They gave away this game for free on Humble Bundle. I thought I got the game when I got the key, but it turns out it doesn’t work like that. I have gotten the key for the license to use the game, but I did not get the content of the game itself. All those 30 gigabytes of content this game has to offer are hidden behind the paywall. Here is how it works for people who do not have the Steam key for this game:
First you have to purchase this game. After that you have to buy the game content if you intend on using its basic features. If not, you will be stuck on paid trial, with in-game content screaming “Buy me! Buy me!” in your face every time you go into the main menu. Not only that, some campaign modes are locked behind the paywall as well, because Sega got away with what they were doing in their Total War games.
This game is Real Time Strategy, and we all expect several playable factions in it. Right? Well, Sega begs to differ. Yes, there are several game modes and playable factions into those 30 gigabytes you’ve downloaded, but it’s just not all of them are available to be played, at least not with the standard license you obtained by purchasing the game. No, my friend. You need to pay more.
You get two basic factions: Germany and Soviet Union. We all know that Germany and Soviet Union were not the only countries to fight in World War 2, because we all know that was a global conflict, which means many nations from almost all continents were involved into it. And this is how Sega’s business model works – “You want other playable factions? No problem, you can have them right away, in fact, they are already part of the 30 gigabytes you have downloaded, but you need to know magic words which unlock them: ‘more money’.”
With more money you will finally be able to get the basic game content, how it was intended to be played in the first place, before it got chopped, and sold into several different packages. Not only they locked three other factions, but Sega managed to make up one of those factions. You get to play as Oberkommando West. What the f*ck is that? Sega describes it as: “The Oberkommando West, battle hardened and newly equipped, are a resurgent and very dangerous foe. Despite being challenged by an economy nearly shattered after years of continuous war, the Oberkommando West still manage to field some of the most impressive heavy armor yet seen: the technical prowess of Germany is on full display as devastating armored force equipped with a new generation of super-heavy tanks repeatedly counterattack the US Forces attempting to drive into the heart of Germany.”
No doubt about German forces being elite and bad-as$, otherwise they wouldn’t have had shattered communism and capitalism in Europe for 6 years while being outnumbered at every front they fought, but they were Germans, not some random, separate faction.
As you can see, this review is not about the game itself, but about greedy Sega’s business model. Sega didn’t develop the game, but they are the ones who butcher the core game, and decide what is going to be sold as a standard edition of the game, and what is going to be hidden behind the paywall.
Capitalism doesn’t have its greed limits, since capitalism is the greed itself.
In the near future I can see standard pc games being served like those Facebook or internet browser games, with free access, but all about microtransactions and DLCs. With business model like that you might get carried away with the overall expenses, because the new DLCs and microtransactions get released over extended periods of time after the game's release. Do not support this business model.

A game which came before Undertale, and should be given double the amount of praise.
LISA tells a gritty and dark story of a broken man who's life is thrust into chaos following the end of the world, and his struggle to redeem himself through raising the only girl left on the planet. The tale weaved throughout the game utterly crushed me at its ending and penultimate climax, and left me feeling empty and sad as I realised just how much I cared about the characters and their depressing journeys.
Honestly, I was utterly blown away at the detail of sprites, clever jokes and one of the most compelling worlds I've ever had the honor of exploring: Olathe, a post-apocalyptic wasteland wrought with heartless gangs and qwerky characters. LISA plays like your average classic RPG, having the ability of collecting and managing party members and items, encounter-styled fight sequences and tough turn-based battles. Overall the combat and general gameplay is nothing special, many aspects have been done before to different degrees, but LISA makes it much more enjoyable, as each fight doesn't feel like a soulless grind fest, but a genuine, life-threatening encounter.
All in all I've no gripe to pick with the game, as it does an excellent job of creating enjoyable gameplay and an incredible story. This is a must have for any fans of darkly written plots or turnbased RPG gameplay.

2017 Review: (Final Verdict: 5/10 - If you like building games and watching them get demolished then don't read any further just buy it)
Well I never thought the day would come but this game is finally out of Early Access.  I personally have been waiting for it for 4 years, others about 5.  The main gripe stemmed from the period of 2 - 3 years where pretty much nothing happened with the game and the dev's heavy handed tactics of dealing with the criticism.  Nonetheless all that is history now and I shouldn't be dwelling on that alone.
The game now is OK.  There is a variety of modes and maps, performance has greatly increased as has some of the AI and building options.  I would agree with some of the sentiment in the comments that the game is worth something like $10-$15 dollars if you are a fan of this sort of thing.
What the game does well:
Performance is decent.  Just about everything in the game is visible.  You don't just put resources and items into storage, the little characters will mine and craft things right before your eyes and place it into appropriate storage where you can see it.  Even when you craft the weapons kits every piece is always visible wherever it goes.  Say you want to craft an arbalast, the crossbow, hat and bolts will be carried one by one from the crafting table to the weapons rack where you can see it hanging there.  This might not mean much to some people but to me it's a great touch.
It's the same when you are building your castles.  Each section can be destroyed individually and if some parts don't have enough support they will fall where they will lie until your bricktrons pick them up and rebuild or place them in stockpiles.  It makes it cool to watch the resources how they are collected and stored, transformed, and become parts of the construction.
The mechanics of the game are pretty solid and in my experience unique.  The enemies are a little bland but they serve their purpose of creating danger and tension in the game modes that include them.
The tutorials and explanations are great and acceptable for those new to the game.
Also the community leader (Shato) I have to mention here.  He is a much better people person than the previous one.  I feel bad for Box because he copped a lot of flak but he also deserved it with what he was doing.  Whether he was doing that under orders from the devs or not I have no idea but for a while there was a really really bad environment for the game community.  So the guy that replaced Box is a big improvement, he seemed to have the will and patience to connect the devs with the public again and that is an understated accomplishment.
Things that are not so great:
Well this is a difficult one as I am slightly biased but i will get into that briefly at the end.  The main issues I see with the game is a lack of content.  The concepts in the game are great, it could have possibly been a genre leader with a little more building options and a little more creativity when it comes the enemies and gameplay.  I really think a decent story (Castle Story???) and even a campaign could have been worked into this game.  Working with the awesome concepts this could have really shined.
I would have been willing to bury the issues of the past completely and give this game a thumbs up.  But alas even though there is a decent variety of maps there isnt much to do after a while unless you want to mess around with some friends in the limited multiplayer.  Now this is just me, I am sure that there are plenty of people around that would be quite happy to play the game just to create different buildings so if that sounds like your thing then disregard my opinion on content.
So just to briefly sum up my reasoning for still not recommending this game, it is a personal taste and morality of early access issue on my part.  This is THE game for me that made me very wary of early access, the years I spent waiting for content and arguing for more transparency left me coming away from the game wondering why I was stupid enough to buy it.  Without the Early Access issues or with some decent utilization of the concept of the game I would have given it a 6 or a 7 out of 10.  But in the end I am going to have to give it a 5/10, it's not bad but its definitely not good.  For me if given the choice I wouldn't have bought it.  But for you if you like building stuff and a little bit of resource management then go out and buy it.  You won't regret it.

Lemme tell you a story. Fourteen years ago I was a sixteen year old boy with teenage angst dripping out my ears, parents in the middle of a very messy divorce, and a high school life that was like Saved by the Bell combined with the nastier bits of the Dante's Inferno video game. During this time my only solace was video games and, for Christmas in 2001 I recieved two things: a Playstation 1 system and my first game for it, Final Fantasy IX. This was the start of a large library of JRPG games including Xenogears, Lunar: Silver Star Story Complete, Wild ARMs 2nd Ignition, and more.
Seeing this game appear on Steam for me is like running into an old dear friend that you haven't seen in a very long time. Its been years, but you're just as happy to see them again and hear their stories as you were when you first met.
So, what do I like about this one?
- The character and NPC models have all been redone to appear much sharper and more detailed than the original release. Its neat to actually be able to see non-pixelated details on their faces and bodies compared to the 1999 version.
- The game controls well and I've only had one issue so far in the Ice Cavern (one of the contextual spots where Vivi uses his magic to melt a path to a treasure chest refused to respond. I already had a Mage Masher so it's not a HUGE deal, but irritating nonetheless).
- The music is every bit as good as I remember it, I had to pause for a moment the first time I got to the overworld just to sit and listen to that song for a while. I've heard some people complain that the music sounds 'tinny' and 'not as good as the original' and, honestly, I wonder if they're just not remembering it right. I mean it came out seventeen years ago. Its been a while.
Things I didn't like:
- The game is fully compatable with my 360 controller... but the default button for Yes/Confirm is B? As in the button that, nine times out of ten, is the EXACT OPPOSITE OF THAT?! To quote Messir Ben "Yahtzee" Croshaw, "Are you taking the ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥". Thankfully you can edit the buttons immediately, but it almost feels like they picked that one just to screw with people.
- ... thats actually it so far. Square did a pretty good port this time. Now all that Square needs to do is re-release games like Final Fantasy XII, Dragon Quest VIII, and Kingdom Hearts on the PC. Seriously Squeenix, what are you waiting for? Do you not WANT every gamer to throw their wallets at you?

This game is pretty good. It's obviously inspired by Sonic the Hedgehog (even started as a fan game and steals many elements from Sonic) but still has an identity of his own and is fun enough with its combat that it deserves to be bought for people who enjoy 2D Sonic-type games. Lilac is the most like Sonic (You'll be hearing "Cyclone" every five seconds), Carol is more combat oriented (with a Wario bike), and Milla is a slower, defensive platformer (not puzzle-platforming no matter what PauseBreakReviews says). The story is long and cringe-worthy at times with inconsistencies and cutscenes can go on for more than 15 minutes at times, but levels are fun and bosses are fun. Bosses are more like Mega Man because they take many tries to get the pattern down, so it strays from Sonic. I originally played the game all the way through before actually buying it on Steam, hence the short play time. All-in-all, It's definitely worth checking out with the demo, or buying on Wii U whenever that finally comes out.

Let me say, going into this, I have never enjoyed Sonic games, even good ones, in the past. I am not a person to who this game appeals intially. The Megaman X elements though, that seemed to be the hooks.
And I loved it. The gameplay, controls, and combat is all very solid. It also has an appreciable, but good difficulty curve. It leads you into the harder parts built on the previous chapters and it all together works well. Some sort of mid-level save system would have been good, but some sacrifices were made for the purposes of establishing it seeming like a early to mid nineties import non-nintendo game (Since Nintendo Imports tended to be different). It also handles quite well on a keyboard, not needing overly complex key inputs just to perform basic manuevers. A gamepad is more a choice than a requirement or even a suggestion. I completed it 90% on keyboard, mostly because my gamepad wasn't recongized until the latest patch.
Story wise? Over the top and Disney-esque describes it well. Don't expect a revolution in story telling, but archetypes are played to well. Liliac and Torque are no holds barred good guys, Shade plays mysterious stranger part, and Lord Brevon plays cackling Villain so well to a T that he breaks the normally kid-friendly atmosphere of the game. It's never so overwrought that it's overwhelming except maybe the ending speech and the introduction to the final level seemed rush in terms of story. It won't wow you, but it won't make you want to gag yourself, and the characters themselves are likeable for what they are. Plus, nobody's voice acting is JC Denton's voice actor.
Music's pretty cool and builds the moments correctly. It's also good for solo listening, but the soundtrack I got has really weird volume level compared to most of my music so it's hard to listen to mixed with other soundtracks.

Straight off the bat yes this game is absolutely worth it if you're pining for retro 90's platformers, no question, believe the hype and get it now.
The one flagrant bit of misleading information about this that keeps getting batted about though is that it's a Sonic game; it really isn't. It bears far more of a resemblence to Rocket Knight Adventures or, more specifically, it's sequal Sparkster on the Mega Drive (or Genesis if you're wrong :p ). It even borrows that whole train section from Sparkster albeit with a less obnoxious boss. Several nods to Gunstar Heroes are in here too, including two bosses that are homages to Seven Force (one of the best bosses in that game), although it's definitely lacking that game's explosive mania (and if you haven't played Gunstar Heroes, play Gunstar Heroes). Indeed there's probably tonnes more nods (especially in Millas levels) that I'm completely missing. The reason I bring this up is that those hoping for a game as fast paced as Sonic are going to be dissapointed; it certainly resembles Sonic 3 and Knuckles a lot but it's not anywhere near as fluid and there's no great sense of momentum that you used to get in true blue Sonic games and that does make a big difference.
On the negative side of things yes the story and voice acting are atrocious, the lives syetsm is almost totally pointless except for achievement hounds, some of the bosses are obnoxiously hard, the last level is especially obtuse with it's incredibly speciific jump timing (I hope you like climbing the same platform section a dozen times) and lacking momentum some of the levels are too big with too few rewards for exploration.
All that said Freedom Planet isn't just a good game because it resembles good Mega Drive games, it's a great game that was wise enough to take what made those games great in the first place and big that all up. The levels are big but never tedious, there's some nice design in here and the graphics are both excellent nods to the 16 bit days of yore and at the same time probably more than those systems could have handeled. The soundtrack is fantastic as well, with a huge amount of effort gone into creating unique stage music and an amazing boss theme that I can (and have) voluntarially listen to on a loop. Freedom Planet is the kind of game I've been waiting 16 years for and I really hope they can move onto a proper sequel with ideas from other, more obscure games as well as taking a few more risks and trying new mechanics to really push this style forward, but for now I'll eagerly await the new characters they're (hopefully) patching in in the not too distant future :)

Short version:
Pros:
+Good Idea
+It takes a while to get every spell
+descriptions and stories are very interesting
+customisation is fun
+Easter eggs in form of unlockable customisations & diaries
+H.P. Lovecraft references <3
(+not very scary)
Cons:
-I have only seen one Map so far
-You can walk around for 10 minutes and not meet you foe
-sometimes laggy
-depending on amount of players: long waiting time (but that's the problem with every low celeb multiplayer game)
(-not very scary)
Long version:
I fully recommend this game! First off, it runs very well on my old working laptop, and that's rare; And in spite of these low requirements the game provides much fun!
The descriptions of each single spell are lovely and funny written, as well as the stories that you are able to find scattered across the map, along with other easter egg customisations.
As a fan of H.P.Lovecraft I was delighted (yet not nurprised, since every Fun Com game has had some references to him so far) to find a bunch of references in this game.
Also despite the seemingly low variation of the game, since it unfortunately only has one map (yet!), it takes quite some time to discover every single Spell in the game.
The techniques used in the game are also interesting, since you may be forced to preserve your spells for a certain opportunity, like trap your foe (e.g. the little springs twerp) or hastily running around a room and frantically searching for a rune to escape a curse of you enemy (e.g. Innsmouth punk) before you get jumpscared.
The jumpscares aren't very scary, it may get you a little bit, when you're totally not expecting it, otherwise it doesn't have a big effect on me; Yet it's quite entertaining to scare or get scared over and over again, even if it's not scary.
To start a match a simple click on the "public match" button is enough, but as it is on every not popular online game: To find your desired opponent it can take quite some time. This can be bypassed by playing a private match with your friends, if you have any...
All in all a really fun game!

First off, this friggin game should come with a trigger warning for abuse victims before the later levels. And personally I wouldn't let a 10 yo anywhere near it, cute though the beginning might be. I know we've all already murdered a million people in games, but games like this come around and manage to use a simple as anything game mechanic to give you goosebumbs, to put it mildly. (Yes, I'm talking about the darn lifeless "dolls" - 'nough said.)
It's not about the puzzles. Don't come to this game for the sense of accomplishment a difficult puzzle platformer gives you. There is no place for competitiveness here, it's storytelling by playing. It's not a walking simulator either though (and I am using the term as a descriptor, not as a curseword). The gameplay is simple without being simplistic, and the puzzles are well, one could say they're easy, but I felt they were appropriate. Basically the puzzles play like the platforming elements do: They flow comfortably, at a natural pace, an average player won't have to stop anywhere long. The atmosphere and the visuals are fantastic, the music and the voice acting are beautifully done. Everything, including the rythym of the gameplay, just flows well and all elements work together to tell a simple story, albeit one we don't often hear in games in this manner.
And btw, it's so insanely refreshing to see minority and lower class protagonists, languages and aesthetics so uncomrpomisingly portrayed in a game.
It's not flawless, but its flaws are totally secondary and besides the point. It deserves every penny we can throw its way, because these developers should be encouraged to try again and do more. So yes, buy it. As for whether you will enjoy it, well, if you aren't coming to it with an all macho "harcore" attitude, then yes, you will get something out of it. I don't know if you'll love it, and personally I wouldn't play it again, but it's definitely a game worth meeting and a little journey worth taking.

Enjoyable while it lasts, but quite flawed! Yep, it's an older game from 2013, but even with its expandalones of more recent times it seems the overal game engine definitely was not optimised very well after the original release. You can see the game can barely handle a further draw and view distance when you rotate the camera to a more level angle. And yes, this is the case even with no units in sight.
The game plays best at an angle towards the ground anyway, but you can't zoom up all that high to really create best overview on the game. To put it simple, this is no Supreme Commander in terms of camera management. You will find yourself moving around a lot to spot ahead. Fortunately, the game is also somewhat designed around using scout units (snipers, certain vehicles like half-tracks or just whichever unit you send ahead towards potential sacrifice etc.), so in a way it kind of falls into place. Speaking of units, this game has a pretty good variety of units, some of which can get upgrades like flamethrowers or anti-tank grenades. You'll get an acceptable historic accuracy when it comes to units for the most part. But be prepared for a lot of narration and story telling that makes the Russians look like total monsters. Yes, I'm sure you've read about it elsewhere when this game first got released, but this game is full of what is best described as American propaganda. If you can't stomach B grade acting with very fake and very overdone Russian accents, then this game probably is not for you.
Anyway, back to performance. It's actually a bit of a let down to see the game run so poorly. It looks acceptable and definitely isn't ugly for the most part for an RTS game (if you don't zoom in), but you can see this game is already showing signs of age. Either that, or the game stubbornly defaults to lower settings than my hardware can handle. It comes close enough to the screenshots for me to think it's actually the game itself though.
I guess this brings me towards the next point of criticism. The AI in this game, or rather the pathfinding of your own units isn't quite without it's issues. I keep finding my tanks are moving backwards when they should turn around first and then move towards the enemy with better speed and accuracy. If you have three tanks moving through a narrow corridor of buildings, you're probably going to see them get stuck and unstuck a few times. The cover mechanism in this game is alright for the most part, but sometimes you will find units won't go to the exact spots the system predicted. It's also somewhat limited in control when it comes to entering buildings.
It's quirks like that which make this military squad 'simulator' game with a heavy focus on micro-management a bit tough to control at times. Especially at the higher difficulty levels you're going to be punished by the flaws of the game itself.
The game also has quite a few situations where it is apparently just fine to fail, only to pretend that was always the inevitable way it would go. It can be unclear about that at times. I don't mind when a game doesn't do any hand-holding, but this game often seems to forget it's an RTS, not some kind of an interactive movie. So yeah, be prepared for a few times where control is taken away entirely only to put you in a new situation. Such events are often a bit hit or miss. I have to say I don't like the way they try to these more cinematic missions at all. It leaves basically no control to the player. For example, in one mission you need to first blow up a German Tiger Tank. After having done so, you're ordered to repair it and drive it back to your mission start. It's literally a mission of following a tank north, blowing it up at an airport, only to drive it back south. And sadly this was one of the more inspired missions. Most of the time it's hardly more than conquering zones throughout a level. Occassionally I managed to completely obliterate the enemy forces only to find the game telling me to retreat 'because mission event dictates so'. At the very least they could have made certain a strong enough force showed up to actually force my forces to retreat. But hey.. whatever.
It doesn't help the game has basically no historic locations or levels. Or at least not in such a way that it is really convincing enough. Kind of a let down for a game that lets you zoom into the action so far.
I would still generally recommend getting this game, but it's by far not worth it's current full price (around $20) anymore. It's also probably one of those games that if you like it enough in terms of  the singleplayer campaign content, you're perhaps going to want to get all the DLC or more specifically the Company of Heroes 2: Master Collection. Not sure if that one ever gets a good discount, but I'd wait for that.

I love and hate this game.  I love to hate it and hate to love it.  Yeah, I recommend it.
It actually reminds me a lot of the first Civilization.  I loved playing the early game, but the mid to late game would drag a bit.  The early game was the most exciting and frustrating part because of the randomness.  Maybe you could expand quickly because of a good location or maybe the barbarians would wipe you out on the third turn.  It was the sense of wonder and discovery of the early game that had me hooked.
FTL is a very random game.  Each sector is random, filled with random events and locations.  The randomness can create the greatest of triumphs or the lowest of defeats.  Despite all the randomness there is still skill involved--a stupid move is a stupid move.   There are several important decisions you have to make: which systems to upgrade. power and target, what kind of crew to hire and how to allocate them, what items to purchase from the stores (which are in random loactions and have random wares), and how to respond to the random events.
You never really know what you're  going to run into out there, and it's exciting.  Sometimes you'll have events which turn into sidequests and you have to determine where you want to go in the sector because time is limited.  You are being chased by a powerful enemy each turn, and while you can push your luck and survive a round or two against them, you really don't want to take that chance too often.  Normally I hate games with time limits, but surprisingly I don't mind it at all in this game.  This is a push your luck game which requires some kind of pressure on the players so they can't just max out.  Players have to make brutal, difficult decisions all the time.  Another aspect I usually don't care for is permadeath, but this also creates that needed pressure.  There are some games I enjoy because I just push my luck as far as I can to see how long I can survive.
Win or lose, there is just something about this game that keeps me coming back.  For such a seemingly simple and random game, there are actually a lot of choices and play styles.

Relatively easy until the Flagship, where it then becomes virtually impossible to win. This is a problem for several reasons:
- Each run takes about two hours.
- There IS some progression in the ships you unlock, but in most runs unlocking one is impossible. Even in runs where unlocking one is possible, you'll likely miss the event or lack something required. So effectively, no progression system.
- If you don't plan properly, it is *literally*, not just virtually, impossible to beat the Flagship. This is especially bad because what you did wrong is inscrutable; your failure could be the result of one of dozens of choices that you made with no indication of which one it was. It's entirely possible that you didn't even do anything wrong but lost anyway, because...
- No amount of skill can compensate for bad luck.
In summary, with each run you fail, you lose two hours of progress for reasons so mystifying that they may or may not even be your fault and have nothing to show for your time.
Is it possible to win after playing enough times? Yes, I believe so. Is it worth the time and frustration? Absolutely not.

I never expected I'd find a game similar to the old Sonic games that would not only bring me nostalgia, but at the same time surprise me with awesome new mechanics.
Freedom Planet is a set-your-pace Action/Platformer game made by Indie developers GalaxyTrail, that features gameplay much similar to the old Sonic games, but brings new mechanics and level design to the table as well such as:
● a
Which consists of various attacks, from a simple punch to uppercuts and dropkicks;
Also, your character has HP, that can be recovered by finding the dragonfruits in stages.
●
These being gems, that will give you extra lives and more, voice lines from cutscenes, stage soundtracks, and achievements.
●
Nothing more to say;
●
That features both oldschool and modern accents.
Mix this up with the oldschool platform gameplay, and you get the fun and beautiful game that Freedom Planet is, with its smooth and detailed pixelated style, gorgeous stages and a gameplay you set the pace to, since you can either try your best at completing a stage as fast as you can, or take your time and explore it to the fullest finding collectibles, gems and power-ups.
The game also features an interesting and well-written storyline, playable from both the PoV of Lilac or her friend Carol.
Of course they both have different gameplay styles, with Lilac being a fast dragon-girl, and Carol being a cat-girl on a motorbike, and another character i won't spoil for new-buyers.
●
An alien dictator who's been conquering planets comes to our 2 heroines' world, Avalice, with the objective of stealing a sacred gem that will give him the power to build up an army that could conquer the universe.
Through the PoV of either Lilac or Carol, we follow their journey as they try to stop the upcoming disaster and meet new and old friends, all of this mixed with comedy, thrill, and more.
Along with the storyline, stage after stage you'll find cutscenes and dialogues.
These both fully dubbed, with the dubbing being one of the best i've ever heard.

As you start the game, the feeling you get from it is amazing, you feel how the developers put their heart and soul into making it, with the game being so detailed and fantastic as a whole.

Normally I preface a review with a brief overview of the game I'm reviewing, but I will instead use that space to tell you that if you are a fan of platformers, especially the "Sonic the Hedgehog" series and "Gunstar Heroes" I would heartily recommend that you purchase this game immediately. This well-crafted game, mixing elements  various of classic 16-bit platformers is very clearly a labor of love, and will instantly hook any fan of the genre.
"Freedom Planet" has you controlling an anthropomorphized dragon named Lilac that stylistically resembles a certain blue hedgehog wearing red sneakers. Lilac, her friend Carol, and an assorted cast of characters search out the fabled "Kingdom Stone", contest with a strange alien force and attempt to prevent a war between rival factions in a plot that is considerably more complex than your typical platform game that simply revolves going from point A to point B in an attempt to track down the main baddie (though you will be doing that too). The story is fairly engrossing and provides ample context for the well-designed and often elaborate levels. The voice acting is surprisingly well done, even if the script provided can be a bit cheesy and melodramatic at times.
As you progress through the game you will visit many varied locales from mines to airships and beyond. Everything from the level design, to the designs of the enemies, environments and the music is very well done and leaves you with the impression that you are playing some long-lost "Sega CD" title. Gameplay is fast and furious with plenty of loops, moving platforms and machinations that will send you flying across the level. Lilac has an auto-refilling charge meter that powers all her moves, from a standard burst of speed to flying uppercuts, a 360 degree spin attack and a savage stomp. The moveset available, and the large and complex enemies and bosses you often face makes the game feel like the lovechild of a Sonic game and "Gunstar Heroes". Controlling your character is tight and responsive, and the collision detection is excellent - Yu Suzuki would be proud. While not as difficult as the titles the game pays homage to (at least at the standard difficulty), the game provides ample challenge and is very rarely cheap or frustrating - careful observation of enemy patterns and patience pay off. Extra lives, obtained via collecting crystals and powerup items are fairly plentiful, and the game provides unlimited continues. In addtion to the standard "Adventure" and "Classic" modes, a "Time Attack" mode tasks seasoned gamers with completing a level as fast as possible.
The team at GalaxyTrail should be commended for releasing a colorful, fast, exciting game that pays proper homage to the platform genres roots. "Freedom Planet" feels like the erstwhile product of a Sonic Team with far more hardware power at their disposal and no platform fan should miss it.

Hide and Shriek is a competitive multiplayer game where both players are invisible.
Two players are pit against each other in a creepy school, with the aim of scaring the living hell out of their opponent.
To win the game, you either have to earn the highest score at the end of the 10 minute round by collecting orbs and setting traps, where as the second option is to scare your opponent 3 times in a row.
The catch is you are both invisible. There are multiple ways to reveal your opponent, and once you know where they are, you can activate your "shriek" which will trigger a floating head jumpscare on the enemy's screen, and get you points.
If you shriek and your opponent isn't close enough, you will be revealed for them to see for a short time.
The most common way to reveal your opponent is by catching them in a trap. You can collect different runes throughout the level, which all have unique powers. Sometimes you can set traps, and sometimes they will give you powers to remove any curses you might have. Runes can even be combined to give unique traits. Some can be very interesting, like sending your enemy to an alternate dimension to waste their time, or allowing you to dash through walls.
Some runes can be shot ahead of you, some can be traps set on the floor, some are on interact-able doors or closets etc. So there's a lot to play around with.
The main way to get points is to collect orbs and put them on your altar. You can even pick up enemy orbs in order to set up traps. I like to put theirs behind transparent cupboards, and then trap them. The whole game is about outsmarting your opponent.
As you level up and get achievements, you will unlock customizables for your character, which is quite fun.
Most stuff is balanced quite well. Although I have a problem with 2 powers. One of them being a wisp that follows your enemy and teleports them to another dimension. Even if you see the wisp, it seems for no matter how long you run away from it, it will catch up to you eventually. I don't know if there's a long timer on it or if it just chases you indefinitely, but that just causes it to be more efficient to just run into it as soon as you see it to avoid wasting time.
The other one, is a power that reveals all runes close to you, and your opponent. It kind of defeats the entire point of the game if you can just see your enemy constantly through walls, there's no investigation anymore. It's not even that hard to get that power, and it seems a lot of people have realised it and are using it the majority of the time, which is why I prefer to just play with a friend and avoid using that power.
Overall, I really am loving the game so far. The aesthetic and music is great, the idea is fun and unique, and it's just funny to hear your friend scream when you trap them!

Pretty fun game! Not sure I can see it having this massive community or anything like that, but it's definitely pretty fun for the price tag, and it's something I can see myself playing with my friends fairly often. It's charming, yet still able to give you a jolt if you're not ready for a spook or a trap. There isn't really any depth to it--there's one (somewhat small) map with random rooms, there's two victory conditions, and a lot of the masks are just re-skins of each other--but it's still a good way to have some laughs and some shouts, be it with friends or with randoms. The mask customization is pretty fun, and has a good deal of options so each mask feels unique. The runes (that allow you to use spells, and can be combined for better spells) are very fun to play with and experiment with. The little hidden bits of lore that you can unlock through books is a fun read. I may be more into it because I dig TSW and anything that spawns from it, but I'd definitely say this is a good game, independent of TSW. It's cute, it's spooky, it's a blast with friends! FTL: Faster Than Light has a lot going for it. It's a skillfully built little roguelike that features interesting races, interesting combat and a seemingly infinite number of possibilities. At first. It doesn't take long, however, for the arbitrary number generator and the handful of events to get repatative or even, at times, seemingly broken. If I had a piece of scrap for every time I ran into the same space station on fire, I'd have enough to purchase the extra upgrades that become useless once you realize there's a ship that can shut off O2 censors and watch you suffucate an hour and a half into a well-played campaign.
One of the largest issues is, of course, the Flagship. Now here's where things get dicey, because no doubt there are many people out there poised to commit Seppuku for their favorite roguelike. Even so, it's pretty easy to say that the flagship battle is, at its very core, poorly designed. It's very easy to make something that is difficult, yet not-so-easy to make a boss fight that is challenging. This is when you realize that your hour to two-hour romp through space testing out your new guns and getting your crew skilled enough to shoot space-gnats with fully upgraded shields and thrusters you realize that none of it mattered as you're eradicated in a matter of minutes.
Now, I know what's going to be said, flocks of people will no-doubt rant about the ways the flagship is supposed to be beated, but that's the point. For a game that boasts so many different upgrades, ships, crew configurations, etc. there shouldn't be a way you're "supposed" to beat the Flagship. Of course there are going to be builds better than others, but realizing that you had to hunt around for a handful of viable builds or your entire trip was for naught is simply a bad design. It's easy to a soup up a giant ship for players to throw themselves at, and then nod saying, "Oh, yeah, that's the way you're supposed to do it" when one of them finally manages to beat the thing and another entirely to create a compelling, well-balanced boss.
In the end, FTL: Faster Than Light is actually a pretty fun little game for all of its flaws, but it just asks way too much of its players without bothering to meet them halfway.

Anyhow, Square actually learned from their mistakes and put thought into this port. Controls can be mapped and they actually show up when prompts are shown. I think this is one of my favorite Final Fantasy games. It doesn't quite edge out VI or Tactics, but it's right up there with IV and XII.
This is a port of the old Playstation game from 2000, and if you aren't a little baby, there's a good chance you've played that version. If you have, you don't really need any type of review, as nothing has really changed. If you haven't played this entry in the series for whatever reason, say maybe VII and VIII were too different for you, IX is very much a return to basics.
Where as in VII the characters are largely interchangeable aside from their limit breaks due to the materia system, in IX we're back to each character having their own set combat commands and feeling like a unique class. Extra abilities come attached to various equipment, and if you wear the equipment and earn enough AP from fights, you can master the ability and use it without having that piece of equipment equipped on the character. This still doesn't let you learn any ability on anyone you want; just because you can equip an item on a character doesn't mean they can use the abilities it has. You're probably not going to learn magic on a melee type character for instance, even if he is using a hat that has cure magic on it.
Like the somewhat recent Steam port of VII (and I assume VIII, I don't have that one on Steam) this version has some added options to help you speed through the game if you just want to experience the story. You can easily make everyone max level, learn abilities instantly, and max out your gil. They've also given us higher resolution cutscenes and character models. These aren't actually new assets or new cutscenes, they just look better than what the Playstation version had since they don't really have to worry about disc space anymore.
Sadly, that's really all the extras we got. It really would have been nice to get some of the extras that VI had in its recent iOS/PC port. With that game you got some extra espers, a new dungeon that was much more difficult than anything else in the game, and a new in game bestiary. I know these weren't made specifically for the PC port, and were carried over from the older GBA port of VI, but still... I mean, couldn't they have at least added some small stuff, like making the right stick turn the camera on the world map?
The lack of new features / content aside, I can't really find anything bad to say about this game. I'm hardly what I'd call a fanboy of the series, and this is still a really good jrpg. If you're into this genre, you could do a whole hell of a lot worse than Final Fantasy IX.

I've been sitting on this game for awhile, and I'm glad that I finally got around to playing it. The game feels like an homage to old Sonic the Hedgehog games, but it has enough of it's own elements that it doesn't feel like a blatant rip off. The levels are fun and colorful, and the soundtrack is retro bliss.
Boss fights are amazing in this game as well. They all telegraph what they're doing extremeley well, and even if you don't know what's happening the first time a boss uses an attack, it still gives you enough time to avoid damage. Pushing a boss to the next phase can add more elements to the fight, or just make the boss move faster or hit harder.
Freedom Planet is one of those games where almost every hit you take is because YOU messed up. Although there are a few moments where you might take damage from an enemy coming on screen that you didn't see, because you were going too fast. But it's not nearly as bad as if you were playing a Sonic game, because the games uses a health bar instead of rings that you have to scramble to pick up when you get hit.
If the game had one flaw, it'd probably be the voice acting. It's okay, just a little cheesy is all. But it's not like the devs had money to hire Jennifer Lawrence to play Lilac, so I'll let it slide, and it doesn't bother me enough to knock points off.

This is what Sonic the Hedgehog should have been after Sonic 3 & Knuckles.
Freedom Planet appears to be a blatant Sonic clone at a glance, and it kinda plays like one too. Begin a stage at the left, and run toward the right until you reach the boss. Run, kill, and repeat.
It's the subtle differences however, that make it more than worthwhile. Freedom Planet takes the Sonic formula and enhances it in unique ways. The playable characters have varying movesets that make multiple playthroughs feel surprisingly fresh, and the level design is very well paced. Boss battles are frequent, and many of them are suprisingly challenging. The overall speed of movement is a little slower than Sonic the Hedgehog, though it actually feels better this way since exploration is also emphasized.
The art direction and soundtrack are also subtly remniscient of Sonic's world and characters, though they mostly take on colorful tones of their own. This familiar universe is vibrant in color and personality, which feels amazingly refreshing after playing countless monochromatic/minimalistic art-focused titles in today's indie game scene.
The story isn't groundbreaking, but it provides a simple coherent flow for the level progression that felt undeniably fun. I'm typically over-critical of story and writing in games, but I let so much slide with Freedom Planet for some reason. It strongly appeals to the childlike sense of wonder and amazement many of us had when playing games when we were younger. It made the story/world a joy to experience even if it wasn't superbly written. It knows it's simple, and it just aims to be fun.
While some may find the characters' voice acting a little silly, I found it to be just good enough to give each character their own charm. Besides the unfortunately mediocre audio quality of the actual voice recordings, the voice acting made each character more likable to me. Still, a "Classic" mode exists which omits all the cutscenes in favor of a Sonic style progression of levels for those who would prefer that.
If you have fond memories of playing Sonic the Hedgehog back in the Genesis era, this game will feel like pure bliss. If you didn't, it's still a must-play for any platformer fan. FREE dlc is on the way as well, which will add more playable characters.
Freedom Planet snugly fits into the massive shoes left behind by the classic Sonic games that modern Sonic has been woefully unable to fill.

Sonic Generations is a return to form for the Blue Hedgehog who has been languishing in bit of a confused rut for many years now, Having played all of the sonic games up to this point I felt that Sega had been trying desperately to bring Sonic back to it's former glory days that seemingly began to dry up after Sonic Heros and finally they've landed square on the money in this title.
It's a very beautiful to look at platformer with puzzle elements that splits the action between traditional 2D side scrolling "Classic Sonic" Stages and 3D "Modern Sonic" Speed fests and from a level standpoint Generations is an absolute treat with classic stages almost perfectly capturing the feeling and vibe of typical classic sonic the hedgehog levels while the 3d levels offer a new re-imagining of classic levels and a full refresh of everything "Sonic Adventure" onwards.
Each Level is beautifully colourful and the HD simply blasts this ultra colourful game making it a real visual delight, controls are also calibrated precisely mimicking the 2D classic sonic physics of the old games and allowing Sonic precision in the 3D "Modern levels" this is particularly clear in the "Rooftop Run" and "Green Hill Zone" Levels. both vividly colourful and precise enough to let you appreciate what’s going on around you. There’s a sense of Vastness in these Levels as well that is really quite unseen in any other sonic game...
This game doesn’t get away completely however with a perfect mark...while the controls are perfect there are a few little bugs here and there which can upset the flow of the game and clipping can sometimes be a real problem (Although thankfully there are no really common clips so gameplay isnt seriously effected) Also the "Story" is really rather Paper thin with some very basic time travel plot implemented that thinly hangs the levels together...personally I would have preferred them to either add a little more depth to the plot or remove it and just have selectable stages...add to this that there was so much potential Scope for Optional DLC (I mean who wouldn’t want to have been able to replay Metal Harbour from Sonic Adventure 2!?) and the fact that the DLC they did opt for is essentially just a pinball machine and it feels somewhat like a bit of a wasted opportunity in my opinion...
Sonic Generations is a great Jumping on point for anyone who hasn’t played a sonic game since the early ones (Or at all) and in my opinion is probably not only the best Sonic game of the last 13+ years but quite possibly one of the best platformers of the past 20 years...it's colourful, creatively laid out and most important of all Fun. Pick a copy up and enjoy cruising around, a real treasure.

An indie post-apocalyptic dad redemption simulator.
But seriously, LISA is an emotional rollercoaster that effortlessly jumps between hilarious dark humor and depressing brutality. Through the main character Brad Armstrong, the player will travel across an absurd 2D side-scrolling hellscape out of a Mad Max parody. Along the way you will have to make certain choices and sacrifices that affect gameplay and carry an emotional impact, but don't actually change the story much. LISA's story is one in which many background details are not explicitly stated and it is up to the player to piece together the truth behind the main characters and Brad's world. If you want to understand the story better, I recommend playing LISA "The First."
The battles are the tried and true turn-based combat utilizing menus, with classic elements like status effects and healing. During the main character's journey, he can collect a large group of party members, many of which have their own unique battle mechanics or abilities. Finding the best complimentary combinations between them or just using your favorites is fun either way. I wouldn't say that LISA is especially hard even on the game's hard mode, but it's not exactly a breeze either. The hard mode will offer a moderate difficulty and there are optional bosses for players who want even more of a challenge.
There's a reason that LISA has a sizable cult following. It's a simple game that reminds us of the fact that games don't need amazing graphics or millions of dollars to be memorable and fun. Its sequel story The Joyful is more divisive in terms of quality and enjoyment, and it lacks some of the charm of Brad's story, but if you liked LISA then there is no reason to ignore it.

Ugh.... I dreaded writing this review. I don't want to recommend LISA because no sane person should play it. But then again it is a good game so I want people to buy it so it does well. It is the equivalent of watching a horrifying (not scary) movie, nearly vomiting, and then recommending it to your friends so you can see them vomit. It is like recommending the manga Berserk or Gantz knowing full well what happens in the first couple of chapters.
Le sigh, guess I'll be a sadist then.
LISA is a turn based RPG that has you traverse through an apocalyptic world with the main goal being to rescue your adopted daughter. And along the way you meet some fun characters, and others that are ... not so fun.
I'm guessing you have figured out by the way I am writing all of this I found the story of LISA to be dark, and you would be right. The things the antagonists and even the main characters do to themselves and each other is just ... mean. Like it stops being sad and just ends up mean. But this is thankfully lightened by some comedic moments. And that is what makes LISA a great game: it has a lot of character. In such a dark scenario I didn't expect myself to be laughing at times. And then the dark moments hit…
The mechanics themselves are meh. It is a turn based RPG, so combat can be boring. Just wiki the right strategy and breeze on by. Things can become tense due to limited supplies which can force you to make risky decisions as whether or not to rest.
If this game only had its mechanics, I would definitely not recommend it. But this dark tale of loss and the struggle to move on makes this game great to go through. Those with weak constitutions may want to walk away from this one though.

I was more excited to find out that multiplayer has returned for THIS Battlefront 2 than I was for the 2017 Battlefront 2.
I played countless hours on the playstation 2 version of this game and it's even better on PC. With mod support, larger scale battles with up to 64 players, multiple modes/maps/classes, and the sheer fun of playing your favourite Star Wars heroes, not even nostalgia is needed to lift up my opinion about this game.

Movement, aiming and shooting can be a bit clunky compared to some first person shooter games today. The hit box detection is not as forgiving either. Does this game have flaws? Yes. Is it still worth playing? OH HELL YES! With multiplayer support back up, now is as good a time as any to start picking this up again if you're an old fan, or see what the fuss is about if you're new to this game.
And there are no pay-to-win lootboxes in this game either.

It's Final freakin' Fantasy 9.
Seriously.  That's all you need to know.  Buy it.
I've been playing Final Fantasy since the first once.  The very first NES FF game.  This is, hands down, my favorite one.  This version is not without its issues, but the core of the game is there.  Plus, it auto-saves to a quick load slot so you don't have to "load" your game, you can just "continue" it, so if you experience any issues you can close out and re-launch almost where you left off.  That's very nice.
While the overhaul of character models is decent, it would've been nice for them to do something with some of the area models.  There are times where you can't tell a door is a door or a hallway is a hallways because the maps, foreground/background, whatever... are all the original low resolution.  I don't have any complaints about the audio quality not being what I remember...  it's still the same.  But keep in mind I haven't played the original in years so maybe I just don't remember correctly.
I have experienced a number of bugs...  from game breaking (Zidane stuck walking in one direction, perma tranced, instant ATB, and invulnerable in battles...  all at the same time), to just annoying (if you play long enough the interaction with stuff begins to take numerous button presses).  It would be nice if SquareEnix patched and corrected some of this...  but let's be honest, lately they just hammer stuff out and move on without giving any support to their products.  And yet we continue to buy it all up.
In the end I recommend this because it is, afterall, Final Fantasy 9.  The characters are great, there's a TON to do beyond the story quests, and it's just an overall fun game.

Alcoholism is destructive. Not only for your liver but for the lives of your surroundings. Especially your family, and even more specifically, your kids. The delirious anger can inhibit a child's imagination and creativity in ways you never thought possible. The shame that comes with a parents insane behavior could possibly mentally scar a child for life. Not giving a child the proper attention, will belittle him or her to the point of extinction. Humans have a bond to their parents, a bond that is hard to break, especially when that bond is held tighter by constant attempts to catch a father or mother's attention, and failing. This need for acceptance is everlasting, and never getting it will assemble a world-view of misconstrued self-hating nonsense. Self-hatred and shame will burn inside of you with the same fire that fueled your father's anger. You will feel so insignificant and, subsequently, depressed, feelings of hopelessness will cover your interests in creative endeavors in a thick goo of inability; a lack of energy, lack of confidence, lack of belief in your own talent. These associative memories will be there however long your experiences of the world stays the same. And this is where Papa & Yo comes in.
The game takes us through an imaginary world - where we are the co-creators and reformers. We are accompanied by our lovely companion "Lula" and eventually we meet the Monster! He seems like a lovable fellow, mostly interested in nuts and sleeping, we provide him with these life-essential things, mostly because he provides us with progression.
Things seems to go fine until we stumble across some cute-looking "frogs". This is where our Monster scurries into a frenzy, he no longer cares about our needs of progression, he just wants to get a hold of this frog and devour it. We are left behind, until we see him coming back, but now the sky is red and our Monster is on fire: charging right at us. What does this mean? We don't have long to think before he grabs hold of us and throw us to the ground with a thump. Huh. This monster is not a friendly one after all, then why are we with him? We run around for a bit and see this blue/purple fruit, described as rotten. Our first instinct is to throw it at him, we do, he calms down. He is back to his pinkish, amicable and lovable form. In this form he only sleeps and eat, he doesn't hurt us, we can manage to stick with him for a while longer. Along the journey his fiery temper tantrums become more frequent and more limiting. We need to get rid of him, we need to let go, we need to move on. We need to exempt ourselves from the grips of destruction, to separate ourselves from the person that is this angry, projecting, mean-spirited Monster. Despite him being our means of progression and survival. Despite him being the reason we exist and survive.
Papa & Yo tackles the subject of a destructive family very well. It illustrates the need to let go of your parents, in general, perhaps not just the despicable alcoholic abuser. A realization: we are separate human beings from the ones which created us, we are our own persons and have our own quirks and dreams. This game illustrates the need to escape when your family life is in shambles, in imagination or videogames. Escapism until you can finally escape it in reality. Papa & Yo gives people a way to escape and even more, it manifests a scenario a huge amount of people are in and gives them validation, a feeling of acceptance and most of all, advice is given. Good advice, helpful advice. Your family is not you, there is a world outside of this small world, imaginative or not. The world is truly yours. Sometimes you just need to let go, of whatever is holding you back.

FTL: Faster Than Light has a lot going for it. It's a skillfully built little roguelike that features interesting races, interesting combat and a seemingly infinite number of possibilities. At first. It doesn't take long, however, for the arbitrary number generator and the handful of events to get repatative or even, at times, seemingly broken. If I had a piece of scrap for every time I ran into the same space station on fire, I'd have enough to purchase the extra upgrades that become useless once you realize there's a ship that can shut off O2 censors and watch you suffucate an hour and a half into a well-played campaign.
One of the largest issues is, of course, the Flagship. Now here's where things get dicey, because no doubt there are many people out there poised to commit Seppuku for their favorite roguelike. Even so, it's pretty easy to say that the flagship battle is, at its very core, poorly designed. It's very easy to make something that is difficult, yet not-so-easy to make a boss fight that is challenging. This is when you realize that your hour to two-hour romp through space testing out your new guns and getting your crew skilled enough to shoot space-gnats with fully upgraded shields and thrusters you realize that none of it mattered as you're eradicated in a matter of minutes.
Now, I know what's going to be said, flocks of people will no-doubt rant about the ways the flagship is supposed to be beated, but that's the point. For a game that boasts so many different upgrades, ships, crew configurations, etc. there shouldn't be a way you're "supposed" to beat the Flagship. Of course there are going to be builds better than others, but realizing that you had to hunt around for a handful of viable builds or your entire trip was for naught is simply a bad design. It's easy to a soup up a giant ship for players to throw themselves at, and then nod saying, "Oh, yeah, that's the way you're supposed to do it" when one of them finally manages to beat the thing and another entirely to create a compelling, well-balanced boss.
In the end, FTL: Faster Than Light is actually a pretty fun little game for all of its flaws, but it just asks way too much of its players without bothering to meet them halfway.

When I first heard about this game back in 2012, it immediately struck a chord with me, though not solely because of what you may think and what a lot of other people got into this game for. It was because it starred Sash Lilac, Carol Tea and Milla, 3 characters whose original creator ZiyoLing I fondly remember following her works on DeviantART back in 2006-7 long before this game was even conceptualized and what got me interested in the world of fan and original characters.  It was great to see these characters these characters star in their very own game and not just remain fan/original characters, and that was enough for me to pledge to the games Kickstarter campaign back in 2013 and eventually get the actual game last Summer via a DRM-free copy.
While this game may look like and can be easy to compare to a Sonic game, it feels and plays differently, more in line of a tribute game to 16-bit character platformers similar to how Shovel Knight pays homage to classic NES platformers. Like this game doesn't just take cues from Sonic, but also Gunstar Heroes with it's hectic boss battles and Torque's gameplay, Kirby Super Star and Megaman X with the attacks along with MMX's wall jumping for Carol, Rocket Knight/Pulseman boost moves for Lilac and Milla's gameplay reminds me of Klonoa.
The game does controls well and each of the characters feel and play very distinctly from one another as well make certain areas or bosses easier or harder depending one which character you’re playing as, almost as if you’re playing an entirely different game with them. The levels are vibrant, have creative design elements, have cute secrets and they as well as the boss fights can get pretty challenging yet fair at the same time, especially in 2nd half of the game.
The story is enjoyable with its mix of both witty & charming moments and surprisingly dark & serious moments. The voice acting is good with special props to Lilac, Spade, The Magister and Brevon’s voice actors, though there are some rough bits here and there like the background noise/static in some of Carol’s lines. And the music is catchy, energetic and overall a joy to listen to.
But there are a few issues (at least for now) like how there are some things in the story they either forgot to tell about or aren’t properly explained which could be due to how Milla’s story wasn’t available at launch which they did say was due to it not being ready in time, yet it’s been over a year now since then and there hasn’t been any word on that nor Torque and Spade’s campaigns which they promised as free updates during the Kickstarter, though the game is fine as it is, these things do make it sorta feel a little incomplete content wise.
All in all, what captivated me about this game is how something that initially started as a fan project that also included fan characters have evolved into things that can stand on their own two feet and be a success.
That was really inspirational to me seeing that I have a passion project of my own in the works along with it's characters who essentially started out as fan creations. That to me is it’s biggest charm.
I'm just a little upset that this aspect and the more tribute nature of the game is being overshadowed by the fact that people are comparing this game to recent Sonic games saying how it's "far superior" or "the true Sonic game we've been waiting for". I wish people would judge this game for what it is on it's own as just a fun and admirable 2D platformer and not by what they want the thing it's inspired by to be. Overall I liked this game a lot and would recommend it any fan of the platforming genre.

(This is my first real review, so I apologize that it sounds amateur-ish)
If you're a fan of classic Sonic games along with Megaman or platformers in general, Freedom Planet is just the thing. The game is absolutely amazing, perhaps the best platformer I've played. Right now you can play as 3 characters, all with different skills and abilities to try out, leaving the game fresh. The voice acting is okay, and if you don't like it there are mods and ways to turn it off. The art style gives it that classic Genesis look and the scenery and levels are absolutely amazing to the point each level has unique paths and ways for the character you choose.
Regarding gameplay, you can choose to fight or flight for most of the game depending on who you choose. It can prove a bit hard at first to newcomers to this type of game (that's what casual mode is for), but proves a fun challenge for anyone. Each boss and enemy has its own pattern that will keep you on your toes depending what difficulty you're on. The soundtrack is also memorable and fun and fits the game nicely. It also works fine with either a keyboard or gamepad, which is a good plus.
Also, it runs really smoothly on my old and cluttered up computer, no lag at all!
It's the best side-scrolling platformer game I've ever played and I'll continue to play it for a long time after. Definitely worth the money.

Picked this up while it was a daily deal during the Steam Summer 2015 sale and turned out to be a delightful surprise. A love song to the 16 bit Sega Genesis era, this game is a rush of nostalgia for older gamers like myself and a glimpse into a bygone era for younger players.
In true Sonic-esque fasion, you are more than capable of rushing through stages. However, you are also capable of exploring every nook and cranny of stages, uncovering various secrets. The stages themselves are beautifully designed and give us a glimpse into the culture of the planet.
Each character has a distinct playstyle:  the fast-paced Lilac, the scrat-and-claw wheelie popping Carol, and the energy shield Mila. The different characters give plenty of replay value to the game. Instead of a ring system, it uses a health bar - a far better idea in my opinion.
As others have quipped in the reviews, it's a better Sonic game than anything Sega has done in ages.
My one gripe I have about this game though is the voice acting. In-game it's passable, but during cutscenes it can be a little painful to listen to. In their defense though the voice acting was done by amateurs. I can easily overlook that though due to the solid gameplay.

Ugh.... I dreaded writing this review. I don't want to recommend LISA because no sane person should play it. But then again it is a good game so I want people to buy it so it does well. It is the equivalent of watching a horrifying (not scary) movie, nearly vomiting, and then recommending it to your friends so you can see them vomit. It is like recommending the manga Berserk or Gantz knowing full well what happens in the first couple of chapters.
Le sigh, guess I'll be a sadist then.
LISA is a turn based RPG that has you traverse through an apocalyptic world with the main goal being to rescue your adopted daughter. And along the way you meet some fun characters, and others that are ... not so fun.
I'm guessing you have figured out by the way I am writing all of this I found the story of LISA to be dark, and you would be right. The things the antagonists and even the main characters do to themselves and each other is just ... mean. Like it stops being sad and just ends up mean. But this is thankfully lightened by some comedic moments. And that is what makes LISA a great game: it has a lot of character. In such a dark scenario I didn't expect myself to be laughing at times. And then the dark moments hit…
The mechanics themselves are meh. It is a turn based RPG, so combat can be boring. Just wiki the right strategy and breeze on by. Things can become tense due to limited supplies which can force you to make risky decisions as whether or not to rest.
If this game only had its mechanics, I would definitely not recommend it. But this dark tale of loss and the struggle to move on makes this game great to go through. Those with weak constitutions may want to walk away from this one though.

Lisa: the painful (aka just LISA on steam for some reason) is an absolutely fantastic RPG. The game takes on an earthbound feel not unlike Undertale, except where Undertale took on earthbound's more cute charm, LISA takes on it's weird and surreal style, in looks, gameplay, and music.
The game's roster of characters is not only large, but a great many of them are viable choices throughout the game. You will want to choose your team wisely, Lisa is not exactly a cakewalk, but it's also not impossible, as saves and resting are generous, backtracking isn't really egregious, and grinding, if you ever feel it's required, isn't long and can be quite rewarding even.
The graphics offer a variety of expression, ranging from charming, to harmwarming, to depressing, to downright disturbing, or even distressing. Accompaning the graphics is the glorious soundtrack, which again, sounds like it could be from a demented earthbound hack.
Overall I would absolutely recommend this game, on sale or otherwise. For me it was worth replaying no less than 4 times, and I'd still be willing to cleanup the last couple of achievements. It is well worth the $10 asking price.

They are another 10 bucks, but it's worth it if they're on sale. Head to the reviews of the specific DLCs on that matter. The replay value of Mafia II when you can just explore the free roam is incredible. The story takes just about 20 hours, but I have played Mafia II for over 160 hours by now. Well, this review is for Mafia II and not for its DLCs, but why not write that down anyways?

Another lazy PC port of a classic Squaresoft game.
- Main character models have been improved, but most other models are left untouched
- Backgrounds are untouched and badly filtered
- Audio is quite inferior and tinny compared to the original, either from over-compression or because of the playback engine
- Menus are straight from the mobile version without any resizing or other tweaking to make them fit better on larger screens
- Original font has been replaced with a generic one that does not fit in with the aesthetic of the game
- No graphical options other than resolution
- Bad controller support
- Reports of crashing and other game-breaking bugs from some people, even when the game was presumably being worked on for a while after the release of the mobile version
- Zero support from the developers so far
This amazing game deserves better treatment, but it's just what I expect anymore from SquEnix.

I would recommend this game. How ever I would only recommend it if you feel you are willing and able to work around the small bugs in the game. The most I ever had to do was save and restart the game (which loads faster than Chrome on my laptop) to fix a bug I couldn't solve in game. This helped a lot with performance issues (and immobile workers) as it caused the clutter from the dead minions to despawn.
I never found a bug I couldn't over come with some simple problem solving. You just have to take into consideration that you need to leave enough room for your littlefolk to manouver through your castle. Having said this, the only areas I found this to be an issue was in my storage area and around stairs (just space the pallets out and manage stair traffic, simple).
Friendly AI didn't seem quite agressive enough and it was difficult using melee guards in any way other than spamming them around choke points and trying to make sure your archers weren't in possitions to catch them in a cross fire.
You can build some really cool castles with this game. Having said that, if you are expecting a minecraft like experience you will be dissapointed. Your buildings in this game need to be structurally sound, unlike minecraft everything needs to be supported.
This isn't hard to do though, you just need to spend sometime testing things out. It also forces your buildings to look good, everything looks like it should exist (atleast in my experience).
Figuring out the controls and intricasies of the UI took about an hour (I think. I picked this up after a few drinks after work). Spent most of that time trying to find a decent instructional video to no avail.
I picked this up 4 months ago*, I think, for cheaper than £15. Not sure I'd pay that now (sorry devs) if you see it on sale then definitely grab it.
*So take this review with a pinch of salt, things might have changed slightly but I doubt they will have gotten worse.

I feel obliged to inform any newcomers who haven't played this game before, that this game doesn't have a happy ending. In fact, this game will make you deppressed as truck and sad, more than it will make you laugh.
tl;dr : This game is an underrated indie gem, it's a masterpiece, which should be regarded as highly as games like Undertale and To The Moon. By the end of the game, you will laugh, you will cringe, you will be creeped out, you will tremble with anger, you will cry, you will do things you don't wanna do. And if you are skeptical about the 2D graphics, don't worry, I've honestly yet to find a game that delivers the atmosphere of a post-apocalyptic world as striking and as cruel as LISA.
The short Steam page description of this game couldn't have described this game any better. LISA is about a (very) miserable journey of a (very) broken middle-aged man named Brad. And you will fully understand this by the end of the game.
Brad is a man who lived through a terrible traumatic childhood, who has some deep regrets about his past and he reflects these on his present. Which makes him have deep issues about stuff. And you cannot really blame the guy up to a point either. Sorry for writing all of these in such a cryptic manner, I'm just holding myself back from giving out a spoiler.
There is also a good amount of world building/lore going on, which will really drag you into this weird perverted horrible world of LISA.
Now that I've finished the game, when I think about this game... The first and foremost thing that is implied in the story is, that how nobody is perfect, and tragedy and reality of this fact. And the revelation that it's okay that nobody is perfect. And that there is no objective/clear one answer to everything. I think that would be the clear lesson that game conveys at the end.
I mean, by the end of both the game and the DLC, you will surely have seen that this game keeps very good checks and balances when it comes to characters' personalities, which makes them feel refreshingly real. What I mean by that is, no character you encounter is pure evil, and no character you encounter is a full-on saint neither. How absurd or fallacious they might seem at the first look, you will see that they each have their own reasons and motivations that drove them to do what they did in order to survive in a cruel world, amongst the shambles of a human civilization which is doomed to go extinct.
About the soundtrack, I've seen better but that being said, the game definitely has a very memorable soundtrack that makes the creepy scenes very unsavorily creepier, which is great.
I really don't know anything else to say other than buy this game and DLC, and experience it.
