Freedom Planet- Sonic the Dragonhog
A fantastic game where they took the old Sonic games, mixed in some Adventure 2 story line and then made it with new characters and a vibrant world.
The game:
I grew up as a Sonic kid in the 90's, where I played up to about Heroes before getting bored of the series (And then eventually going "WTF" to some of the fanbase...).
That being said, I was exstatic to play something similar to the older Sonic games once again! The game features 3 playable chartacters, 2 available at the start and 1 available later on. Each do the Sonic running thing, but with different special moves. Something this game did well by adding that the original Sonic games did without: An attack button. Based on how you aim and use the attack button, you will perform different swings.
Though, gameplay aside, the level design was a total throwback to Sonic 2 and maybe even a bit of Sonic CD. Each level presented a whole new group of enemies and new environmental situations to overcome. Then couple that all with the Soundtrack and its a wonderful experience.
Bosses. Like you'd expect, each level presents itself with mini bosses and big bad bosses. Not nearly as hard as old Sonic games, but in its own mechanics, fairly fun. I will admit though, the last boss and the grey looking dude both gave me a real issue, really made me work for it. I should add that I played on Normal mode, probably much more difficult on Hard.
The Story:
While being slightly cringy and partly bad voice acting (I gotta say, some of the VAing was pretty amazing, just not all of it) it wasn't all that bad. It features a revenge story ontop of a bystander thrust into conflict story. Where both run alongside one another. Though fair warning, the humor is a bit dry. Get passed that and its ending is very fufilling.
The Verdict: My usual scale of 1-10, 1 being bad, 5 being par and 10 being the best: I give it a 7. Maybe wait for a sale, but if you got 15 dollars to spare, this is a great 4-6 hours of fun. Even more if you are a completionist!
My Reasoning: I loved this game to no end, nostalgia was strong within me. However, it was not without flaw. I loved the character, level and sound design that went into the game and was thrown back into the 90's early 2000's, but if I was to look at it critically, a 7 is a good score.

While many retro platformers tend to emulate NES aesthetics, Freedom Planet aims for the Sega side of that era.  I personally enjoyed it even more than Shovel Knight, despite mostly being an NES/SNES kid.  Objectively, I'll admit Freedom Planet is not as good as Shovel Knight, but I liked it anyways.  Freedom Planet is still worth checking if you have nostalgia for old Sega, whether that nostalgia is growing up on a Genesis, or merely playing your friend's/sibling's Sonic games.
PROs
+ Music, graphic style, and speed appeal to those with fond memories of Genesis.
+ Very few "instakill" hazards, so you can actually use your speed.
+ While the Sonic inspiration is obvious, the combat elements give nods to other titles and help the game establish its own identity beyond "just a Sonic clone."
+ All characters play different, especially Milla.  Lilac is recommended for first play.
+ Like Sonic, several stages have a high path and a low path that eventually both meet up, providing a sense of constant progression and a feeling of exploration.
+ The amount of new gimmicks and enemies (not palette swaps) in many stages is a nice surprise.
CONs
- Midgame and lategame bosses get tons of health.  If playing on Normal or Hard they WILL kill you until you learn to dodge.
- They tried with the story and I enjoyed some parts. But the story has major pacing issues after two or three stages and trouble deciding if it wants to be serious or lighthearted.
- (Should get fixed in 2015) 2 of 5 characters are not playable, and Milla only gets Classic Mode.
- Some shared stages/bosses don't feel like they were balanced for all characters.
WTF
? Like Sonic cartoons and comics, Freedom Planet can get darker than expected.  For example, in the opening cinematic
.  There's also a quite effective/disturbing scene about 50-67% through the game, which makes me question how this game got E instead of E10.
? Voice Acting gets no volume slider.  While I found the voices charming, others dislike the Saturday Morning Cartoon or early (pre-PS2) game vibe.
? If you research early builds (when it was still a Sonic 2 fangame) some changes feel more "how do we not look like a Sonic ripoff" than "will this improve the game?"
RATING
7.5/10 RECOMMEND, BUT WITH CAUTION.
Exceptional for a $25k Kickstarter title.  On that scale, the flaws are forgivable, especially given the existence of Difficulty Select and Classic mode. But Freedom Planet is also a 2D platformer normally running $15. Which means it competes with the likes of Ori and the Blind Forest ($20) or the $300k Kickstarter project Shovel Knight ($15).  And as much as I loved Freedom Planet, that is some very well-polished competition.  And it is from that vantage point which Freedom Planet's falls out from the low 8's which I initially inteded to rate it.
EDIT (Aug 17, 2015): Spelling, extra details, and rephrasing parts that sounded more negative than intended.

I wanted to love this game, and got it quite early after I first saw about it. The unique Fightingsystem in combination with the strong artstyle and the solid music performance entertained me for some hours but I never managed to master the combat.
The Fights can depending on the players be a slow and thoughtfull dance or more of a furryfilled rampage, and both ways can be quite funn.
There are several fightmodes, like 1vs1 2vs2 1vs2 and even capture the point like teamgames.
Camera and controlls work fine, despite being a little bit clunky sometimes.
There are many things to unlock but all are purley cosmetic. So it allways is a skill question who winns, and not simply the equipment that winns a fight.
Loading Screens took way too long for me though and the game crashed from time to time when I wanted to switch server.
The Interfaces look nice but could be a lot more clear than they are now.
So in summary it is a great experience with some weakpoints that can be annoing but do not kill the whole game.
But there is one more thing that changes nearly everything:
The game has AI controlled opponents, but they can't (as far as I figured it out) fill in in real player matches. They are restricted to the practice mode. This means that without Friends to play wou might not find a single server to play on with players on it. And if you find one they often are way above your experience level and can stump you into the ground without much effort... Or you find friends playing that do not always want to play with random strangers. It seems there is still a bunch of active players, and with some efford you can surley organize a full server on a sunnday evening or so.
But if you just wanna start the game and play, it will feel like a ghosttown.
Would love to recommend it but I just can't do that in this state, with the exeption for someone who has some frineds to play this with. Not a perfect game by far (For honor could be a good alternative nowadays) but it is certainly not a teriible game aswell. If yo uare still interested just grab it at a sale and give it a try.

Some technical issues first:

This is more of a rollercoaster simulation than a pinball game^^ You can actually change the camera (press C several times) to be fixed on you/the table, that however doesn't even work with these tables as all 5 of them are designed with several flippers in the upper part of the tables and you'll spent most of the time playing on the top of the tables with these flippers rather than the 2 standard flippers at the bottom/the sinks. Knight Tournament - meh... ball keeps draining very unfairly on this table.
Monsters - Decent table, but only really playable with the standard view imho (prepare your stomache).

Dream Pinball 3D is a pretty standard pinball game with several different tables. Sadly, this game is far inferior to Pinball FX2, which is far better and offers tables with deeper gameplay at a lower price.
Let's start with the camera. This game actually made me motion sick. Games never have that impact on me. Heck, I regularly play my 3DS with the 3D turned on, and I've played a lot of games that should really cause nausea without any problems, but this game got to me. That's how bad the camera is. You can choose to zoom out and have the camera be fixed, but then you can't see any of the details on the board, or you can stick with the close-up that moves at the same speed as the ball, so you still can't really see much, and twists and turns to completely disorient you.
Next, the controls. One thing I love about other pinball games is that you can use an Xbox controller and use the triggers to control the pinball flippers. This game supports controllers, but only barely, and it doesn't accept analog buttons like the triggers. Also, you can't use the controller in the menus; you must use keyboard and mouse. I could configure JoyToKey, and I would, but I don't plan to start this game up again.
The tables aren't bad in this game, they're just unremarkable.
Also, when I tried to turn this game off, it crashed so hard I had to reboot my computer (it refused to let me access the Task Manager to kill it). Thanks, Dream Pinball 3D.
From the whole presentation of this game, you'd swear it was made in 2000. Maybe this game would've been fine at the time, but we have better games to choose from now. At $7, this game is a complete joke. I think I picked this game up on sale for $0.70, and while I don't think this game was worth what I paid, I can't be too mad at having wasted less than a dollar. As I mentioned before, Pinball FX2 is the far superior game, and I'd recommend buying a few new tables for that game instead of playing Dream Pinball 3D at all.

Sonic Generations is the game that Sonic fans have wanted for years. SEGA's Sonic team has struggled to make Sonic work in the 3D space. But Generations handles it very well. Having both classic and modern Sonic help to facilitate two very different forms of gameplay. Classic Sonic's levels have a greater emphasis on platforming in 2-d esque stages. Modern Sonic has the bigger 3-D levels. A lot of these levels have sections that are on rails but these help lend a sense of speed. Modern Sonic also has some of his more recent tricks like his homing attack.
This contrast between the two gives the game variety. As you complete levels you progress through a simple but entertaining story. Like Mario; Sonic stories generally never get too deep or overly complex. The game avoids many of the errors Sonic games have had in the past; like shoehorning in new characters. In my time with the game I haven't met any new characters. Old familiar faces like Tails, Knuckles and Amy are present. Visually the game looks very nice indeed which is further helped by a mostly consistent framerate. I did have a few drops here and there however.
Having played Lost World I felt the level design was fantastic and the parkour system was an interesting new mechanic. If they could find a way to take the foundation of Lost World and marry that with the speed found in Generations I think it would make for quite a Sonic game. If you are a Sonic fan and have not played this game. This is definitely one you want to check out.

Easily the best SimCity yet. Don't bother with the new one, this one will suck your time away more and has a lot of cool addons and mods. Be sure to get NAM (Network Addon Mod) to make the traffic better and you're all set.

We still have yet to see a true successor to the immense scale offered by SimCity 4. It has everything from the peaceful zen of settling a farming village in rolling hills, carving out a bustling coastal metroplolis, or the dirty fun of managing the man-made mountains of your region's garbage city.
The modding community has really made this game shine. At the minimum I recommend the Network Addon Mod (NAM) because of the improved traffic simulator - even if you choose to not increase the road capacities or include new highway and rail components. A full NAM install will add a good bit of content, so choose carefully when doing a custom install if you dont want your menus to get too bloated.
I have also managed to get the game running smoothly on my modern hardware (3770k + Radeon 7850). This game is known to erroneously detect moden Radeon HD 7xxx series GPUs as the old non-HD 7000 series. In the game's GraphicsRules.sgr file I commented-out the entire section on "radeon slow path for partial depth buffer copies" and added a new rule for the "AMD Radeon HD 7000 Slow-Down Fix" posted in the simtropolis forums - this resolved choppy scrolling issues.
I also use the following launch options set in steam:
-intro:off -CustomResolution:enabled -r1920x1080x32 -d:directx  -w -CPUcount:1
These options: disable intro, enable and set custom resolution, directX video output, windowed mode, use only one cpu.

I'M SO INTO THIS GAME!
Unable to sleep, your character (which you can choose to be either male or female) goes for a late night stroll to clear their head only to get pulled through a portal and into a strange world filled with odd beings, an abundance of cats, and lots and lots of puzzles. Solve all the puzzles to make your return home.
For the most part, there are three main puzzle types, and three main chambers which house 25 of each type as they're displayed on a wall panel that fills the entire screen. The first type involves moving a block through a series of mazes so as to fill in all the empty spaces behind you as you move, but being careful not to trap yourself in the process. The second has you controlling the movement of multiple boxes simultaneously as they slide along tracks, with the goal being to manage the position of the boxes so they each rest within an outlined area. And in the final type you'll be presented with a board filled with crosses/plus signs, each of the four arms of every cross being either black or white, with the objective this time being to rotate the crosses so that all connecting points of every arm match colour.
They all start off easy enough, introducing you to the most simplistic form of each puzzle to teach you how it works (showing rather than saying, since there isn't a single word of text in the game beyond its title), but they gradually raise the difficulty or complexity as things slowly ramp up throughout the course of each set of 25. It's tough to judge how difficult others will find it, as is always the case with puzzle games. Some may breeze through it, while others may hit roadblocks at points as they just can't see the solution, but all told, I imagine most will take about an hour to get through the main challenge. Though there is some additional content for those willing to dig into it.
As well as the main story puzzles, there's a whole other larger puzzle hidden away in the form of the game's own language. This is a language based on symbols which you can draw to a handful of NPCs littered around the world. It's completely non-essential to the story puzzles and you can complete the game without ever even knowing it's there. But, still, even though I admit it's not really my thing and I had no bloody clue what was going on with it and quickly resorted to using a guide for the achievement related to it, I love the fact they went to the trouble of including it in the first place.
Presentation wise, I adored the greyscale art - fairly pixel heavy in "cutscenes", really clear and detailed whilst actually playing - and the music never stopped putting a smile on my face the entire time, either. I'm still in awe of the fact such an incredible product was given to us for free, so much so, in fact, that as soon as I add some more Steam funds, I fully intend to buy the non-playable DLC as thanks and support to the devs and really hope others will, too.
Part of me wishes there was more content, just because I had such a great time with it, but then again, maybe that's for the best, as, if it were made any longer, it could risk outstaying its welcome. I had a perfect little experience, and I'm happy with the memory and feeling that it left with me, so I really can't ask for anything more. It may only take you an hour to complete, but what an hour that will be.

"FTL: Faster than Light" is best described as a unique survival rogue-like where you travel through space while being chased by a huge enemy fleet. Each playthrough feels like a series of Star Trek episodes where you are the captain. Explore alien planets, battle space pirates, trade for supplies as you try to save the galaxy.
The gameplay mechanics are carefully designed to be both challenging and balanced. Enemy encounters and events are interesting and well written. The music and graphics are quite decent for an indie game. Overall, I highly recommend FTL to any player who enjoys sci-fi strategy games and survival roguelikes.

Mafia II might not be what you're expecting when you first boot it up and start playing. It looks like GTA, plays like GTA, but it excels in one major area that GTA does not: delivering a story. Rather than have a bunch of filler content like minigames or sidequests, Mafia II keeps straight to the point without erring too much. This could be seen as a benefit or a negative. Personally, I see it as a positive since the setting's atmosphere is so rich that I wouldn't want the game to feel TOO gamey, if that makes any sense. I would say the game does a good job at being a period piece, but I haven't done much research to back up that claim.
My primary issue with the game is its checkpointing system. I played the game on Hard (which I recommend) and didn't have that difficult of a time progressing. However, there were sections where an enemy would kill me midway through a 15 minute mission, and I'd be plopped all the way at the beginning of that mission. Not all missions are like this but when they are, it will just♥♥♥♥♥♥you the hell off.
Mafia II clocks around 12 hours which is pretty short in my book, but it's worth the play if you can get it at a decent price.  And it should be since it's pretty old now. If you think you are buying a simple GTA clone that you want to mess around in, do not get this game. If you want a decent mobster story with well-acted cutscenes and great setting, I would pick this up.
EDIT: I am not ashamed to admit that the primary collectibles in this game are also some of my favorite. >:)

Hard, but that doesn't mean not good.
while simcity 3000 will remain my favorite for the rest of the conceivable future, 4 has a certain charm and depth of mechanics that makes me itch for more.
the budgeting system has been overhauled allowing for much, much more customization and indepth management of your city's utitlities, waste management, and tax revenue. whereas in 3000 you could only manage RCI taxes as a sort of umbrella for each type, in 4 you can raise and lower taxes based on the pay bracket (for commercial and residential) or the subtype (industrial, separated into agricultural, dirty industry, clean industry and high tech industry). this management allows you to pinpoint taxes where you want them, potentially driving out a class of residents or commerce, or inviting in the same.
the zoning rules have changed dramatically. whereas in 3000 you simply designate a plot of land and let the sims do the rest, in 4 each zoned lot has a facing and transportation/utilities needs that have to be met before the lot will develop. designating a large area will automatically add roads so that you don't have to micromanage each lot's transportation needs for the most part.
on the topic of transportation, roads in general have recieved an overhaul, splitting them into four classes of road, with separate capacities for travel: streets, traditional roads, avenues and highways. while the avenue, the highway, and of couse the road were availabe in 3000, the avenue was constructed by putting two roads together, and the highway was bank-breakingly overpriced. the newest addition, the street, is a low capacity form of transport that requires very little maintenance.
coming back to utility management, each utility building (water pumps, power plants, landfills) has a seperate funding slider that can be adjusted to change the output or intake of the facility in question. such a mechanic can be used to set power systems into standby, or to limit usage of over-producing plants; all very useful for a city that has just begun.
the region system is where this game really shines, however. the ability to create dozens of cities and have them all work together is simply incredible.
in short, simcity 4 is a very deep, very complicated game, but the rewards are very high. the amount of fun I've had here despite losing is roughly .75 times what I've had in 3000, which is saying something considering how much I've loved 3000.

Rarely do I finish a game and immediately start up again, yet this game has forced me to do just that. LISA is a side-scrolling, turn-based battle RPG where you play the most selfish man in the post-apocalypse as he murders, tortures, and turns tricks to hunt down the last woman on Earth, his step-daughter.
What I really like about the RPG aspects of LISA is that there’s so much here. Turn-based is often accused of being boring and bland, yet I think the developer has really hit the mark here. The huge number of status effects keep things fresh BUT ALSO inform us about the character. A few actions only exist to clue us in on how our main character is feeling. What else I love about the combat is that every encounter feels like something new, because it is. Nearly, if not, every enemy in the game has a name and move set. You will never be fighting that wine throwing skeleton for the umpteenth time because every mutant and bandit is handcrafted and unique. This is what so brilliantly sets LISA apart from other turn based combat games.
You have a huge roster of potential party members and each one of them handles differently. Most developers would just balance out the roster with tanks, bards, glass cannons, etc. In LISA, every party member has their own move set tied to their level progression. For example, one character has no primary attack, but can fill a rage-type bar that will allow him to make a powerful support move on the next round. Everything about the combat is teeming with life, which is why it’s so easy to overlook the nearly static battle scenes.
I won’t spoil anything, but the story is wonderfully told with a great interconnectedness that makes for a tight narrative, even when things look like they’re getting out of control. Throughout the game, you’ll have to make a series of choices. Your decisions don’t effect the story so much as they effect your character. This is a great way to make us care. Players don’t care what happens in the world so long as they’re powerful enough to handle it, but LISA is the type of game that beats you in the head with a shovel and then gives you a permeant -10 luck.
I could go on about the music, the character designs, and all that, but you really need to see LISA for yourself. While the tone may waver like a pendulum for the first hour, it quickly finds its place under the wasteland sun. I really cannot recommend this one enough.

LISA: The Painful is the perfect mix of violence, humor and evocative storytelling. Although it's been compared to Undertale and OFF (even Kindergarten) before, the comparisons don't set up fair expectations. LISA is a completely unique beast in its storytelling, humor, combat system and explorative world. I have to say it's my favorite Indie RPG.
I admire how Dingaling doesn't tiptoe around harsh implications. At its core, LISA is about a broken family and the road to madness one man takes to preserve the one speck of goodness he found in his miserable life. People have said before that it's not for the faint of heart. I consider myself a sensitive soul and I wasn't as broken or anguished as some reviews led me to believe I would be, but it did stay with me for a very long time. Months after I played the games, I still find myself thinking about Brad, Buddy and the lingering psychological effects of childhood abuse.
Despite the dreary backstory of its main characters, LISA is surprisingly hilarious. I can't remember the last time I felt genuine excitement about exploring a world. There are 3 main crossroads you can reach in the game, and each of them has various doors that take you to unique areas. For such a small amount of game time, LISA doesn't take any shortcuts or pull any punches: I enjoyed the unique environments and the different creative ways you could traverse them, as well as the crazy characters.
As you can probably tell from my lengthy dissertation on LISA's story, plot is an important part of gaming for me. LISA is fantastic in that it incorporates gameplay in refreshing and exciting ways to ensure that you are never brought out of the game experience. From impacting your story through character deaths, to giving each character a unique battle style, LISA kept me engaged for every minute of my gameplay.
In short, LISA is a hidden gem that I wish more people would notice. I keep recommending it to my friends, but they all think I'm strange for liking a game wherein you play as a fat, old bald man as much as I do.

Great game. By far the best Final Fantasy game in the series. I highly recommend to anyone looking to try an FF game for the first time, or relive one of the best in the series.
For the port, it has some good and bad.
Good:
- F-Keys add a bunch of functionality like multiplying speed, adding levels, no encounters, etc.
- Graphical updates. It looks much prettier now, especially combat, characters, and tetramaster.
- Smooth. The game wasn't very choppy back on the PS, but even less so now. Even with multiplied speed it works great.
- Great port to Unity that functions similarly on a lot of computers. Easily modable and decompilable, at the time of this writing.
Cons:
- Resolution is weird. You have to play with it quite a bit to get rid of the bars
- Oddly slow at several points. There is literally more lag at times than on the PS (to be fair, its much faster most times)
- Controls. The mouse tends to get stuck at the center of the screen, xb1 controller has problems being registered. This might be due to not playing well with multimonitor. To fix I often win-key out and click on the titlebar of the non-windowed app or alt-tab out and in to fix it.
- The backgrounds are not HD. Since theyre pre-rendered, they look about the same as they did before.
All of the cons could easily be fixed, with the exception of the backgrounds. I don't expect many of these to last more than an update or two.

Anyway, I found the game to be rather great. The level design was good, I liked the characters, the music, pretty much everything about it. Although, the game does have a bit of challenge, especially in later levels, but that just adds on to the fun of the game.
And the game isn't hard to run at all. While I usually use my desktop, this game actually runs (at around 60FPS in fact) on my Toshiba notebook from 2010 running Linux Mint, so I doubt you'll run into any optimization issues or anything.
Overall, I definitely recommend this game. Whether you're a fan of retro games or just want a good platformer, this game is rather fun. From me, this game definitely gets a 10/10.

What If 2D Sonic Actually Had Combat Worth A Damn: The Game
Just so we're clear from my ridiculous playtime, Freedom Planet is not a game I merely think is good. Freedom Planet is a game that I think makes most other games in its genre look bad by comparison.
The game completely nails a seamless blend of fast, intuitive momentum based movement that feels really good and meaty combat with satisfying strikes and a wide variety of moves across 3 extremely different characters that all have unique uses and can be combined in very logical ways in both movement and combat to do literally anything you can think of provided you have the balls to try and the dexterity to pull it off. It's complex in its variation, yet extremely elegant, remarkable game design. There's a completely insane amount of stuff in this game to chew on if you're even remotely speedrun-inclined (see the playtime. That's not a joke, this game is a monster.)
Most games cannot pull off either fun and varied movement or satisfying 2D combat so the fact Freedom Planet pulls off both with such seemingly effortless panache simultaneously is an achievement worth lauding.
Soundtrack is also killer and the art and set-pieces are a colourful treat on your senses.
The story is bad. It's paced badly, seriously overwrought and has some scenes that are just plain confusing in their existence. I respect the attempt but uh, maybe next time? But it's about the only negative thing I have to say about this game. Otherwise it's an incredible video game and one you absolutely should play.

This is an indie 2D platformer with cartoony anthro characters and a well done 90's era aesthetic that takes inspiration largely from the oldschool Sonic and Megaman X games (though more on the Sonic side than Megaman). The story is cheesy, as to be expected in these kinds of games, but the voice acting is pretty competent; I would go so far to say it's better than most older games and indie games, definitely better than the acting in the later Sonic games that I've played. Most of the game follows the philosophy of "easy exploratory levels with challenging bosses", though even the bosses are easy in the beginning. You'll be glad you accumulated tons of extra lives for the final levels, though, where the game actually gets challenging. (but still not TOO challenging, at least on 'Normal' difficulty it's still easy enough to complete.) It's nowhere near as hard as Super Meat Boy or the like, but then this game isn't about precision platforming, but about running through levels and beating up enemies and bosses.
This game does a number of things that make it more fun than most oldschool platformers, IMO:
-The controls are very responsive, and your attack and move animations can be interrupted by other attacks and moves at will.
-Some attacks make you invincible during parts of your attack animation, which you have to take advantage of against some of the later bosses.
-Contact with enemies and bosses doesn't hurt you, only enemy attacks or spikey bits hurt you.
-Bottomless pits are very rare. This, combined with the ability to run through enemy sprites make it a lot easier to run through levels than in the older Sonic games, which punished speeding with enemies and pits out of nowhere.
If you like oldschool platformers, especially the bits where you fight enemies and battle bosses, you'll like this game.

As of January of 2014 the game remains in prototype stage and the company developers have stated they are continuing to work on the game with no timetable for completion.
Adding insult to injury, the game is now available as "early access" on Steam for $19.99, less than the original Kickstarter package.

Allright, so I love this game. And for the gameplay, I will give it 1,000 stars, and will always play CoH 1 and 2. But I personally, from the bottom of my heart, want to say a big F*** You to the a##hole company ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s that makes so many d*mn microtransactions. If I buy the d*mn game, make a little bit of content grouped into expansion packs or whatever, but COME ON. The amount of additional transactions is ABSURD.

It's not a bad game, but it's a bad sequel. Long before I got it in the giveaway I knew I didn't like what Relic did, I had seen some of the game and I was more disappointed after I actually played it. It's fun and all, but it's below the standards set by the first CoH and its expansions.
First off, concerning gameplay, it has indeed a lot of cool new mechanics but most of them are just there for the show and don't really change the big picture of the game. As far as I played, you can break ice to sink tanks but it freezes almost immediately afterwards, providing only a cheap cinematic (it's not even particularly spectacular) kill, little more than an execution in a third person game. Line of sight does change a couple of things but I can't say I'm immersed more than before, it works though and maybe has some potential for more experienced players. Other than that I didn't notice any other changes in terms of the core game.
Moving on to combat, it feels a bit more uncertain, I have had AT guns hold their ground for 4-5 encounters and others just being overrun by the first tank, they don't seem to pack as much of a punch. MGs are a bit more reliable in their role of suppressing infantry, flamethrowers are very effective just as before. Vehicles are weird, my Ostwind got a few hits from a T-34 but survived, but it seemed to be overrun by infantry later, I did not notice any AT weapons or grenades but maybe I missed something. Halftracks on the other hand seem very resilient, although they did have some armor (up to 15mm, which should stop your average infantry weapon) they seemed to survive a lot better when faced with anything smaller than an AT gun or tank. Artillery is nerfed as it almost can't touch vehicles with any amount of armor (there goes my excitement for being able to build field howitzers with anything other than the British), and even buildings don't take near as much punishment from direct hits by 105mm guns.
Commander abilities have me torn, I like the definite progression and the fact that XP keeps on showing after you've unlocked everything, but so far they don't seem particularly useful. Also the fact that you load three commanders out of six or more available is a bit weird, I'm not sure what purpose it serves. But mostly I just don't think they're that useful.
Graphics are nice and all, being more detailed and stuff, but the combat has become a bit cartoony, tank shells fly at a very low speed, explosions and fire feel a bit exagerated and in general, any claim for more realism leaves me unconvinced.
What determines for me, though, that it is not worth buying this game, is two points:
The units are just about as many as in Tales of Valor (I think fewer actually), sure you have one more faction but you still have a limited selection of units. A couple of new additions may stand out (the rocket-bearing halftrack is nice) but they replace equally good stuff (the Nebelwerfer), so I don't feel that the game has made much progress, if any. The thing is, though, that just about anything you find in this game, you'll find in almost all major mods for CoH:ToV, which is cheaper too, plus you'll find a ton of other great stuff and improvements that match this.
The other point is, I noticed you can buy some stuff for your army, I don't know if it's decals or if you can actully buy commanders or something, but you have essentially IAPs or permium stuff (no idea ont the specifics) in a game you presumably already paid for, plus more than half the factions are actually in separate expansions so you're paying even more, and though the original CoH had expansions, they were two expansions released over a course of 4 years.
Just go buy Company of Heroes: Tales of Valor, and install the Blitzkrieg mod, Europe At War mod, or the NHC mod, and you'll get a lot more content with much better mechanics, richer and more useful skill trees, more realism, and in some cases great graphics (tipping hat mostly to BK mod here, those explosions and the burning hulks of dead tanks look awesome!)

Very much enjoyed this game. First game I bought on steam over the summer sale and glad I did, because it seems to have been taken down.
There wasn't anything too groundbreaking here but everything this game tries to do it does very well.
It may seem at first like a GTA clone and the game play is pretty similar but you'll quickly notice it ignores some the mechanics that have become hallmarks in the GTA series.
There are no side missions. There is no upgrading your character or characters status. There's nothing to do in the engrossing but empty open world.
These may seem lacking but this game does just fine without any of it and I'm glad the devs didn't force it into the game. Instead the game focuses on a well told and straight forward story with a great cast of characters.
The voice acting is among the best I've heard in games, it really stood out. If you close your eyes,  you would think, you were listening to a real Scorsese movie, if only the dialogue were a little stronger. The dialogue is at times not as punchy as I might hope but it's by no means bad, just doesn't quite match the grade A standard set by the voice acting, character models and overall atmosphere of the game (which is largely thanks to the stellar 40s+50s soundtrack. I noticed a couple songs also in Fallout 3 and New Vegas). I wouldn't even mention it in any other game, the voice acting just sets such a high bar, I wish the actors had some interesting lines, or at least had them more often.
The game play largely revolves around third person cover shooting and it's extremely fun, especially with a mouse. I play GTA with a game pad but Mafia II on M+K since there's more focus on shooting.  You feel extremely badass laying down 200 goons in a bar with your pistol or Tommy gun.
I hope Mafia III sticks to what made this great and doesn't truly turn into a GTA clone

What can I say? It would be a sin if I didn't review this.
Final Fantasy IX isn't only my favourite game from the series - it's my favourite game of all time. It's the first Final Fantasy I played, and it's the one I could return to every single year until I expire. I played this continuously when it was first released back on the Playstation.
As a huge time fan/writer of medieval fantasy, this game really does have it all for me. The plot is, for the most part, a gripping tale of intrigue, romance and adventure. The (main) villain is one of the most charismatic of all, despite their very questionable fashion sense. The character development is second-to-none, easily the best from the series (Zidane and Vivi, especially.) It also features my favourite female protagonist from the entire series.
The setting is wonderful. No two places look the same, and the environments are all unique and memorable (though in the case of one particular dungeon, you're likely to remember it for all the wrong reasons...)
The music. My God, the music. This soundtrack is a masterpiece and the work of a true legend of composing, Nobuo Uematsu. I want to be Uematsu. Seriously. Character themes, environment themes, battle themes and that beautiful, beautiful world map theme - there's not a single track that I don't like.
The sidequests are fantastic (a couple are a little irritating, like one involving a skipping rope, but all entirely optional.) The Chocobo one is easily unbeaten and rewards you very, very well for your time. I also think I'm the only person on Earth who actually enjoyed the card game.
I could honestly write more - so, so much more - about why I love this game. But I would be here all day. Let's just say that I enjoyed the original release so much that I actually got the Excalibur II in a repeat playthrough because I wanted to see EVERYTHING that this game had. Buy it. Just...buy the damn game. Please.

When I first downloaded this highly praised title (not on Steam) I was immediately surprised at how much depth a 2D game with RNG and permadeath could have.  I finally bought it through Steam (an embarrassingly high amount of hours later), and as an introduction to the genre I am now a huge fan of rogue-like and rogue-lite games.
You're given a starter ship and a small crew to outrun the rebels and eventually face off against their flagship through 8 star systems.  While in flight you have to manage everything from power distribution of desired systems to crew locations to ammo, shield, and fuel management as well as system and weapon upgrades, hiring more crew etc etc.  In combat there are things like fire suppression, crew healing, oxygen management, weapon power management, target selection, shield management, etc etc etc.  Your attack abilities can range from multiple projectiles that wear down an enemies shields, drones that keep up a constant attack while your weapons recharge, porting over to the enemy ship and doing crew combat, targeting specific systems so they can't fly away or use their weapons, using lasers to destroy their hull, etc etc.
Putting them all together can be intense and overwhelming and is a bit punishing at first.  I quickly learned that I needed to start the game in easy mode to make any sort of progress.  The further I made it the more I learned which weapons I liked, which upgrades worked for me, and how to manage my scrap for purchases.  The game has many RNG elements, and no two playthroughs will feel the same, but as you continue to play your progress consistently increases. The first time I beat the flagship by the skin of my teeth but then I began to beat it pretty easily and was ready for the next ship design or difficulty.
There is a huge amount of replay value here.  It has to be one of the few games on a short list that I've ever replayed after beating it.  As you progress and unlock achievements you unlock different layouts and better ships.  Each of the ships has their own style of combat and crew eg. more focused on using drones for attack and defense or the crew is mostly a race that is better at porting over to a ship and attacking or has quick repair and heal ability which allows you to ignore medical upgrades and focus on others etc.
I would definitely recommend picking this up on sale and giving it a try.  Very addictive and really polished.  I would just recommend starting it on easy mode!

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Papo & Yo is a delightful platformer/puzzle game with a very interesting theme. Though the game might at first look seem like a fantasy story of a boy and a monster being friends, it really is about growing up and coming to terms with your childhood. It is a game about how our imagination can help us cope with difficult times, until we are strong enough to take the masks off, see things for what they really are and accept reality for what it is.
In essense, Papo & Yo is not an extraordinary game, but it is a very good one. It has a strong and very personal message, one which I believe most people should be able to relate to one way or another. You can't go wrong with it.

When I bought this game half a year ago, I wasn't familiar at all with city-building games, but it was on sale and SimCity was of course a known franchise, so I bought it. When I started up the game for the 1st time I saw that I sometimes suffered from unexplainable graphical issues (colored lines ramdomly appearing on the screen). I went on. Then I noticed that the game sometimes chrashes (it happened to me about 10% of the times that I play it). I went on. Then I saw that I had been playing for hours. I went on.
This game is just so good that I dont't really mind these issues that I have from time to time. It is just so nice to start from scratch and create the city of your dreams (or the City of Death, for that matter). But that's just the start. After you're done with one city you will want to start up another neighboring city and connect both. and then a third city. And a fouth. There is just so much replayability because every city has different terrain. And while I can say that it's definetely not easy to make (and keep) your city healthy , it's not too complex to handle.
Since I bought this I have played more than 140 hours in 5 months time. For someone who also plays numerous other games, that's quite something. So yes, I'd definetely recommend this game if you have only a remote interest in city planning/management. It's already quite cheap normally, but when it's on sale there should definetely be no excuse for not buying this game if you think you will like it. It'll be worth the money.

Yes, Worms Reloaded can be considered to just be Worms Armageddon +, and in many ways this is right. The premise is exactly the same, the weapons are exactly the same (save for a few new ones), the physics, humour, & the modes which people will be spending 90% of their time are exactly the same. However, this is really refinement at it's best. The new bells and whistles make this incarnation of Worms into a 2010 and beyond experience. Seamless Steamworks support, achievements, HD sheen and interface, DLC, and tons of customizability mixed with the proven gameplay is the perfect molotov cocktail to keep you still coming back for more.

Furthermore, I think the TOTAL playerbase for the game was about 10-15 people during the time I played, worldwide.
This in itself would be okay if the players were friendly and willing to help teach someone new some tricks. (When first getting into M&B Warband I actually had some helpful players tutor me in how to play.) However everyone I met in the several hours I played seemed fairly elitist and would only speak to insult me for losing. Bowing before a fight? Enjoy a throwing knife to the face. Had a close match? Prepare to be teabagged. (Or teabagged in general, I usually was)
I think with the right community and some populated NA servers this game could be decent, certainly worth the five dollars, but as it stands, I wouldn't recommend this. There are better games with better melee mechanics, and much more friendly and populated servers.

I'm glad the focus is back on horror but at the end of the day all that matters to me is how good the game is. Fear is subjective and all but Resident Evil 7 wasn't scary to me. Not at all. It's still a decent game/teaser but I don't get the point of a demo where you don't actually get a sample of as core mechanic that is being in danger of being killed as you aren't being stalked by anyone. Yes the house groans and creaks but it's just ambient noises not the enemy. The point of puzzles in a horror game is to make it so your worried about solving them without being killed in the proccess by it or an enemy or killed on your way to the puzzle but here it's just dull wandering and lazy oops I fell off a shelf happenings.
It's not like you'll be hiding from your captor patrolling the house as you search for puzzle peices, trying to pu the peices together when ever there's a gap in his patrol for a breif moment before you go back into hiding. Instead you'll wander until you beat the demo and a cutscene kills you. I assume what I described above about hiding from hillbilly ganados will be in the final game but that's just an assumption. It does at least put the Resident and Evil back in Resident Evil. Try it for yourself as your milage may vary.
It controls well too but there were some bizzare immersion breaking flaws in the camera man section related to his hands being at his sides on his shadow {meaning that his head is a VHS camera) and how he climbs down a ladder with both hands whilst still supposedly holding a camera.I'm impressed by the port/version. Great new engine when compared to the MT Frameworks engine that was last used in Resident Evil Revelations 2. This and MGS:GZ/MGSV:TPP are the best "ports" I've seen in recent memory. Turn off the shader cache if your having trouble performance wise and watch the frames soar. It has a lot of graphics options for tweaking and thankfully the FOV can be defaulted to 90 which will make sure you don't get motion sick. My only complaints are it's lack of proper 8 MSAA or 21:9 support PC wise.

I wasn't alive at the release of this game, give or take a few months, but I was certainly playing it growing up. I had completed it fully, with no stone left unturned. I remember it was perhaps not one of my favourite games, possibly because I was too young to fully grasp the emotional rollercoaster the story turned out to be, but I remember it was up there with my top 5s on the original Playstation. And now, here it is on Steam! I immediately bought it as soon as I could and couldn't wait to jump back in, and I have to say, I am not disappointed in the least! The game is just how I remembered it only with boosted graphics. The gameplay is smooth, no lag whatsoever, the menus are slighty larger from what I remember but I think that is because this PC version was adapted from the IOS and Android version? Correct me if I'm wrong. Anyway, moving on, the adaptation seems to have brought on no problems. I read a few complaints in the reviews about controller support issues, thankfully I can say I have had none of those.
All in all, the game is (still) perfect! No problems, and SE didn't mess it up by trying to implement Microtransactions or DLC!
Definitely a worthy purchase for the nostalgia and a truly fantastic, wonderful and inspirational game!

A very good port!
- no dumb keymapping, no NumPad etc. You mostly need X, C, V, and B with either arrow keys or WASD for movement, turn on "Always Run" in the menu and you won't need the mouse. You can also navigate with the mouse like in a point-and-click adventure.
- graphical update is mostly good. In a few cases the low-res backgrounds are jarring, the originals have been lost apparently. Runs well on my 5 years old laptop, but no widescreen, there are constant gray bars on both sides.
- F1 ALL THE THINGS - 2,3x speedup via F1 makes long fights with summons bearable, also great when you're stuck in a location and missed a door somewhere, it's easy to visit all screens in a few seconds. It's a godsend when the game makes you watch something boring like that dance in Cleyra. F1 can also be used as a cheat: when you're in one of the missions with a time-limit the clock isn't affected by the speed-up. I've encountered a minor bug: A few times I've managed to F1 the animated cutscenes with no way to turn it off, you have to hit F1 at exactly the right time for the bug to trigger.
- The other F-keys are cheats, the only useful one is F4 which turns off random encounters (that includes the "good" ones!), good for exploring or when you're running low on supplies.
- Autosave! You still have the old-school save locations, but you also get a autosave every time you change the location, good for when you lost a valuable Tetra playing card, or when a boss is far away from the last savepoint. Apparently this save is only accessible over the "Continue" button in the main menu.

When I first downloaded this highly praised title (not on Steam) I was immediately surprised at how much depth a 2D game with RNG and permadeath could have.  I finally bought it through Steam (an embarrassingly high amount of hours later), and as an introduction to the genre I am now a huge fan of rogue-like and rogue-lite games.
You're given a starter ship and a small crew to outrun the rebels and eventually face off against their flagship through 8 star systems.  While in flight you have to manage everything from power distribution of desired systems to crew locations to ammo, shield, and fuel management as well as system and weapon upgrades, hiring more crew etc etc.  In combat there are things like fire suppression, crew healing, oxygen management, weapon power management, target selection, shield management, etc etc etc.  Your attack abilities can range from multiple projectiles that wear down an enemies shields, drones that keep up a constant attack while your weapons recharge, porting over to the enemy ship and doing crew combat, targeting specific systems so they can't fly away or use their weapons, using lasers to destroy their hull, etc etc.
Putting them all together can be intense and overwhelming and is a bit punishing at first.  I quickly learned that I needed to start the game in easy mode to make any sort of progress.  The further I made it the more I learned which weapons I liked, which upgrades worked for me, and how to manage my scrap for purchases.  The game has many RNG elements, and no two playthroughs will feel the same, but as you continue to play your progress consistently increases. The first time I beat the flagship by the skin of my teeth but then I began to beat it pretty easily and was ready for the next ship design or difficulty.
There is a huge amount of replay value here.  It has to be one of the few games on a short list that I've ever replayed after beating it.  As you progress and unlock achievements you unlock different layouts and better ships.  Each of the ships has their own style of combat and crew eg. more focused on using drones for attack and defense or the crew is mostly a race that is better at porting over to a ship and attacking or has quick repair and heal ability which allows you to ignore medical upgrades and focus on others etc.
I would definitely recommend picking this up on sale and giving it a try.  Very addictive and really polished.  I would just recommend starting it on easy mode!

There is good games, and then there is great games. Freedom Planet turns out to be latter, thanks to developers paying attention to detail more than i remember seeing in quite long time.
Story is not exactly Shakespeare, but the voice acting is decent with the standout being Lord Breven with his growly voice that makes him over the top and charismatic, The atmosphere is both exciting and charming. Partly thanks to visuals that actually looked slightly better in-game than elsewhere. Music and sound effects turn out to be top notch as well.
The most important thing, however, is gameplay, which is mix of various classics such as Mega Man X, Gunstar Heroes, and of course Sonic The Hedgehog. This is without ever using retro-style-indie-game cliches, and it works incredibly fine as long you adjust sensitivity settings to fit your taste. But what is game without it's meat? Level design here is surprisingly varied and detailed, with lot of interactivity put into worlds. Enemies and Bosses are the main challenge, though, but even on their worst they seem decent. Game even occasionally has some clever tricks and strategies to use against them.
Extra stuff includes collectible cards in levels to unlock stuff in gallery, mahjong and Shang Mu academy, series of mini-challenges so fun that it must be illegal. And the best thing about this already content packed game is... there is still more to come...

Jesus, this game was hard.
Freedom Planet is inspired by sonic but really is very much it's own game. After finishing the game as Lilac, I feel both pleased and relieved that I managed to survive the onslaught of bosses this game throws at you, without throwing my controller out of the window. Key take home messages:
I found the level design to be particularly satisfying as it wasn't always just 'run from left to right until the end of the stage'. Level navigation is a key concept in the game, and there isn't always a single path to the end of the stage. There's also other challenges which involve interacting with and navigating your environment. This adds some welcome variety to the gameplay and can serve to slow you down from just running all the time so you can think about how to tackle the next obstacle.
The sound effects are crisp and have that retro feel, and the soundtrack is really great, and compliments the situations in the game well. The pixel graphics are done very well, and the use of vibrant colours makes this a beautiful game world to look at. I found myself screenshotting away on the regular, as there were many grand screen filling elements of the game. WHich brings me on to the use of screen real estate.
There's always something going on somewhere in the screen. I found there few if any dead spots, when it came to filling my monitor with game assets or just background artwork. This is not something I ever paid much attention to before when gaming, and I believe it's only really something to be noted in 2D platformers. It doesn't really detract from a game if it's not taken care of (it can even be an aesthetic design choice), but when it's taken care of I feel it can add to my enjoyment of a game world. The game as Lilac was of a good length, and seeing as you can play as other characters, there really is plenty of game to be enjoyed.
Freedom Planet is best enjoyed on a controller. I used an xbox 360 controller, but I got it to work with a Dualshock 4 controller also. This is unsurprising as it's inspired by games like sonic which were initially made for the Sega (and later Nintendo) consoles, which would have used controllers of their own. Keyboard and mouse work fine, but the controls for this game are really basic, and the analogue stick really does compliment the fast paced running and jumping really well.
The story of Freedom Planet is what I can only describe as lovely, with many warming moments and some nice use of drama. It's not a spectacular story by any means, but it doesn't need to be, and it doesn't advertise itself as thus. It's nice, it adds context to the gameplay and I found it enjoyable. Not every game we play needs to be hard hitting, nitty gritty and I can definitely appreciate a light hearted, but immensley challenging game to sink my teeth into. Ultimately I found Freedom Pplanet to be a well put together, fun, fast paced, pretty, challenging but ultimately rewarding experience.
But most of all, the best way to describe this game is - fun.

I was watching a review of Sonic 2 for some reason, and in the video, they mention that there's a game called freedom planet, which is a Sonic game, that isn't a Sonic game. That was enough to peek my interest in this title. Before I played this game, my favorite game of all time was Donkey Kong Country 2, for the music (still my favorite), the level design (most the time), and the length of the game. Then I came across this game, and this, as of now, is my new favorite game of all time. It takes the sonic formula, and then amplifies it, while adding in things that made other platformers great. The soundtrack, while it isn't my favorite, is really good, and kinda gives me Starfox, F-zero, Megaman, and vibes from other platformers. I liked how all the characters played. Lilac is the one I reccomend playing on your first playthrough, as the levels seem to be made around her abilites. The other characters are kinda like variations on how to play, Carol can scale walls, and has a super fast motercycle, and Mila has an exelent double jump, and defensive capabilities that can damage the enemy units. This game also has a story, and while it's really not the meat and potatoes of the game, it's still good for what it is, and is lightyears better than any story in a recent Sonic game. The story starts out somewhat innocent, and there are moments that feel like they belong in a kids movie (and a good one too), but then the story gets really dark, slowly, but surely, kinda like growing up now that I think about it. I also didn't mind the voice acting too much, and a lot of the actors/actresses felt really down to earth, and I can dig that. Now this is the best part of the game, the bosses. If you like the bosses in Gunstar Heroes, Rocket Knight, or Contra Hard Corps (Probotector on the Megadrive in europe), then this game is worth it alone for the extravagant and over the top bosses, that can be daunting in pure size.
Now here are where the cons come in. First and foremost, and this only aplies to the versions on pcs, but the game is a bit of a technical mess. If you are running a monitor that is above 60hz (like a 144hz monitor), then you should externaly turn Vsync on, otherwise you will get exreme amounts of stuttering. There's a lack of an in game Vsync option, which just adds an extra step to turning Vsync on, and there isn't a proper resolution option either, and the game runs at 30fps if you don't run it in fullscreen, and if you do run it in fullscreen, then it runs at 60fps, which isn't too big of an issue, it's just that I would prefer to take advantage of the refresh rate that my monitor runs at. Other than that huge wall of technical infromation, the only cons I have, are on the bosses, and the difficulty of them depending on the character you choose. Some bosses may be extremely easy with Lilac, while that same boss can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥for Carol and Mila. It's not a huge issue, but just something that annoyed me a bit, and should be noted.
Other than those things, this is the perfect sonic game. You need to own this title if you are a fan of either Sonic, or the Sega Genesis (or Megadrive), or even retro games in general.

Sonic Generations is a fun game. I don't remember ever owning a Sonic game. I've only played some flash copies of it in browsers. So I guess this is the first actual Sonic game I've played? Possibly. And it's a great introduction to Sonic!
In Sonic Generations, you go through various levels from various Sonic games. All the levels are ofcourse redesigned for HD graphics and such.
You get to choose if you wish to play as old Sonic or as new Sonic in EVERY level! What this means is basically weather you wish to play the oldschool sidescrolling Sonic or if you wish to play the 3rd person Sonic. The 3rd person mode is way better than previous Sonic games! A good game with an excellent, although at times dark, campaign. It definitely has some replay value.
Pros:
— A reasonably lengthy campaign.
— Fighting in the Pacific theater offers some much-needed variety. The Japanese have a very different fighting style compared to the Germans. You must constantly watch out for banzai chargers, snipers hiding in the palm trees and ambushes from soldiers hiding in the brush. The array of new weapons such as the Japanese Arisaka rifle and Type 99 machine gun breathe some fresh air into the game.
— This game feels a lot more mature and serious than previous CoD games, especially the Soviet Campaign which brings moral ambiguity into play. This makes the game more psychologically engaging.
— The soundtrack adds to the overall more serious theme of the game. Particularly the menu theme is eerily calm and foreboding.
— Zombies mode. Gotta admit, I never really got on board the Zombie hype train, but there is no denying that the Zombie mode is a ton of fun.
Cons:
— The Soviet campaign might start dark and gritty, but once you get used to it, it feels a bit like a rehash of the Soviet campaign in the first CoD. It starts with the very same battle, Stalingrad, and end with same triumphant conquest of the Reichstag building. There is only so many times you can fight the same battle before it gets boring.
— No British Special forces or any British campaign? Really? They were always a highlight for me in the older CoD games. I miss their cynical, dry sense of humor.
Mild spoiler alert
— The Catalina Mission. Sigh. The entire game goes for this more realistic feeling, where you have to figure out your next move carefully and strategically. A single wrong move and you kick the bucket. Now suddenly a single Catalina can take down wave upon wave of enemy fighters and Patrol boats, survive the lot of ‘em and save some sailors in the middle of a raging naval battle. Don’t get me wrong. It’s very cool and dramatic. Just seems really out of place in the middle of a serious, realistic campaign. Might have worked better as its own game mode like Zombies.
Overall I give this game a 8/10.

Papo y Yo is a 3rd person action platformer. Its basic controls and easy to understand mechanics allows its charm to shine through. The story is centered around Quico, a south american boy, that sets out to find why he is cursed. He follows a mysterious girl around in search of the answer to his quest. He comes to find that his curse is to be paired with a monster who is usually disinterested in him but will turn in a moments notice and attack Quico when presented with some mysterious tree frogs. Quico has the ability, or the task, rather of manipulating his world. The south american favela setting is both oppressive and beautiful; at times the world is vivid and imaginative. Traversing the various puzzles can drastically change them in ways you would never expect.

Very much enjoyed this game. First game I bought on steam over the summer sale and glad I did, because it seems to have been taken down.
There wasn't anything too groundbreaking here but everything this game tries to do it does very well.
It may seem at first like a GTA clone and the game play is pretty similar but you'll quickly notice it ignores some the mechanics that have become hallmarks in the GTA series.
There are no side missions. There is no upgrading your character or characters status. There's nothing to do in the engrossing but empty open world.
These may seem lacking but this game does just fine without any of it and I'm glad the devs didn't force it into the game. Instead the game focuses on a well told and straight forward story with a great cast of characters.
The voice acting is among the best I've heard in games, it really stood out. If you close your eyes,  you would think, you were listening to a real Scorsese movie, if only the dialogue were a little stronger. The dialogue is at times not as punchy as I might hope but it's by no means bad, just doesn't quite match the grade A standard set by the voice acting, character models and overall atmosphere of the game (which is largely thanks to the stellar 40s+50s soundtrack. I noticed a couple songs also in Fallout 3 and New Vegas). I wouldn't even mention it in any other game, the voice acting just sets such a high bar, I wish the actors had some interesting lines, or at least had them more often.
The game play largely revolves around third person cover shooting and it's extremely fun, especially with a mouse. I play GTA with a game pad but Mafia II on M+K since there's more focus on shooting.  You feel extremely badass laying down 200 goons in a bar with your pistol or Tommy gun.
I hope Mafia III sticks to what made this great and doesn't truly turn into a GTA clone

Should you get this game?
In short: yes
In long: let me try to explain.
The game definitely takes you on a very entertaining rollercoaster with a very decent story, nice cutscenes, a very good environment that feels lively yet also date enough to make you feel what it must have felt like to live in the 1940's/1950's. Be it the looks, the people, the shops, the billboards, the cars, it's all there.
Another plus to this game is that this game makes you feel more to be part of The Godfather, than The Godfather I and II games ever did. Godfather I was great, don't get me wrong, but it felt a bit artificial where it tried to combine movie scenes and stories to the game, where this game doesn't.
The controls are very easy to understand, the difficulty levels can be a plus to everyone, depending on your gaming preferences.
On to the cons. It's short, seriously it is, too short for its own good, and the ending...well that ending. If you read other reviews you'll understand the ending leaves to be desired. I had no idea I was so close to the end, got the cutscene and was like "great let's get on with
Ending credits?
Dissapointing. Dissapointing also cause the linearity of the game makes you forget you're in an open world sandbox. And if you ever want to explore that world, chances are high you get shot or arrested after a few minutes anyhow.
The lack of length, the linearity and the ending cost this game points, what could have been a 9/10 ends up with 7.5/10 and that's partially due to the fact I like this genre.
But in the end, L.A. Noire is superior. I don't regret getting this game and I'll probably make another run in it, but it falls short to its potential. L.A. Noire does as well, but not nearly as bad as this one. Still if you like this style of games, you'll enjoy it though.

If you are not familiar with this game, perhaps you should read another review, but...
If you loved the original game on PS1, you'll love this one too.
If you loved the original game on PS1, but you DON'T like this one... Wow... Look at yourself. What sort of person have you become?
Sure, some of the backgrounds and secondary assets at times seem a bit... "fuzzy" and not quite on par with the new character models that they are so often awkwardly juxtaposed with, but the overall visual presentation exceeds that of the original game while still maintaining the same spirit and feel. And yes, the battle UI is a bit too big. And yes, the "Boosters" feel somewhat out of line with the spirit of the original game, seeming to cater to the now much-maligned "casual" gamer. And OH NO, it's a mobile port, and OH NOOO it's 2016 and the game is still in 4:3! How terrible!
If the original game enchanted you, but you are now put off by these superficial flaws... are you happy with the person you've become?
As for price, well, I look at it like this: In my adolescent carelessness, the 4th disc to my original copy was scratched and unplayable by around 2003, I never got in more than 2-3 playthroughs, never got to sink in the countless hours with IX in the same way I did with VII, VIII, and X. Making up lost time is more than worth this price.
You really can't ask for greater depth or charm out of a Final Fantasy game than this. Final Fantasy IX is a shining example of the greatness of this franchise in the days of old. Few (if any) subsequent FF titles have surpassed it.
Turning it on, and hearing the music of the intro cutscene: instant, warm, gooey nostalgia.

TL;DR
+ Aesthetic
+ Performance
+ Lightning-fast gameplay that'll leave you feeling like a badass
+ Realistic sword fighting with cool fantasy elements
+ Beautiful OST
----- No player base, but play it anyway because that's the only way to fix that (also it's very fun)
REVIEW (Early Access, 17.8 hours on record as of writing):
This game is amazing. Everything from the aesthetic, the performance, the lightning-fast action, the music, the variety of sword and combat styles on display, the different moves blending both realistic sword combat and techniques with some fantasy elements (such as running on walls and aerial attacks), it's all great.
However, there is one major problem with this game that hurts it very much - there are almost no players. Only very few people still play this on a regular basis, jammed into the same server, practicing every day/week and not getting any worse for it. The result is, any new players get stomped and beat into submission. The tutorial does nothing (it can't, really) to prepare you for the level of♥♥♥♥♥kick you're going to get before you start to learn the tricks and subtleties that make the difference between winning or getting your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you by yet another longsword-wielding Phalanx. The learning curve is a serious brick wall because of this, and the player base isn't large enough to split people up into multiple tiers based on games played, win ratio and whatnot.
This is the only fault I've really come across (other than Early Access Limbo) and there isn't much to be done about it, other than this - which is to say, recommend it. Anyone who reads this: give it a shot and with a bit of luck you'll like it as much as I do.

Not much to say about this mod at the moment, since it's rather short, although it's supposed to get a couple new episodes in the future. Even then, after having played it, I feel it appropriate to write a review, as short as it might be.
Half-Life 2: DownFall is a mod set after the events of Half-Life 2: Episode Two. While I'm not really fond of mods trying to continue Episode Two's story, considering the way they usually conflict with its ending, I can still appreciate them for their quality, and even their storytelling if it's good enough. In the case of DownFall, there's some minimal storytelling, and that's not bad; it feels somewhat similar to Lost Coast in that regard.
As far as the gameplay goes, well, it's pretty much in typical Half-Life 2 fashion, nothing fancy there. I feel the pacing is pretty good, with some intense battles here and there. However, a few times I found myself confused as to what I was supposed to do, but I don't really blame the devs, since taking a good look at their level design, it seems they took a few cues from Valve's way of guiding the player; they just need to improve the implementation.
To conclude, I'd say this is a pretty good mod, with a nice level of quality. It's not something I'd see as a continuation of Half-Life's story, but it still feels very fitting into the HL universe, like Lost Coast. So, in my view, this would be part of Half-Life's "Expanded Universe".

Company of Heroes 2 is one of those games which i love and hate at the same time. It's always been a very unstable game across the years with lots of downhill and uphill stages, firstly with pay to win commanders back when it came out, then it seemed incredibly imbalanced across the different units and factions moving like a pendulum back and forth without finding any sense of stability in multiplayer, which by the way is why you would buy this game.
The Soviet campaign is awful and the Theater Of War missions just seem like unnecessary busywork, although i do think the Ardennes Assault campaign was pretty alright since it reminded me of Company Of Heroes 1. If you want a good singleplayer campaign buy Company Of Heroes 1.
So if we look at the multiplayer currently it's completely transformed since it first came out, in a good way. It is alot more balanced than previously and it doesn't solely center around what commander you choose anymore which is great! The gameplay is addicting as hell once you get the basics going which will probably take you about 10 hours of ingame time. It's a relatively hard game on the surface if you are new to Real Time Strategy games but you can find multiple guides and tutorials in the forums and on youtube to get you up to speed. The small coh community is still very passionate and active, and on top of that they are still releasing patches and trying to balance the game to perfection. It's far from dead.
Now the only real frustration i have with this game is some of the imbalance between the factions particularly in 2v2 and 3v3 currently. If you have a player that is just as good as you are playing the US or British faction, then you will most of the time lose the game. I've had this experience a lot in multiplayer, allies are at this moment a lot easier to play which just makes it frustrating when you play as the axis most of the time since the allied factions can pump out more, and better units. At the same time it feels more rewarding to win :)
Now hopefully the Winter patch coming out this, well winter, will fix a lot of these issues and make everything more rounded. Or it will fix it and break something else. It seems like game balancing maybe isn't relics strong point, but at the same time. This game is incredibly addicting despite some of the unbalance and ultimately, there is a reason I've reinstalled this game i think 50 times now after telling myself i have to quit (i have another account with 300+ hours) and yes there is something wrong with me.
7/10
