I felt the storyline was a skewed portrayal of the Soviet Union as murdering its own soldiers and civilians without hesitation. If someone wants to call a country to account for war crimes, in the medium of a computer game, it should be specific ones and not as part of an imaginary drama story. Because then we see pretend victims when we could have known the stories of real ones
Early on this game shows a blocking detachment machine gunning their own retreating soldiers - this wasn't the units' function, or how Order 227 normally operated. It must have happened somewhere, the Soviet Union did shocking things - but the game characterises them through this one lens selectively, rather than as a rational army. As well as dramatizing, the focus on one commander and the superficial summary text between missions obscures the wider context of the Soviet Union raising 30 million troops and defending in a war of extermination
One thing I found sickening though, was that in the second mission you have to burn down some farmhouses with the flamethrower unit, and after you do this you're shown that the buildings were not in fact empty: because some people run out of one of them. Now this is historically accurate, but if a game is going to put you in the role of a paramilitary destruction battallion about to carry out the Kautla massacre, then it should give some advance warning of this so you can make an informed choice about whether or not you want to play it
Bias penetrates into the unit design, mission objectives, and voiceover: "another unit of conscripts is at our disposal". Even the Red Alert games didn't make the Soviet units so expendable. I found the combat mechanics peculiar (on medium difficulty) - the soldiers look realistic in the way they move, but then they do things like walking right up to an enemy unit in cover to attack them, or across the line of fire of a machine gun - and they can survive like that for a while. The atmosphere, artwork, and (close-in) mission scope and field of view don't suit stylized combat with health bars gradually wearing down. In a mission about fortifying a small village against a German advance, it was strange being able to replace lost soldiers by standing units in the radius of a command post and clicking the "recruit" button
"In future, Komandir, do not retreat the conscripts toward the blocking detachment. Instead spam the recruit button."
"Komandir, enemy forces are destroying our farmer units in Belarus, please press the recruit button two million times"

I'll start off by saying for those who see the trailer and think just a sonic ripoff you need to do more research as it is heavily inspired by sonic, and started off as a sonic fan-made game, but has evolved into a game its own.
Gameplay
Now the game plays a lot like a sonic game, so classic sonic gamers shouldn't have to much trouble with this game and to offer a comparison, the stages are easier then a classic sonic game's but the end of the stage bosses are harder so I'd recommend new players that have no sonic experience (classic sonic anyway) to do there first playthrough on an easier difficulty. A big difference from classic sonic the the presence of a life gauge rather then the ring system, you have health and can recover it but you can't pull pro skill grab your last ring and stay in the fight tactics, you genuinely need to learn enemy patterns and avoid there attacks. For fans of the classic sonic games you have the option to play the game in adventure mode (have the full story with cut-scenes) or classic mode (more like the old sonic games) as well as the option to play as 1 of 3 characters in the game. Overall the game play has a nice feel to it but I'd recommend a game pad any day for it, 8/10
Graphics
Now for you fancy graphics gamers you will hate this as it is more for classic Sega graphics so by the over-hyped standards of today there not great but more retro gamers will be pleased with it as it gives a nice refreshing taste of old classic games. 8/10
Sound/Audio
Another good spot as the music for the game is great having a slight touch of old school game music but withy a larger sound bit option so the music sounds great, and for those playing the adventure mode it is fully dub so you get the full experience that modern game take for granted. 9/10
Story
Now the story is where I'm in love as it is refreshing, a long time ago a dragon descended onto the world and become the kingdom stone, a jewel of great power, three kingdoms where founded and have lived in relative peace till a warlord appeared to try and steal the kingdom stone using one of the kingdoms as a puppet to do so, you follow/play as lilac and Carol (and later Milla) to stop lord Brevon from succeeding. Overall the story was great my only real beef is that it doesn't have much back story (it feels like it starts partway into the story, there isn't any origins for some of it, such as who is lilac and carol, how they meet, there dark past, you get some idea but nothing to really explain it, I'm personally hoping this game expands to become its own thing (kinda like sonic but I'm hoping without the cluster **** that sonic is, it is so far divided its not funny) 10/10
Overall
This is a great game that I'd recommend to almost anyone and is a great way to kill time and give a good old classic sonic feel to games. 8/10

This is a surprisingly thought provoking game. On the face of it a USA developed fruit farm themed time attack game from 2009 which employs the characters of Flora and Old Jim (who is an Uncle Sam figure in the tutorial passing on the old ways to the young, vivacious, hard working and obliging Flora).
Every good resource based game echoes the struggle for survival which humanity faces and this game does do that.
What I liked about this game is that it has on the face of it an almost educational potential to prepare the young for a career in a service industry and help older players laugh it off. I was curious that it embraced the almighty dollar and could teach gamers of all ages a thing or two about free market economics which also had a slightly dry edutaining feel, when games like this usually opt for gold coins or piles of gems. Also I liked how cheap it was to buy and how the fruits make a farty noise when they turn bad.
What I didn't like was what was left out of the game, which is as thought provoking as what is included if not more so. One gets the feeling that, intentionally or otherwise, Honeyslug created an ironic microcosm of power struggles within the US bread basket, which raises questions about modern forced farming techniques and the validity of the free market as an overseer of the long term health and happiness of the human race. Flora's Fruit Farm provokes thought about all that and more because it isnt anywhere to be seen, if you can make sense of that. Let me explain.
Maybe the games fruity theme was an in joke about fruit themed hi tech gadgetry, I dont know. But if it was it doesnt show and instead is thoroughly innocent agricultural gameplay in the sense it includes no references to gadgets or to controversial biology which is instead represented as "magic" growth, shine and vermin removal tied to dollar purchases of "fairy dust" and no hint of the related ecological or health issues arising from hormones, GM and pesticides which were the first things which sprang to my mind when I played it and imho should be seen in an agricultural game because it is part of the public debate today. The subversive nature of this innocence can be seen as acting subliminally for big chemical business in the way it neglects the inconvenient truths and responsibilities of agriculture, which speaking personally is why it fails to catch the whiff of the zeitgeist which Angry Birds for example didn't, giving as it did, players the chance to attack the greedy fat egg stealing pigs head on instead, which I think we all enjoyed. Flora's FF is just a bit too innocent to have that kind of appeal and studiously avoids any hint of the controversy which could make it funny.
I ended up wondering whether it was designed like that unconsciously or in irony because it feels like such a Macdonalds ready staff training game. But I am not sure if in the artistic process of true artists it is even possible to tell these two kinds of inspiration apart. Either way it ended up being just a little too innocent to be believed.
In addition the pacing and balance of the game make it something of a repetitive grind of mouse clicking, perfect for testing mouse to eye coordination and preparing the uninitiated for the arduous realities of holding down a job in a service industry but not actually that much fun to play for long periods given my life long aversion to such modes of employment, though in short bursts maybe if you like that kind of time attack thing its engaging uncomplicated fun. I do love how the trees grow so tall and full.
I was only a little disappointed that it lacked the glimmer of hope for the future which every tech savvy gamer knows robots will one day provide, assuming they don't try to take over the world first that is! ;o) What it did have was lots of fruit and we all know how food items go down well with the punters.
It is a curious early game from Honeyslug who went on to produce such amusing timewasters as Ric Rococo : International Art Thief and it would seem success changed their perspective on the work ethic somewhat when comparing Ric to Flora. I preferred Ric tbh. I cannot condemn them for what they have made here, its just too sweet and innocent and I dreamt about Flora all night long, in a very innocent way I hasten to add, for some reason I was lecturing her in forest pool ecology and she was a very good listener.
I can say that there was only one minor bug apparent when I played it in Win7x64 and I was able to reload the game and play on without major issues (just one tree not appearing in the plot map after restart, but it was there when you played the tree spot).
Because I am Flora's friend a thumbs up. Its sweet if you like that kind of thing. There is at least one gameplay video on YouTube and I advise prospective customers to go take a look at it, it is the ethical thing for me to do :)

In general this is the best version of this game around especially if you were like me and still played it on an emulator.
Pros:
- Models (character, NPC, monsters) look fantastic and have great detail
- Graphics in general much improved
- Good controller support (xbox 360 controller in my case, have not given the kb and mouse a shot)
- Original audio and it sounds fantastic
- Still one of the best FF titles IMO
- The text looks great and is really readable
- Skipable cutscenes
- When you select continue on the title menu the game picks up right where you left off, nice feature
Cons:
-  It's a port of the mobile release so it's graphical options are limited to resolution.  Wish we had some basic AA or     something.
-  While the models and cutscenes in the game look awesome the pre-rendered backgrounds were not given verry much love they could really use some additional touch ups
-  The battle UI is god awful for a PC game.  It's friggen gigantic and spread out all over the screen.  I wish we had the original PS1 UI at this point.
-  The cheats are OK but I was really hoping we could get two things: and increase in difficulty (tougher battles) and a sensible increase in battle speed.  I know you can speed the whole game up like crazy but that's not really what I was hoping for.  Was hoping for 1.5x the speed of the max battle speed setting in game options.
-  No in game controlls to set the sound level, have to do it with the Volume Mixer in Windows.
-  Minor gripe but I hate how getting close to any NPC causes "!" to pop up.
In short, I love this game and this port is pretty decent.  It could have been better for PC players but whatever, still beats playing on an emulator.  I hope that it gets some slick mods like FF7 and FF8 got but I am slightly doubtful because of it's mobile origins.  99/100 Nobels were impressed.

I'm writing as somebody who has only beaten the game once so far on easy, playing with AE on; from the outset I'll say that you should play with the advanced edition additions on. Also, it takes a little bit of time to git gud, so be wary (I'm still not there yet).
As of right now, FTL has risen to become one of my favorite single player experiences in gaming. Whether it be the balanced weapon systems, the micromanaging, the alien races and their specialities, the different ships you can use, the different strategies to combat and resource management (varying from a focus on boarding parties, to drone control, to laser spam etc.) Each aspect of the combat and the storytelling is super polished and seamless. 95% of the time you die, lose hull points or crew members, it's cause you stuffed up; you made the mistake. Whether that's preparation issues or wrong choices. Furthermore, the last stand is one of my all time highlights when it comes to boss fights, seeing that thing for the first time and taking it in, trying to break down how to win piece by piece is an experience. The gameplay here is spot on for a roguelike, it's a challenge, but a manageable one. The two difficulties I've played in Normal and Easy were both brutal initially, but Easy gives you plenty of opportunity and currency to make up for your mistakes, Normal does not. Hard sounds like it will kill me, but I look forward to being able to take it on properly once I beat Normal.
Something I'm passionate about in gaming is the soundtrack, as for me, sound design generally can make or break any type of media. The soundtrack for this game is far above average. It should be noted that each song in game (with the exception of the last stand) has both an explore and combat piece, which crossfade beautifully into each other when each phase ends. To summarize, the overworld music is incredibly atmospheric and sets the tone nicely, while the battle themes add suspense, but not in an 'in your face' way. The weapons and alarms you'll hear in game are all quite distinct and add levels of immersion to the experience.
The background art is decent, but not super noticable when you're spending the whole time busting your balls trying to stay alive. Each ship class, both yours and the enemy's is distinct and well done, it's really the smaller details that speak for its ingenuity; for example moving your weapons to different ports in the action bar shifts them on the ship, which is a neat detail.
This review is intended to sway you to purchase the game, I unfortunately have to leave halfway through writing this, so I urge you to check out at least one negative review of the game (if you can find one handy), to balance out this review. The main thing that comes to mind is that the game can sometimes be unforgiving, and once you figure out how to manipulate the enemy crew's ai, it isn't nearly as difficult as it is early on. Boarding is good, perhaps too good; the mind control, crew teleporter combo is tough to beat. Furthermore, having to unlock each ship can be tough as some of the quests you simply won't see because you avoid sectors or they just don't generate.
All in all, if you're looking for a challenging roguelike that pushes forward an immersive experience, brilliant combat system, choice a plenty, a seamless mix of game and story, awesome soundtrack and one of the best three phase boss fights ever. Then Star Trek episode generator, AKA FTL: Faster Than Light is the game for you.

Papo & Yo is a delightful platformer/puzzle game with a very interesting theme. Though the game might at first look seem like a fantasy story of a boy and a monster he befriends, it really is about growing up and coming to terms with your childhood. It is a game about how our imagination can help us cope with difficult times, until we are strong enough to take the masks off, see things for what they really are and accept reality for what it is.
The game itself isn't very challenging, but the platformer controls can be a bit finnicky from time to time. The environments of the game are well made and it is fun to see how the world shifts as you solve the puzzles. The game is fairly short but it definitely keeps you invested in it until its very appropriate and memorable ending.
In essense, Papo & Yo is not an extraordinary game, but it is a very good one. It has a strong and very personal message, one which I believe most people should be able to relate to one way or another. You can't go wrong with it.

Autobiographical game and a surreal parabole about a relationship between a child and abusive parent with drinking problem. That alone makes Papo & Yo stand out. However actual gameplay consists of series of puzzles that are inventive and satisfying but never bring greater challenge as it is almost always obvious what to do. Jumping is imprecise at best and sadly there are few sections where you have to perform a double-jump in a very specific way which is not fun at all. I reccomend Papo & Yo for tackling with difficult topics and for creating a memorable experience.

This game is pretty much the way you remembered it back in the year 2000. If you haven't played the game before, then mostly everything is left untouched (story, game mechanics, etc) and you should read a review elsewhere for how the game is in regards to that. I'm going to talk about the port itself and what changes it brought to the table.
Off the bat, the character models had their textures bumped up to higher quality. No longer are faces blurred out because now you can see them with great clarity. Even NPCs had their textures bumped up too! However, the backgrounds are still in their old Playstation low resolution versions and rumors state that the developers lost the assets for the backgrounds. It's very distracting and clashes heavily with the new high res character models. While it doesn't bother me too much, it may be a deal breaker for others. The FMVs also had a bump up in quality and are not fuzzy or blurry anymore, which is another nice touch.
The port also has several game boosters that you can turn on and off at will, such as making the game go faster in turbo speed, always do max damage, disable random encounters, and always have full ATB and Trance bars. The other boosters such as max level and magic stones, instant learn abilities, and max gil can't be disabled once turned on. The boosters are nice to have if you want to screw around or just want to get to certain parts of the game with little hassle and you can easily enjoy the game without them. However, it is quite easy to accidentally turn a booster on by mistake if you're aren't careful.
There are a few bugs, but they're mostly minor. There's the infamous "character moves to the right" bug when it comes to using controllers, but so far I have managed to get around it by only enabling the controller after the game has loaded. In certain battles or battle screens, the dynamic camera can get screwed up such as zooming in too closely on a character or the camera focusing on the wrong character when an enemy readies an ability. While distracting, they're just minor annoyances.
Overall, the port is pretty solid and the extra features are a welcomed addition. Minor bugs are present, but nothing too deal breaking.

They're too far apart, or they're before an unskippable cutscene. Oh yeah, this game has (some) unskippable, also mostly useless cutscenes. The actual story-cutscenes are skippable, the nonsense-cutscenes (like a dude walking through a door) aren't.
Aside from the infuriatingly annoying checkpoints, the health-system in this game is kind of weird, too. You have to eat, but oftentimes you don't have anything to eat when you actually need health - no medikits, anything beside the automatic regen system, which only helps to restore a portion of your health makes some missions incredibly difficult.
And the third thing that annoyed me most is the very dull and boring fistfights. Also they're frickin' hard if you haven't got enough health at the time they come.

This game is quite phenominal, one of the best indie-platformers I have ever played. The visuals are incredibly SEGA-eqsue, as if this game were a smash-hit on the Sega Genesis or Saturn. It has a retro-inspired look, without using low-resolution as a crutch; it is truly a beautiful game. Although on the surface it appears to be primarily inspired by Sonic the Hedgehog, it finds its own footing through inspiration from many of the 1990s best platformers, including Mega Man X, Castlevania, etc. Each of the characters abilities offer a variety of ways to traverse a level, making each playthrough with a character feel very different.
The music is phenominal; it reminds me of Sonic CD, one of my favorite Sega soundtracks. It has a nice old-school MIDI feel to it, but with some more instrumental complexity that you would find on consoles like the Saturn or PS1.
The voice-acting and cutscenes aren't particularly memorable, but they are good for, well, being "indie". Personally, after one playthrough of "Adventure" mode, I played through again in "Classic", completely skipping nearly all voice-acting and cutscenes.
Controls were simple enough, I played on a DualShock 3 and it felt like any other platformer. It uses a three-button control scheme, well suited to the old Sega controllers. With only have Jump, Action, and Special, you can really map it to whatever you feel like.
As an aside, I loved the addition of Casual mode, which halved enemy damge and added in passive health regeneration. It takes away quite a bit of challenge, but is a godsend to people who love speedrunning, or those who would like to playthrough levels many times over for completion, without having to worry about carefully traversing the levels each time and playing it safe with bosses.
All in all, this game is like the best platformer that time travelled from the 90s. If you enjoyed any action-platformer from that decade, this game is for you. If you liked indie titles such as Cave Story or Shovel Knight, this game is also for you. Give it a try!

I've never played Sonic nor any other game similar to Freedom Planet, so I didn't quite know what to expect going into it. It ended up being an uneven experience, but one that was overall enjoyable and clearly worth the (sale) price I paid for it. The separate soundtrack DLC is worth purchasing, as it's one of the strongest parts of the game.
Pros:
- Great environmental art. The stages are all quite different and consistently impressive in their creativity.
- Great soundtrack. There aren't any absolute classic tracks, but the OST taken as a whole is strong and worth owning.
- Generally clear level design. This isn't universally true, sadly, but it was usually clear where the game wanted me to go.
- Enemy design. There's a huge variety of enemies in the game, many of which only appear on one or two stages. Not all of them are incredibly original, but they're well drawn and explode satisfyingly.
-  Precise controls. I wish Lilac's hover-spin could be cancelled easily, but I otherwise never felt that the controls got in the way. I did not play as either Carol or Milla and can't say how they control, but I'd be surprised if it was significantly worse.
- Almost always perfect checkpoints. If you finish a frustrating section, you'll almost never have to play it again because you died. One particularly frustrating boss has multiple stages without intervening checkpoints, but that's the only notable flaw with the system.
- Unlimited continues. If you die - which will happen a lot if you're like me and have no experience with Sonic-likes - the game will never kick you out of the level unless you want it to. Continues are infinite and start you at the same checkpoint you'd get if you'd simply lost a life.
- All inter-stage scenes are skippable and mid-stage scenes do not repeat if you die after them. Every game should do this.
- Early bosses are well designed and fun. Unfortunately, I have to make the distinction with "early" bosses because...
Cons:
- Late bosses are infuriating. The checkpoint system is the game's saving grace here, but it can't alleviate the frustrating of high health, multi-stage bosses loaded with patterns that can only be consistently dodged through trial and error. More than half of my 118 deaths occured on just two of the games bosses, and ~70% occured on the last third of the bosses combined.
- Story is forgettable. There are some great silly moments interspersed throughout, but the plot is entirely unremarkable. These are all characters and situations you've seen before.
- Voice acting is inconsistent. A few characters are done well, but it's clear that this game didn't have a massive voice over budget. I skipped most of the voicing in the game.
In spite of the unbelievably frustrating end-game bosses, Freedom Planet is largely well done and worth playing. I liked much more about it than I disliked, and even if the ending frustrating proves too much for your patience, I think you can get your money's worth out of the more forgiving first 6-7 stages.
This game has amazing level design, fluid gameplay, and even better music. If you liked the classic Sonic games, you'll love this. If you didn't, this might actually make you appreciate the genre.

Sonic Generations is a platformer games of Sonic franchise and a main one at that, not spinoff. It was released in 2011 and is celebrating of the 20 years of Sonic series, still surviving, with lows and highs and crazy fans, swapping gameplay between 2D and 3D. It was released on modern consoles and PC. It sure was running on 30fps on consoles, so you know that you will want more or less modern computer to run this game. 3DS version was also released, it's more like a serapate game, not a port, so can go ahead and check that one out someday.
Technically, it's pretty nicely done. Well, if forget that it takes more system requirements than what most expect. And that you will need program that translates non-Xbox360 controllers into Xbox360 ones for the game so they will not glitch out. Preferably older version, that I found in the forums, by the way, with command promt window.
And then it often crashes when you are trying to do time attack, usually in the menu. Doesn't show your results properly either. But don't worry, if it crashed after you beat the level, it still will save result. Yay achievement hunting.
And as for last, here is a protip: There is a challenge mission where you use Espio for swinging on a hook. If you use controller then you should use D-pad in this mission, for some reason Sonic doesn't jump high enough with analog.
So, yes, it's a celebration title and it was put together with love and sane game design and it shows. Though some may agrue that it's kinda short and not really a main Sonic game.
And well, it does have only 9 levels. If forget that all nine of them come from 9 main Sonic games, being the most memoriable stages from them, so you know that they all are worth it and not just space-fillers. And then each level has two acts, so it makes 18 stages. And then you also can go and try to get S-Rank in each one of them, even if it's only requires you not to suck. And then there are 5 Red Rings hidden in each stage, making you explore stages, which also have few paths in them, in the best tradition of Sonic. And then you also got 7 bosses, each with hard mode. And then you also got 90 challenges, which are also quite unique at times, changing layouts of stages, including unique objects, like huge enemies, and some challenges even let you interact with Sonic's other friends! Like, using Tails to fly over the gap. And you also can try to get S-rank on them as well, they are fun too. And you also can unlock additional skills by doing some challenges and getting all red rings will let you get Skills that you can use on both Sonic to "personalize playstyle". Well, if forget that most of them feel more like small cheat.
So yes, this game is a rip-off, lacks content and is too short.
This is a sarcasm.
Anyway, aside this game has expected qualities of Sonic games that are awesome music, multi-pathed levels and quick action speed. But this is also a Sonic game that remembers that it's supposed to be a platformer, not just a bunch of speed sections where you don't need to ever jump. And then it got two Sonics, two different approaches to gameplay.
Classic Sonic stages are always 2D and he is quite simple to control, only being able to jump and spin dash. It's pure platformer and it also uses mechanic where after any kind of enemy hit the Sonic will jump a little higher. You can use it to reach bonus areas. As said, they knew that game is platformer, yep yep. Though, the physics are more on the level of 8-bit Sonic, yet surprisingly the old-school fans of Sonic didn't complain about physics like they did with Sonic 4. Whatever, level design matters more.
Then Modern Sonic is for those who want to pull out tricks and want more complex gameplay. And hopefully, "old-schoolers of all-new-hating" didn't call them horrible either. Hopefully. Anyway, it's a mix between 3D and 2D stages. Though I would have prefered staying them as always 3D. Sonic here knows quite a few tricks, like sliding or stomping the ground. He also has "boost", which I never digged in Sonic games. But oh well, Sega said it will be the last game with boosting. Gameplay is incredibly fun and it's satisfying to pull off some tricky shortcuts, none the less. It's a shame that Sonic may have too much abilities that are used only in some parts of games. Like, he can slide over a line of rings like in SA2, but only on special lines where control tutorial will show you a sign that you can press a button to do that. Or just having a serapate button for sliding, which is required very rarely.
And best part, as said, is that due to celebration nature of the games, it includes only best from the best, so to say. All stages are memoriable and fun. Especially Classic Rooftop Run. Like, wow, it has cheerful atmosphere of exotic celebration, awesome memoriable music and even adventure feel to it. It even made stage from Sonic 06 awesome. And even challenges are awesome. And you get to unlock concept art and music from previous Sonic games.
The only truly weak parts of the game got to be final boss. Let's just say that instead of fast action or such, it just feels like you are dragging and dragging on. And Sonic friends, like in few previous Sonic 3D titles, just will not shutup about obvious things. Which bothers some people. At least you can disable omochao in options in this game.
So yes, grab it for sure.

Please click read more to see full review of Missing Translation. I talk about lots of things from genre, game play, graphics, cons/let down, and more. If you also find this helpful or not leave a rating!
Overview:
Missing Translation is a pixel, puzzle, indie game, that’s free to play and over all is very good. It offers a good hour or two, depending on how good you are at solving puzzles. The game has a unique story, which I found to be interesting. The game play is simple and the puzzles are pretty simple, a little hard towards the end of them. The graphics fit well with the game, I couldn’t see it be anything other than pixels. Some other things included are steam achievements, 6 in total which are all possible to get in one play though. I personally was able to get all 6 and I can now add this game to my 100% completed list. Lastly, there’s no language needed to understand this game, it’s all symbols, so anyone can just download it and play.
Genre:
Missing Translation is a puzzle game that offers 3 different types of puzzle for you to complete. Each type has 25 puzzles you can complete, this totals to 75 puzzles to complete. The puzzles are pretty simple and start off easy at first, then they start to get harder and harder towards then end. I personally liked all 3 different types of puzzles and I was able to complete at 75 puzzles in one play though. The only downfall I could find to these puzzles is it’s a bit repetitive towards the end and they could off added some more. Also if you’re not good at puzzles or just don’t have the patience to take your time and solve them, you might find the last few to be a bit hard. But other than those couple reasons it’s a very good free to play puzzle game.
Graphics:
Missing Translation is a pixel and black and white game at its heart. The graphics work very well with the game and I couldn’t see the game using any other type of graphics. I love the graphics personally and I couldn’t find any flaws with it. Overall the pixels and the black and white theme really work well with the game and add to its charm.
Game play:
The game play for Missing Translation is really simple, first move around the area you’re in, then just come across doors that take you to puzzles. After that you complete the puzzles and move on to the next ones, very simple. As you do this, the story will revival intersecting plots in its self. I won’t talk about the story; due to it being simple and you should download the game and just see it for you. The controls are simple, just moving around and a activate key. Overall the game play is simple and works very well for this game.
Content:
Missing Translation offers about 1 to 2 hours of game play, depending on how good at puzzle games you are. There are 3 different types of puzzles, totaling up to 75 puzzles, for you to complete. There are also 6 steam achievements that you can get; these are all possible to get on your first play though.
Cons/Let Downs:

FTL: Faster Than Light is essentially a simulation of intergalatic space travel mixed with all of the threats present.  Being a rogue-like video game it's clear that you may or may not wind up with your ship scattered in a million debris particles, irritating runs, and many many failures that can shatter a budding astronaut's dream.
My kind of game!
FTL is centered around a very "complex yet simple when you get used to it" mechanic, or rather, mechanics.  The player is tasked with managing a top-down perspective of a spaceship and the crew operating everything down to the ship's high tech future weaponry or the vessel's door controls.  That seems dandy and fine but FTL is special in the spaceship department in that it requires you to keep track of every little bit and bolt if you want to make it out of this space journey alive.
(Or at the very least to the final boss before you die anyways)
For instance, if you're a total ignoramus and let the medical bay of your ship get taken out, do not be surprised if during a heavy firefight some poor shipmate happens to be blasted to smithereens.  Same with your engines.  Letting an engine die on you prevents you from dodging enemy fire which can result in some poor soul shipmate being blasted to smithereens.
Basically keep good care of your ship if you want it to be smithereen-free.
The game, despite being centered around a rogue-like gameplay element stressing the fundamentals of managing your ship, is also actually rather text heavy for its kind.  A majority of the events in this game are captioned by boxes of text that detail the problems your ship and crew face.  Unlike other rogue-likes which generally throw you into action expecting you to get through with your wits and reactions, this game focuses on your strategy and your ability to not let your ship explode.
The fun in FTL is essentially making the game as stressful as possible for the player.  Subset Games did a wonderful job throwing in as many terrifyingly painful ways for your ship's crew to die on their way through sectors.  Whether it be bandits, solar flares, alien spiders, you name it, they will create a stir and a problem which your decision making self is responsible for keeping on the down low.
It is up to the player to keep track of and manage everything.  It's a strategic game suitable for space tacticians, rogue-like video game enthusaists, but not for those who dislike multitasking.

You know its a special kind of game that is amazing in a lot of areas yet... can be amazingly frustrating at times. Mainly due to these massive through the roof difficulty spikes that seem to come out of nowhere.
Pros:
+Amazing soundtrack
+Graphics, though retro, are still great with only a few glitches when moving at high speed
+its apparently like a new, better sonic?
+gameplay is almost flawless, with the exception of some enemies that can be a bit annoying at times, even they can't blemish its feel
+feels amazing to zoom through the map when you do everything right
+loads of gameplay options, from its selection of characters, to time attack, to the wide difficulty options (normal gave me challenge in the right places when it didn't feel like I was throwing lives away to climb the difficulty spikes)
+moments where I was actually astonished at the game and outraged at the main villain.
+I can easily see speedrunning this game would be fun as hell, even though its not for me as every level has multiple paths to take through it, with secrets and shortcuts everywhere
Cons:
- I feel like the camera is too zoomed in at times, kind of makes me feel like I'm running blind
- those massive steel wall road blocking difficulty spikes that just suddenly hit you. I'm glad the dev is fixing some of these in the next patch, which means this point could be dealt with
- maybe a bit on the short side if you only intend to play it through once, with my run clocking in at 7 hours.
- some combat issues, varying from getting mini-stuns when you're hit, meaning rapid fire attacks can chunk you for your full HP if you get hit once, to issues with "safe" areas against certain attacks
-running boss fight controls feel awkward as hell, as you dont go left to right, you slow down and speed up. The distinction being slowing down goes fast, while you take a long time to speed back up (even freeze in place on screen)
A lot of these cons are really just niggling irritations I experienced, they really aren't that big of a deal but to people that get frustrated at BS you might experience frustration here.
Regardless, I liked the game. It takes a lot to leave a bad taste in my mouth yet still be savoury enough to continue eating anyways. Highly recommend if you intend on playing through more than once, which is certainly doable with multiple characters that all behave and play differently! I think even the levels play out differently depending on who you are playing, so theres that. I do see myself having a second go through with this game, which is a rarity considering all the games I still want to play at the moment. So yes, buy it

Final Fantasy IX is one of my favorite games of all time. So this review may be biased.
First of all, should a person who likes Final Fantasy or Role Playing Games in general buy this game? The answer is yes! As other reviews have stated this game has charm oozing from it.
The story, in my opinion is wonderful and heartfelt. The setting is a living fairy tale world with just enough steampunk to keep it entertaining. The characters are wonderful.
Enough about the old stuff. What about the new? The new character models are excellent. The ability to speed up battles is also great. Turning off random encounters, while not something I would usually do, is becoming tempting because of the encounter rate in certain areas. There is a lot of good. I have especially enjoyed the sharper graphics and enhanced cutscenes. I am seeing details that I didn't know were in them, and I have played this game countless times through. This is the best version of Final Fantasy IX.
So...what do I wish was better? The backgrounds and some of the NPCs could have been touched up a little. I know that replacing backgrounds would have required phenomenal effort, but I know there are some high quality backgrounds floating around the internet. Perhaps a future update could gradually improve the visuals that way. Honestly, it's not a deal breaker. This is the best version of the game.
In closing, if you are at all a fan of the JRPG genre, this game is for you. A great story, great side quests, and a lot of depth. Enjoy!

HOLY CRAP THIS GAME IS GOOD
Okay, imagine you're back in the glory days of 2D platforming, and Sonic was far in the lead. Let's say Sonic CD just came out and you love it... It's different than the other older sonic games and it's still really good dispite being different. Fast forward a bit to when the Sega saturn came out. Where are the good games? Where are the memorable platformers with great music, and excellent 32bit pixel graphics?
Turns out, they're to be found in 2015. Freedom Planet feels like a long lost Sega Saturn game with crisp CD quality audio and pushing future graphics on new hardware.
So much of this game FEELS like a traditional Sonic platformer, but it IS NOT a clone, or a shoddy fan game. And I like it that way.
Simply put, if you love fast paced 2D platformers with a lot to offer, just click the buy button now.

I love this game from the bottom of my heart. It brings back the feeling of amazement I once had playing Sonic the first first. I still remember sitting down with my first Sega game and listening to the crisp music, abosrbing those vibrant colors and beautifully designed levels. Moving so fast you got a true sense of motion Sonic really launched you into a whole new world that Mario never really touched upon. Freedom Planet has this same sense of wonder for me, the graphics are beautiful the controls perfect and the music and sound a delight for the ears. It is as if an A + developer made a new game for the Sega after all these years and put all their talent and heart into the creation. I cannot recommend this game enough, if you have any fond memories of Sega games or old pixel games in general you will not be disappointed.
That being said ths is NOT Sonic, your character cannot jump on the heads of the enemies instead you have to attack them with a button press, in a way it combines the fast pace platforming of Sonic with the perfectly timed attacks of Ninja Gaiden. Your charactrs have a large number of moves to help you get around and find hidden locations and they're so adorable! Stop reading this and buy the freaking game already!

I wasn't expecting much from Papo & Yo but ws very pleasantly surprised.
Papo & Yo tells a very sad (and very real) story through a compelling narrative and clever gameplay. While it may seem to be a game for children, it's mature subject matter means some parental guidance would be advisable before letting them play.
While the story may not be for kids, the visuals, audio and gameplay certainly are. The environments are more less variations of the same favela theme but some certainly do stick out as particularly pretty. The audio is great and befits the environment. The soundtrack especially is outstanding; a beautiful selection of Latin American instrumentals.
The gameplay is a mixed bag. The puzzles while simple are fun to solve thanks to some unique mechanics and smart level design. The only gripe I have is with the lack of an auto follow camera forcing the player to control the camera manually all the time. The game is short but fulfilling nonetheless.
Papo & Yo is a fantastic little game masking a touching story of some real world issues. It is well worth a play through, if only to experience the story, mechanics and level design.

Pretty much the best citybuilder and one of my most played games of all time. I own a physical copy of it, and I recently picked up this Steam copy... definitely one of my favorite games ever.
You need to mod the game in order to make it playable, and the game tends to crash, lock up, and run slowly. There's no autosave and you'll probably lose a lot of hours of gameplay. Loading a custom region is cumbersome, installing mods is archaic, and the whole thing is just clunky. Using some mods will require literal hours of patience... ask me about custom highways or building a mass transit network. Piece by piece, slowly, surely, but satisfyingly.
Beneath all the clunk is a diamond, the absolute best city builder of all time. Every game that comes out can't seem to match a well-modded Simcity 4. You can install a massive amount of options for mass transit and building variety. It's intoxicating, if you're into it.
If you just want to build a pretty city, you're going to need to work slowly and learn how to do it. This game honestly isn't friendly or accessible for new people... But if you work at it, and you enjoy the genre, you're going to love it.

Half Life 2: DownFall is a community-made mod set in the white forest seen in Half Life 2: Episode 2. The player, as Gordon Freeman, aims to find the Citadel Buster before the Combine do.
It isn't the longest mod ever made. I took eighty minutes in my playthrough, but only because I was slow and wanted to check every single area. For someone not so slow, it might take more like 40 minutes to an hour. The length isn't a detriment, however, as the developer intends to expand upon it on a later date.
The level design is well polished, and the NPCs make you have to go to some difficulty to advance to the next area, though it still isn't hard enough in my opinion. At least not on normal mode, which I played on. Don't expect any great story to the mod either. The story is only really explained to you on the store page, and not in the mod itself. Still, the difficulty of coming up with a comprehensive story, implementing it into a small timeframe and doing the voice acting for the characters substantiates the minimalist story. Perhaps my only severe complaint is the difficulty finding the path to the next area, though the actual game suffered from this at times too, so it may just be intrinsic to Half Life 2.
I didn't come across any bugs or exploits in my playthrough, with the exception of one where I hid in a toilet stall and couldn't leave because zombies swarmed around me and prevented the door from opening. Such a bug though was more to my amusement than annoyance.
Overall, DownFall is well implemented, and I'm curious to see what future expansions will bring. It deserves a 7.5/10 in my book.

FTL: Faster Than Light is essentially a simulation of intergalatic space travel mixed with all of the threats present.  Being a rogue-like video game it's clear that you may or may not wind up with your ship scattered in a million debris particles, irritating runs, and many many failures that can shatter a budding astronaut's dream.
My kind of game!
FTL is centered around a very "complex yet simple when you get used to it" mechanic, or rather, mechanics.  The player is tasked with managing a top-down perspective of a spaceship and the crew operating everything down to the ship's high tech future weaponry or the vessel's door controls.  That seems dandy and fine but FTL is special in the spaceship department in that it requires you to keep track of every little bit and bolt if you want to make it out of this space journey alive.
(Or at the very least to the final boss before you die anyways)
For instance, if you're a total ignoramus and let the medical bay of your ship get taken out, do not be surprised if during a heavy firefight some poor shipmate happens to be blasted to smithereens.  Same with your engines.  Letting an engine die on you prevents you from dodging enemy fire which can result in some poor soul shipmate being blasted to smithereens.
Basically keep good care of your ship if you want it to be smithereen-free.
The game, despite being centered around a rogue-like gameplay element stressing the fundamentals of managing your ship, is also actually rather text heavy for its kind.  A majority of the events in this game are captioned by boxes of text that detail the problems your ship and crew face.  Unlike other rogue-likes which generally throw you into action expecting you to get through with your wits and reactions, this game focuses on your strategy and your ability to not let your ship explode.
The fun in FTL is essentially making the game as stressful as possible for the player.  Subset Games did a wonderful job throwing in as many terrifyingly painful ways for your ship's crew to die on their way through sectors.  Whether it be bandits, solar flares, alien spiders, you name it, they will create a stir and a problem which your decision making self is responsible for keeping on the down low.
It is up to the player to keep track of and manage everything.  It's a strategic game suitable for space tacticians, rogue-like video game enthusaists, but not for those who dislike multitasking.

This is probably the best 3D Sonic game to have come out. The retro takes on newer games created some really great levels. Modern Sonic has also never controlled better. The music is fantastic, the visuals are pretty, the level design is amazing, the boss fights are cool. I won't lie, there are a few small missteps here, such as some of the challenges involving sidekick characters controlling poorly and its weird that 4 of the 9 locations in the game are city-themed, but even these don't really spoil what otherwise is, surprisingly, an incredible Sonic game.

Sonic Generations takes what we loved about Modern Sonic gameplay and what we loved about Classic Sonic gameplay and sort of meshes them into this anniversary title. Throughout the game, you'll be traversing through classic and modern zones reimagined. Classic Sonic is strictly 2D while Modern Sonic is Boost like what we saw in Unleashed and Colors. The controls for the most part are responsive although the occasional unresponsiveness can happen. The graphics are simply great and take you back to the days of yesteryear and today. There is a gallery where you can view various pieces of concept art, listen to music, or watch cutscenes. The game does seem to have missed potential as they could've done much more with this idea but Sonic Generations should not be passed by if you're a Sonic fan.

Mafia II is a great game with a great atmosphere, nice cars, good songs, the missions are realistic and the story is pretty good. I really liked the graphics of this game, especially the effects during winter period, like snow, cars getting dirty and other cool stuff. The only major problem with Mafia II is the lack of side missions to encourage free roaming, I mean the studio put a lot of work in designing this game but the missions don't actually allow you to explore everything the map has to offer and the posters aren't quite interesting enough to collect when you already have playboy magazines to worry about.
They could have made side missions without cutscenes, I mean there are a lot of characters in the game that tell you to come and see them later for missions but this actually never happens and you feel stupid after you went several times to someone to ask for a mission. They could have put more effort into this, they already have GTA as a great example of the amount and diversity of missions, so no excuse.
Apart from the lack of side missions another issue is the AI, in my opionion it's way to easy even on max difficulty. I never had to struggle killing enemies and rarely died during missions (except during some chases where you have no possibility to shoot back and you can only hope that your idiot AI partner will kill them before they kill you, which never happens, so you have to drive really well).
A third problem with Mafia is the lack of diversity in general: diversity in clothing (just a few clothing models with different colour options - this is unacceptable when they already created multiple outfits for the people walking on the streets), diversity in house options (you are basically poor the entire game and even when you get a decent house, you'll keep it for 2 missions until♥♥♥♥♥♥happens), diversity in activities (actually there is zero diversity because there are zero activities, even though the options were limitless - pool, chess, betting etc.).
Even with all this problems, I cannot give a bad score for Mafia II, because the positive aspects are great, good story, nice characters, amazing atmosphere and the fact that I really love the time period, I just wish they would have done it better and hope they'll improve the next title. It's worth buying but don't expect for hundreds of hours of fun, because it's actually very short without the DLC's.

Now, this is a Mafia game. Mafia II follows the story of Vito Scaletta, who has started making a name for himself on the streets of Empire Bay. As someone who can be trusted to get a job done, he and his buddy, Joe, become members of the Mafia family and rapidly climb the ladder of status.
The gameplay of Mafia II is truly "Action-packed", However... The gunplay seems quite repetitive and extremely easy. After completing the game on Hard difficulty with ease, it came to me that the gunplay seems very scripted. Hide behind a piece of cover, lean over, shoot, get back down, repeat. Hand-to-hand combat is fun: when in hand-to-hand combat, the camera locks on to the enemy and it truly feels like a one-versus-one fight. Everything around becomes irrelevant as you try and knock the guy out. The finishing moves seem a bit 'dry'; it would be nice to have some more enviromental KO's rather than just punching them to finish the fight.
Driving in this game is something different. Different meaning amazing. It gives a sense of realism as you will actually slip and slide on ice and rain. You cannot speed, or do a hit-and-run or you will be chased by police. On top of that, you can actually get a ticket for speeding, instead of just being shot like other games.
The story is intriguing and leads you on an adventure with Vito and Joe. Somehow, it manages to convince you that Vito and Joe are the good guys, but they are the Mafia. That's how good the writing is. On top of this, there is a good amount of humour mainly from Joe.
I can't stress how much this game is worth it. If you find it on sale, it's a no-brainer.

This game recieved 877.5% of its funding goal on Kickstarter almost 2 years ago now. Making just short of 3/4 of a million dollars, you would think that the game has improved slightly from the beta build that came out almost a year and a half ago, right? No. I come back the this game every couple of months or so to see if it has improved, and almost nothing has. I am fine with bugs and glitches and even total save rollbacks, but this game is literally unplayable. The AI of the bricktrons is atrocious, the gameplay still feels like a prototype, and almost no new content has been added. This is one of a few games that I have run across recently that has fallen into the trap of having too big of boots to fill, and has consequently caused me to become a very staunch opponent of Kickstarters and even Steam Greenlight.
Getting $702,000 on a game that the dev's probably just wanted to make in their spare time causes an enormous amount of pressure to make the game more grandiose than it needs to be. The devs apparently scrapped the entire engine after the kickstarter because of the amount of money they generated. Instead of taking their time working on the game, Sauropod Studio now had to send posters, soundtracks, plush toys, and all sorts of other things to thousands of donators of the kickstarter.
So why do I keep coming back to this game every few months even after 2 years? Simply put, I still have a lot of hope for it and would like to see it blossom. I have nothing against early access games and I have never asked for a refund. I support small early access developers 100% so long as they continue their work and stay in touch with their backers. Sauropod Studio  is still very much in contact with us and still continues to make regular updates on their progress. Im torn as to whether or not to recommend this game and I have come to the conclusion that I simply cannot recommend a broken game. When the time comes that I can play more than an hour of this game without having to restart because the bricktrons refuse to move or the interface refuses to function, only then will I recommend this game to buy.

Congratz, Sauropod Studio, It's been 2 years since you released the game to the public and It's still in Early Access. Really, I accomodate you and your hard work for this terribly optimized, bugged game. It seems improvement has obviously been made. (Obvious Sarcasm)

I have 400 hours aprx. I've been with this game for 2 years through thick or thin. This is part review, part history.
tl:dr   This isn't what it used to be. The playerpase is small, but its very tight knit. It's the kind of community where everyone know's everyone by name. The gameplay itself is wonky but often fun when you get it right. The learning curve is a brick wall. You're going to lose a lot when you start. Don't be afraid to ask for help. Almost everyone in master rank would be more than pleased to take you udner their wing, all you have to do is ask.
Don't expect this to be a hardcore fighter with lots of fierce competition. Thats what Blade Symphony used to be. Today theres an average of 10 different people who log on per day. I can say for sure that I'm one of those 10. This game is what most would be concidered dead. To the newcomer this game will seem like theres nothing here for you. I'm here to tell you you're wrong. You're simply unable to see it for what it is.
Where this game excells is in the high level community. The issue is the skill gap between those dubbed "newgen" and those from the old gen and alpha gen. The majority of regular players have played for years. I have played for 2 years, and over a year of that was solely training the class I use. Many people who have played less have attained my skill level and beyond, but it still takes a conciderable amount of time. On top of that this game is impossible to play without a lot of resiliance. Put short, you will lose. You will lose often if not constantly. However thats how you learn. If you can take a loss without suffering the weight of defeat then you'll make it far in this game. The people who sit atop the skill ladder are there not because they have inate tallent, but because they simply kept trying. And you too can join them, all you have to do is not quit. Keep at it. Learn from your mistakes. Reach out to masters for help. Reach out to me for help. I'll tech you how to play if you really want to become better (disclaimer: I'm a bad teacher).
My final reason Blade is good is the community. Some parts of it are toxic, some are sweet. Overall it's tight knit and diverse. If you play more than a week you'll recognise everyody. 3 weeks and you'll know everybody. In no other game have I seen this many freindships form and hold over time. I have my mixed feeling with the people I play this game with but the one thing I can say about the people of Blade Symphony is that thay're the only people here I really trust. We're not here to beat you back to cs:go. We're here to be your freind and have some fun. Thats what this game is about. Its about having a good duel and not climbing the ladder.
If you're hesitant about this game pm me, and I can talk to you about it and why you should play.

The best RPG I have ever played, and that's a feat, with my other favorites including Mother 3, Earthbound, Bowser's Inside Story, Thousand Year Door, etc.
The story, the characters, the throatpunching decisions are all executed wonderfully as the game batters you through it, and LISA: The Joyful wraps everything up very well.
My highest recommendations.

I gotta say I was intially on the fence with this game despite playing games very similar to it like the MOTHER series, OFF, and arguably Undertale. When I first saw this game, I thought it was just going to be a generic edgy RPG where you breeze through the combat and after going through the story, you'd just stop thinking about it. How wrong I was about that.
LISA takes place in a post-apocalyptic world called Olathe after an event known as the White Flash occurs. After looking a bit into the past of the main character, Brad, we eventually end up in the present where his daughter named Buddy was stolen from home and now it's up to him and whoever he comes across willing (or unwillingly) to help on his journey to save his child. Things aren't all they seem however, as the reason that Buddy was stolen from home was not out of petty ransom or revenge, but rather she was kidnapped because she is actually the last known woman alive in the world of LISA. Brad is trying to get his daughter back from the people who took her because he wants to keep her safe and the people that took her want to use her for the future of the world and I just love how much these points of view clash with each other during the course of the game. It makes me feel like these characters have actual motives for what they do and I just want to learn more about them.
They don't dissapoint in the character department either. You get to witness Brad who started out with hope about seeing his daughter again become this absolute monster that doesn't have any qualms about killing the friends that he's known for years just to save his one chance for happiness and it's disturbing to say the least. The companions are diverse and interesting and while they mostly don't get much of their own dialogue after being recruited, their designs and attacks in battle allow you to imagine how these characters might act in this world. In terms of enemies, you have your standard evil gangs, junkies, and these people that have changed into these grotesque creatures known as Joy Mutants that have these very elongated and creepy designs to them. You will also encounter people from Brads past who want nothing more than to either make him suffer or want to use Buddy for their own needs and they are definitely a pleasure (or not) to deal with when you encounter them.
For a game made in RPG Maker, the combat is suprisingly deep. You have your standard high damage attacks of course, but this game has many different status conditions that you can take advantage of. Do you try to weaken your enemies over time with stuff like poison, burning, and bleeding? Do you prefer trying to keep your enemies locked down by tripping, stunning, or scaring them? How about just debuffing the enemies stats with statuses like crying, blindness, or just making them feel weird? Because you can take three different companions of your choice alongside Brad, you have a ton of options for diversifying your teams and trying to go through the game with a different party on a new playthrough can lead to many fun times.
Would I recommend this game to you? Yes absolutely, as long as you aren't offended by the dark themes you'll end up encountering through out the experience. This game was an absolute gem to play and there wasn't a single moment where I regretted playing it. If you're looking for an RPG that has plenty of depth and story, then you should go ahead and give this game a shot, it is a "joy" that'll leave you craving more.

By itself, I think the choices would have been enough, but some enemy attacks permanently kill your party members.  This is balanced by having a roster of 20 or 30 party members.  As a result it causes your party to seem expendable, and I started to look for my favorite type of character instead of being attached to individual ones.
I found the setting to be far more interesting than the characters they didn't bother to give more than a few lines to.  It's a shame, because the world is incredibly unique and it feels like it's window dressing.

So I was a bit of a fool and tried to play this game and Night in the Woods one after the other. But this game is almost as much of an emotional ride as the other. I wasn't exactly prepared for the emotions this game brought up.
This game is great though, every character is designed so well. The soundtrack for most of the game, as well as the settings, the characters, the battles, and the dialogue, it's all silly. But behind all the funny or strange things happening, there is a really dark story. It's not even hidden, just as the game progresses, the silly front begins to fade. The game is also well balanced as far as challenge, it's not too easy, it's not impossibly hard, and getting lost for a long time is rare.
The beginning and the end are dark but everything in between is dark humor.

Lisa is a blasphemously magical side-scrolling RPG brought to us by Dingaling. You play as Brad. A broken old balding junkie in midlife crisis.
As you get to know, Brad has had a genuinely rough childhood, coming home in a beat to sh*t state right into his drunkard father's hands. Then, something uncanny happens, and here comes the postapocalyptic women-less world. Coincidence?
Out of nowhere, Brad finds a baby.

So the promising story begins. Brad, the broken old balding junkie in midlife crisis, raises the only girl in the world.
Terry Hintz aka The Lord of the Tutorial aka ´that guy with a huge fanclub' appears, offering you his skills, which are legit out of this world. The girl is taken hostage, and guess what. Brad has to find her no matter what.
The dialogues, which are beautifully crafted, I find the dearest. They abound immeasurable number of darkly humorous passages, which I've hardly ever seen in such concentration. You get to play a game, which has been made via RPG Maker - truly a sympathic choice, I adore it.
Mentioning the soundtrack, I love it, that's my jam right there. I mean, the developer had to choose such tunes to underlay the game's impact, and it worked.
So, I did mention the graphics, the friendly vibe I get from playing it, and now it's about time to get myself over to the story, which I have kind of summarized in the first paragraph.
It's easy to proceed, the story as a whole is no big deal to follow. Meeting a new character equals more unanticipated fun & joy. But, what I do recommend, is playing the game regularly until the very end. Do not make the same mistake I did; going for a hiatus.
The maps (or areas)  are to a certain degree complex - numerous entrances leading to yet another maps. Taking a break means you may forget which way to go, where was the latest save point, and that gets you easily frustrated.
That said, every aspect is worthy and there is a sincere place in my heart for this game.

While the first impression is that this is a child game, this game is actually as fun as Plant vs Zombies.
It isn't tower defense style, it is more of a timing management game (ie. store management, flight controller, etc), you have to keep an eye on your customer queue and your "factory" (tree) and make sure your products (fruit) will be available on time, or at least so that you don't lose too much money if you fail.
The game is easy at the beginning and if you rush starts getting hard after world 3, you are allowed to grind for upgrades on the previous levels, although with diminishing returns. You are also given a lot of bonus items to make your life easier on the later levels, or whenever you want extra help. The UI is excellent because it doesn't force you to give each command on time, you can queue comands and just watch the level unfold (and this has its own mechanic as you can't cancel them, so you may screw yourself up if some future event doesn't unfold as expected).
You play as a diabolical Herbomancer vying for total medow dommination. Enslave the feeble fruit trees and sell their children to the pathetic inhabitants of the village.

TL;DR: Game good, buy if you like Star Wars.
This game is beyond words. Such a simple game means so much to so many people. This is a big chunk of what got me into gaming, and if I could see my statistics of every platform I played this on combined, I'd most likely have somewhere near 1000 hours.
But how is the game?
Well for starters, there's the campaign, which isn't canon anymore if you care about that. It's a good story that can keep you engaged for the duration of it, but personally there are some levels that I never cared for (Naboo).
The Galactic Conquest mode is simple, but very fun. It makes me want an updated game with more complex management of your fleets, units, and upgrades. Think the Galactic Conquest from Empire at War, but the battles play like Battlefront 2.
Instant Action is where most of your time with this game will probably go. I know it's what I've played the most. Choose a map, choose a game mode, hit play. Simple and fun.
As for multiplayer, I haven't gotten to play much of it aside from a couple of private matches with friends. While I can say (at least from my experience, could just be my bad internet) the revamped multiplayer runs better than the old method of using third party programs to connect, I found there to still be a few latency issues. (But again, could just be my end.)
Lastly, I'll go over the gameplay. The movement and shooting mechanics are awesome for the time, although I've found that every now and then, you'll think you're shooting somewhere, but in reality you're hitting the wall you're using for cover.
The classes feel diverse and unique, with 4 universal classes (trooper, heavy/shock, sniper, and engineer) and two unique units per faction. Additionally, two classes for space combat, with 4 classes of ships. Each class, with the exception of the unique units, has unlocks you can get by playing the game and honing your skills with that class. The unlock lasts until you die, then you have to earn it back. This goes on for some time, and each unlock has reduced requirements to earn it  the more you get it, until eventually you can perminatly unlock it. This truly gives the player a sense of pride and accomplishment.
I would absolutely recommend Battlefront 2 (this one anyway) to anyone who is a Star Wars fan. Even for someone who isn't a fan, this could be a great tool to get them into the original and prequel trilogies.
Side note: This game has an amazing modding scene, with space to ground maps and even sequel trilogy mods being made, and much, much more.

I'm an experienced operator so I already know about heavy equipment. So I will make my comparison based on that.
For the most part, the stick controls are correct. It does feel like a real excavator. So all my skills and nuances translated perfectly into this simulation, albeit a few changes. The controls for the tracks, however, don't feel right because of the right shoulder used as a modifier. It just feels weird pressing that then the sticks.
The digging aspect seems nominal at most. You don't see every grain of sand going into the bucket due to game engine limitations so its mostly graphically and mathematically simplified. What it doesn't do is (1) sloping, (2) bucket grading, and (3) platforming.
Sloping is important because you need to have certain trenches at a certain angle of repose; an angular ratio between its verticality and its horizontalness. Most common sands are good with 1:1 ratios, wetter stuff could be like 3:2 and it matters greatly because of the chances of a trench collapse. The game doesn't do sloping very well, nor does the sand contour with the bucket at all, so you are left with pregenerated, precalculated sloping angles that it thinks sand can do.
The bucket can't grade those slopes either. All the bucket does, on its back side, is bump into the sand (even with just a tiny windrow) or bounce off it. Even the bulldozer got stuck on a simple windrow. Not very realistic... which is fine, but I prefer the ability to manipulate sand to my needs.
Platforms are one such need. Most times, ground isn't always level. In gravel pits, you dig and dig and dig until all the sand around the machine is gone. And each time you grab a full bucket, you already chancing to tip over unless you have a stable foundation to dig from. Even then, depending on your counter weight, you might tip if you grab wet stuff when fully extended and perpendicular to the tracks.
Sometimes you gotta fix your foundation or slope yourself up it before grabbing. And when you're done, you gotta get off the foundation (which is probably a platform by then) which is no safe feat. Sometimes you gotta make a platform to get up on to grab the fill. The game doesn't let you spear into the sand to pull the machine, nor does it let you push the machine up or down the hill. Nor does the angle of the machine's tilt matters, you dig without worry of tipping.
The camera controls are wonky and it's weird operating from third person. I don't know whose idea it was to have the horizontal controls of the camera to spring. That was just an idiotic design decision. You need the camera to follow the bucket or look where you need to without these interferences.
The other machines (loader, truck, and dozer), kind of follow the flaws of the excavator too. The dozer can seriously do without the right shoulder modifier being pressed. I also noticed that there's no vertical tilt or horizontal angling on the blade. It's just a raise and lower dozer blade. (Might be a feature exclusive to D4 Cat dozers though). This makes the final grade an annoying task not because of the top level, but the sloping can't be done very well or at all.
And as I said previously, it stops dead on a simple windrow. In the real world, even a small D4 bulldozer can cut through gravel like its butter. Here, the game doesn't do that.
No real comments about the front end loader or the truck. Ultimately, I think the game is only fine as a simplistic digger only game. It does not have the additional nuances I wished it did have. I recommend it only as a taste of heavy equipment but nothing more serious than that.

If there is anything that really defines LISA, it would have to be how damn refreshing this game is.
At its core, LISA is not a terribly unique four person party RPG that has you trekking across a large span of ground to meet an end goal, not particularly fresh.  But where this game shines is in its writing and its design.  The world of LISA is funny, frightening, and cruel, all at once.  It's unbelievably interesting exploring this world because there truly are no limits to how zany or dangerous the next area can be.  I found myself loving characters one minute and hating them another, many NPCS are much deeper than they first appear.  But what truly makes this game stand out is how it is not afraid to absolutely♥♥♥♥♥♥on your day.  Party members you've had for hours can be killed in battle, every campfire rested at provides high chances of terrible things occuring during the night, and surprise attacks at your weakest is the norm.  And I couldn't praise this game without mentioning the FANTASTIC soundtrack that accompanies you on your travels.  Even if you're not considering purchasing the game, the soundtrack is very much worth a listen.
HOWEVER...
This game is not for the faint of heart in any sense.  You will be challenged to make some of the hardest choices I've seen in gaming.  There is never a third "Make everything better" option.  There will be loss, and it will be permanent.
During the first few minutes of gameplay, you are offered to choose between either "Painful" or normal mode.  I would recommend normal mode to anyone that doesn't take loss easily, as painful mode essentially prevents any form of save scumming, but at the same time, Painful mode fits the motif of the game much better.  If you think you can handle it, Painful is the way to play.
AS A NOTE:
You may as well purchase the DLC now, it picks up right where the main storyline leaves and wraps up alot of questions you'll likely be left with and puts a refreshing spin on the gameplay.  Main game runs ~20hrs and the DLC ~4hrs.

Papo & Yo is an emotional experience about a young boys escape from the reality of his abusive drunk father via the power of imagination, told in the characters actions with the surrounding environment and Monster, the allegoral representation of his father. The story is not told with text, nor with spoken audio. It unfolds differently for each player, as you must imagine what you will as the visuals and character interactions further the narration of the story. While Papo & Yo is short in length, it delivers in excellence a touching, beautiful, and heartrending experience. Visuals are top knotch, audio is clear, and mechanics are stable and concise. While not a AAA experience, Papo & Yo far exceeds expectations both in format and design, and is an incredibly underrated title. This tear inducing social commentary in artistic form is a must have, and is well worth it's current asking price.

"Final Fantasy IX" is definitely my favorite in the series, and one of my favorite games of all-time for that matter. So upon hearing that this game would ported to PC, I got super excited. This is a game that I feel (or rather now felt) didn't get the recognition it deserved. Admittedly, I did get a little worried, considering that the ports of FFV,FFVI, and even FFVIII weren't well-received by fans (not including the graphic and music mods inputted in those games).
So after playing at least 7 hours of this port, I would have to say, YES!! THEY DIDN'T SCREW IT UP!! NO CRAPPY RESOLUTIONS, NO MIDI MUSIC, NO LAGGING!!
*ahem* Anyways, I was pleasantly surprised that this port was not only great, but also a decent contender of the most definitive version of the game, giving the original PS1 version a run for its money. The graphics are updated and more crisped, the FMVs (cinematic cutscenes) have gotten an extremely HD boost and looks absolutely spectacular, the music is the same as it should be, the mouse support really helps in some parts, and the battle system is more helpful,giving you the option to change and defend in on menu (though that's kind of a small thing).
The only nitpicks I have with this version is that one: the battle swirl is a little less fluent than in the PS1 version, two:  it's kind of a hassle to exit to game, having to go to the menu to exit it instead of doing so pressing ESC, and three: I kinda don't like that this game is not fully controller compatible. When I use my PS4 controller to play the game, Zidane walks either to the left or right. But again, like I said, they're nitpicks. A keyboard works fine as well.
Overall, SE managed to not screw up this port of the game. I say if you want to go on an nostalgic trip, or if you want to play this game for the first time, buy this port! :)

Blade Symphony is a sword-fighting simulator where players fight 1v1 or more with balanced controls on a handful of maps.
Now for it's Pros:
1) It runs really good for such great cinematic graphics.
2) Great arsenal of different swords to try.
3) EVERYONE, and I mean EVERYONE can have their unique sword style thanks to the excessive ways to attack your enemy.
4) Semi-skillbased. (I'll get to this in one moment in Cons).
5) Despite being semi-complex, tutorial clears all hardships in knowing the game.
6) Has AI offline training.
7) Your sword fighter can be customized real good with colors and plenty of armors. (Thanks to Workshop).
Now for the cons:
1) Swords aren't completely balanced, thus there is a slight meta. (That can still be overpowered by skill).
2) By the time I was playing this, servers were completely empty so I didn't have some online fun.
3) Camera problems, wish if devs would add FP mode.
TL;DR If you like competitive sword simulative fights then get this game, although for fair warning you'll be upset by no online mode and meta of several weapons over each other.
I thought it was great, but didn't really have the patience to master it, so that's on me.
