Pros:
-Excellent soundtrack
-While being a "Sonic game" at heart, it has many innovations to lift itself above boring traditional map-memorizing Sonic gameplay
-Better-than-expected voice acting (YMMV. I'd much rather an actor make a decent attempt at sounding passionate and concerned than just having characters sound like they're aware they're in a video game). Lord Brevon's voice actor is just solidly VERY good as a villain.
-Highly epic and challenging boss fights
-Character variance with a lot of favoritism. I can't really imagine not playing as Lilac, the protagonist, but other people really liked the other characters and even found certain bosses easier.
Cons:
-Difficulty is fine, but I felt like a few boss fights felt unfairly difficult. Not particularly in execution, but in being not particularly clear in time what you would need to do to avoid a certain attack. Once you know the patterns, the challenge is managable, but it can take a lot of tries to learn those patterns.
-Kinda pointless infinite lives/continues system that leaves you right back at the same checkpoint
-"Cyclone!"
Other thoughts:
-The game has a storyline, and some long cutscenes. I enjoyed it, I know many people didn't and grew tired of the dialogue. I'm an Ace Attorney fan, so I don't mind some character development and something to give the levels agency.
-Very difficult. The game has difficulty levels, which I think primarily change the amount of damage enemies do. I would LOVE to see AGDQ/SGDQ speedrun this, if it's not one of those Sonic 1-esque wall-hacking glitchfests.
PS: There is mention of a "Turbocharged" edition I don't think I played. My best guess is that they rewrote the game outside of the very cheap engine they had it in beforehand. If so, that just doubles the fun!

Ico-esque adventure game where your companion is [very explicitly] a big, hulking metaphor for the game creator's abusive, alcoholic father. Subtle this game was not ... but it *was* unique, and in the end it did have a real effect on me. I'm very glad to have played it, but it's heavy enough that I'm unlikely to play through it again.
Strengths: Really striking and original visuals / artistic direction, superb music, refreshing protagonist [the opposite of the powerfulwhitemale we so often see in games]. Short length, ~3.5 hours [a big plus given my schedule].
Weaknesses: The gameplay itself is a bit repetitive [though the constant introduction of new visuals and mechanics does liven things up]. The puzzles are trivial [this is an adventure game, not a puzzle game]. Some minor control+camera wonkiness. Complete lack of subtlety in hitting you with the game's central metaphor [this game's creator is making a very personal, cathartic game.]

Well,there barely is any and what's left of it can be ignored but if you play a Sonic Game for the story then I have some bad news for you.
Basically,Sonic friends are kidnapped and you have to free them by beating the level.You will go back to levels and settings of previous Sonic games like GreenHill Zone (Sonic the Hedgehog; what a surprise), Rooftop Run (Sonic Unleashed), or Speed Highway (Sonic Adventure). Dr.Eggman is obviously also involved in the story.
The game is devided into two part: The Modern Sonic Gameplay and the Classic Sonic Gameplay.
The levels with Modern Sonic are 3D and 2D similar to Sonic Unleashed or Sonic Colors and also play similar to these games. Classic Sonics levels on the other hand are all in 2.5D and are much more similar to the classic Sonic games (Sonic the Hedgehog 1, 2 and 3&K) and
like Sonic 4.
After you have beaten Act 1 & 2 of an era (each era consists or 3 Zones, there are 3 eras) you have to beat three challenge levels. There are alot of challenge levels to choose from and they are mostly rather easy so that shouldn't be a problem. Beating challenge levels can also unlock news skills that you can then use in Act 1 & 2 and you also unlock music from older Sonic games that you can then listen to or select as the music to play in a level.
Then there also are the Rival Battles and the Boss Battles, there is one Rival and one Boss Battle in each era and each of the are similar how you originally fought the boss but they are different enough to feel completely new.There are also 5 Red Rings to collect (only in Act 1 & 2) that also unlock new music and skills.
The Soundtrack is as good as always and since this is an anniversary game it consists of a lot of (great) remixes.
And like I already said, you can unlock new,old music that can be used in levels and challenges.Summarized, the soundtrack is great.
The PC port is functional. It does everything it has to. I haven't had that much problems with it. Sad thing is that the Online Mode doesn't really work in the PC Version and you can't play Sonic the Hedgehog 1 like you could on consoles (but we can buy the pre-order DLC, which they can't :P )
Also,each time you change your PC set-up (like for example the monitor) you have to go the the files,delete all .cfg files, then re-start the Conig Tool and then you can play the game.This is rather annoying but when you don't change your set-up this shouldn't affect you.
The game only shows you the Xbox 360 controller icons but you can change the key-bindings so that shouldn't be a big problem, controller is still recommented.
So yes, I recommend this game but not for 30€
Also,this game has some great mods which you can have fun with like for example play the Act 1 level of Sonic Unleashed or change the character model to Shadow.

First up, I'm pleased to announce that I was able to run this demo, with no lag, on a laptop not much better than a "potato". So for those, like myself, who've been a bit anxious about how the final game might run on their machines, things are looking pretty darned promising (be nice if they came up with some better pre-purchase incentives, though: things which merely increase or decrease the difficulty factor don't exactly get my credit card all hot and bothered, I'm afraid).
Secondly, despite popular opinion, this is NOT a return to old-school Resident Evil roots, in anything bar perhaps "spirit". Anyone who has actually PLAYED one of the earlier RE games can see this as clearly as the nose on their dead dog's face (unless said dog was blasted with a shotgun). In fact, anyone who's kept even remotely in touch with horror gaming in the past few years can see that games such as Outlast have played a significant part in influencing the new direction which Capcom is taking, to the point where I won't even ponder the similarities in setting between this and the also-upcoming Outlast 2 (though I suspect Red Barrels could cheerily murder someone at Capcom right now).
Me, I'm gonna buy both games quick-smart anyway, and I have a sneaking suspicion one of them might get the honour of being my number one game of 2017. And the other, well...might still end up being my number TWO game of 2017. So chicken, egg? Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn. Let the best game win.
Oh, and this demo, specifically? Short, no real "action" to speak of, but if you have enough imagination to mesh the extraordinary atmosphere of this demo with the promise of action we can all so plainly see in the trailer, you can tell the main game is gonna be a significant improvement over RE6 (unless your idea of good "horror" is lots of kickboxing and enough explosions to make Michael Bay soil his pants). I for one cannot wait...though I still wish they'd come up with better pre-purchase incentives than an uber-Difficulty level and A COUPLE OF ♥♥♥♥ING PLANTS.
Verdict: 9/10.
UPDATE: I was wrong about the "action" bit. This game has a few secrets you'll probably only find with multiple plays and/or Googling, and yes...there IS a use for those pistol bullets you find! Quite the cheeky, multi-layered little demo, actually...
Updated Verdict: 9.5/10 (self-contained demos - with content which apparently won't be in the main game - simply don't get any better than this)!

Note that I received this game for free, due to being gifted LISA: Complete from a friend of mine.
LISA has been one of my absolute favourite gaming experiences in recent times. I can't go into great depth of why without spoiling the game for others, so I will list the positives I have with this game.
The game's overworld in its post apocalyptic state is really quite interesting to travel through and explore throughout the course of the game. I was scared to explore because of the possibilities of what could happen, but that was nothing compared to my strong curiosity to explore. The game also boasts an enjoyable turn based combat system that even manages to be unique in its own way. This game is one that is definitely replayable, due to the number of possible party combinations you can have when playing the game.
This is a story rich game and it does a wonderful job at being serious and dark, while also not pessimistic. I'm not an emotional person generally, but this game did a great job at twisting with my feelings. After doing everything I could do in this game, I would read up on the lore and found it to be highly fascinating. Easily one of the strongest highlights of the game for me.
You can guarantee that when playing through the game, you will have to make some decisions. These vary from quite easy to sacrifices that I had so much trouble deciding upon that afterwards I wondered if what I had done was worth it. These choices will definitely make an impact across the entire game, not just to the game but to its player. An excellent and highly notable system in my eyes.
Despite being made up of FL Studio samples bought from other composers, LISA has a whacky and highly suitable soundtrack. After playing Adventure 2, formerly my favorite Sonic game, again on Steam and realizing just how bad that game really was, the franchise was not in good standing in my mind. However, once I fired up this gem that I bought on the same sale, my faith was restored. Sonic Generations is undoubtedly the best Sonic game, and arguably one of the best platformers out there.
To start with the basics, you play as both Classic and Modern Sonic, in nine different worlds, each with one stage per Sonic. Classic Sonic controls just like in the old days, totally 2D. Modern Sonic switches between 2D and 3D, as seen previously in Colors. The stages we see are among the most memorable ones in the series, usually the first for their respective games, and they're all changed enough to keep the feel of the original without feeling like they just copy-pasted the level design in. Race through Green Hill Zone again, try desperately not to fall into Chemical Plant Zone's water, and see City Escape's GUN truck return with a vengeance. Even the Sonic '06 stage doesn't suck.
Each stage has five challenges to complete (at least nine of which must be done to beat the game) and five red rings to grab, for a total of 90 each. These unlock the various concept arts and tracks that comprise the collectables. These are mostly fair challenges, only a few of each got on my nerves. There are seven bosses, three of which are structured as rival battles, and these are mostly throwbacks to classic fights. Bring down the Death Egg again- with RINGS, this time- and use Modern Sonic's water-running ability to beat Perfect Chaos without going Super.
On the graphics end, this game is like the New Super Mario series: they're not trying to do anything groundbreaking or realistic, they're just taking the capacity of modern technology and using it to update the visuals without really changing the style. And it works. On the sound end, the tracks for stages and boss fights are remixes of the original BGMS. Some are better, some aren't, but you always have the option of playing any of the tracks you've unlocked instead.
The achievements are quite fair. A good count will be unlocked during normal gameplay, and most of the rest involve going after the unlockables. Some involve performing certain actions on certain levels; manage to not fall into Chemical Plant Zone's water? You'll agree that's worth an achievement. A chain require S-ranking all 18 stages, which is way more doable than it sounds; all you gotta do is run through at a good speed without a death, and it should happen. The hardest achievement is to beat the endboss without taking a single hit, but when you can swap out the BGM for Open Your Heart, Live and Learn, What I'm Made of, His World, or Knight of the Wind, you won't mind the practice.
TL;DR: 100%ing this game was 23 of the best hours I've spent this year. 9/10, Sega please, stop trying to change the Sonic formula, you already perfected it, just make more Sonic games like this, no Naughty Dog rejects required.

Truly a fantastic adventure game! Papo & Yo will not only present you with interesting puzzles and fun gameplay, but also challenge you to look inward to the demons we all battle throughout life (and more importantly the places we go to escape them).
This is a game about a boy named Quico and his seemingly magical action figure Lula, as well as a giant - and normally docile - beast named Monster. As Quico, you will explore various facets of the dream-like favela he escapes to, where the laws of reality itself bend to the whim of one little boy.
The core gameplay focuses on solving environmental puzzles, many of which involve magic chalk-like drawings on the walls and floors of buildings that let you manipulate this strange and beautiful world in a variety of different ways. There is also some light platforming and some interesting mechanics which involve Lula, who straddles your backside like a knapsack and acts as a sort of jetpack that can also carry out some basic commands (such as flipping switches for you at a distance). Monster will also play a big part (no pun intended) in solving a lot of said puzzles and offers his own unique mechanics; when he is asleep his massive gut can be used as a trampoline of sorts and of course that brute strength of his also comes in handy! You have to be careful, however, as Monster also has an unhealthy addiction to poisonous frogs which cause him to burst into flames and go on a rampage!
All in all this is a refreshing take on 3D puzzle-platformers, that also reminds us just how beautiful and robust the Unreal Engine can still be when in the right hands.

The description does not the do the game any justice and is completely misleading.
Quico and the monster are not "friends" in the slightest, you are not "playing" with the monster, and you don't "build a friendship" together. The description makes the game sound like a bright, cheerful, Boy and His blob type game. It's not.
Watch the launch trailer to get a better feel for what the game is about.
*SPOILERS*
I don't want to give too much away, but here's the jist:
The game is an intriguing and harsh look at alcoholism, anger, neglect, child abuse, and even murder, through the eyes of an innocent child who, being unable to understand these things, creates a fanciful world they can escape to and make sense of them in their own way.
The monster altogether ignores you throughout the experience, try as you might to interact with it, like a neglectful parent. When it's not ignoring you, it's eating or sleeping. It only pays you any attention when you have food, or when it is actively trying to harm you. Yes, it "helps" you solve puzzles and progress through the game, but you're not in anyway develping a friendship with the monster.
The world is breathtakingly beautiful, with some really innovative and engrossing level design. There's a lot of detail in the mystical favela landscape, and exploring it is equally as enjoyable as the controls are tight and responsive.
The game moves very fluidly with excellent pacing and hitting all the right emotional cues. The music is also top notch.
Overall, this is a very polished game, and an excellent experience. The whimsical setting and levels juxtapose perfectly with the deeply emotional and dark subject matter. If I had any complaint, it's that the jumping is a little shoddy at times, and since the game has such an emphasis on platforming, that's a bigger deal than it should be. But that doesn't take away from the overall experience.
Definitely reccomend it to anyone who likes to play games with a good story, a lot of emotion, and a lot of layers. The fact that the controls are great and the graphics are fantastic is merely icing on this bittersweet yet delectable cake.

Call of Duty: World at War throws you into the conflict that held the world in it's hands. You'll watch limbs tear from the bodies of soldiers as grenades explode right under their feet, and through impressive set design and nice voice acting, it will convey the war as realistic as arcade FPS game can get.
The campaign is extremely well done, featuring the voice talents of Kiefer Sutherland and Gary Oldman, moving on to the sprawling ruins of Stalingrad and unforgiving warzone of the Pacific Islands. The story itself is fairly good, maybe clocking in at just under six to seven hours depending on the difficulty you play on. I will refrain from discussing story points as I don't want to spoil the experience.
The multiplayer extremely fun. The map design has a good mix of open areas and cover-based buildings, and it can really go either way in a gunfight as a result which is pretty neat. While the customization is pretty primitive by today's standards, it's still nice to have some options.
To wrap up, let me state that this is the last Call of Duty that featured mod support excluding a patch for Black Ops 3. But the game itself has an incredible atmosphere that is only surpassed by games that intend to make a realistic WW2 game (Red Orchestra, Day of Infamy, etc...). Don't get me wrong, there are going to be some balancing issues, and since Activision don't exactly shed a tear over the fact that their old Call of Duty titles seem to be overrun with hackers, it can be intimidating to play online; but luckily there are some good people who host servers, and are willing to kick those ♥♥♥♥♥ out.
In the words of Joe Bob Briggs, "Four Stars, check it out!"

It's FF9, which is arguably my favorite Final Fantasy of the PSX era.
PROS: The game is largely unchanged and the the port is overall pretty good, the models are updated, the pre-rendered is updated for HD.  Music is unchanged unlike ff7 and ff8 ports.
CONS: Backgrounds were not updated for HD which makes for some striking contrast.  Some changes don't make a ton of sense.  There is no ability to exit the game from the title menu, exiting to title and exiting the game are buried at the bottom of the config in the menu (should just be a new main menu item or from pause.)  Some interfaces were changed to optimize for keyboard but take away controller only interface (notably naming characters requires a keyboard.) FMV framerates are pretty awful.
Overall.  It's a must-play final fantasy and if you like classic final fantasies you should just get it.  As this is my 3rd time purchasing, it's not an amazing port (there could be added extra features like a FMV theater or NG+) however as far as I've seen there's been minor upgrades and minimal bugs.  If it's worth a purchase as a pure psx port (which I think it is) it's definitely worth a purchase with the revamped models and FMVs with almost no negative changes.

IQ tests don't get cuter than this! Don't let the adventure game trappings mislead you; at its heart, "Missing Translation" is a cleverly concealed, charmingly packaged,  non-linguistic IQ test. There aren't any nonsensical adventure game puzzles here ("put the tape on the cat to get the hair to make a fake moustache"), just straightforward logic challenges like "determine the next pattern in the sequence", accompanied by adorable cats, staring cows, and some oddly spud-like people.
There are a lot of games on the market that claim to boost your brainpower, with bright graphics, loud music, and rapid-fire math problems hurled in your face. (I'm not sure who came up with the idea that being able to do math in your head faster than other people was a sign of intelligence, but that's what most of those games  seem to promote.) It makes more sense to have high-contrast black and white images presented in a low-stress environment if you really want to improve the way your mind works, and that's just what "Missing Translation" provides. Intelligence is like typing: it's better to work on accuracy first, and speed will come with time and practice. This game understands that principle, and rewards you for thinking correctly, not quickly.
Come for the logic puzzles, stay for the cats. Definitely worth the download!

*SLIGHT SPOILERS*
This game brought soo much to the table. This game feels like a spiritual successor/ predecessor of the classic Sonic games, yet operates much differently despite the closeness of both engines. I can feel the magic in this game lol. Felt like I was 5 again. Anyways, let's delve a little deeper into the review.

Design 95/100
Right off the bat, I have to say that the design is do or die in these type of platformers. The space between enemies, the setting of the loops, the different situations in where you utilize all of your skills with whatever character you have, etc was amazingly done right. I have never felt that one thing was too much in any of the stages, save for the final stage (final stages in every game are always a bit too much design wise anyhow). They perfectly paced this game out, almost as good a pace as the classic 2D Sonic games. Each and every one of the bosses are extremely unique and challenging. That alone is easily the most rewarding part...bosses that make you scratch your head and think a little bit about your actions.
Controls 90/100
The controls are pretty good, haven't had a bug or problem yet with it. I've only finished with one character, so I can't rate this on all of the characters.
Plot 78/100
The story isn't revolutionary, and can totally opt out of its cutscenes with classic mode. In fact, I dare say that classic mode is probably more effective story wise. The voice acting is great, but the plot didn't match the quality of everything else that made this game stellar. Classic mode fixes that IMO.
Originality 85/100
The environments weren't cliche'd to death, and the character design was amazing. It kept me engaged long enough to gaze at the artwork, and not just fly through a scene as quickly as possible.
Gameplay 85/100
Overall gameplay was smooth, save for a couple of times where the FPS dipped (mostly during boss fights). The developers did a bang up job ensuring the smooth playrate.
Overall, this is more than just a throwback to the prime of Sonic games, it's its own world. Recommended.

Stands on its own as an excellent game (READ:  NOT JUST A SONIC CLONE!).  I went into this expecting a Simple Sonic Clone, but it was on a good Steam Sale and the reviews looked promising so I figured, why not?  What I wasn't expecting was the fresh, original story, very balanced mechanics and tight gameplay that danced that line between challenging enough to feel something was at stake and loose enough to be fun as hell.
If you allow yourself to be immersed in the lore they make a little, you'll suddenly find even slaying a lowly baddie feels significant somehow, like it has meaning.  Nothing ever feels just "slapped in".   Unlike Sonic, that would have "Lava level becuase lets do one of those."  There's a lava themed level tied directly to an alien Foundry that you infiltrate, that was alluded to for its significance to the antagonists and had a reason to exisit beyond "Here is a Laval Level!".
It is obvious this story was lovingly tended to.  Even secondary characters had moments of significance that surprised me, or that spurned the tropey direction I had assumed they would go in the best way.  I knew they'd done something special when, even after the victory fist in the air at the end of the game I was going "But what about <redacted> character??  What happened to him?  What's the deal with this Council,  are there other people like Lialac who can literally tear apart sophisticated alien super-tech with their magic energy hair?"  I was both befuddled and hungry for more.
Yes it's a fantastical world, yes it leans very hard on some of the good staples of your old Sonic games, but in my opinion, it greatly improves on them too.  Not only is it its own world, but there are subtle moments where I went "I WISH Sonic games had done this!", such as the quasi-health bar instead of "lose all your rings, then die if hit again" flow-breaking mechanic of the Sonic Games.  Or the fact that, while Lilac can get up to speed, its never to seizure inducing, too fast and hard to follow motion, the pace can feel fast and light but, unlike even the best of Sonic games, at top speeds I can still keep track of♥♥♥♥♥♥
This is an indie game doing everything right, and had I payed the full 14 dollars for it, I still would have gotten my money's worth.  However, if you DO see this on sale, grab the soundtrack too, its bloody fantastic and it makes excellent workout/study music!  Nice added bonus there.
In conclusion:  Better than all your expectations, don't expect this to rest on the laurels of Sonic or just be a "Sonic Clone".  It's not,  its an excellent game fully deserving of its own clout and absolutely worth your time and money if you liked any of those old side-scroller style games.   Two Thumbs way up and Kudos to the Game creators, I hope you guys make more stuff like this soon!

Okay. Papo & Yo.
My first attraction to the game came with its visuals. The bright, colorful design of the favelas instantly caught my attention in a market saturated by grays and sepias. It stood out, it was new, it was charming. I picked it up, played it for a short while, and then set it down for a week. This should not speak poorly for the game but, rather, for my lack of attention. It took a little bit to get started. But when it did get started, oh man. It got started.
I have since finished the game, and I can now safely call it one of the most important games I have ever played. Not because of anything that it does in the gameplay that is new. The gameplay is only ever average, an affair of finding gears to push and plungers to pull. It has its difficulties - the frame rate will sometimes skip for no reason, and the platforming elements feel strange. Quico, the protagonist, has a strange weight to him, making jumping a bit of an unusual effort. The gameplay is the weakest part of this game.
But it is everywhere else that it shines. It can be terribly dazzling when it wants to be, offering a magically real landscape of favelas that twist and turn and defy gravity, and houses that walk on legs made of chalk, and an enormous pink monster with sun-cracked skin and a dangerous addiction to tropical frogs.
And for every wonderful moment there is a counterpoint, a realization that this experience is inspired by Creative Director / Writer Vander Caballero's relationship with his alcoholic father. Later in the game Monster finally gets his hands on one of those irresistable little frogs, and gobbles it up. He is instantly wreathed in red flames, and he turns on you with a stomach-gnashing roar. Poor little Quico suddenly seems very small against the rampaging Monster, very fragile.
The story's focus is on Quico's quest to cure Monster. You go on a journey to find a shaman, aided by a mysterious girl and an endearing toy robot named Lula, and of course Monster. Sometimes things go quite well. Sometimes they go very wrong.
There are moments were Papo & Yo is absolutely childlike in its wonder.There are moments that are dark and threatening. And there are moments where you have to do things that are painful and liberating. This is a game of powerful, startling, painful moments, strung along to lure you deeper into its narrative.
I feel Papo & Yo is best experienced in a single sitting. The puzzles never become inhibitingly difficult, and you can finish it in about 2 - 4 hours. Which, honestly, you should.
If you want to know more, read the reviews put out by Rock Paper Shotgun and the New York Times.

Papo & Yo is a metaphorical story played out within a child's imaginative mind. Adhering to its theme, the gameplay and puzzles are simple and childlike. The story progresses, driven by the nostalgic innocence of childhood, and ultimately unfolds out into a darker, more mature theme.
Recommended to those who can appreciate an emotionally engaging storyline, vibrant visuals, and a uniquely magical soundtrack.

This game looks so simple, it can hardly be any good, right? Wrong! What a gem!
It's a fairly small game. This is good because it won't make a playthrough dragging on forever. It also has a very high reply value. Didn't beat it? Try again. And a few minutes later you're blazing through the galaxy in yet another attempt to beat the crap out of that final boss or die in the process.
And you'll die. Over and over. Don't come in expecting to win every round or even win on the first ten tries, beause you probably won't.
When you first play the game, it's very very hard once you get through the first few sectors of space.
It's a process of failing and learning from it. Try again, fail and adapt, try again, fail and adapt, try again... yeah.. ragequit, ten minutes later: lookup some tips on youtube.. try again.. and fail.. but it's SO much fun!
It's also based heavily on random events, so don't expect one strategy to work all the time. Take your time. Use the pause button a lot to rethink strategies or to better time your actions, because correct timing is vital.
Replayability comes from the fact that the galaxy and events are randomized and there are several ship types and layouts to choose from. Ships and layouts will be unlocked by acquiring certain conditions. So even if you've finally been able to defeat that boss, you'll want to come back for more.

text:
LISA is one of the pinnacle games RPG Maker has to offer, while unfortunately flying under the rader for most people. For me personally, I found it after the whole Undertale craze while looking for similar titles. On a whim with little more than this knowledge I purchased both the main game and DLC, LISA the Joyful. In the end I personally enjoyed LISA quite a bit more than Undertale and even felt like the two were very different genres of games. While Undertale focused on pacifism, LISA had a large focus on violence, conflict, and darker themes.
The plot of LISA starts off pretty generic, a man named Brad and and his few pals live together in a post apocalyptic world where theres only men left, until one day he finds a female baby. From here on Brad raises what could possibly be the last woman on Earth. Eventually the child, nicknamed Buddy, gets taken and Brad must track her down. Throughout his journey he meets some friendly and not-so-friendly people that decide to either accompany, help. or hinder his journey. While the world can seem very grim and dark at times, there are also some light hearted, fun moments too, albeit dark humor is weaved into these moments. As you progress you learn more about Brad and his past while also making decisions that affect the future. At certain points in the game you make decisions that have real consequences that are by no means easy. Morality plays a large part in this and while playing I questioned many of the decisions I made. We learn that many of the characters are by no means perfect but that many are just trying to do the best they can.
For the gameplay of LISA it is similar to most RPGs, health, some sort of special attack resource, leveling, etc. Brad serves as the only essential character of the game while other companions can be skipped, abandoned, and used. (There are only 1-2 forced companions if I remember correctly). Brad's basic attacks are combo based and use the WASD keys to use  his special attacks which at first makes combat fun but later becomes a headache when you have more special attacks. Luckily you can bypass this by simply selecting them from the menu, making you lose a few basic hits but without having to remeber the key combo. Brad aside, all of the other companions uniquely fulfil their roles while also varying in usefulness. Some may be very powerful but suffer from Joy addiction, the main and only drug in the game, giving you one more resource to balance. As you build up your cast of companions you will also lose some. Permadeath for companions is another part of the game that really messes with not only your gameplan but emotions aswell. Although for the most part an ally can faint and be revived by either items or resting, there are also enemies and attacks that can cause permanent companion death. As you lose characters you will find yourself rebuilding your team to fill roles that you may lose characters in. This is made further impactful by Pain mode, a selection made at the beginning of the game that makes save points usable once before exploding. While this makes the game much more difficult, it also made every fight more risky. There were times where I contemplated redoing an entire section to try and keep certain companions alive. The enemies are also varied and creative, with many of the human enimies having names along with both pre and post fight text. These little aspects were charming and helped to build the world and atmosphere. Exploration also plays an important role, similar to RPGs such as Undertale or Earthbound where you can find extra goodies or useful equipment. This also plays in with the companions, some being very easy to recruit while others may be a pain to find or convince to join you. This adds quite a bit of replayabilitly as you may want to go back and try to find what you missed.
Another small point I want to add is that the games soundtrack, while being very catchy and questionable at times, is overall really good. Going back to atmosphere and world-building, the songs really help to tie everything together. One second you're exploring a rural area while some peaceful music plays, then you enter an area full of body builders where the music is composed of grunts from Shenmue, to an air raid siren-esque track while fighting some thugs. It's actually cheaper during sales to buy the game, DLC, and soundtrack bundled together during Steam sales then it is seperate so theres no reason to skip.
Praise aside, LISA does have its shotcomings. The first of these issues is the ability to walk off (almost) any cliff in the game, some causing fall damage while others will simply give you a game over screen. This annoyed me many times, especially during Pain mode where I'd often have to redo some fights. The difficulty of the game is a double-edged sword that, while making decisions and such impactful, can also be very frustrating. As the decisions become more and more impactful you constantly wonder if you made the right choice since the game can be a slog at times. There is one section where you must play Russian Roulette with the lives of your companions to progress and this was probably the worst part of the game. The lack of decisions that is avalible when it comes to other tough decisions in the game makes the deaths feel forced and as if they are just trying to make the game harder for the hell of it. Luck is also a factor so you can lose 3+ companions before you can progress. Other than this I feel like other complaints may just be nit-picky or personal choice.
In the end, LISA is a very powerful game that manages to use RPG Maker to blend an emotional plot to entertaining combat and characters in a well fleshed out setting. As more and more people try to make thier own games hoping to make the next Undertail or OFF, games like LISA really give you hope and look towards the creativity and innovation these games can have.

Let me start by saying this is the perfect game to kill some time with and get some easy achievements.
This game is very short, although there is some dlc available, which, after playing the game, I'm more than willing to try.
The game graphics are black and white pixel graphics, but this doesn't subtract from the game, only adds to it - in the best of ways.
Game play consists of 3 main sections which includes 25 puzzles each. These puzzles can be fun and challenging, but not frustratingly so. Pretty quick to get through most of them, but they are hard enough to leave you feeling accomplished afterwards. There are a few outside mini puzzles as well, coupled with the games non existent hand-holding, makes it quite fun to figure things out. If things get to hard, there is a dedicated community here with very exact guides to help you out.
I loved the music - got that tune stuck in my head. I also loved the cats, I wish you could do something to them/with them.
The only cons: One is the very short gameplay - you kinda want more, and you can see the areas where the dlc enables certain things. The only other one seems to be a memory leak somewhere, which causes a slight stuttering every 5-8 minutes, with a overflow in the memory upwards of a gigabyte. Seems to effect multiple people across different os.
On the whole I would definitely recommend this game, it's quite enjoyable.
<sidenote>
Even though it says Windows 7 and up, it will play perfectly fine even on Windows Xp.

It's a testament to how good the game actually is that it can remain super fun and enjoyable despite its problems, and the biggest problem in Freedom Planet is how deceptive the game is about it's difficulty.
Normal difficulty is well named up until the airship level. Past that, the game gets extremely difficult very quickly. Actually completing the game on normal difficulty requires a high level of skill.
If you're a strong platform gamer you'll probably still manage to complete it, but it will absolutely test your skills. Even if you do complete the game, you will likely feel frustrated, as the difficulty comes unexpectedly.
There are segments you will not complete on your first try, simply because you can't anticipate the danger. "Gotcha!" moments are way too common in the late game.
This can be very discouraging at times!
If Freedom Planet called normal mode "hard mode," and hard mode "very hard mode," that be an improvement. It'd at least give the player an honest idea of what to expect.
I really, really enjoyed Freedom Planet, but it is absolutely not a game I can recommend to everyone.
At the very least, I'd advice anyone who isn't confident in their platformer skills to play on Easy difficulty first.

*Edit*
I'll explain in a wall of text why you should try it anyway XD (TLDR, buy it!)
It may seem like a Sonic clone a first glance, but that's far from the truth. This game is like Shovel Knight in that it takes elements from 2D action games from the 90's and impressively manages to stand on its own as not just a great 2D action game, but also one of the best in the genre.
The gameplay features speedy platforming similar to Sonic's 1-3, but also mixes it up with satisfying combat. Each character also has different moves. Lilac has the powerful Dragon Boost that allows her to charge through enemies and bounce on solid objects, plus a Cyclone spin that can be used to kill enemies above or get up to higher ground.
Carol can use her claws to scratch enemies or can do a powerful pouncing slash. You found a gas-can as Carol? Grab it to summon her physics-defying motorcycle!
Milla can construct a shield or a throwable block of death. Combine the two and she now has a laser attack! She can also fly for a bit and find items buried in the ground.
The game also has an awesome soundtrack(my favorites being Fortune Night and Sky Battalion).
The only problems this game has (though the pros heavily outweigh the cons) is that the story is kinda run of the mill and basic and has a few cutscenes that last way too long (maybe FP2 can improve on story and cutscene issues?), and the fact that the lives you get don't matter since you start at the last checkpoint after pressing continue (though I personally prefer it like this, it's still a bit weird having lives that do nothing).
The lives issue can be fixed if GalaxyTrail adds an option where lives count, since I'm sure some players would appreciate the option.

Many others better than I will tell you about FF9 as a JRPG, so I'll leave it to them. Just wanted to weigh in my experiences technically.
Works fine with Xbox 360 wired controller for me. Doesn't have the annoying pre-boot screen like FF8 and FF7, meaning I can boot this up and not have to go near a keyboard. Haven't tried it on the Steam Link yet, but I'm not anticipating any issues based on the above. Controls feel fine. In-game recognises Xbox buttons (telling you to press Y, etc.).
Sound is same as PSX. No midi here.
Graphics are along the same as FF7/8. Hi-res models, but muddy backgrounds. Occasionally jarring, but not too bad.
There have been some changes to the GUI, but aside from some resizing I'm honestly hard pressed to notice and/or care. The ones in this version work pretty well, that's all that matters to me.
Only thing I don't like is access to the game boosters from within the menu, rather than outside the game. Not end of the world, but occasionally worried I'll accidentally hit one of them (it says they're irreversible so would probably require a reload).
Game is not widescreen. Original game wasn't, so it makes sense. It has some textured edges to fill the sides. Honestly would've preferred it if they'd made it black, but it's neutral enough to not be too distracting.
Probably the best PSX>PC FF port I've played so far. Nice to see that lessons have been learnt.
EDIT: For clarification, there is a launch screen, but unlike FF7/FF8 you can actually navigate through it with a controller. However, I did have some issues when trying to change resolutions and had to go back to my PC to actually do it. Once set up, I've been able to go through fine each time.
I've spotted a few graphical issues. Nothing major, but still annoying. Steiner's victory pose in battle, if the camera focuses on him, causes him arm to vanish.
Other than that, still seems to be running well. No other issues encountered.

To be honest, I wasn't really expecting much of this game. The mechanics of flying through the air looked fun, but I really didn't expect much of a story. What this is, however, is a beautiful cascade of visuals, soundtrack, and a rekindling of child-like imaginations that I'd long since forgotten. The story starts out with a father telling his daughter a bedtime story...a story about his Uncle. In this story, the father retells an adventure from his childhood when he set out to find his missing uncle.
To me, this game was uplifting. It's genuinely refreshing to play a captivating game that is challenging, touching, and completly lacking in violence. Beyond the brilliantly simple controls, the game consistently kept me intrigued with increasingly exhilarating challenges, and the promise of answers at the end of the road. And as we explore what appears to be the vivid imaginations of a child, we learn a more poignant truth behind this experience, one that as an adult, is incredibly close-to-home.
I highly recommend this game

Apparently, you can only move your legs *or* your sword at any given time.  What?
I don't know what to say... very stiff controls.  Very awkward to play.  I want to like this for being a new attempt at making an interesting swordfighting game, but I just can't find it enjoyable.  Even in the fast stance, my character freezes up completely during swings.
I would recommend that anyone who's interested in this, pick up a copy of Unreal Tournament 2004, install the ChaosUT2 mod for free, and try out the melee dueling.  This game seems like a remake of those mechanics as a standalone game, down to the 3 stances, the controls for sweep attacks, etc.  Problem is, the Chaos mod's version is just more *fun*.  You can move fluidly while attacking and it just feels more like a good action game.  The one thing I liked gameplay-wise in Blade Symphony is the way heavier attacks can break through a parry.  In the Chaos mod, it's a little silly when daggers parry a hammer blow.
Good effort, but I hope the developers give this "your legs freeze during any attack" mechanic a hard look.  Just changing it to a speed penalty could go a long way towards making this game playable.  I do miss the melee duels of ChaosUT2 and will be open to a good challenger.

I spent years playing this game for PC. The CD is still in my laptop right now. For those that don't know, SimCity is the originator of being a mayor, placing down your roads, zoning area for buildings, watching them grow and balancing the budget. This isn't for everyone, but to a lot of us, this is huge fun and SimCity 4 is probably the best in the series.
This is all single player, instead of the more current SimCity 2013 that is focused on multi-player. The game can cycle from night to day, but its just a look and doesn't seem to do anything special. You have terrain control like previous versions of SimCity before you start each game.
You start out in a region map of dozens of land plots. Large, medium and small. You pick a plot of land and make your city. You can then save that city, load the region and start up a new city on a different plot of land or go to a previous city. Why does this matter? Because you can trade between cities, you can export and import water, garbage, energy and so on. Not just that, but the sims / citizens can travel back and forth. Such as living in one town and going to another for work. You'll also have pollution effects that seep into other towns as well. This is all single player, so you need to jump between cities. Because two or more towns can thrive off of one another, you can put your heavy polluting industries in an extremely profitable town on their own with no residents living there to complain about how awful it is. There is no need for police, hospitals or schools if no one is living in your industrial city. Then just make some mass transit system for them to get to and from work.
When you play, you have full control from the start with only a few things locked away unlike Cities XL that requires your city to grow before it unlocks things for you. Because you have full control, that may set you up for failure quickly. Highways, big hospitals, deluxe police stations and so on cost big money and until your city is big, you should keep it small. Once your city grows, the game has ways to tell you that your hospital is too small, such as your staff workers will go on strike. How do you know if its too small? Sadly you can't just hold shift and click the building, you need to click the ? and then the building. It seems tedious, but you'll see what the building can handle and adjust its budget. If you can't adjust the budget high enough, its time to make a bigger version of the building or just plop down another building to do the same thing.
You need to keep your budget balanced, everything will cost monthly money, so you either need to cut spending from places like roads, schools, utilities or raise taxes, which might make some businesses, commerce and residents run to away from your city. When you lower taxes, of course people move in, but then your hospitals, schools and so on will be overcrowded, your buildings will grow larger. Its beautiful.
The game will tell you what kind of zones you'll need, such as low, medium and high density residential, commercial, industry and even agricultural. Its your job to plop them down. It has a graph to show you if you need more and less. If you need less, raise taxes for them, or replace the zone with a new zone. Luckily the game makes it easy to replace zones.
There are all sorts of charts and maps, such as pollution, both water and air. Crime, fire safety, land value and so on. If you want to raise land value, put down police, fire, schools and so on. Then add parks and various things to drive value up. Replace dirty industries that pollute with cleaner industries like medium density manufacturing.
You can also click on zoned buildings to see the crime, water, power, pollutants, and even the driving pattern of where the residents go and where the employees come from. Its a very nice feature. Especially if you're trying to reduce traffic. You have control over roads, avenues, streets, highways, trains, subways, busses and so on. Its fun to see just how far people will ride a bus to work. The game has plenty of charts too, in order to demonstrate how far the average drive is, how much garbage you have, the age and education of your population. Its all a lot of information.
On top of that, you have advisers that will tell you what's good and bad about your city. The game sadly uses pop up windows to tell you what's up, but thankfully there is a setting to turn it off, or else before you know it, you'll have nothing but popups. Instead you can look at the ticker at the bottom of the screen and even go into the advisers section to see their specific needs.
After all is said and done, you can then summon a natural disaster (or truckasaurus) to come and destroy your town. Why you'd want to? Just for the laughs I guess.
Because this is the deluxe edition, it comes with Rush Hour expansion pack, which gives you the ability to take over vehicles and drive them on the road. Not first person, but still from the normal almost top down perspective. This content gives you missions that will give you cash and other rewards, but really, it doesn't feel like a great addition. Its just there.
This game is a classic, but after 10+ years, I don't think that its aged very well. After months of playing Tropico and Cities XL, those games just seem to run smoother control wise and have explanation to them. Having a hot key for pause would have been nice. Fires break out in your town extremely frequently, no matter how good your fire coverage is. It just breaks the flow of the game, you need to send your fire fighters out to stop the fire and wait while they put it out. That's just not fun.
There are also a few minor bugs, but some that will crash the game. Since there is no autosave, you can lose an hour's worth of progress if not an entire city.
It is still an enjoyable game and I can recommend it more than SimCity 2013. Is it worth the $10 - $20? No and yes. If you enjoy mayoring sims, you can sink days and months into this game, then its worth it, but you should wait for a $5 sale if not cheaper.

This is one of the best Kickstarter games out there.  If it had nearly the attention that Mighty No. 9 or Bloodstained had, then this game would have been even more overfunded than it was with a measily 2,000 USD goal.(It gained 25.000 USD)
Now for the actual review.
I paid 14.99 USD and used a 360 controller for Windows.
Starting off, the sprite work is excellent.  I'm a sucker for pixel art, but this is some great stuff.  They even use it for cutscenes in a rather intelligent use of budget.
Cutscenes are well voice acted, humorous, and can have some genuinely inspired and well written dialogue.
For the actual gameplay, it's the best game inspired by Sonic that I've played in a very long time.  However, it doesn't play entirely like Sonic at all.  For one, if you play as Lilac, do not try to do the Spin Dash.  Fight the muscle memory, because it will not work.  Another thing more specific to the game is that enemies cannot hurt you until they attack you.  Meaning you can run right past them...unless they are already attacking you.  Another thing are the boss battles which are insane.  If you've ever played Gunstar Heroes, you are in for a treat.  If you've never played Gunstar Heroes, you are in for the fight of your life.  It's impressive that the characters aren't just built around speed based platforming but for one on one boss battles as well.  They even combine the two for boss battles that involve racing through levels.
Not once was there ever slow down that wasn't intentional.  What I mean by this is that some bosses are so big that when they drop, there's weight to it.  The game ran smoothly from beginning to end.
My only gripe is that the tone of the story mode clashes too much.  At one point it's humorous and pleasant, and then it gets insanely dark.  It happens randomly and it's jarring every single time, especially in the second half of the game.
This game is awesome and well worth the cover price.  There's even free content coming soon where you can play as Torque, who will play like a Gunstar Hero which I mentioned above, and Spade, who uses playing cards.  There's already 3 characters to play as and a few collectibles to obtain.  It's a damn good game, so buy it.

FFIX is what the other previous PSX ports should have been.
Videos are wow.
Backgrounds got a decent upscale+filtering (some transparency on the layers could have been cleaned up more though)
Character models got a few more verts here and there, and the textures look like they got an uprez/median filter with some additional cleanup work.
If only I could avoid the stupid launcher as I have to use a mouse for that one part.

tl;dr: Overall it's a good port. There are changes to the UI, sound effects have been updated, videos have better resolution, characters are great, controls are ok.
- If you're a fan of Final Fantasy games, don't miss this release.
- If you have neve played this game on PSX, here's your chance, do it.
- If you played it on a emulator, It feels like playing it on a decent emulator, with the best possible quality, and also some dark magic improving models and textures (things a emulator can't do properly). Plus, it has all the charm of various language options, Achievements, Cloud Save and Trading Cards.
--
Comparisons to PSX version
UI: The UI was basically remade. It has touch support, which translates to mouse clicks on the PC side, and navigation using a controller feels mostly the same as it was in the console version. Player portraits inparticular look great. The downside is that it runs at a faster framerate than the gameplay itself, making some UI graphics shutter when it tries to follow a model character, such as damage text when a creature dies.
Music: It features the same music used in the original game, with a small difference. The PSX game had its music done using a sequenced with specific samples. The game can be speed up using the F1 key, which makes the whole game faster, except the music, making the battle encounters and battle spoils moments completely gone, and would make Mr. Uematsu quite unhappy. This version uses a compressed recorded version of the original PSX music, which leads to the best fidelity, but with a small impact on quality. If have a good ear for subtle things like this, it'll bother you a little; most people won't even notice.
Controls: Using a gamepad, it feels like a PSX, except for some parts of the UI, where it behaves slightly different from the original counterpart, such as the battle scene, where selecting the target of a skill is easier to select using up and down in the enemy list instead of selecting the enemy looking at him, using left or right. Inputting the character name is also different and quite counter-intuitive: I had to grab the mouse and click on the text box, and then click Confirm.
Models: The character models are great, and their textures also look great. The battle scene models remain the same as the original PSX game, which makes it look a bit outdated, which is fine, since we're playing a port, not a remake. Also about the battle scene, the level textures uses some filtering. It doesn't help, but doesn't hurt to have it. The prerendered backgrounds are fine just the way they were, also featuring the same texture filtering, also not helping nor damaging.
--

A LONG(ish) REVIEW OF WHAT TO EXPECT.
***EDIT-  Just found out that SE lost the original HD renders of the backround scenes, hence why they didnt put them in the game.***
Pretty much as expected from what the other remastered FF games have been like. I was hoping that SE would of included HD versions of the game backround scenes as they made HD versions when the game was developed then they downscaled them so the PS1 could run the game, it was a bit of downer that they didnt include them. The NPC's are sharpened up to the same standard as the other remastered FF games. The cutscenes have been tidied up and there are the cheats (if ya want to use them) as seen in the other FF games.
Alot of the Negative reviews are due to a 'Xbox controller' bug but i have not come across this so far or because they where expecting the graphics to be better and it being scaled to 16:9 Aspect Ratio, well i dont really know what those people where expecting. It's a PS1 game that is 15ish years old so dont get your hopes up if ya thinking this is a full on redo of the game cus its not xD.
After installing the gameplay was jittery but a quick PC reboot sorted that issue.
Pro:
- The best FF game ever made has now come to PC
- sharpened NPC's (no more blurry characters) happy days \o/
- 100's of hours of great gameplay and story from a time where RPG's where in their prime.
Cons:
- No HD backround scenes in the game (though not surpised)
- Cutscene's locked at 15fps/ Gameplay locked at 30fps
- Maybe a bug or two
- Looks like its a port from the mobile version of the game
Final Words:
Not much to say really, it is what it is. People who have played the remastered versions of FF 7/8 will know what to expect. Its a shame that they didnt include HD versions of the backround scenes as they where made when the game was develped, SE have had 15 years to implement into the PC version of the game, however, that is prob my only gripe.
Dont expect a full-on redo because you will be left with a bitter taste in ya mouth. All you should expect from this game is a vanilla game with sharpened NPC's a few pointless cheats, cloud game saves & steam trophies.
With all that in mind i am very happy with my purchase, i get to play prob the best FF (yet under-rated) game ever made on pc. Veteran's of the game will be happy with just having the game on PC and for those who have not played the game then give it a go. Its a very relaxed gameplay style with some of the best storytelling that has ever been created for the gaming industry.
Hope this review was helpful, thumbs up/down if ya liked/disagreed with my evaluation. Enjoy & Good luck

Before anything, I have to say FF IX is my favorite game ever (I played it on psx and on the emulator). I'm a huge fan of rpgs and j-rpgs and I've been waiting for this release for a very long time. And they didn't mess it up, thank you square enix!
Now that you know a little bit about me, would I recomend this game? If you are a FF fan like me, yes definitely. If you are new to the FF saga but you love rpgs, you should wait for a sale (and a good one!).
I'll be honest, this game is a port from Android (more like an adaptation, but it feels like a port), and they've done a good job on some parts of it, but were really lazy on other parts. Let me explain:
++ Character remodelling: the characters you control and most characters you interact with, have been remodeled and it looks really good *.* (I've been playing this game on a 1366x768 resolution). Also, the text balloons have better quality too.
++ Cinematics: The movie cinematics have better quality then it had on psx. It could be better, but I'm happy they improved it a bit.
++ Battles: New options like being able to disable the battle intro or no encounter mode are welcome. I like the battle intro, but when you're grinding (it's not like you need to do a lot grinding on this game, but still) it will get boring to watch the same intro over and over again (that takes about 10 secons on each combat).
++ Music: I absolutely love the music themes on this game. The composer is Nobuo Uematsu, I don't think I need to say anything else.
++ Feel (this is a personal plus for me and FF IX fans): It feels like FF IX. It plays like FF IX. It sounds like FF IX.
++ Story: The plot is simple and easy to follow. It's not the most original plot ever, but it's well presented to the player, you can actually feel the story growing, gaining complexity, you care about what's happening in this world. And a very well built world to say the least.
++ Characters: The characters jobs are cliché. You have the happy, good-hearted thief, the angelic white mage, the strong worrior and so on. But their personalities, oh my, their personalities are just... wow... Even years after playing this game I can still remember every main character name, their motives to fight, their roles on the story, what they're trying to acomplish, what they went through that made them change and the conclusions they find out... You can feel them grow up, their pain, you care about them and what is happening to them... d*mn FF IX is the only game that ever made me cry.
-------------------
-- Graphics: They've done a good job remodelling most characters in game, but the backgrounds and minor characters (like the villagers on a farm or citizens on a city)... not so much. It's the same backgrounds and models, no HD or remoddling whatsoever... On Android maybe it doesn't look that bad, but on PC with a 1366x768 resolution, it looks bad for a game released on 2016... A little remoddeling here would be welcomed.
Also (and probably because Square Enix didn't touch on the backgrounds), the game is locked on a 4:3 aspect ratio (no widescreen option).
I also detected a minor animation glitch when one of the characters is celebrating a battle victory.
-- Price: it doesn't feel good at all when you pay 17€ for an Android port on PC, even more when this game was released  16 years ago and it's basically the same game from back then with a little remoddling...
----------------------
+/- Controller: I played this game with an Xbox360 controller, and it works really good. Only a small problem when using the joystick to move the characther on the map, the character for some reason keeps moving on it's own sometimes...

What is it like being the father of the world's last girl? PAINFUL.
Brad Armstrong, a bald middle-aged man, is the protagonist of this game. One day he occasionally picked up an orphan, the Buddy, which might be the last girl in the world, and thence his life track has tremendously changed.
Though raised under a disqualified fatherhood, Brad did devote 100% of himself onto Buddy. He treat her as if she's his blood-related daughter. And he decide to hide her from the outside world, believing his daughter will never be the savior of the dreadful world.
But the secret got debunked one day, Buddy was kidnapped. He was forced onto the way of finding back his daughter. Waiting ahead is the cruelty of the world, the betrayal of his close friends, continuous hallucination of his suicided sister, Lisa, and de facto revenges from Lisa, the Buzzo's torturing him once again.
The part hurts me most is, Buddy rejected to come with Brad and argued that staying with Marty for a few day shows her what's the true fatherhood. And after hours of struggle, the dying Brad finally reaches the heart-broken Buddy. Brad's effort only hurts his daughter completely.
Someone holds the opinion that Brad is wrong for not giving up Buddy to save the world even she wants to. But I could understand Brad, savior or not doesn't matter, Buddy is just the daughter in his eye. The taste of true fatherhood is painful, so is the taste of the game.
RIP Brad.

The game's plot like is basically a mixture of the Godfather, and Goodfellas, you're a war hero, come back from the war and fall into a life of crime with your friend. The open world nature of this game is not the same as GTA, which to me is a good thing, there aren't a million half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥mini-games to play. Each section of the city feels different, China-town feels different than Little Italy. I'm not going to list any spoilers but I do feel like this plot is decent, the voice acting is pretty good for the most part, the in-car conversations are pretty humorous a lot of the time. The driving is a HUGE improvement over the first game, the cars feel like real cars would from the 40s that is spongey suspension and sluggish acceleration, this is not bad design, it's how the actual cars behaved back then. The map is actually displayed in the radar instead of the lame "map" that's in the first game.
The guns are all fun, though the pistols pretty much all seem the same power, even the magnum (and the magnum sound a little goofy, like a cartoon gun). There is an actual cover system in the game, and overall the fights are much improved over the first game. This is a great game, it's heavy on graphics card, so I recommend looking into mods on how to disable the physics of the clothing in the game.
Overall I've really enjoyed this game and don't understand why people are criticizing it for NOT being just a GTA clone.

On first sight, Papo & Yo could be made for a younger audience. And if you'd leave the story-elements aside, Papo & Yo would be just that. The Gameplay is simple, the mechanics are easy and it is no challenge to beat the game. But Papo & Yo doesn't try to be challenging, it tries to tell a story. The story of a boy who escapes into his own imagination to seek shelter from his alcoholic father, the "monster" if you will. And in his imagination, still, he tries to "heal" the monster from its addiction to frogs.
Papo & Yo tells this story in a metaphorical but so profound way, sometimes you just need to turn off the game and think about what just happened. As a game Papo & Yo is nothing special, but as a tool to express a story it is unique.
8.5/10
PS: The Soundtrack is superb. I bought this game without the Soundtrack and after playing trough Papo & Yo I feel pretty bad about it.
This is such a beautiful experience. Unmissable, in my opinion.

This game is a masterpiece! It's the only game I've ever played that left tears in my eyes. Highly personal, and very fun, Papo and Yo is a game about a boy trying to cope with his abusive father. This game opens wounds, but not in a bad way. Instead of determining to make a statement, and pointing it out to you, Papo and Yo immerses you into the story, letting you dictate how you feel about the situations presented.
The gameplay is puzzle based. It's inventive and very imaginative, but not difficult. Do not expect to burnout your brain trying to solve the puzzles. This game is more about the storyline and your personal reaction to it. Your first play through will probably be 2 - 3 hours; so it's not a bad game to play on a lazy afternoon. The graphics are done well with a rich color palette and tones to make you feel you are in the slums. The voice acting is spot on.
I know I'm lavishing over this game, but I really can't say enough good things about it. If there was ever a game I wished everyone would play at least once, it would be Papo and Yo!

First, I'll say that I enjoy games with immersive atmosphere, story, and a unique artistic vision.  Papo & Yo manages to get all three of those to work together to create a truly unique experience.
Above all else, I would call Papo & Yo a 3D adventure game, and the puzzles are worked into the environment in a way that makes them engaging though not the most innovative in the genre.  That's ok, however, because the real star of this game is the immersive experience of wandering through this fantastical favela, appreciating the colorful artwork, and dissecting the meaning and symbolism behind it all.
I don't know if my interpretation behind some of the imagery was intended by the developers, but when a video game can rise to the level of having multiple interpretations, you know it's something special!  The shift from colorful and sunny to drab and rainy...  The graffiti so intentionally placed in each scene...  The act of moving great buildings and how it relates to both boyhood imagination as well as the main character's role in his troubled father's life...
I experienced no bugs.  The visuals are stunning when using the highest graphical settings.  Look around, pause and enjoy the music, and take it in slowly to make the experience last.
The little gems of creativity, the perfect soundtrack, a story unheard of in the game industry, and the sense of wonder you feel as you explore this world simply cannot be missed by any gamer who believes that games can be art.

Good, but...
I like this game. It's bright, colourful, the music's inoffensive, and even the characters are likeable. As far as 'love letters to 16-bit Saturday-morning-cartoon-show platform games' go, I'd compare it to Sonic 3; where, instead of HOLD RIGHT TO WIN, you're expected to feel your way around a stage, taking on general platform-game-type enemies and getting to the end of the stage in one piece. There's a nice amount of variety in level themes - and I loved the nod to Gunstar Heroes for one of the level bosses, and the design of the bonus stage.
However - I feel that somehow, despite getting a handle on how to make an
platform game this decade, GalaxyTrail really dropped the ball, hard, when it came to the level bosses. If you have little tolerance for trial and error gameplay, untelegraphed lightning-quick attacks, or undodgeable screen-filling bullet-hell moments, you're going to start seeing red pretty quickly. Bosses attack to a pattern, and to proceed you will need to die over and over and over
until memorised - or at least mash the attack button in the boss' face and pray your life bar doesn't run out. It might be 'authentic', but given that the level gameplay experience seems to have been given careful attention - no blind leaps into the unknown! - it's disappointing that you're almost expected to grind through your accumulated lives. It's a mercy that the story dialogue doesn't repeat each time you restart the boss encounter, but c'mon.
In a nutshell: gameplay inspired by the nineties, updated for the noughties, but boss design lifted from the eighties. Recommended, but with a (hand gesture indicating
).

If you've just gone through a bad breakup, lost a loved one, had a pet die, or are otherwise in a bad place, this is what you need to do:
1) Set aside 15-ish hours of your life where you won't be disturbed.
2) prepare some light, bland meals and drinks for those 15 hours.
3) Play LISA. No breaks. No interruptions. No contact with the outside world for any reason.
It isn't going to make anything feel better, if anything it'll make you feel worse. But as you feel the inside of your soul rusting and peeling, you may find some shreds of catharsis. There are jokes, placed like a breadcrumb trail, to keep you holding on just so long to see what is going to happen to the sad, sad man you're spending your time with. At some point you may hit a wall and consider giving up. Don't. I played through the first 3-ish acts of this game, and then put it down for a year, and it still punched me in the gut when I went and finished it. I can't imagine how unpleasant it'll be to play it straight through.
But why am I telling you to play a game that makes you feel awful? Very simple: for the same reason that a cultured individual should watch Irreversible, or Come and See, or Magnolia or Requiem for a Dream, or read Exquisite Corpse or Funeral RItes. Because it's a stunning, beautiful piece of art, and sometimes, it's healthy to expose yourself to complicated, unpleasant, scary feelings. You will come out the other side purged.
Once you're done
1) Have a shower
2) Make some tea
3) Call your parents and tell them you love them
The only game that made me feel worse than LISA was probably Demonophobia, and I stopped playing that after twenty minutes when I realised that people were supposed to be getting off on it.

What an awesome experience. I recently played Sleeping Dogs and thought that it gave a great insight into Triad culture but it pales in comparison to Mafia II. I really can't find fault with this game at all. I suppose you could say it only lasts 10 or so Hours but its a very intense 10 hours.
You play the role of Vito an Italian/American who with his buddy Joe takes his shot at becoming a Made man in the Mafia.
I can't really say much about the story without giving big spoilers but lets just say it gives us an excellent look at how life in the mob would actually be. I always wanted to play a game version of Goodfella's and Mafia II is just that.
+ Graphics still hold up today. The character models and expressions are great.
+ Old 50's music, i personally love the period and setting.
+ The Story has so many twists and turns, its better than many movies. Keeps you playing to see what happens.
+ The gameplay is also fantastic, its unforgiving unlike many shooters you need to use cover or you die.
- It comes to an end a little after 10 hours. I wanted more.
- You can no longer buy it on Steam. Get a copy elsewhere its really worth it!.

The game is short, and further playthroughs are much quicker than the first time around once you become proficient in the game's controls and KNOW where you are supposed to go. The background music is calm and reminded me of the one for the game Myst--it was good for exploring.  There is not much complexity to the story, but what it does it does well. The narration along the way is helpful to immerse oneself in the exploration--it makes me want to BE a part of the story, of the world.  There is no gore (or violence), just pulling oneself by grappling to walls in caves or floating rocks. This game is definitely kid friendly. I got it on sale, but wouldn't pay more than 5 dollars because it is short and somewhat small (although the areas are large)--but it is lovely.  There are unlockables you can find on each stage which unlock some features, but so far they don't add much to the experience (goat mode, for example, where you hear goat sounds instead of the usual human ones for the main character). I would have prefered more surfaces on which to grapple to and explore, just for the sake of exploring and aesthetics. I love looking at the waterfalls, caverns, etc.

I wish I could give this game a mediocre rating but as it stands I'm tending more towards the negative than the positive. First-Person platforming is tough to pull off so I'm giving the devs a lof of credit for this game. However, they didn't do themselves any favors with the grappling hook functionality given the inconsistent control scheme. Sometimes you can latch onto objects, other times you can't, even when it's at the same distance. The margin of error is so small that on massive rocks right in front of you there's only a tiny area you can actually latch onto and it's often more luck-based than anything else whether you get it right. There were plenty of sections that I enjoyed but more than enough areas that were just frustrating beyond belief, not because it's hard to pull but because the controls get in your way. I really wanted to finish the game to see where the story would lead but once I got stuck at the falling blocks section in the ice area for more than half an hour I was done.

Where Shovel Knight is a tribute to NES games, Freedom Planet is a tribute to Genesis/Mega Drive games. It borrows a little from Sonic the Hedgehog, Sparkster/Rocket Knight, Ristar, and Gunstar Heroes but still manages to feel completely fresh. Throw in some quirky and lovable characters and a decent plot and you've got yourself the best Sega game never made.

I've only finished it with one character so far (Carol) and I really intend to play with the others, but I feel like I absolutely need to recommend it already. I had a blast.
At first I played one stage with Lilac and it felt like a Sonic game with changed characters, the similarities are obvious, thrown right in your face, the level design, the abilities, the sound effects, the graphics. After that I decided to try Carol and it felt so different. Her abilities are much more slow-paced and focused on combat and exploration. I never really got into the Sonic series, so playing as her made me enjoy the game much more.
The game can be speed ran and finished in under 1.5h or played calmly exploring everything and finished in 6/7h (with one character, worth pointing). The level design is outstanding.
I found the story to be quite annoying at times and to be honest sometimes I couldn't even understand what was going on, but it gave the characters lovable personalities, so it was worth it. It can be completely ditched by choosing the Classic mode.
The boss fights are the highlights, there are several of them, between mini and main bosses, a few are quite easy but most put the surprisingly good battle system into test. A bit of pattern memorisation is necessary which can be bad for some but I really enjoy it.
So, overall, if you are a Sonic fan you will enjoy it, if you don't really like Sonic but enjoy 2D platformers you'll also enjoy it. Just buy it already.

Freedom Planet does Sonic better than Sonic does Sonic. The characters control smoothly allow you to perform platforming and combat with grace and style. However, I strongly suggest using a retro pad with a good D pad, as using analogue will be noticeably detrimental in harder modes and levels. It is as action packed and over the top as Gunstar Heroes and its bosses are just as creative. The story is suitably over the top and delivery melodramatic, that any 80's kid will appreciate. As for the music, it keeps you pumped up and driven forward, with some good tracks, and some excellent tracks. The seasoned gamer will feel challenged all the way through, and face a serious challenge towards the very end. For new players the challenge may seem intimidating, but i'd urge against using the regen health difficulty. If you ever enjoyed a Sonic game and yearn for the time where SEGA new what they were doing with him, you need this game. Frankly if Sonic dies out and Freedom planet becomes the great franchise that Sonic used to be, I think it is for the best.
