This game only speaks to some people, and I'm part of those some people.
The game pretends to control like Sonic, and the world pretends to be a Megaman Game. The story is what you'd expect of that mixture and gets serious later on in. If anyone's ever played Dust: An Elysian Tale, the combat can be a lot like that, as you have 3 buttons for actions rather than the one you get in Sonic. People argue about this, but from how I see it, the game acts like Dark Souls by i-frames and learning your opponent so you can minimize deaths. They argue against it because of the fact that a few bosses are repetitive and have set attack patterns.
I've beaten the game 5 times now and I can say that after the first final boss run I did... He never was the same. Brevon started playing dirty. He changed up his attack pattern to personally hold me back. The game'll try to confuse you with lots of shinies and enemies but your goal is collecting gems and speedrunning. Your max speed on a flat surface can hardly match Sonic, but the acceleration and grip on the environment is far less slippery. With Lilac and Carol, you have control and finesse. This game cannot be compared to Sonic, as it's innovative and clever. The game cannot be compared to Dark Souls, as it has it's own stylization and feel to it. Don't forget it's also 2D which is a luxury from the past refurbished for the future.
I can honestly say, I'm gonna buy Freedom Planet 2. The game put me through a whole sea of emotion that by the time I finished it, I was glad for the tale it told. There's a lot of promise in this for the second game too, but I'm gonna let Galaxy Trail do what they do best. Trust me, it'll be hard not to impress after this game. There's so much to imagine that anything could happen.
The beta offers up a new character, Torque, in the playable set, and his combat prowess is unmatched, but his health matches that of Milla. He runs like a glass cannon, and has interesting mobility which is extended by the crystals you collect. I had a LOT of fun playing Torque, and cannot wait for his full release, even more so the release of FP2 which is getting closer!!!

A Story About My Uncle is game that invites you to relive that a long lost part of your life, where adventure and mysterious places dominated your imagination. The movement, flow, and world building all accumulate into a very well made game/story that left me pondering what will happen next.
The gameplay is fun and builds upon itself to make an increasingly difficult, while fun, 3D platformer. The programming that went into each ability, perfectly coincides with the surrounding world, creating a feeling of true skill when you achieve a tricky maneuver.
While having a good story, I won't say I don't have critiques. The voice acting is definitely a little cheesy at times. However, for the smaller development teams like Gone North Games and Coffee Stain Publishing, I would say they did what they could. Additionally, while a beautiful story, I felt it could have used a bit more pay off in the end. By introducing another character, Maddie, and not utilizing her properly, this game missed the opportunity to create a deeper emotional impact. Action, suspense, and conflict build a story to greater levels. Understandably, it is a bedtime story so it shouldn't be like an action film, but every good narrative (especially one that took about three hours to beat) could use a subplot, or additional conflict to flesh out the world a bit more.
Overall, I give this game a
It kept intrigued until the end, but it is not a masterpiece.

Let me begin by saying that this mod will have a second chapter. I was extremely confused to see the game end with a sudden cliffhanger, and the unseen detail of the last level. To my relief , the mod is still a work in progress, so expect more chapters to come.
Overall , I think that this mod is great. The attention to detail is amazing. Although I've been stuck in a few places , it rarely lasted for long as I could always find myself back on the track in seconds.
The placement of supply crates is very smart. The game doesn't throw ton's of ammunition at you. It encourages players to use the gravity gun whenever possible. I've played the game on Hard difficulty and fighting enemies was a breeze.
The level design is stunning. Despite Half-life being a series with linear gameplay , the mod gave me the sensation of freedom that I've never felt in a Half-Life game.
The only issue that this mod has is the amount of detail that was poured into it. Some large areas ( Like the woodmill ) are so detailed that it drops my framerate significantly. In addition, there are lots of props and areas that have strange lighting effects, but thats more of an issue with the engine and not the level design.
I enjoyed every minute of playing this mod and I can't wait for a second chapter.  If you have spare 30 minutes, I suggest you give this mod a try.

The story is good, when you really think about it. It's the story of a man going to the literal ends of the earth to save his daughter. But he lacks clear eyes.
Also has some of the funniest music and moments I've ever experienced in a game. Like seriously this♥♥♥♥♥♥is weird.
I would rate this game a 9/10, as it has some bugs, nothing that actually affects the story or anything, just sometimes things will not happen the way they were meant to be presented. It doesn't even affect the game. So no biggie.
But really, this game is hardcore, and it will break you down, slowly. You are presented with fairly hard choices, and you'll be left either googling what to do or wondering what you could've done better. Permadeath is a real thing. RNG will be your worst enemy. And depending on your choices, this game can be a cakewalk, or death at every turn.
There's a bit of strategy to this game, too. You can't just blunder your way through, because you will fail. Guaranteed. You have to pick your battles, pick your teammates, and learn things the hard way. This game WILL trick you. Sometimes it won't even disguise that. Regardless this game is deep and wide, and makes for a good game, especially for the price.
All in all, great game.
By the way, this is the middle game of the LISA trilogy. If you'd call it that. LISA: The First, comes before, then LISA the RPG, then the dlc.

Perhaps the most emotionally powerful game I've played. Those of you who have read about the game or watched one of the trailers know what the game is about already, but if you haven't, the game is full of metaphors that become clear by the end of the story, and it's devastating.
The gameplay itself is wonderful - it's a puzzle platformer, with some neat puzzle mechanics (changing the world to complete your objectives), with one bit right out of "Inception." The puzzles aren't too difficult, and there is even a hint box in every level in case you need a hint. The art direction is terrific (with street art commissioned from actual artists); combined with the music and sound design, it really immerses you in a favela like nothing else.
If you are looking for a well-told story that immerses you in the world of a young boy in a Brazilian slum dealing with a monster - I can't recommend this enough.

Hey, kids!  Do you remember the good old days when Sonic the Hedgehog was fast, cool, and fun to play, with great music, tight level design, and amazing controls?
Well, since Sega couldn't be bothered, someone else decided to give you a brand new Sonic game.  Freedom Planet is a 2-d sprite based game that pays massive tribute to the old Sonic the Hedgehog games on the Genesis, HOWEVER, it is, in my opinion, even better than those old classics.
First, the graphics.  Beautiful sprite work, with tons of expressive characters who can laugh, cry, hug, tease, hang out and watch a movie...the graphics are amazing, with a mix of polygon esque sprites and traditional hand drawn images.
Gameplay is tight and works well, with three different characters who all move fast, but all have different specials.  Lilac is my favorite, who has a double jump and a charge move for massive damage.  The speed is great here and the platforming even better.  There's lots of unique and organic level design that is just awesome.
Music.  Excellent in almost all regards.  Very power rocking but also somber at times, with a lot of variety.  Better yet is the timing and the sound effects, used for dramatic effect and comedy all in one package.
Story...wait, story?  Yeah, unlike the early Sonic games, Freedom Planet has an impressive story mode to go along with the classic arcade mode.  It's got tons of great humor, likable characters, and some truly gut wrenching moments here and there...showing just how powerful sprite art can really be.  The entire game is voice acted too and while some consider these actors unknown, they rival the best VAs I've ever heard in film or anime.  Able to emote and carry a story with the force of their voices mixed with the sprites on screen.
Freedom Planet is the total package.  It's beautiful to look at, it's got great music and gameplay, and a story that is, honestly, shocking in how engaging and powerful it is, as well as fun.
Now, no game is perfect, however.  The levels go on for just a tad too long and while I had plenty of lives up to the end of the game, the final boss is pretty cheap.  Still, that aside, the developers give you infinite continues and lots of check points, so it never gets too frustrating.
This game is amazing...please, support these devs.  I'd love to see a sequel.

Freedom Planet is an action-platformer that's heavily inspired by Sonic. It has smooth controls, multiple characters to play as, great music, lots of replayability and nice voice acting. I'm normally not a fan of Sonic-ish games but this one I'll highly recommend.

This game perfects the "gotta-go-fast" platformer better than anything SEGA has ever put out, including the original Sonic games.  The physics feel much more satisfying than sonic games, but they have that "Genesis/MegaDrive" feel of momentum and speed.  This game's mechanics really feel like they were meant to combat the common frustrations of 2D sonic games.
1. Sonic games use momentum so the player can run fast, but this makes platforming finicky at slow speeds.  Freedom Planet gives you a meter that builds up so you can instantly run your full speed; because it is easy to get to top speed, the designers can make the platforming physics and momentum feel better.
2. Sonic games use homing attack to let the player extend their jump, but this leads to easy deaths if you miss.  Freedom Planet uses a cyclone attack as your second jump, letting you float in the air for long enough to land safely.
3. Sonic games bind many functions to one button: spin dash, jump, homing attack all use one button.  This leads to whiffed attacks.  Freedom Planet uses three buttons: one for punches, one for jumps, one for the speed dash.  Even though each one of these buttons is bound to many different punches, jumps, and dashes, this compartmentalization really helps to keep the controls intuitive and fun.
4. Sonic games use a rings system to gauge extra lives and health.  This means that an unlucky series of two hits can always kill you, regardless of how many rings you have.  This makes death frequent and often surprising.  In a fast paced game like this, quick deaths feel cheap and unfair, making the game unfun.  Freedom Planet uses a leaves system where each attack takes away about one leaf from a total of 7.  This makes the game feel fair because you always have about 15-20 seconds of warning when you're about to die when your leaf count drops.  It also has a gems system that carries across levels.  150-ish gems for an extra life and the 1up music is excellent.
5. Sonic games train you to go right and up all the time, making the rare exploration segment feel slow and making the main segments feel like "hold right to win" as if the game is playing itself.  If you ever miss the upper path, you are almost encouraged to backtrack to get back on the upper path.  Freedom Planet is all about exploring and non-linear platforming and never lets you feel too lost.
6. Sonic games always feature unfun water sections, with an unclear breath meter and slower movement.  Freedom Planet keeps your movement speed fast in water, and the amount of air you have is listed in a bar.
This developer put a lot of time into fixing Sonic.  They succeeded.  The game has an Adventure mode and a Classic Mode.  Adventure mode inserts story cutscenes between levels; even though the voice actors are a bit amateurish, the voices manage to sound endearing instead of cringe-worthy like most 3D Sonic games.  "I'LL TAKE IT BY FORCE, THE HARD WAY."
Definitely worth it.

So, I thought I should finally review this game. This is Sonic Generations. The game was made for Sonic's 20th anniversary and so they wanted to include stages from past sonic games. To mix it up, each stage featured has a Classic and Modern sonic act.
Classic sonic's stages are all 2D, taking you back to the Sonic 1,2 and 3& Knuckles days. And I have to say that I was pleasantly surprised at the way they pulled it off. The control is good, the mechanics are familiar and the stages are beautiful. However, I prefer Modern sonic.
Modern sonic's stages are set in 3D. Like previous sonic games you are given the ability to boost, homing attack and lightspeed dash through stages. The control is perfect, the mechanics can be fun (although frustrating at times, I'm looking at you lightspeed dash!) and the stages look beautiful (although a little too linear). Although Modern sonic has 3D stages, portions of the stage are played in 2D. I feel this is to mix it up a bit, and it also adds a bit more complexity to the stages (albeit still quite linear). Sometimes you feel as though you don't need to do anything due to loops and straight paths. Overall, the gameplay is fun.
The story is, at best, ok. But, I don't really play sonic games for a deep story, I play cuz I wanna go fast! Anyway, the plot involves a mysterious being ripping through time and space, making you go through old stages to bring back colour. I won't go much further than that but you get the idea. The 2 sonics meet and work together to save the world. Moving on.
Now, this game is soooo much better than the abomination known as Sonic '06, however, it is incredibly short. Overall Rating 7/10
The Good
Storytelling is not only excellent but also the game’s strongest factor. The main narrative and conflict are morbidly captivating and deep. The art certainly helped contribute to the mood. It takes risqué, sprinkled with quirky comedy, and nails it. Major characters play their role very well and, if not relatable, at least understandable in the stances they take. Secondary characters are numerous and incorporated nicely. Consequences of your choices are reflected both in gameplay and story. Recruiting and exploring are emphasised and greatly rewarded. Mini-games are enjoyable where they are. Effort for implementing unconventional mechanics is generally appreciated
The Bad
There are a lot of unfun and overly frustrating game design choices. The core gameplay is boring and monotonous—battles, discovering new locations and missions play out the same way too often and lose excitement. Different sections of the world feel and look too much alike. Audio can also be unpleasant at times; this extends to music as well. A small number of minor question marks, relating to the main plot, were left without an answer at the end.
The End

Gorgeous, brilliant, intelligent, beautiful, surreal, magical. A treat for the eyes, the heart and the mind. This indie game cleverly mixes metaphor with gameplay in an amazing, colorful presentation. The puzzles themselves are not too challenging, but still provide a comfortable feeling of accomplishment when you conquer them. The platforming could have used a tiny bit of tweaking though. But the game's real goal is to let you share the emotional journey of the silent protagonist. Unfortunately, as the entire game is a metaphor I don't want to explain it too much by giving away the meaning (sadly the trailers, while beautifully made, blatantly tell the hidden meaning so I recommend to interested parties that they do /not/ watch them). Still, it's hard not to emphasize with the pint-sized hero as he explore his magical world even knowing what is coming. Definitely one of the most interesting games I've played this year.

Why so much hate for this game?
Yes it does have issues. There aren't a lot of players out there, and some days I genuinely won't play it because there isn't enough players. However, there always at least 5.
Some say the movement system is clunky, and i thought that at first. However, I quickly realised that if movement was too fast, the game would simply be running. In my opinion, it is great, and allows evasion of attacks without gifting excessive movement to new players. It also encourages parrying as a way to defend, essential to the game's mechanics.
There aren't a lot of variations either- 5 swords and 5 characters allows for 20 different combinations, and not all of them are used. There are enough though, and each person's play style is different enough to create a different experience for every person you fight.
The combat system is delightful, and creates many different ways of manipulating spacing, positioning and damage output.
I am only 10 hours in to this game and loving it already. I find the player base agreeable and helpful, and love the combat system.
TL;DR -- A great game with a tough learning curve, but has no limit to the skill that can be amassed. Slight content issues and a small player base doesn't stop this game from being great.
Pros-
Great combat system
Helpful player base
Cons-
Lack of content
Small player base

Freedom Planet was prior to its current incarnation a Sonic fangame. Once the producer realized he would never actually own the game, and Sega would boot him for it, he turned it into something original.
The game looks and feels just like the 16-bit platformers of the Sega Genesis/Mega Drive era. Whoever the spriter was managed to nail it right on target, it's so well crafted and put together, which is rare in modern day especially in the sense of true pixel art. I also feel it was developed under the limitations of the Genesis, but that may be a bit of a stretch.
The levels are extremely expansive and are about 3x larger than Sonic 3's levels, spanning about 7 minutes at least, and 15 minutes normally. It works in acts similar to Sonic but isn't labelled as such, it also has level transitions very similar to Sonic 3.
Gameplay-wise, it's like a lovechild of Sonic CD's platforming and Sonic 3's speed. Many have expressed their opinion that this game is a spritual Sonic 4, unlike Sega's version. I would have to agree, it's definitely got a lot of love and time put into it along with never really straying away from itself.
Oh yeah, the soundtrack is also AMAZING

TLDR First
Pros
-Fun Game, not starcraft 2, but something that can be a chill or an intense game depending on the game mode
-Very, very enjoyable with friends
Cons
-Pay to win commanders (this has been fixed but only after as the lifespan of the game is declining, they can now be earned, grindy but if you know which ones in each faction are the best it's not terrible since you might want 2 for each faction)
-Pay to win factions upon release (this has been fixed), almost as if to entice you to buy them before they get balanced months later, happened each time whereby new factions were very much notably stronger then base factions
-PvP netcode is still playable but has a delay, could be do to less players online, PvE is usually good
Controversial Game Play Wise
-RNG (some might say it implies realism but I personally think it seems to hampers the gameplay
-Slow to kill with infantry before mid-game but this may be balanced to the developers wanting matches to last longer
-Upkeep of army means less resource income (some say this mechanic allows for comebacks of worse players) but it seems semi-realistic and if you're grinding them down they're almost certainly going to lose unless they outmaneuver you
-Suppression mechanic
It's a fun game that's nice to play anytime, dropping mortars on supressed squads feels satisfying as does outflanking the enemy with tanks and other units. The main thing that grinds my gears (yes, I'm guilty of it though mostly versus bots) is the pay 2 win commanders up until a year ago. The AI pathing or missing shots in front of them can be frustrating but taken as a whole with your entire army it's not game breaking. The supression mechanic is  arguably a bad one though it may be realistic, it could have been better if they changed it for a large or possibly moderate increase in damage output to set up machineguns and that way infantry would have more of a chance to use grenades on them early-mid game especially on city maps. As it is right now it appears machineguns are the op go-to unit of choice, yes you can get rid of them, but that seems to only be much easier late game.
If this was on release with OP pay to win commanders and super OP pay to win factions I guess it depends on your view of whether or not a game is worth it with the release of other games doing the same thing...but it's been changed. Overall as it is now I'd buy it and just do PvE to get the hang of things and earn some supply currency. 300+ hours of playtime, worth the purchase even just for the initial non-dlc factions, all factions appear to more or less be balanced now.

A frustration machine. Play only if you enjoy rage and, subsequently,  rage-quitting. A game I played far too long because the story and setting are rather lovely. The attitude of the game, though, is YOU WILL LOVE MY PRECIOUS GAME MECHANICS.
I don't love your mechanics, though. While a good idea, overall, they are flawed by: (1) a horrible cursor that obscures targets, (2) a targeting highlight policy that's all-or-nothing, both in direction and distance, so you don't get any idea if you were barely there or way off, (3) a targeting highlight policy that's all-or-nothing, so you get zero advance hint about when a grapple might be successful, (4) level assets with poor graphic design that give little cue about distance but have very similar appearance, needless yinterfering with distance estimatation, (5) a seriously bad horizontal momentum system that brakes far faster than air actually does (braking is proportional to the square of velocity, but you die most often falling straight, straight down), (6) and which also means that it's harder to swing around grapple points, meaning you run into them more often, (7) no visual concept of your own body size, so it's impossible to estimate in advance when you will run into a grapple point, (8) a policy that insists that you click only on top of grapple point, not nearby, making it impractical to plan on grappling edges, (9) level design that insists that YOU WILL BECOME PROFICIENT IN WHAT I WANT TO YOU *RIGHT* *NOW* DO OR YOU MAY PROGRESS NO FARTHER (there's a good reason I have no desire to play NES games), which could readily be addressed by smoother presentation of skill challenges, (10) route-finding by trial-and-error when only the first part of the route is even visible and the route has to be done dynamically, leading to an utterly implausible mesh of story and mechanics, because no teenager is going to magically find all those routes and live to tell the tale, and (11) I'm sure there's more but I don't care right now.
tl;dr: Not fun. Don't play.

It seems like I've had this game forever and never installed it.  I was told it was like Grand Theft Auto so I thought I'd give it a try.
First, I'll say that I didn't feel like it was GTA.  It has driving and you can steal cars and such, but I rarely felt like I needed to just go driving around to do side missions.  In fact, there wasn't really much in the way of side missions, and the city, although large, was nothing compared to GTA V.  If I had to guess I would say it is closer in size to Liberty City from GTA 3.
Pros:
1. The story was great.  It was pretty fast paced but kept me engaged pretty much the whole time.  It took me 14 hours to finish but some of that was me walking away from the pc for various things like making something to eat.
2.  The melee combat is pretty good.  I didn't care for the hand to hand at first but came to enjoy it later in.  It is a shame they didn't have you do more of it.  The missions that required it were a lot of fun to me.
3.  Shooting felt good and fluid.  The shotgun was the only weapon I didn't care for.  I spent most of my time with the 1911 .45 because it felt good.
4.  Voice acting was great.  This isn't normally a big deal to me, but I was happy they took it seriously.
5.  I thought it did a great job of balancing the cost of being in the mafia, with the benefits.  It is always a worry that someone will glorify being a thug but I never felt like they were doing that.  You were constantly in trouble and someone was out to get you.  Not a life I would want for sure.
Cons:
1. Lack of side missions.  I was almost reluctant to call this a con.  On one hand it is nice to have focus in a linear story line, on the other, it is a shame to create such a large place to play in and have almost nothing to do in it.  It is a sandbox that someone forgot to put sand in.
2. Again, this is a con to me but I suspect a lot of folks might call this a pro.  The cars.... I'll say they were 'too' authentic.  I know the game's purpuse is to drawn you into the time period and the cars surely helped that immersion.  The problem I had with them is that every damn one of them drove like♥♥♥♥♥♥  Even the rare fast one couldn't handle very good.  With the game making you drive all over the place and almost constantly run from police, I quickly found myself wanting a better car.
3.  Money...  This game you need money almost constantly and you almost never have it.  There are things to buy and upgrades to get but you never seem to have enough to do any of those things.
Overall I enjoyed the game and I'd recommend it to any gamer.

XBOX 1 / PS4 gamepad issue temporary fix:
Wait to turn the controller on until after the game has started. This works for me with my XBOX 1 controller, but I haven't experimented enough yet to make it work for my Dual Shock 4 while using the DS4Windows app. After doing a quick search, it's clear that I'm not the only one who had to fight with Zidane constantly moving left as soon as the game gives the player control.
This controller issue is another derpy performance from Square Enix, which I think many of us have come to expect, especially in their PC ports of classic Final Fantasy games. I enjoyed my playthrough of it back when it was originally released on the Playstation 1. Anyone looking for a more detailed review of the games content can easily find one with a quick online search.
The framerate is unfortunately locked at about 15-20 fps during battle and on the overworld map (though the damage / healing numbers strangely seem to be animated at about 30 fps over the slide show), but since this is how the game ran originally, I'm not going to hold it against my recommendation of this port.
A few quick button presses from the start menu allow you to double the speed of the game, enable always full ATB/Trance/HP/MP, constant 9999 damage, or disable random encounters. The double speed is a nice way to counteract the slow pace of battle (there are frequent pauses between character and enemy turns that slow down the pace), and disabling random encounters will be nice for areas with weak enemies. A 1.5x speed option would have been nice since the 2x is so fast. The other 2 are cheats of course for those who can't handle a bit of challenge, just want to play around, or don't want to grind :)
The graphics are nicely done. The new character and enemy models have some extra detail on their textures, and I think there have a been a few more polygons added to the main characters. The movies have been very tastefully up-scaled to look good at a higher resolution. Environment backgrounds have been given a smoothing effect, which is an improvement, but not quite as nice as the character models. The text font looks sharp.

This is a fun one. Absolutely one of the more interesting RPGs I've played in quite some time.
This narrative is♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ And only through the act of playing it all the way through does the player gain a smidge of understanding about what is really happening.
So, the world is over, and the surviving old men are busy being depressed, doing absolutely nothing, or dressing up as women constantly. And it really makes sense once you think about it. A world with no women is a world with no hope, and the NPCs in this game generally act the part; that is, when they aren't meming like champs. There in lies the crux of the conflict; what to do when you have to balance something that has value to you, and something that has value to literally everyone in existence.
Lisa as a narrative piece often shifts between the wacky to the disturbing to the sobering. It's easy to get whiplash, and I know I did. Between the main storyline, the just plain creepy episodes, and the levels full of people ready to get womped, its hard not to get sucked in. There's a charm to this tone; sort of like a fallout game that has more focus on being gross than being entertaining. Brad's struggle to destroy every major gang leader on the face of the planet is an endearing one, considering the circumstances and the difficult choices posed when one plays this game. The game plays around a lot with the concept of value. Specifically, what is the value of a human life. Tough stuff.
The gameplay itself blends very nicely into this; though in reality it is standard RPG maker fare. Everything feels balanced for the most part. Bosses are beatable, if a bit unfair at times. If I were to complain, the biggest part of the game that let me down was the constant problems with trying to heal my party. I can understand that this is the wacky wasteland, and you're actively trying to waste my time, but poisoning my party, or randomly taking someone out of my party is just going to make me reload my latest save file. And, that it did. Several times. In fact, I would probably attribute an hour of my total game time alone to just reloading save files from unfair events; hell, lets tack on another hour for just backtracking to a safe resting location once I actually found one. A stronger man would play through it, but really my priorities are to actually keep my strongest party members with me, thanks.
Speaking of party members, there are a metric ton of them in this game. A huge amount of variety on offer here, though your mileage may vary on who exactly you deem to be useful enough to keep around. In my playthrough I found a couple party members who were reliably able to deal 1K damage a turn; and I also kept a member who was able to blind opponents; which is a skill that I would probably say is required to finish the game. By and large, If found healing characters to be obsolete by the half way mark, and instead opted for members who were tanky but also able to fight effectively. Again, your mileage may vary.
Without spoiling anything, the ending messed me up in a very unique way. Lisa is a very lengthy game, and by the time it feels like closing, things were getting a bit contrived. But still, things wrapped themselves up in an interesting, but not entirely satisfying way. Then I booted up the DLC.
Lisa the Painful is Brad's story. Lisa the Joyful is Buddy's story. It's a direct continuation of the main game, and it really puts some closure on things, though most of the tone and lingering difficulties remain accounted for. This time, you actually don't have an objective other than to kill everyone. So, I guess that's more straightforward. Balancing feels way off in the DLC, basically creating an environment where you are forced to take drugs. No followers. No new party members. No nothing. The end of the world is here; and boy does Lisa the Joyful make it obvious. It's not difficult, just boring. The bosses have inflated HP values, leading to long drawn out battles that consist of CCing the enemy, attacking, and then CCing the enemy. What a bore.
But the ending of Lisa the Painful is where it really comes together. Somewhere, it looses focus, and then spirals into mediocrity. It's more obvious to me that this is just extra content to be thrown at the wall. Nothing too much to write home about, aside from some telling dialogue. Otherwise, it was a complete wash.
I recommend Lisa for anyone looking for a ride in a wacky wasteland's clothing. I'd also say that the DLC generally isn't worth it unless you're really hurting to see whats next. Just be aware that there really isn't much more Lisa has to say that it already hasn't in the base game.

Okay, I love sword fighting. That's pretty much the only reason I bought this game. This review isn't all positive. I wish I had nothing bad to say about this game... sadly that's not true. If there was a button between Recommended and Not Recommended, that's where this review would be.
Blade Symphony is a sword fighting game combining parkour elements with various sword fighting techniques. Unfortunately, the wall running doesn't work 100% of the time. Granted, it does work the majority of the time, but sometimes when you attempt it, you'll just roll at the wall and get stabbed in the back.
The combat mechanisms are all right, nothing really that great. The combo system does add a bit of repetetiveness to the combat, because you're doing the same couple moves EVERY time, some of which don't help your situation at all. It would be a lot better if they gave you more freedom over your moves.
The combat itself is a bit buggy at times. Sometimes your stabs don't register on the enemy, your sword sometimes will just slide off the person you're fighting like they aren't even there. Also, the throwing stars you get can be a bit annoying, seeing as they're nearly impossible to actually dodge, you have to block them with your sword. sometimes the enemy will have their sword behind them as they charge you, throw a star at them and their sword instantly snaps up to block it. It's not very fair, making attacking from a distance if you have low hp difficult and just annoying.
The art style and the animations though? They're pretty awesome. If the devs would actually update the game now and again, it would be pretty fantastic.
That's all I can really say for now. Don't get me wrong, I don't hate this game, however the bugs make it a little hard to enjoy.

The game starts with an advertisement screen for the company's other games.  Later, it pops up a nag screen to rate it.  I paid for this game.  It's not freeware.  So, here's the rating it demands:  Not Recommended.  Fish poops.
EDIT:  After a total of 15.9 hours (9.8 hours to complete the base game on Hard without maps, 1.8 hours, similarly, for the Bonus Chapter, and 4.3 hours to get the remaining Achievements (on Easy with maps)), I've now finished the game.  So, here's some information on the game, itself.  It basically plays almost exactly like the previous game (Lost Lands:  The Four Horsemen (TFH)):
- A lot of good work went into the story, graphics, and puzzles.
- The voice acting is fairly terrible (about par for the genre).
- The puzzles aren't Hidden Object Games (HOGs), they're Chain of Object Games (COOGs).
- The collectables (particularly the morphing objects and the statuettes) are so ridiculously camouflaged that they're essentially impossible to get.
- The key/lock pairs are so far apart physically and temporally that it's impossible to remember what belongs to what (or even that it exists).  This gets much better when playing with the map, since then you merely have to look at it, see what's active, jump there, and use any new objects.
Also, getting left over mini-game Achievements is helped since we can do them in the Extras area once the game is done.  But, HOGs and collectibles have to be done in game (which means starting over if we didn't get them the first time through).
I'm not changing my rating from my initial Not Recommended, though.  I rated TFH as a just barely borderline Recommended.  But, the starting advertisement and the rating nag screen here just pushed the game over into Not Recommended territory.  However, if you liked TFH and don't mind the ads/nags, feel free to give this a try.  You might like it.

Freedom Planet caught my eye on the front page of Steam during the summer sale with its cute and colorful art style, and once I watched the trailer and read a couple reviews I decided to impulse buy it. And wow am I glad that I did.
This game is an action platformer that is similar to the original Sonic the Hedgehog games. Now I've never been a huge Sonic fan, only playing a few of the games casually, but I was instantly hooked to Freedom Planet the minute I started playing. It's fast paced (without the same momentum that Sonic games have that kind of force you to keep moving), has a colorful pixel art style, a great soundtrack, and the story is exciting and packed with creative characters and a cute sense of humor. Plus, if you're not a fan of stories and just want the gameplay, you can play on classic mode. The gameplay is fun and challenging, with unique levels and boss fights, and there's a time attack mode if you are looking for an extra challenge. And each level has a lot of room for exploration, plus there are collectible cards in each level that will keep you playing over and over again.
Seriously, Freedom Planet is an amazingly fun game with lots of replay value that I wish more people knew about. It is well worth the price, whether you get it on sale or decide to purchase it for the full price.

Freedom Planet is about the adventures of Lilac and Carol. The evil Lord Brevon have sent the planet into chaos in order to steal the kingdom stone. After Carol and Lilac meet Torque and Milla, they all join forces to foil Brevon evil plot. The story progresses like a Saturday morning cartoon, which for me wasn't a bad thing. I like that nostalgic feeling and brought me back to my younger days of watching cartoons where our heroes must stop the evil villian. With all the characters voiced, you can tell that the people who made this game had fun with this. Honestly it was a great story and worth playing again just to take it all in.
The gameplay is where this game really shine. This game doesn't have Freedom in the name for nothing. This not just linear 2D platformer. Often time I found myself going left, right, up, down, etc to reach my goal. So often do side scroller 2D platformers like Mario or Sonic just have the player go in one direction to reach the end. But with Freedom Planet, I found myself going in many directions, yet it always seem to progress me forward toward the goal of the level. You can play through the main story with either Carol and Lilac, each with their own style. Lilac plays as a Sonic like character; she can charge up and shoot herself at light speed in a direction and have a hover jump attack. Carol can climb up walls and zip through levels on her motorcycle. And if the play styles for these two characters wasn't enough to encourage a second playthrough, then you must also know that each character got a few unique levels to their single player. Second thing I like about these characters is when you play as Lilac, Carol or Milla may show up to help you attack a boss or give you some help. Sonic Team take note, this is how you should handle all of Sonic's friends. Don't force the player to learn their play style but rather have them show up to help you!
To make a long paragraph short, the gameplay style is fast pace and with challenges ranging from different type of enemies to just challenging platforming section. From the beginning to the ending level boss, you'll find yourself having fun with these levels.
This is what indie game should strive to be. This game is easily one of my all time favorite indie game. Between the story, voiced character, fun levels, challenging enemies, hidden items to find, and amazing soundtrack there really nothing to not like about this game. If this wasn't enough, there are more characters coming to game (from the stretch goals being met). I hope to see you all on Freedom Planet!

On the surface Freedom Planet may seem like a pretty straightforward Sonic the Hedgehog clone, and if it was that'd be fine and dandy, but it's something quite a bit more. It's a celebration of all things Sega Genesis, and feels just as heavily influenced by Treasure's classic game Gunstar Heroes. The colors and sounds will all be instantly familiar with anyone who grew up in the 16-bit days, and what you will find is a beautiful game with fast action, tight controls, gorgeously designed levels that beg to be explored and replayed, cute characters and even a pretty entertaining story with some endearingly camp voice acting. Give it a shot.

This game is an interesting Sonic inspired game that has a lot of good things going for it with only the occasional fault causing a bit of distraction in what is otherwise a very fun experience. As of writing this I have only played from Lilac's route so will be using that as my baseline.
The game is a very solid platformer that has a good mix of enemies, items, platforming areas, and areas of rewarding speed. The bosses are interesting, diverse, and are difficult enough to challenge while not so hard as to be frustrating. The gameplay overall is very satisfying and the key strength of this title. It is fun to play and proves that at least someone knows how to make a Sonic-like game.
The design of the game is interesting, as I can not tell whether or not I like it. The character designs are very reminiscent of the Sonic series not only in their anthropomorphism but in the proportions and sizes as well. The pallette that was chosen is very diverse and pleasing, characters standing out and the levels feeling very distinct from one another. While I generally like most of the character designs, I have found several instances of animations or sprites that could use improvement, for example the most common seen within a game of this type: running. Lilac runs with her arms spread behind her which leads to a still top half and her feet stop as they hit the ground. This gives a bit of an odd feeling to the game at times and distracts from the goodpoints of the game. This is, admittedly, a nitpick, but worthy of attention as a lot of praise is being given to the spritework of the game.
The voice acting in the game has both strong points and weak points. The voice cast chosen are all very capable voice actors and actresses which is good to see. I am not used to the bright, anthropomorphised characters with rather normal voices, but this is simply a personal issue that many might not find troubling. The voice of Lilac can occasionally grate by simple fact of her chatter in the game. Specifically, yelling 'Cyclone!' every time you use the jump extension technique, which in my case is very frequently. Again, a very small complaint, but can be quite distracting at times.
The writing is a bit... cheesy. I personally am not a fan of most of the dialog. While not painfully bad by any means, it comes off as very adolescent at times to which I am not personally a fan. This may not bother many people though, as again the voice acting is done well and even through the criticism here I wouldn't call the writing horrible. The world it takes place in is a mix of Chinese and Japanese culture. Much more leaning towards China, really, with the occasional interjection of Japanese as well. Personally, this comes off as a bit confused and I would have liked to see a stricter choice to one or the other extremes. I do not think that a mix is bad, just that it was not realized to an extent that justified the mix in this case.
Overall all the complaints are rather minor, as I do find the game fun to play. Something which, in the end, is the most important part of any game. I enjoy playing and think that it is worth the full price even before delving into the other characters available.

What happens when you attempt to merge Classic Sonic mechanics with Ristar mechanics, Sparkster mechanics, and Socket/Time Dominator mechanics but do it terribly, slap on some mediocre OCs, and complete it with a terrible story and awful voice acting? You get this clusterf*ck. Freedom Planet is about Lilac, a dragon, Carol, a wildcat, and Milla, a basset hound dog as they attempt to stop a 3 way war breaking out from the Kingdom Stone being stolen. The game plays similar to the previous games stated above. Lilac has a meter that automatically fills your dash meter like Sparkster. The dash is very similar to Ristar when he lets go of a lever at full speed or Sparkster when he dashes when the meter is full. Carol can spin like Sonic. She also rides a motorcycle (What?) like Shadow. Milla plays strangely like a mix of Mario and Mega Man. She can create a shield which can then be turned into a short burst of energy and creates blocks that can be thrown at enemies. However they have different melee attacks which REALLY slow down the gameplay. Each character runs at at jogging pace and they only speed up in certain areas, if you use dash as Lilac, or if you're on the motorcycle as Carol. The controls are slippery, stiff, and floaty. You'll always be sliding off platforms. The gameplay tries to switch it up here and there but it doesn't work. The story is convuleted and it doesn't help with the horrendous voice acting. It just drags on. There are times where the game wants you to feel for these characters but you really just can't take them seriously. Also, we have generic character archetypes such as the edgy bad-boy, the misguided hero, and the mind controlled friend. Speaking of dragging on, the levels are not only unnecessarily long but they're tedious. The design is terrible. You'll sometimes feel lost because everything looks the same and due to the camera being too zoomed in, you can take hits from from off-screen enemies which is incredibly annoying. The theme of the game seems to be inspired from Asia. Even the moral has a wise grand master like feel to it. When there's only just one theme for your art design though, it just comes of as generic and lacking as there is no variety in the graphics department. The bosses are too frantic and unpredictable making them irritating and will waste a chunk of your time when you keeping dying. Great music, and lovely graphics aside, this game is just bad. It fails to capture the essence of momentum based platforming and tries too hard to be unique in its own way with the ideas they tried to implement. DON'T waste your time or money on this disappointment.

tl;dr Mafia II is only worth play is you can enjoy a linear game that looks and feels like a sandbox game
Minor spoilers ahead
Mafia II is deceptive in that presents itself as an open world game, whilst actually being a highly linear experience with the trappings of a sandbox. The game holds your hand all the way through to the point that there is little to do outside of the main quest series. Even in the main quests there is no expression of choice or freedom - the hallmarks of a sandbox game.
Having said that, I have not played Mafia I, so for veterans this may be tried and true formula. Mafia II does in fact execute aspects of the game adroitly. Namely, the visuals, soundtrack, level design, pacing, story-telling and the main quests. The visuals are by far the best aspect of Mafia II. The game is rich with references from the 50s (at least I think so) and captures the atmosphere with grace. Judged by visuals alone, it is a game that is brimming with potential. Unfortunately it remains unfulfilled.
SPOILERS: Despite expert story-telling, the plot itself is lacklustre. While starting off strong in Cuba and telling the tale of a soldier's homecoming, it succumbs to certain sins of narrative. Mainly that the plot progresses barely through the actions of the protagonist but mostly through random and unexpected things that happen to him. Most instigators to entire sections of the game are meaningless and seem so contrived as to insult the player.
It's not a bad game per se, but I would still consider it a poor man's Godfather (PS2).

Papo & Yo is a quiet game , but it's telling a story contains lots of strong emotions and deep feelings , it needs us to pay a little bit attention to listen and find out .

In the begining , everything looked so peaceful , brought me some kind of calmness . As I was going deeper , I couldn't help realizing that Quico has been bearing a lot , that he must protect the ones he loves , help the one who hurts him......that I must help Quico to fix all of this . I think this is the main reason I continued playing .
We all make mistakes , grown-up might have a childish immature heart , doing irrational things that only hurt oneself and others , while a little one might have the strongest soul . It doesn't matter how much time that one has been living , what matters the most is that we have the ability to help each other .
So I thought the game is about saving an angry monster , and I believed I'd done so . But in the end , I realized there's something beyond salvation . I played as Quico , had to do the final steps by myself , all the conflicts within was about to explode . When it's done , we might understand something .
Papo & Yo is a beautiful story , and the story has been being told beautifully . The art is gorgeous in it's own way , very bright and colorful , lighting up the dim raining days , along with the music , creating an exotic world that you want to stay and explore , the ending song is very touching . Lots of elements in the game are symbolic , but it isn't hard to understand , instead , finding out the meaning of these elements by continue playing makes the game more fascinating and engaging .
Another thing I love about this game is the level designs . The puzzles are so brilliant and inspiring , you solving them by interacting with the imaginative environment . These two parts are blending in with each other beautifully , for several times I was just "Wow" . But every time the monster was in madness , the whole world was immersed in red color , it felt really uncomfortable . And I admit I'm scared of the mad monster , when I was being chased , I could hardly see myself because the monster was so big . The game is a little bit short though , It only took me 4.6h to finish , but I didn't find all the hats , it might be a glitch because I couldn't wear any of them .
Papo and Yo is not a perfect game , but it's beautiful and good enough , I strongly recommend it !!!

A Story About My Uncle was the most captivating yet short stories I have played. I have been following the development of this project for years, and after finally getting to play the finished version I have to say it was well worth the wait. The music, atmospheric level design, and the short story mix beautifully to create an artistic and immersive experience for the player, and I was enthralled for the entire journey. Every leap and jump across the visually stunning environments felt so real, despite the fantasy aspect of the game.
One of the two downsides of the game has to be certain parts of the levels, where almost pin-point accuracy is needed to successfully progress through the story. This can become slightly frustrating at times, but definitely do-able eventually. The other downside is that, at times, I lost my sense of direction and had to spend time searching corners and edges of the map that could be the way foward, which slightly took away from the immersion.
Overall, the large positives drastically outweigh the small negatives of the game, and I highly recommend buying this game as a beautiful, story driven, peaceful piece of art.

Sonic Generations is a game where you play as Modern Sonic, and Classic Sonic. Modern Sonic's gameplay is very similar to how Unleashed played just with better physics and remapped controls. Classic Sonic is very reminiscent of how it was in Sonic 2.
The story is about as basic as a children's book. But that's good since we've gotten "edgier" Sonic stories in the past and nobody liked those. It's just padding between stages and I'm fine with that.
The levels are short and snappy. Filled with fun elements and tons of shortcuts. (You'll have a blast finding all of the shortcuts and figuring out how to get the best times.) The graphics and textures for these levels just pop straight out of your screen. I was playing this game while a friend was over, and he said the colors were almost overwhelming. Just like how colorful the classic games were.
The gameplay is fun for both Sonic's, but you'll be spending more time with Modern Sonic. Modern Sonic's gameplay is far superior than Classic Sonic's. If you love the old gameplay style, you probably will feel a little odd with Classic Sonic. His levels are long and drawn out for his new speed. If I wanted to blaze around the stage without a care, I would pick Modern Sonic. (And I do.) But if you just want to have tight platforming, I'm sorry. (This goes for both Sonic's.)
This game is great in it's vanilla state. But it also has a humongous modding community with thousands of mods you can sink your time into. (And I reccommend checking them out.)
Sonic Generations story is nothing interesting, the gameplay is fun for both Sonic's, (though I enjoy Modern Sonic's gameplay way more) the levels are fun and creative, and the graphics are simply stunning.
I reccommend this game at full price, since the mods add alot more content to the game. But in vanilla form... I still reccommend it.
I give Sonic Generations a solid 8.5/10. Would definitley buy it if you're a diehard Sonic fan, or a newcomer. Both groups will love this masterpiece of a game!

I will not say that this game is like Sonic the Hedgehog, as so many other fools have said. Sonic is like Ozymandias of the sonnet, a spectre in time who was king, claiming a supremacy that history did not deliver; indeed, the very ruins and vestiges of his empire embarrass his legacy. Freedom Planet plays as new, as it should; it's gameplay of smooth platforming and light combat serve as a model of evolution. It's better than Sonic's best. It is as far removed from Sonic as it is from Pitfall.

This game is pretty much a fan made spiritual sequel to 16-bit Sonic games. If you enjoyed them, then I highly recommend this game! While it is obviously inspired by Sonic, it still plays differently enough to have its own identity. There are three different characters that all play differently. All females, and the main character Lilac really looks like a character that could be from Sonic series. She totally looks like a hedgehog (well, as much as Sonic does), apparently it says she's a dragon.
There is a story mode with full voice acting, something I did not expect from a game that uses 16-bit art style, so that's pretty nice. I have to give my respect for the developers and voice actors, for actually making a quite lenghty cutscenes for a retro platformer. For those who don't care about the story there is Classic Mode, which removes all story and cutscenes.
But the main thing is that the gameplay is good and fun. Pixel graphics are well done and the music is nice too. Stages are mostly good, but it kinda makes me wish there would be even more possibilites for going fast. Boss fights are mostly good too.
The bottom line is that it's a well made retro platformer, and all platformer fans should try it.

Tired of Indie games that your friend insists is one of the best games ever, but only plays once every four years? Well, get ready for the indie game that your friend insists is one of the best games ever, and plays once every THREE years! It’s just that good.
Freedom Planet.
Freedom; a word the evokes uninhibited exploration. Planet; a word used to describe worlds so big, Pluto doesn’t make the cut anymore. Get ready to explore a sprawling Metroidvania that is worthy of its title... what? It’s a level-by-level platformer with no upgrades? Then why is it called Freedom Pla [cut]
Welcome to planet Avalice. Embark on an epic two-and-a-half hour adventure with your choice of character. Blaze through over ten stages as Girl Sonic…-Ristar...-Gunstar...-Ryu...-Dragon... Okay, that’s awesome. Leave something for your sidekick, why don’t you? [clip of sidekick driving a motorcycle up a wall] Nevermind.
Use your skills to speed through huge lovingly detailed levels with multiple paths, then spend eighty percent of your time stuck trying to defeat bosses again and again in vain because you’re too stubborn to lower the difficulty. Ughh, how am I supposed to beat this guy?! He just punches out of nowhere and takes half my health! I’m not even playing on Hard! Patch this already! Oh good, they did. All right! Time to download… wait, I already have it? NOOOOOOOO [cut]
Get ready to experience a loving homage to Sonic, Ristar, Treasure, and every other awesome Sega Genesis \ Mega Drive and Saturn game every made, with quarter-pipes, crazy loop-de-loop structures, high-speed launches,  sweet music and sound effects, elemental shields, the dread of running out of oxygen, really big lasers, really big explosions, really big bosses that shake the screen when they attack and lag the framerate when they die,  and those cool spiral elevators that were in..,. uh… Launch Base Zone? Hydrocity Zone? You know, that zone with the cool spiral elevators in it. They’re in this game.
Then watch it burn your childhood nostalgia into a crisp by pointing out all the problems your favourite games had, and fixing them with simple features like: difficulty selection, more than one useful move per character, a perky 1-up jingle that only plays when the mood calls for it, a reasonable difficulty curve that ****s with you on purpose instead of drunkenly stumbling between too easy and too hard, the ability to pause cut-scenes, the ability to skip cut-scenes, the ability to not accidentally skip cut-scenes just by looking at the controller funny, an icon that tells you when something’s about to kill you from off-screen WHY DON’T SONIC GAMES EVER HAVE THOSE?! [breath], and swimming.
Use your cunning to conserve your health bar and cherish health pick-ups like water in a desert… or play on Easy and watch as your health regenerates before your eyes. You might as well; the achievements don’t care. And you can change the difficulty any time you want. See? This cleared save file has 100 deaths because I played on Normal, but do you see the word “Normal” anywhere on there? For all you know, I lost all those lives on Casual. But trust me, you guys, it was on Normal.
Cringe, at a, well, honestly, a surprisingly well-fitting story featuring: Decapitations, Brainwashing, Worldwide War, Making New Friends, Political Intrigue, Wholesale Asskicking, Playful Teasing, Horrifying Mutations, Cold-Blooded Torture, and All-You-Can-Eat Sushi. Mmmmm. Sewwwwsh.
Once you’ve played out the Adventure Mode, take on a variety of extra modes such as: Classic Mode, which is Adventure Mode minus the cutscenes, Time Attack Mode, which is Classic Mode plus a level select menu, and… ummmm…
Then, hunt for 100 cards hidden throughout the game, and try to collect the achievements, which are one part speedruns, one part card collection, one part challenges that would be tough if you couldn’t do them on any difficulty, and three parts wacky bull**** like “notice our dance easter egg”, “let the AI partner get the last hit on this boss”, and the ultimate bragging rights reward: “stand on a ledge.”
But seriously you guys, you think I’d write a review this long for a game I think is just ok? No. It’s tons of fun. Buy it now!

This game is amazing. It has interesting characters, levels, and a good story, and amazing voice actors. That's right this game is fully voice acted, and all of them are great. Every level has new enemy types so you'll rarely see them reused, the maps are just as diverse. There are three playable characters Lilac the Dragon, Carol the Wildcat, and Milla the Basset Hound. All of them play wildly different and have different levels specific to their particular character meaning that even on your third play through you'll still be seeing new content. That's not even counting the time trials or collectables.
The game loses point for being quite hard to play without a controler, not impossible, just hard. On the topic of hard the game is difficult but you always feel like it's your fault you died. The bosses are difficult and require you to learn their patterns to beat with any level of ease. You'll quickly find which character is your favourite and start ripping through the opposition... mostly.
You'll see a lot of people comparing this to Sonic games, as someone who has never played a Sonic game (aside from Sonic 06) this is exactly what I imagined Sonic games to be like. It's fun, it's fast, it's interesting, and it's full of content. I've played for 8 hours and I've only beat the game with one character, have next to none of the time trials done, and about 10% of the collectables.
Do yourself a favour and buy this game. My friend introduced me to it, so play it, love it, and tell all your friends. If this game can become a series I'm certain it will eclipse Sonic games very soon. While Sonic is surely a great series I don't have to play it to know there hasn't been a good one in ages.
If I had to rate this game I'd give it a 9/10. Full of interesting content, hours worth of fun. but there are some glitches and I'd highly reccomend playing with a controler if you have one.

Papo & Yo was a bit on the easy side, even though I was pretty stumped at the scrapyard scene with its colossal tower-in-building. The game was solid. Everything worked and it did not glitch to my recollection. I liked the game a bit, but despite its shortness it was starting to grate on me nearing the end. Not because the end was bad or anything -- the game simply wore out its tricks.

A 3D puzzle platformer set in a fantastical favela. Inspired by the personal story of one of the creators, Papo & Yo explores some dark themes.
While the game quickly became find-the-chalk-drawing, all the contraptions were always fun to watch and filled with child-like imagination.

A very endearing, moving, sad and yet sometimes whimsical game. It does what Alice in Wonderland tried but much better.
I was surprised I've never heard of it before and hopefully it was successful enough to guarantee the next game from this team.

Papo & Yo is the story of a boy who wants to save his friend Monster. On the surface this seems rather silly and simplistic, but it is a metaphor for a very real and heart wrenching tragedy. It is highly uncommon to see real world social issues brought up in games, especially social issues which no one wants to talk about, but Papo & Yo does this beautifully. The core gameplay is a puzzle platformer. The puzzles are quite easy to be honest, and if you get stuck it has a built in help system. The world you are in is very surreal and fantastical (think Salvador Dali), and is set in a bario neighborhood somewhere in South America. The soundtrack in this game is just fantastic as well. You must play this game to the end, or else it will not make much sense.  While this is certainly not the best game I have ever played, it is by far one of the most memorable. Papo & Yo takes about 3-4 hours to complete.
9/10

A Story About My Uncle is a unique twist on puzzle platformers. It begins with a father telling his daughter a bedtime story about an adventure he went on when he was younger. The player is a young nephew who gets lost on an alien world in search of his missing uncle.
The platforming mechanics are done well, however they quickly become repetitive. The player unlocks a few different tools to help navigate the world, however the main one is the grappling mechanism. The grappling mechanism allows the user to swing/pull it's user towards an object. The other two tools at the users disposale are the rocket boots and the super jump.
The levels feel unique and are well designed, however the difficulty is problematic. The difficulty has no real curve, it is all over the place with giant difficulty spikes preceeded and proceeded by dull, easy, repetitive sections.
Along the way, the nephew can find cleverly hidden objects that can unlock fun additions to the game like changing the color of the grappling beam, the funny goat mode (changes the players audio to that of a goat), midas mode (everything you grapple turns to gold), and acrobatic mode (spins the player around while in the air).
I was really looking forward to a good story, and the intro leads you on into thinking there is one. Sadly it is quite flat and not very flushed out. The game is rather short, however that is not always a bad thing if the story can keep me captivated, but I found myself wishing the pace would pick up and it never did. It took me around five hours to complete the game. The ending is also quite bland and sudden. I was hoping for some kind of major twist or a final boss like in the Portal series, but it let me down...
Other than the main story mode, there is also a time trial mode where the player competes against the clock on the various levels, and can be rather challenging at times.
For being a good platformer I have to recommend the game if you have a few hours to spend and can find it on sale.

This is a fun one. Absolutely one of the more interesting RPGs I've played in quite some time.
This narrative is♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ And only through the act of playing it all the way through does the player gain a smidge of understanding about what is really happening.
So, the world is over, and the surviving old men are busy being depressed, doing absolutely nothing, or dressing up as women constantly. And it really makes sense once you think about it. A world with no women is a world with no hope, and the NPCs in this game generally act the part; that is, when they aren't meming like champs. There in lies the crux of the conflict; what to do when you have to balance something that has value to you, and something that has value to literally everyone in existence.
Lisa as a narrative piece often shifts between the wacky to the disturbing to the sobering. It's easy to get whiplash, and I know I did. Between the main storyline, the just plain creepy episodes, and the levels full of people ready to get womped, its hard not to get sucked in. There's a charm to this tone; sort of like a fallout game that has more focus on being gross than being entertaining. Brad's struggle to destroy every major gang leader on the face of the planet is an endearing one, considering the circumstances and the difficult choices posed when one plays this game. The game plays around a lot with the concept of value. Specifically, what is the value of a human life. Tough stuff.
The gameplay itself blends very nicely into this; though in reality it is standard RPG maker fare. Everything feels balanced for the most part. Bosses are beatable, if a bit unfair at times. If I were to complain, the biggest part of the game that let me down was the constant problems with trying to heal my party. I can understand that this is the wacky wasteland, and you're actively trying to waste my time, but poisoning my party, or randomly taking someone out of my party is just going to make me reload my latest save file. And, that it did. Several times. In fact, I would probably attribute an hour of my total game time alone to just reloading save files from unfair events; hell, lets tack on another hour for just backtracking to a safe resting location once I actually found one. A stronger man would play through it, but really my priorities are to actually keep my strongest party members with me, thanks.
Speaking of party members, there are a metric ton of them in this game. A huge amount of variety on offer here, though your mileage may vary on who exactly you deem to be useful enough to keep around. In my playthrough I found a couple party members who were reliably able to deal 1K damage a turn; and I also kept a member who was able to blind opponents; which is a skill that I would probably say is required to finish the game. By and large, If found healing characters to be obsolete by the half way mark, and instead opted for members who were tanky but also able to fight effectively. Again, your mileage may vary.
Without spoiling anything, the ending messed me up in a very unique way. Lisa is a very lengthy game, and by the time it feels like closing, things were getting a bit contrived. But still, things wrapped themselves up in an interesting, but not entirely satisfying way. Then I booted up the DLC.
Lisa the Painful is Brad's story. Lisa the Joyful is Buddy's story. It's a direct continuation of the main game, and it really puts some closure on things, though most of the tone and lingering difficulties remain accounted for. This time, you actually don't have an objective other than to kill everyone. So, I guess that's more straightforward. Balancing feels way off in the DLC, basically creating an environment where you are forced to take drugs. No followers. No new party members. No nothing. The end of the world is here; and boy does Lisa the Joyful make it obvious. It's not difficult, just boring. The bosses have inflated HP values, leading to long drawn out battles that consist of CCing the enemy, attacking, and then CCing the enemy. What a bore.
But the ending of Lisa the Painful is where it really comes together. Somewhere, it looses focus, and then spirals into mediocrity. It's more obvious to me that this is just extra content to be thrown at the wall. Nothing too much to write home about, aside from some telling dialogue. Otherwise, it was a complete wash.
I recommend Lisa for anyone looking for a ride in a wacky wasteland's clothing. I'd also say that the DLC generally isn't worth it unless you're really hurting to see whats next. Just be aware that there really isn't much more Lisa has to say that it already hasn't in the base game.

Freedom Planet is my favorite game that I've played this year. I bought it during the 2015 summer sale last week for about $4, but if I knew how good it was I probably would've been willing to spend ten times that much on it.
I was always more of a Nintendo kid than a Sega kid growing up, so I don't have too much nostalgia for the Genesis games that Freedom Planet tries to emulate. However, I did enjoy Sonic 2 and Sonic 3 & Knuckles, and I feel like I enjoyed this game just as much as those. Sonic is definitely the most obvious design inspiration (most obviously in the level structure), but Freedom Planet also takes a lot of ideas from other 16-bit games like Rocket Knight Adventures, Ristar, and Mega Man X. The bosses in particular are some of the best I've ever seen, and are just as good as anything in Gunstar Heroes.
It's clear that a lot of work went into making the 3 playable characters feel very dynamic and fun to play. They are all VERY different, and none of them truly play like Sonic as you might expect. The game is balanced around Lilac, who is sort of a hybrid of Sonic, Ristar, and Sparkster with some fighting game moves like an uppercut and a dive kick. However, I initially played through the entire game as Carol, who is much closer to Zero from Mega Man X4, with a fast combo-oriented claw attack and a wall jump. She also has a bizarrely awesome motorcycle that can double jump and drive straight up vertical walls. I'm impressed that the game still felt well designed and balanced despite playing with a character who works completely differently from Lilac.
After around level 3, the bosses become extremely difficult, absurdly so relative to the stages themselves. And there are a lot of them, generally 2-3 per level. However, they are not truly unfair. Even with the notoriously difficult final boss, I was able to figure out his pattern enough to know how to beat him without taking a single hit... though I'm unable to play with enough skill to actually manage that. Fortunately, the game is generous with lives and checkpoints; I died 70 times throughout the entire game with Carol on Normal (20 of those deaths were on the final boss), but I never saw a game over. So the game is definitely hard, but it does encourage and reward skillful play.
A lot of people don't like the story, but I found it somewhat charming, reminiscent of all those early 90s Saturday morning cartoons starring anthropomorphic animals that took themselves slightly too seriously. It is admittedly darker and more violent than those ever got, as you'll see during the introduction. However, the characters themselves keep things lighthearted 99% of the time. The voice acting is excellent (apart from the overly hammy king in the introduction, who gives a lousy first impression), and it's clear the actors had tons of fun during recording. Some of the cutscenes do go on far longer than they should; the worst offender is between levels 2 and 3. Fortunately, if you don't want to deal with cutscenes there is a specific option to play story mode without any of them.
My only other complaint is that the levels, while well designed, are probably longer than they should be. Not so much because they get boring, as the game introduces new mechanics and environments at a good pace, but because they can be exhausting. The game is generous with checkpoints, but saves only happen between levels, so you'll have to complete each of the 15-40 minute levels all in one session. I would have preferred that each level be cut in half, much like how Sonic's Zones have two Acts; the levels are clearly designed in halves, even with different music for each part, so I don't know why this wasn't done.
In summary, Freedom Planet is an excellent game, and I give it my highest recommendation. This and Shovel Knight should serve as examples of how to do retro gaming well, reaching a level of quality that stands shoulder to shoulder with the greatest games of the eras they seek to emulate.

Something about this game seems really familiar, but I can't quite put my finger on it... Let's see, quick anthropormorphic animals going through a momentum-based, 16-bit platformer with the goal of stopping a robot invasion involving a big gem... I swear, I've seen it before. Nah, must be my mind playing tricks on me.
But seriously, this game is what Sonic 4 wishes it could be. It's a fantastic tribute to the old Sonic games, with plenty of unique mechanics that set it apart from the aforementioned rodent-based platformers. The soundtrack's amazing, the art looks like something straight from the Genesis (which isn't a bad thing at all), and it plays like a dream. The only gripes I have are that some of the voice acting is inconsistent, and there are a few technical hiccups. All in all, though, Freedom Planet's pretty good.

A barely disguised allegory, the game is occasionally overbearing in its message.  The puzzling and platforming is usually just this side of tedious.  Nevertheless I love this game as it's a perfect example of the interactive form being the correct choice for telling a particular story.  Fear, frustration, and the magical beliefs of a child thinking he can change what is through the few options available to him make for a near seamless intertwining of feeling, meaning, and gameplay.  There were times when I refused to do what the game asked of me; other times it gave me chills as I tried to process how I felt about what was happening.  The art and music are glorious.  Well worth the 3 hours it will take to play to completion.

TL;DR - Overall, I'd say that this is one of the best games in the CoD franchise, with one of the best campaigns and a very enjoyable multiplayer. If you like the CoD franchise, old or new, you'll enjoy the hell out of this.
Full Thoughts (Mainly Campaign Stuff)
------------------------------------------
Campaign - The campaign in CoD: WaW is refined and fun to play, with a few dragging stages in between. The beginning mission (Semper Fi) places you as a man known only as 'Miller' in a Japanese POW camp. This is an appropriate start to WaW, with the player witnessing the brutal and often horrifying depictions of war that this game brings to the table. Now, from this mission onwards, here is my complaint: All of the Pacific Front (American/ Japanese) missions (Excepting the first) are considerably worse than the Soviet ones. There are many cliche and boring moments in the Pacific Front's story overall, and the levels are bland and repetitive. Often, your goal is doing one thing over and over again until suddenly your commander says "I think we've done enough for today.". For instance, you'll be assaulting mortar pits repeatedly many a time as Miller, with the gameplay being moderately frustrating on Normal difficulty, but teeth-gratingly frustrating on Veteran. You'll often see that Japanese soldiers have no qualms about tossing grenades precisely at your position until the sun goes down. You'll have to relocate often enough for it to become more of a difficult chore than an action-packed, life-threatening stunt. The Soviet (Eastern Front, whatever you wanna call it) missions are the highlights of the campaign. Don't get me wrong, the Pacific Front has its jaw-dropping moments, but they are few and far between compared to the Soviet campaign. Pvt. Petrenko is your character, with the first mission starting directly after a massacre of Red Army soldiers by the Wermacht. This is also where you meet Reznov, your campaign-long companion with a taste for brutality. This mission (Vendetta) has you stalking the ruined buildings and streets of Stalingrad, recreating the confusion and vulnerability displayed in the soldiers who fought through that siege. This mission does most things flawlessly, having all of the brutality, action, story, and gameplay that CoD: WaW promises. You duel with a sniper, duck under flamethrowers, and kill scores of Wermacht scum (Getting into character a bit), all while being inspired to push forward by the great performance put forward by Gary Oldman (Reznov). The voice-acting in the Soviet stages is superior to the Pacific stages, the gameplay is superior, the environments are far superior, and the Red Army Soldiers are too! URRRAAA!!! Ahem... So, if you're looking for a good campaign, just tough it through the Pacific levels and you'll have one of the best of the franchise.
