The Armament Project is a cool throwback to 90s FPS in style, substance, and inspiration. Armament offers a level based design (3 levels) in the vein of Wolfenstein 3D and Doom, but with the subtle maze-like structure of Quake. Likewise, Armament offers a nod to actions films like Terminator and Aliens (which inspired early FPS). But instead of aliens, machines, or Nazis, Armament offers a battle through a prison in the context of a dystopian society and government class wars.
Though brief, the game is a fun little FPS experience. I like the storyline (I’m biased in enjoying a deeper story to my FPS), but the story is a little too complex for a shorter game. I think such nuanced storytelling will prove useful as DYS Top builds more complex games.
As a nascent developer and publisher, DYS Top shows promise for future games with the likes of Armament. I look forward to checking out their sophomore release.

I used to love SimCity. I used to play it a lot on a Mac. I would still love to play it.
But not this releaes, not this version. The tools and interface are clunky in the best situation. That's the nicest thing I can say about it.
Here's this great game, but you ... just ... can't ... quite ... access it. The interface has a mind of its own, which bears little resemblance to what you want to do (let alone any kind of reality-sim). For example, why, on a completely flat and empty plain, can a cloverleaf only be placed at a 45 degree angle to the grid? Why can't I decide for myself how I want to place it?
You end up building a highway, destroy it, build it again .... and so on until you get something vaguley like what you were after. Or your budget runs out.
There it is, just out of reach, the fun game I used to play. It is an exercise in extreme frustration. I am going to delete this game and hope I can erase it from my memory.

The world is beautiful, and just my cup of tea, part fantasy but realistic. I love the imagination that just shows in the game, and the controls are tight, great quality apart from the camera being a bit too close when the monster's chasing you.
Now on the emotional part  - the creator said himself that it's based on his experience of being abused in his childhood, and while I have not gone through emotional or physical distress like that personally, the way this game showed me these emotions was simply genius. It was gentle, yet it was a completely new emotional for me. That a video game could do that really earned my respect.
All in all, I'd recommend this game though it's short and maybe not your style if you're looking for a challenge, but it's something I cherish and am glad I've played.

I am perhaps a bit biased, being the voice of Slightly Panicked Generic Radio Guy, but I know a great Half-Life mod when I see one, so I'm reviewing this anyway.
Anyone who's paid a modicum of attention to the Half-Life 2 mapping scene for the past few years knows exactly what to expect from marnamai's work (e.g. "Overflow" from The Forgotten Journey and "Raining Down Hell" from CityStreetsVille), and will not be surprised that his usual flourish shows up here. Slick brushwork, refined lighting, balanced combat; it's not present "in spades", exactly, but the limited scope of this release left me feeling excited for more as opposed to unsatisfied and grumpy.
I was especially impressed with the extra effort put into the modeling. In particular, the lumber mill is home to a few assets that are clearly brand new upon close inspection, but that feel right at home beside Valve's content. Later on there are even what appear to be custom train tracks that actually use the same gauge as the train models! I have spent the past thirteen years being unreasonably angry about that and it's nice to find someone else who cares.
My only real criticism would be the occasional dead air as far as audio is concerned. I didn't notice much in the way of music, and a couple of the soundscapes were a little flat, which dampened the atmosphere somewhat. It's not much, though: this was still a fantastically tight, polished piece of level design that I had a ton of fun wandering through, and I can't recommend DownFall highly enough!

The Fantastic-
-An actual native port of one of the most beloved games in the Final Fantasy series. The graphics look fantastic, it plays smooth, the horrible 'wobbly' textures and warping of models as seen in the PSX version is gone, gone gone. Attention to detail has actually been undertaken to make this game a rare gem for me to play.
The Good-
It's got cheats, or 'boosters' yes they will come in handy but I've always been a fan of the grinding, so I won't be using these but I can see other players might like to use them.
The Bad-
Controller support is woefully inadiquite. The Xinput plugin for unity used is way, way out of date and lackluster. The Backgrounds, although I know myself they have been replaced with higher resolution versions than the PSX, they stand out really bad on higher resolutions.
The plain ugly-
Where do I start? First of all an older version of unity has been used making the game prone to game-stopping bugs (which I will report below). There's zero graphic customization, there's a horrible aspect ratio fix and ugly grey bars, forcing me to create my own mod just so I can enjoy the game, you know, so it stretches to my screen. Heck a PSX emulator can do better. But don't fear, my mod for this is up on the guides section in the community.
Although it has been claimed that the movies are 'HD' the one at the start (where vivi walks around and the alexandria text comes in) is plain awful. Pixellated, blotchy, low res rubbish. At least use a slight blur and a sharpen Square to get rid of this. And why the heck are the movies been renamed to .btyte when they are clearly theora? Why make it so hard for the modder community to improve a classic game further?
And the big one. The game, for some, doesnt work. Period. Getting into the first battle is impossible for some and the music plays, but your world will go black. And here's why.
I was able to reproduce the issue people have been having, it seems it's related to a really dogdy plugin that square enix made for this game, called FF9SpecialEffectPlugin.dll, it's in the Plugins folder. A look in a hex editor at it mentions bones, SFX and framebuffer effects. Deleting this plugin results in what people have described, cant get into the first fight, the music plays but the screen is black. This is definately what is causing the problem. Square if you are reading this fix your buggy plugin or should I do it for you?!!!
All in all, I do recommend this game as it is *almost* a vast improvement on the PSX version. However, Square, you need to fix all these bugs, upgrade your unity version, allow people to mod your game more easily (this is 2016, not 1996 anymore) and stop treating your PC fans like idiots.
Buy for the price and the possibility of this getting fixed but steer clear if you want to play now.

- Not a lot of PC options and key rebindings can only be done in game and will only affect that specific file
- I believe they still kept the original PSOne framerate, so expect 30 frames locked and dip to 15 in battles

For some reason, the controlls are really wonky because it can't use the analog stick right. That said, the game is still fine and Keyboard controlls work just as well. Very Hesitant Positive. There are several grammar issues (tough instead of though, poor wording in sentences, etc) that make me feel this wasn't originally made in English.
However, the branching is neat...but it is the kind of game that almost NEEDS Achievements to really warrant trying to explore each and every branching path.
+Cute little pixel game with easy mechanics
+Good price point
+Each level shows how many branching paths, so you aren't spending forever trying to figure out how many you have left
+While poorly written at times (grammar) it's a neat little story that is playing out
-Seems Short. I've played for only 15 minutes and not only have a feel for the game, but have unlocked about 10 levels and done all their subsequent branches to completion (save the ones moving the story forward)
-The Grammar and word choice is really, really bad sometimes. Either ESL, or someone who didn't have a proofreader. It's not a full deal breaker for me, but it can be for others
-No Achievements. While I know this may not matter to some, for the type of game this is, they would almost enhance it ten-fold; a reason to go back and find the branches, which may not be all that interesting on their own.
-Repetitive. You have to go back to the levels and replay them, but there's no way to skip past text so it can be a bit of a slough.
TLDR: Decent game, good price, not the best grammar.

LISA is a game which, by design, has many chances to fall short and become more irritating than enjoyable. However, the game is immaculate in execution, and LISA appeals perfectly to its audience. To understand if you fit the audience, there are a few things to consider about LISA:
LISA is set after an apocalyptic event killed every human female. The resulting society is essentially running on fumes, falling into depravity, and finding diversions as the human race inevitably comes to an end. On the surface, there are Russian Roulette players, and a town with a cult-like worship of a still-functioning McDonalds. Beneath that surface, an investigative player may unravel the story of how the world got to be the way it is.
One of the main draws to LISA is the dialogue. LISA's sense of humor is a bit PG-13 (reaching to more of an R rating at serious parts), but it does not fall back on sheer shock value to get a punchline through. To give an example may ruin a joke, but the first fight (shown in a trailer) generally sets the tone: A small dog named Cheeselegs is frightening a man in a tree, kill Cheeselegs (it should only take one turn) to get the man as a party member.
LISA's gameplay can be summarized as a fairly standard turn-based RPG. Some characters use directional-inputs, some simply have commands. If a player is keeping on-pace, they should not need to grind for any fight, but the combat is still a relative challenge. The endings are defined by the player's usage of an item called 'joy', a drug which greatly decreases the difficulty of the fight, but at
costs to the player.
The party can have up to four members, the main character plus three of
characters which can be found across the world. Save for the main character, any of the other party members can die in combat. Falling to zero may not necessarily mean that they die, but some powerful enemies pack an ability which can kill off a party member. As well, there are events outside of combat which can potentially kill the party. Most notably, there are occasions where either the main character can suffer a permanent penalty, or a party member is selected to be killed.
LISA is a game with memorable humor, a unique world, flexible gameplay, and a few choices-matter mechanics sprinkled in. If you do decide to try LISA, do yourself a favor and save 'Painful' difficulty for your second run.

This is definitely one of those cases of "games as art". While it's a pretty standard puzzle platformer, Papo & Yo is dealling with some pretty interesting concepts. The setting is some sort of South American chanty town outside of reality, and the main character has to navigate the world by manipulating the landscape, and through the assistance of his little robot friend Lula, as well as a large placid creature called Monster.
The "arty" aspect comes to play when trying to use Monster to get to new places. Monster has three priorities, sleeping, eating coconuts and eating frogs. You can wake him up and lure him to places you need him using coconuts, but you want to keep him away from frogs. If he eats a frog he'll start rampaging and only care about eating more frogs and hurting you. This fact comes to play in the plot with various cut scenes that show there's more going on than it seems.
The puzzles are fun, the art style is pretty (I quite liked the landscape manipulation effects), the music is atmospheric and has an odd nostalgic quality to it, and the plotline is engaging. My only gripe is that it's a bit on the short side and a little too simple. Oh, I also wish the dedication made at the start of the game was made at the end of the game instead, and it was a little more subtle with its "plot twist". All in all I enjoyed the experience though, and feel it was a successful "arty" game that still managed to be fun.
I strongly suggest avoiding trailers if you plan on playing it, so you can avoid spoilers.

There has been a significant amount of improvement on this game.  I would definitely recommend it to anyone who feels on the fence about it.  Yes, there still are some bugs, but they are not major, game-stopping bugs anymore.  The development has been slow, but it is still chugging along.
For the first time since I've owned this game (which was when it first came out on steam), I was actually able to load up a multiplayer game and have it just work.  That is astounding for this game.  The way the multiplayer used to work was complex and hard to even get going.  Most of the time, when you did happen to get the weird server panel running, the other player connecting wouldn't even be able to play with you, see your creations, or interact with your bricktrons.  I will say it again just because it makes me so happy to say: it just works.
The bugs have had a noticable amount of squashing, particularily game-stoppers such as the bricking of bricktrons, pathfinding loops, and having bricktrons get lost during a task.  Sure it's not entirely bug-free, but its more than playable now.
Is the game perfect?  No.  Is it polished?  Somewhat.  But what the game is, is just plain fun.  The mechanics and the core functions are all there.  Everything you need to enjoy the game, whether singleplayer or multiplayer, is working.
It seems silly to say that a game is good because it works, but for anyone who has had this game for as long as I, they understand just how astounding that truly is.  This game was utterly broken when I first bought it.  And now it is slowly, but surely, becoming the intense and creative game I hoped it would be from the kickstarter trailer so many years ago.

I don’t consider myself a Sonic fan and I really don’t have any nostalgia for the series as a whole.  Most of my good memories come from Sonic and Knuckles, so it has been a long time since I played a Sonic game for any real length of time.   I discovered a nostalgia and love for Sonic through this game that I didn’t know existed. Its gameplay is simple but effective and its graphics and art charming.  No matter your level of respect or disdain for that little blue rodent this is a game worth exploring.
The story starts off as Sonic celebrates his twentieth birthday, with a monster known as the Time Eater crashing the party and dispersing Sonic's friends to various stages in history. Sonic is knocked out after futily taking on the monster. He wakes up in the White Space dimension and encounters Tails, as well as his plumper, black-pupiled younger self. The two Sonics have to free their friends in two different versions of levels that have emerged over the years, and eventually defeat the monster summoned by Dr. Eggman. Modern Sonic utilises the game mechanics used in 3D games like Heroes and Colours. His homing attack allows him to lock-on to an enemy when he jumps at them and can boost through levels for additional speed. Classic Sonic handles the traditional side-scrolling levels, sporting the ability to spin-dash. Levels run at a slower pace as they require some more caution, and he also can’t auto aim at enemies or jump as far.
Generations is something of a healthy montage of what comprised the first twenty years of Sonic games. The nine stages are all throwbacks from three console eras. Three zones from the heights of the ‘Classic Era’ have been lovingly reimagined, including the signature Green Hill. The ‘Dreamcast Era’ touches up Adventure’s Speed Highway and City Escape plus Sunside Beach from the later Heroes. The ‘Modern Era’ even revitalises Crisis City from the disastrous 2006 reboot, as well as Rooftop Run and Planet Wisp from Unleashed and Colours. Boss fights are dispersed between each era, but can only be unlocked upon completion of three side missions. These are usually comprised of another objective within a level, such as a ghost race or collecting items. Some are fun and others are less so, but aren’t a necessity to reach the end. Similarly to secret special stages in the originals, hidden stars encourage exploration of the multiple paths in each level. There are also the Red Rings hidden in the main stages to encourage players to explore every nook and cranny as both Sonics to find them. Ample rewards await players who take up all of these challenges in the form of new powers, which can be added to either Sonic's play mechanics to make old stages new again. These powers are hardly throwaway, but they're also hand-picked from Sonic's rich game history. Prepare to relive the fun of using the special elemental shields from Sonic 3, give Classic Sonic the Homing Attack, give Modern Sonic unlimited boost meter in exchange for one-hit death (one of my favorites), allow either Sonic to stop on a dime, or even endow the time-slowing skill from Secret Rings. There are dozens of these, and they're great for playing around in stages, exploration, or for finding the best combination for the fastest times.
Bottom line: If you are or have ever been a fan of Sonic the Hedgehog during the series' two-decade history, then this is your game. Sega made this for us. If you've been away from Sonic for a while or have been wondering what he's all about, then this is actually a great game to start with, as it features the two best-playing versions of Sonic in the series, along with his greatest stages, all in one place. Play it however you can, even if you rent it, but whatever you do, don't call it "short" or "over quickly." There's enough game here to last potentially ages.

You don't need to play or even like Sonic to enjoy Freedom Planet.
Personally, Freedom Planet is probably one of the absolute best indie games I've ever played. The amount of polish and love that has clearly gone into this game is pretty hard to one up, even by a triple-A developer.
So much exhausting detail was put into every inch of the game. The sprites and pixel art are absolutely gorgeous, up there with Axiom Verge and Shovel Knight. The Sega Genesis/Megadrive-era Sonic inspired aesthetic was masterfully replicated, and the well-done animations give the game an incredible amount of life.
The music is almost unreal. It's obviously a homage to the earlier days of video game soundtracks, full of harmony and melody, very upbeat, and fast-paced. At LEAST buy the soundtrack, if anything.
The story, while introducing a few elements that causes you to wonder "What'd I miss?" is very well written. The characters are all very memorable, and those that aren't, don't waste your time, or aren't thrown away to try and get an emotional response out of you. The ending is extremely sequel-baity, but it wasn't done as poorly as Halo 2.
The gameplay is a blast. The controls are tight and responsive, the level design is fantastic and there wasn't very many times at all where I felt like a hit or failure wasn't my fault. The difficulty is paced well, and becomes a tough but rewarding challenge later on. Normal feels just right because of this. Bosses are designed in almost Capcom-esque perfection, with clear patterns, good telegraphs and plenty of attacks to keep them from getting repetitive.
There is definitely no shortage of content, either. The game has 3 unique characters to play as, each with their own cutscenes and playstyles, as well as more characters and stages coming down the pipeline, completely free of charge.
Like Axiom Verge (or even more so), the game sets itself apart from Classic Sonic very well and it becomes very apparent that the game is it's own different beast, especially when you fight your first boss. I can't recommend this game highly enough, and the only real complaints I can give are nit-picks. Like the main villain's design. Dem eyebrows.
Buy it, even off sale. This game is absolutely worth full price. I personally will definitely be following this developer and will support everything they make in the future.
Now, excuse me while I beat the game again twice over.

-one of the laziest single player plots I have seen in a while, If you were to sarcasitcally say "what could go wrong?" before each mission you'll find that very cartoonishly and repeatively something goes wrong in pretty much every mission. Essentially, your given a mission and half way through something goes wrong and you have to deal with it. Rinse and repeat.
-The Mofia itself feels lazy and generic, lacks personality.
-even though your in the mob, you never get a sense of the mobsters being good people, most of them are just kinda creeps. Unlike the godfather in which the characters can feel good, at least to some extent.

But there are many times where you have to slowly fight through several guys one at a time in this way, you can't use guns or anything else, as if they were really proud of this system and wanted you to use it. Final Verdict-5/10- unfortunatly I felt that the bad really outweighted the good in this game, to make it not horrible but just pretty mediocre. For a cheap steam purchase it may be worth it, but to be honest to me there are just simply a lot of better games out there to be played. Sonic Generations is the best way to acknowledge good Sonic games that doesn't involve playing the older good Sonic games. The PC version of Sonic Generations is a good enough port, with high framerate support, modding support and decent fast visuals. However, running mods such as the Unleashed Project require a decent modern CPU due to the relatively poor CPU porting, and some mods, such as the most popular visual mod for the game, add graphical effects that are present in Unleashed and the console version of Generations that skipped the PC release, while somehow improving performance in some places. This also means that people with slower or less powerful processors may have some problems running busier levels, due to the games poor handling of multiple CPU threads. I did not encounter any framerate problems, but there is always going to be users who do encounter these issues, and my warning is simply ensure that you have a decent CPU. The gameplay itself blends the best of older Sonic, with modern stages built around the best ideas of Unleashed and Colours.
I've only played it with a controller, so I can't judge the PC controls. I can point out that there is sometimes some delay between the pressing of the button, and Sonic actually doing it sometimes. Besides these occasional problems, the game controls very solidly and I have no actual complaints involving the controls beside this small problem. Sonic also has some problems with precise movements in some levels due to speed and sometimes eratic camera movements. The game also sadly lacks in the number of main courses, which is a shame because everything that they've put in, both modern and classic are brilliant. Game length is instead lengthened by short challenges that are required for progression, or unlock bonus tracks on the soundtrack for use in the game levels. Sadly, these challenges aren't really that interesting to play compared to the actual main games levels, and even with this, the game comes out on the short side.
Visuals and port wise, graphical options are limited, but with mod support and game support for high resolution textures and shadows, the port works well most of the time. For the speed that Sonic moves at, the visuals are acceptable (and improvable with mods), and run at 60 FPS, something not available on the console versions.
Sound-wise, the game for the most part shines. It features many tracks from older Sonic games, most of them are remixed and sound really good. Voice acting is a bit strange, minor characters such as those from Sonic Heroes, or ones like Shadow sound really stupid, but the main characters are voiced fine enough I suppose, although Eggman/Robotnik is the only one who I think sounds close enough to what I asscoiate the character with (that's what happens when you change voice actors when I'm not paying attention, so stop doing that). There are some issues with audio sychronisation that I've encountered and have been unable to ever replicate, such as out of sync audio or no sound in the cutscenes at all, then again, the only thing you miss in this case is cheesy writing. No gameplay affecting issues though in terms of sound. The soundtrack, although consisting mostly of remixes, is still a great soundtrack, probably being one of my favourites for the series.
The major disappointing factor, because every Sonic game has to have one, is the challenge stages. The core game is extremely short, so to pad it out, they have these challenge stages. They range in quality from good enough to boring, long and frustrating, and are not a highlight of the overall package as it pulls you out of the game constantly so that you can play around on these challenge maps before you can unlock the next boss and the next group of stages that take around 10 minutes per modern and classic stage.
Overall, its a good Sonic game in an age of disappointing Sonic games. It ends up being a bit too short, which is sad because awful Sonic games like Sonic 06 are many times longer than this for the average player, even with all the bloating from the little stupid side missions. Despite that, I'd say it is worth getting, unless you really hate Sonic. This game does almost everything right, fast colourful visuals, a story that doesn't get in the way of the game and a good varied soundtrack.
Mods improve everything, graphically and performance wise, as well as ported stages from other Sonic games and new creations, and again add life to what is otherwise a very good tragically short platformer, while also stripping out the unwanted bloat.

Oh boy, where to start with this one?
I went into LISA expecting a game full of penile jokes and such, seeing as how there's no more women left in the world, and a non-serious game about an old balding dude trying to get his adopted daughter back with his band of misfits. Instead what I got was a rollercoaster of choices, a lot of which I still regret making, genuine feels and enough depth to keep everything interesting and entertaining.
There were certain occasions, ones that I won't spoil for anyone because it's better to go in blind, where I had to force myself to do the wrong choice just to proceed. To defeat certain people, people who didn't deserve it, all for the sake of plot development. This game, this ♥♥♥♥ing masterpiece, has made me question every single decision I've made in my life and how that has affected both my own life and the lives of others around me. Putting aside the post-apocalyptic scenario and the lack of women, so many characters are easy to relate with simply due to their experiences and views on life.
In terms of length and difficulty (unless you're playing on Pain Mode), LISA is perfectly paced. If you're on a casual play through then it will only take a small level of grinding, or none at all if you build your party/manage your items right, to get through the game. You'll be able to both enjoy the fantastic music, appreciate the characters and design and all without feeling like the game isn't progressing.
If you're a fan of Mother 3, Undertale, or just any sort of RPG, then LISA is the game for you. Combined with the DLC and the various ways the game can go, you'll be getting more than your money's worth. If you can handle the tear-jerking level of emotion this game will have you going through of course. LISA will always be a game that I will recommend to people, no matter how old it gets, and for that I can easily say that it is one of my favourite games.

I think the best part of strategy games is often learning how everything works and interacts and actually experiencing the learning curve first hand. It can be frustrating because you'll die because of something you didn't know about- but you remember it for next time and forge ahead and slowly climb the ranks.
FTL is excellent at this process. I've died in this game more than I've died in just about any other game and I've barely been playing it over more than a few months, but rather than getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off and ragequitting I'm encouraged to try something new, to adjust my upgrade order, to select a different interaction with a ship, to mix up my weapons or combat technique or any number of different approaches to avoid or deal with the same problem in the future.
It's a game that relies on RNG heavily, which normally makes for a really boring end game, but with FTL there's tons of end-game content and once you think you've learned everything and mastered the intricacies of turns, combat, crew members, upgrades and everything else there's still a heap of goals to strive for, new challenges to attempt and things to do.
It's a fantastic game that never makes me feel rushed, and in those moments when I do feel pressured because I'm losing it's alright because I know I can adapt and try things a little different next time and get just a little bit better and a little bit further.

What a glorious adaptation (not a port) of my all time favorite video game. To people coming back to the installation, you will love the updates, nothing is ruined, in fact things are improved (if that was even possible) slight touches here and there make the game so much more enjoyable - things like autosaving before a boss battle to the updated sprites; simple touches, nothing overdone, they even keep the amazing original soundtrack - keeps the nostalgia alive. Also for those that want to have fun messing around with speed runs, or expirimintation - cheats can be enables in game! Things like auto earn abilities rather than leveling them to keep them, or auto level 99 are all in this game so you can tweak it how you want it, or play it like it was in the glory days, your choice. Also added to the adaptation - STEAM ACHEIVEMENTS!
To those new to the game - enjoy this beautiful masterpeice, there are too few games out there that warrant the title "work of art" but this game hands down is one of the best in the long running Final Fantasy franchise, and ultimatly one of the best games EVER made. The turn based combat seems slow at first, but if you dive deep into the core mechanics that is this glorious RPG; it will make you think. You will fall in love with the fantasy/steampunk environment and will be enamored by the complex ability system. Saving every peice of old equipment to be synthisized into something completley new with brand new abilities is a refreshing turn from tossing things out just because you have something that hits harder. From the main story to the side quests and mini games, this game will keep you hooked - the character development is something you don't see in video games in this day and age anymore (so good that I did my creative writing thesis on it). So much to do, so many secrets to find, every time I pick up this title it blows me away, this is how games should be made.

When I jumped into this game, I didn't have many expectations for it. I just knew that it was something that was originally going to be a Sonic fangame before the creator decided to turn it into an original IP instead using the same engine and that people were going *crazy* for it.
I may not really care for Sonic that much these days, but these people're right to go crazy for this. This is the snappiest, most enjoyable platformer I've played in a REALLY long time. I'd even say that I enjoy this almost as much as "Rayman Legends", even (and that says a LOT). Beneath the Sonic-esque character designs and familiar (and very nicely handled) level design riffs that tip their hat to classic Sonic games, you have a platformer that somehow takes the familiar and makes it feel fresh again.
Really big, long levels that never really lose their momentum and fun despite their lengths, fantastic controls and ultra-fluid combat, the nicest looking pixel-centric graphics an indie game of this type has had in a really long time and REALLY nice music that rivals even some of the best music from classic Sonic games IMO just to name just a few of the things that work so well in this game and elevate it to more than just "a Sonic fangame that isn't".
Honestly, I like to think of "Freedom Planet" as more of a loving, thoughtful tribute to 16-bit/32-bit 2D platformers in general rather than just a better version of *one* of those classic franchises. And if you did that sort of stuff, then go right ahead and check it out. It's a lot of fun!
(PLEASE NOTE: If you're a Mac user, as of 20th June 2015, I recommend you turn off Steam Overlay before playing this game. There's a weird bug right now that doesn't let the visuals show up that's all to do with Steam Overlay for some reason. I'm sure its a bug that'll be fixed in time but for now, bare that in mind before you play. Thanks!)
EDIT: Just after writing this review, I found out that at some point in the game, it gets VERY suddenly hard really, really quickly so unfortunately for players who aren't immediately fantastic at tough-as-nails platformers, then your enjoyment of the game will only take you to the 3rd stage or so before you hit a mental wall.
So I don't readily recommend this game to as many people as I did before now, but its at least worth a try.

Freedom planet is everything I could have dreamed it to be. Not only is this game a calll back to all the games that I grew up with, but the absolute fun oriented with the gameplay is fantastic. While I know that this is a common sellingpoint for this game, I'd say it goes deeper than just retro style enjoyment. The music and characters are all amazing, creating actuall personalities while still maintainging an ecellent pase to the game. While the story might be the weakest part to this package, the plot is still much better than some modern games that follow similar game styles. I ftill found myself genuinely caring for the heroines, and at the same time disliking the villians. Props to the voice actors as well. This game contains well designed and thought out levels, with tough and fun boss fights to end out the action. Often, there are games that have trouble maintaining a level of difficulty without making it too hard. Freedom Planet has no trouble with this. The difficulty is very stream lined, and is incredible near the end. Don't fear though, because if the difficulty gets to hard, you can always turn it down in the options. This game even includes a casual difficulty.
There are tons of things too do wihtin the premise of this game. There are OPTIONAL collectibles and a vast number of hidden secrets. I had tons of fun finding these. In addtion, (and a personal favorite) there is a Majong minigame within the stage select screen.
Freedom Planet is a downright amazing game that I suggest you chech out. The people at Galaxy way were really on their toes. I look forward too a sequel.

Sonic Generations succeeds in crafting a coherent game from a 'Greatest Hits' collection. Classic and Modern Sonic exist side by side in stages ripped from past and present games adapted to suit each Sonic's play style while maintaining the spirit of the original design. The controls are solid, the levels are gorgeous, and obstacles don't destroy momentum. It's everything you could hope for from a Sonic game because it's made up of every other Sonic game alongside modern sensibilities. The Red Ring collectables hidden in every stage give an incentive for exploration without requiring Sonic to rein in his mad dash just to complete the stage. Challenges present the stages in a different way, calling into focus the individual elements that made that stage/game special. And both extras feed into Generations' function as a nostalgia-fest by rewarding collection or completion with art, music, and abilities from previous games. Every part of the game comes together to support a celebration of the Sonic series and it all just works. This stops in the last third of the game, when the stages start to represent the games in what is known as the Dark Age of Sonic. These stages are chock full of random holes in level design, ledges that are just a little too far while maintaining momentum, and enemies that are timed to hit at the exact moment of contact. The simple fun of quick decisions made while dashing as fast as possible though beautiful landscapes drops away after the fifth life spent on a bottomless pit there was no way of knowing about or an enemy standing just out of range of the next jump. The final boss doesn't change the tone either. The previously tight controls kind of just fall apart with the rest of time and space which just so happens to be blocking any possible view of what the boss is doing. The flaws of the game's final third try to cloud out everything the first two thirds did so well, replacing an easy fun with frustration. But this hasn't stopped me from coming back to Generations time and time again. Maybe it's a good game with a few bad parts, just like the series it seeks to celebrate. Maybe I'm nostalgic and delusional.

DownFall is a fantastic little piece of Half-Life action. The problem is it's incredibly short - my playthrough took about 30 minutes and while YMMV, it won't get much longer than an hour or so. However, Marnamai does plan on releasing a continuation, which is great, because the ending cliffhanger really stung.
But that's just a testament to how great DownFall is. The levels look, feel and flow really, really well. You've got some really strong gameplay, making great use of the Half-Life combat and exploration loop - you end up in some novel situations that you haven't played through before, have to engage enemies in different ways than you're used to, and the slow build-up in terms of weapons and enemies means even a novice player isn't going to get stuck. It also makes for great pacing.
Overall, highly recommended. If you own HL2, go for it - if you don't, buy HL2 and then play this. It's worth it!

SimCity 4 is a game that I spent a lot of time with in my early 20s. It had its fair share of bugs when it was first released and I remember a lot of frustration on forums early on. Crashes were frequent and the performance was not great despite having hardware more than capable of handling it. These many years later, the game runs much more smoothly than it ever did and it's a joy to go back and play. It's complex without being irritating (I will never understand where to put bus stations to get them to work properly, though). I've played SimCity since the first game was released in the late 80s (I played it in the early 90s), and SC4 ranks high on my list - perhaps below SC2000, but slightly higher than SC3000. The beauty of SC4 is the size of the maps, the inclusion of regions and the varied building style. The customisation of terrain is also the most advanced of all of the SimCities (in the latest one, terrain editing is sadly lacking). The latest SimCity is not worthy of the name and this represents the last of the good ones.

Ooh, another review!
PROS:
- Game looks amazing, with highly detailed sprites and backgrounds. The art style too is very good, with a lot of Chinese/Japanese elements.
- Characters are immensely likeable (or hateable) and have disctinct personalites. Well, the fact they HAVE personalities at all considering the source of inspiration is a plus in and of itself.
- Gameplay is more than just "gotta go fast"; rather, there's more focus on the platforming than the speed. You know, where the focus in a platformer SHOULD be.
- Speaking of Gameplay, combat is good too, as it is smoothly intergrated into the gameplay and doesn't feel out of place, unlike, say, Sonic Boom.
- Music is astounding, but does weaken a little compared to standard Sonic soundtracks (or hell, even the Sequel fan trilogy).
- There are moments in the game that are actually gripping and make you feel whatever emotion the game wants you to feel. Considering that this is the first game in a LONG time to do that to me, it means that the writers are doing their job for once.
CONS
- Ths game is HARD. Granted, it starts out challengining hard, but quickly spirals into DIMPS levels of cheapness, espcially the bosses. The final boss in particular is one of the cheapest bosses I have EVER fought in a video game.
- The story is...pretty sucky. Nothing really happens in an interesting or strucutred order, they just kind of...happen. Think the Hero story in Sonic Adventure 2, where some of the levels just happen with no real set-up or reason.
- There are also a lot of copouts, which make the story's gripping moments (described above) feel kinda redundant in hindsight.
- And leading on from THAT, the story is perhaps a bit TOO lighthearted for its own good. Such as a scene almost from a cartoon leading on from a very unpleasent scene. Perhaps the story could do with being a bit darker, with more death and a larger focus on the protagonist's state of mind after some of the more...disturbing moments.
- The voice acting is mediocre. Some like Dawn M Bennet (the voice of Lilac) certainly try, but others...kinda don't.
- Some of the characters in the story are worthless to the story and don't actually DO anything.
FINAL VERDICT:
Issues with the story aside, this game is a GEM. One of the best games I've ever played, and certainly the best indie game. While Shovel Knight is more well known and Five Nights at Freddy's has the better story, the former is a bit too popular for its own good while the latter is a pretty poor "game" to begin with. Freedom Planet is Sonic the Hedghehog++ and after the childhood♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥atrocity of Sonic Boom: Rise of Lyric (as well as the addtional sledgehammer to the nuts with Sonic Boom: Fire & Ice and, of course, Angry Birds in Sonic Dash), Freedom Planet helps revive my hopes, purely by the fact that SOMEONE out there still cares about Sonic in some fashion.

I am an Australian, and the playerbase is probably 0.1% Australian, perhaps the Aus vs. US tournament that has begun is changing that but as it stands no such luck, there are very few servers and the ones that are there lag like nothing else, and in this game, lag is a big deal.
Lag the difference of whether or not you can snipe that quick hit, or make that jumping lunge, or make the decision to dodge or block your opponents att- Oh wait he already jumped back and you couldn't tell, oh wait she already hit you before you could even consider making a decision, The lag makes this unplayable.
On top of this, the players who are left are all of the elite, beaten countless opponents and have their swordplay honed to a razors edge, and they will beat you down time after time without fail, because they know all the ins and outs, all the skills and tactics and how to counter them all.
And I end by saying this, if you enjoy skill based games, believe you can bear the lag and believe you can weather through a thousand soul crushing defeats for a single victory, I say without question to get it.
If however you cannot, then find something else I'm afraid.
Honestly this game is pretty fun only if you really enjoy fast paced intense 3d physics PVP that requires you to really think. If not, then maybe you shouldn't play it.

I found myself thinking "amg so pretty" as I went through the game. Sure, this has been my favorite game since I first played it back in 2000, so I'm probably a bit biased. Still, if you played this game in the past and enjoyed it, you'll likely enjoy reliving it in slightly upgraded game graphics, and wonderful HD CGIs!
If you're only trying this for the first time in 2016, keep in mind it is an old game, and things were a little different 16 years ago. For anyone who's never played it - Final Fantasy 9 is perhaps RPG at its best. The story is simply amazing, with lots of humor, the game has endless  optional adventures (I say "adventures" because nothing in a Final Fantasy like this is as rigid as "a quest"). The amount of depth this game has, and how well everything was designed, is outstanding even for today's standards. The (now in HD!) CGIs were used perfectly in this instalment, as they helped tell the story with beautiful and often touching scenes, and I can't wait to see them all again.
If you've played and liked it: You will love it.
If you played games of that era: You will probably love it.
If you never played a Final Fantasy: This is a great one to start with.. play it!
If you like other Final Fantasy titles but never played this: You will likely love it.

Absolute classic. Probably my favourite game of all time. I have never wrote a Steam review before but feel like I owe the game a positive review.
FFIX has a brilliant story with well written characters, gorgeous pre-rendered cutscenes, has an emotion inducing soundtrack and an intuitive ability/leveling up system. There's also a card duelling mini-game which is pretty neat. The game lasts around 35-45 hours but can stretch for much longer if you try to do everything there is to do.
Now, for the PC port. There are a few small issues. The battle UI is rather chunky and takes up way more spare than it should do. The new and improved character models look great but they clash rather horribly with the 2D backgrounds. Hopefully this is something mods will fix? Who knows. These are the only negative things I have noticed so far.
The controller support works brilliantly, you can rebind the buttons if you wish. Battles load faster than the original PS1 version and you can enable a bunch of cheats like infinite gil or max level if you so desire but these cannot be disabled on the save file you activated them on, so if the story is all you care about this should cater your needs. All in all I would recommend this port wholeheartedly.

The game tutorials introduce you to the core mechanics and an overview of how to balance your finances with your cities growth, and then allows you to develop the neighbouring cities into fledgling cities. My only suggestion is that if you do buy Simcity 4 Deluxe, ensure you visit the modding community, who have poured years into the various mods which not only increase city variation, but offer complete rewrites of various features (Such as NAM, a transport network mod which offers unprecedented levels of control of how your city traffic flows, and how it appears)

I love this game. It's fantastic! The similarities to Sonic are the first thing everyone mentions, and while Freedom Planet's inspirations are clear, the game is far from a clone.
The game has engaging combat, very tough but very exciting and rewarding bosses, a pretty good (but, imho, very poorly paced) story, some memorable characters (if you are into the story), large and varied level design, excellent 16-bit-style pixel art, catchy late-90s "CD-quality-audio"-style music, and 3 characters, each with their own unique movesets and playstyles (like, seriously. They play TOTALLY differently).

Blade Symphony is honestly a great game. I have always wanted to love fighting games, but I could never get around the ridiculous learning curve required to memorize and input the button strings required to pull off special moves. I love games that are easy to pick up, but hard to master, and this game is one of them. The developers attempted to recreate the kind of fighting atmosphere that was in Jedi Knight 2: Outcast, and I feel like they suceeded.
Basically, there are five playable characters, and each character has their own move sets, as you would expect from any fighting game. However, that is not the most important element of the game. Just like Jedi Outcast, there are light, medium, and heavy stances. These stances are like a rock-paper-scissors kind of deal, and each one cancels out the other. What makes this important is that if you hit a character using medium stance with a heavy attack it does extra damage. Really, this makes the combat extremely simple: figure out which stance your opponent is using, switch to its counter stance, attack. I was able to win a duel in my first play session using this strategy. This doesn't mean you can win by button mashing/spamming, because the more you play, the more you memorize the moves of the five characters, and can easily dodge their counter stances and move in to use your own. This is just a basic summary, because you can also charge attacks for each stance, and there are also five different weapon types to choose from, which mix up the formula quite a bit!
There is one major drawback: low player base. Unfortunately, it is rare to see more than 10 people playing this game at one time within a reasonable ping. Once you go over 100 ping the game is really unplayable (which is not any different from any other game), but that is often the only way to get on a server with any players!
I definitely recommend that you get it, especially if it's on sale, so you can be part of the solution and increase the player count! you won't regret it!

Final Fantasy IX is easily one of the best Final Fantasies out there. Zidane was a breath of fresh air after Cloud and Squall depressed us with their emo mannerisms. All of the characters were fun and exciting. The story itself seems to transcend its own seriousness in lieu of light-hearted silliness and many many opportunities to get sidetracked with other activities, like Chocobo Digging and Tetra Master.
The PC release offers us help in the form of fast forwarding, easy skills, and max gil. I will admit to being tempted to use them, and I would recommend it for any buyers who lack the patience for an old grindy game, but there has been and always will be a feeling of satisfaction that comes with seeing your efforts pay off when you finally learn a new skill or level up after a lengthy grinding session.
I have heard a couple of reports of controllers not working, though my lame Steelseries 3GC works just fine, and I have seen people using the 360 controller reporting no issues as well.
The polished character models are fantastic! I can, for the first time, appreciate the detail that went into these characters. Faces that simply looks like colored blobs of pixels, now actually look like faces and their bodies have details I had only noticed in cutscenes and closeups. Unfortunately, the backgrounds were not upgraded. I have read that this is due to much of the original material being lost over the years.
All-in-all, I'll say that this game is worth the price, especially since it is discounted off the bat. I would have gladly paid $25 just due to the sheer amount of content in this game. You will get your moneys worth in this. Don't fret over how old the game is until you've seen how much is in it.

Mafia II has a really great episodic story structure and mostly avoids being just another GTA clone, but the cast and some of the questionable game design choices just cannot compete with its predecessor. Still, if you like mob stories, it is a very solid pick.
Mafia II is a decent GTA IV clone with emphasis on story and characters over the sandboxing elements. It follows the exploits of Vito Scaletta, the son of an immigrant to Empire Bay (New York), who, with his friend Joe, slowly finds his way into the Italian Mafia.
His tale is not a classic rise the power one, more like a series of schemes and jobs to raise money to pay back his latest debt. This creates a very realistic motivation but serves as a poor game element, because the developers regularly just wipe your entire in-game account to create a reason for the “next big plan”.
Since the plot follows a get rich, lose money cycle for almost an entire decade, it is very episodic in nature, divided into 15 chapters. The large time span and almost self-contained chapters were a good tool to build the world, but not so great when it came to character development. The cast does a great job, but when you see only a small glimpse of the characters’ lives, even they cannot do too much. To compensate, all the missions feel unique with just few enough GTA-like shooting sprees to not turn it into another dumb TPS.
On its own, Mafia II is an enjoyable plot-oriented shooter/driver game with a small map (that feels more like a fan-made GTA IV mod project). Compared to its predecessor though, it feels shallow. Mafia 1 was like the Godfather trilogy with an excellent main character you could relate to: a good man who ended up in a bad life. Mafia II is more like a weaker season of Sopranos: grittier atmosphere, lots of cursing, and a main character that is nothing but a two-bit thug. It is a good game with a good story, but it had the misfortune to follow up a much better one.
The unique climate and the plot makes this game timeless. Instead of wasting the time for GTA V or SR4, just come back to Mafia II! <3

There were some nice moments, there is some nice art and vistas, but the gameplay is glitchy, the pacing awful, the direction unclear, and the checkpoint system frustrating as hell. Having to target those crystals to recharge your grapple with pin-point accuracy while swinging around is horrid, especially when I tried with a gamepad. I absolutely had to switch to keyboard+mouse.
I did finish it, but it became an exercise in extreme frustration too many times. A real shame, because I was somewhat captivated by the art and the world (I even liked the low-poly character art that others dislike. I found them charming.) Some of the reveals are quite breathtaking.

A Story about my Uncle was a unique experience for me. The game is quite short and it took me a little less than 6 hrs to complete it. The story is fairly simple and straightforward as the protagonist narrates a story to his daughter about a journey that he embarked on to find his beloved uncle's whereabouts when he was a kid. Coming to the gameplay, this is exactly the department where the game has something new to offer to the players. The core mechanics of the gameplay involves crossing various levels ranging from frozen caverns to paradisal floating city to mystical landscapes by means of a grappling hook. It can be quite frustrating at times to progress through some parts of almost every level given the challenging level designs. Timing and patience is, more often than not, the key to successfully cross those hurdles. Barring those, the gameplay is actually quite fun and somewhat makes you feel as if you're a superhero as you fly high and soar through the levels. The visual fidelity is quite decent. It is more of an artwork with good colour contrasts. The enigmatic and imaginary elements of the game world adds to the overall graphics quality as well. The ambience in-game was very good as it incorporates a sense of calmness and keeps you hooked to it throughout its entirety. The controls were quite responsive. Didn't have any problem in that regard as well. On the other hand, the achievements are tough to unlock in this game too. So a heads up for the achievement hunters out there. There's also a time trial mode where you've to complete the previously completed levels within a limited time. And that pretty much wraps up my review.
P.S-There's not much replay value to it to be honest. So get it on a sale. Once installed sit back and relax and enjoy this game on a Sunday afternoon. You won't be disappointed! :)

EGAD this game is beyond phenomenal! Initially a Sonic fangame, it eventually evolved into its own amazing thing. Think Sonic meets Rocket Knight and you're on the right track. What makes it amazing is that these people are CLEARLY hardcore Treasure fans and I do NOT throw that around lightly. There's a difference between "We were inspired by Treasure" (which I swear EVERYONE says) and "We STUDIED Treasure". It's like they refused to finish the game unless they themselves were blown away or something!
As for that "pesky" story? Guess what? You can turn it off. When you start a new game you get a choice of "Adventure" or "Classic" mode. Classic removes all the cutscenes. Mind you the story is pretty solid and the voicework is at worst on-par with Working Designs but if you REALLY hate it? Turn it off.
The pixel art is phenomenal, the music is great, the gameplay is fast-pace, responsive, and fun. The stages are incredibly varied, the amount of enemies is unbelieveable, and the game is LONG. This is the single greatest Indie Game I have ever played. No joke.
The fact that this isn't getting more love is outright criminal. This is the digital equivalent of Shantae in that respect, a game that gets tons of praise but nobody plays and then 10 years later is worth $300 on EBay. It's a shame this doesn't have a physical release because yes, it seriously would be one of those.
Get it. Just...get it. (Ignore the time stamp, I play it a lot on a different PC in offline mode)

Another classic Star Wars game that simply does not hold up. Has the same issues as it's sequel/expansion Jedi Academy but is worse off because you have to play the innacurate and poorly designed FPS sections for a number of hours before you get to play the just as innacurate and poorly designed (but more fun) lightsaber/Jedi sections. Enemies ping pong everywhere, hit detection is horrific, and weapons feel ineffective. The level design is actually quite excellent, but the environments because tedious quickly and you're esentially tasked with a escort mission right from the beginning, but the game is designed as a fast paced and exploratory FPS, so you will fail a lot as your partner dies. Also, Jedi Academy has SIGNIFICANTLY better graphics and presentation despite only coming out a year later. I know that these classic games are from a different era, but if people would take their rose tinted glasses off, they would see they shouldn't be recommend to anyone in 2017. Jedi Outcast, Academy, and especially Republic Comando, are all garbage now. The cores of these games are profoundly broken and the designs don't hold up. Save your money and play KOTOR or Battlefront 2, both excellent games that have aged beautifully, and allow you to make your own fun and stories.

I first got the demo for this game in 2002 or so from a disk wrapped together with- I think PC Gamer magazine. I would always look for the magazines with demo CD's in them at the local supermarket. The CD caught my eye through the plastic wrapping because the cover said STAR WARS in big letters with an awesome looking blue and white symbol. I got home and put the CD in, ignoring the other demos on the disk and quickly installed it (Quickly being subjective as game installation wasn't a short process back then). I finally started it up, and it was the most mind blowing gaming experience I had had up to that point. I beat the level the game came with and then had hours of fun with cheats and console commands. A few years later I was able to get the game at either Circuit City or CompUSA or something. I never got around to beating it. I played a lot of multiplayer then, which was also great fun. Some guy taught me all these crazy moves and harmless glitches of sorts you could do in multiplayer that only a select group of people knew about, which was so much fun. People would be mesmerized and I always enjoyed teaching them the secrets. I can't remember any of it anymore. But, if you're out there, guy who taught me Jedi Outcast multiplayer secrets, thank you for the fond memories.
Well, I'm finally about to finish the game all these years later. Everyone is right in saying it hasn't aged too well in some aspects. But, back then, the things we think about games having or not having today, we didn't really think about. The standards we have from games today didn't exist then, so I've been trying to play it as objectively as I did back then. And it's still a blast. It can be difficult, and frustrating at some points. But man, is it fun. You progress from not being able to hit anything with a blaster to feeling like a practically indestructible god of the force.
I just want to thank the team that made this. I had a lot of great memories playing it when I was younger, and still am 15 years later.

As one of the less people who played this game maybe a bit longer (next to the main Dev of course), i guess it would be time now to write a review about this game - next to this i waited a bit before i write the review since the dev added a lot new things and stuff into the game and those might would have changed the review ever i would written it.
So after he also told me its now a good time to write one, i do it now.
Actually in the Screenshot i made, You might can see that the dev & I worked a bit together. Said that, I have to say here that the Dev is really a nice guy and maybe one of the closed "down to earth" guys/devs i met so far (Konami, Capcom, you guys should learn something from this guy, srs!).
Said that, he also asked me to review the game.
So first, i bought the game (i didnt got a free key) coz i wanted the game. Now i have it, played it and can gladly review it.
As the dev already uses the main line "If Lemmings meets Boulder Dash", thats kinda the gameplay this game offers.
You have a Number of "Miners", which looks a lot like the classic Lemmings (if you compair them you can see a bit changed but still, they REALLY looks like the original Lemmings) which also act like the Lemmings:
They walk around till they hit a object and turn around, falling off cliffs & like, drown in water, die if they explode and like.
Already with that in mind, you get this "Lemmings vibe".
But where is the "Boulder Dash" part now you will ask?
Well, the "main part" (i use this word with caution, you will see later why) of this game is to use abilitys with this said Miners in the style of Lemmings to dig around the map you choosed from, getting Gems/Jewels and like, avoiding ice, boulders which can fall and crush your Miners, explosivs, gas-pockets and other things which can easy destroy/kill your Miners.
If you got the said Gems/Jewels, here begins the other part of the game: Get the Miner back to your Home with this Gems/Jewels in one piece.
So its not only a "How deep can you dig" Game, its also a "How can i dig and be Save to come home" Game.
As i got the game, I already loved it but a lot stuff was missing or made the game kinda feel "unfair". I shortly after talked with the dev and i gave him some ideas like:
- A Jewelbag a Miner loses if he dies so another Miner can collect the Bag with all the lost Jewels.
- Coins which give you some cash instandly (unlike Gems/Jewels which have to be brought back home first).
- More Weapons like a Bomb for laying, Lasers for destroying explosives or other obstacles and a flamer for digging out a smaller area
- Mini missions which gives you a small challange.
Of course, the dev had some own ideas and thrown them in (its his game, after  all) and just with this "little things", the game makes a whole lot fun. The Jewelbag makes it not so hard if you lost your Miner on the way back home, the Coins let you buy some abilitys wile youre digging and the Weapons work more as tools (at least that was my idea) you can use if you need them.
It sure is a nice game and i played it for a long time as i got it and as the Dev build in all the new ideas and co but after a wile it got a bit "boring" and now i play it more "ones in a wile". Again, i really
the idea and the game, mixing 2 great games from not only my childhood.
The problem i have (at least) is that this said "main part" (here i come back to it) has not really any kind of "goal".
Its not like Lemmings where you actually have to save a number of Lemmings or Boulder Dash where you have to collect a number of gems and find the exit.
It sure mixes the gameplay very (
) well but it misses the side of "complied" something:
You dig around with abilitys which you also have to buy again after using a said ability. You get money by either collecting a coin or bring back gems/jewels back to your home. If you bring said gems/jewels back to your home, you buy with the money you get from them said abilitys and go digging, returning into the circle ones again.
Its not like it is a bad idea, the problem is just it misses something "why" youre going to dig in the first place.
Let me explain that:
If i buy me a pickaxe
to dig around and get a jewel, bring it back home, selling it
for buying myself
pickaxe.....i guess you see what i try to explain...
It misses a kind of "goal" to be honest. Something like you "have to do" or "upgrate" or like. I said in my review what Lemmings & Boulder Dashs goal was. Those might not fit for this game but i could image like you have to build a city with that money or upgrate your Miners with it - a bit like in Terraria or games like...(not in the gameplay)
So is the game really worth playing?
I
since it is a good game and a good idea. Next to this, you can talk with the dev (who is begging for feedbacks to make the game better (in a good way)) about ideas and he might add those. The game plays nice but you will end like me maybe, playing it a bit longer at the first time and ending up playing it ones in a wile. Thats actually not bad but as i already said, "Its like a raw diamond which needs to be cut and polished", meaning that it lacks of a goal why youre going to dig around at the first place. It is really nice and it can keep you busy (i played it ones 3 hours in one sitting, forgot the time wile i did) but after a longer time you might begin to ask yourself the same question, where is the goal behind it.
I will say, for 5 bucks, it really is a nice game and for that what you get you actually cant complain about a really nice old-school digging game. Still, as i said, something like a "reason", a "goal" why youre going to dig would be really nice.
If i would give it a score it would be a 7 our of 10 since its nicely made but missing a "special something to make it whole".
And at the end for this review, here a fanmade trailer (so yea, i really like this game)

A little indie game by one of the friendliest devs I've ever encountered on Steam. A hybrid of Boulder Dash & Lemmings, in this game you release miners which you control in a similar manner to Lemmings, the aim being to have them explore the map, dig & find precious materials, whilst avoiding dangers such as explosives, gas, long falls & so on. To receive any rewards once the gems & other elements have been collected you need to get your miners back home which is often the hardest part.
The game seems pretty stable though it could do with a little more polish. Although gameplay is fairly easy to pick up I would have liked to see an in game tutorial. Whilst the game is score based there are a nice collection of achievements to offer additional objectives.
I wouldn't hesitate to pick up this game in a bundle or when discounted 50%+. Given the current depth I'd struggle to recommend it at full price, however although not in early access the dev is still working on the game & is both very enthusiastic about this project & accommodating of suggestions. This fact alone sways my decision in favour of suggesting anyone who thinks they like the concept to give it a go.
As the dev himself suggests, try it & if you're not happy, get a quick refund. I get the impression that if just a handful of Lemmings fans get into this game & give the dev good feedback, he'll be able to take the game that bit further & with a smidgeon of luck turn it into a tiny sparkling gem.

MANIC MINERS, as it advertises, is basically what happens when Lemmings has a baby with boulder dash. The game comes in 3 difficulty settings, Easy, Medium and Hard. No gamemodes beyond the current one, of course, but why would there need to be?
The game is simply explained aswell. Release miners (basically your lemmings) from the house and go about controlling them in an almost identical fashion to the Lemmings games to traverse through every nook and crany of the map, collecting gems and other valubles which increase your highscore if you manage to successfully get them home.
I bought this game myself shortly after coming into contact with the developer on steam. He was very kind and so I thought I would do my part and at least give his game a go. I'm glad I had. I had issues at first with the key bindings, but upon asking him about it, the game was soon updated to include tool-tips to remind the player of the keybindings. I have never met a developer who is so considerate of the needs of his customers.
This brings me on to his dedication. This game appears to be, despite what the update logs say, recieving updates (be it minor or large) on almost a daily basis. I can't deny that I'm surprised. I've genuinely been given the impression that he really, and I mean REALLY, cares about his work.
More about the game though. It plays a little clunky, I have had troubles from time to time controlling my miners but that may be entirely down to how incompetent I am at the game. I don't believe the game looks particually polished graphically and I can't help but feel like the game would have been better in early access, in the sense that the developer is planning for so many more features to be added that it almost seems like it's not quite finished. However, for this kind of game, graphics don't matter anywhere near as much as they might in other games.
Non-the-less, I believe the game for such a small price of £4.99 is definitely worth a shot (there's always the refund system if it doesn't turn out to be what you're looking for), there's a lot of fun to be had. Perfectionists will love doing the same levels in order to get the highest scores possible and casuals will love to pop on, play a short game and come off again. It really does feel like a new lemmings game but with more replayability, so if you were looking for more Lemmings or just a game that brings something completely different to the table unlike the usual over saturated♥♥♥♥♥♥on steam, you may be pleasantly surprised to find that MANIC MINERS might tickle your fancy.
I really, whole-heartedly, recommend taking a look at this game.

well, close to it lol.
The Sonic series has had a lot of ups and downs. 06's buggy mess, the storybook series, the Werehog stages, Sonic 4's broken physics.
It really hasn't been that great for the blue blur, but Generations has truly restored the famous hedgehog to his former glory. Colors was pretty decent (Worth playing on Dolphin if you haven't) but this game is so much better.
There's a great blend of sidescrolling and full 3d platforming. The stages are very well designed and its just what you'd want out of a modern Sonic game. Like the old classic games, there are so many alternate routes and paths. While Unleashed day stages were enjoyable, they were quite linear. That's completely gone and improved so much. This FINALLY feels like a modern take on the classic Sonic series and really what else should an anniversary remake be? The speed here is fast like Unleashed and the platforming isn't blocky like it was in Colours. There's a great blend of everything. No forced gimmicks, with the exception of optional side missions and those are actually quite fun as well. Speaking of which, this game has a nice amount of content for a Sonic game. Apart from the mentioned side missions (and there's a ton), there's a bunch of unlockables such as powerups you can equip for playing levels and music tracks.
My only real complaint with the gameplay is, once again, there's much more sidescrolling gameplay than 3d. Not as bad as Colors but I would really prefer at least a 50-50 cut. The modern stages have sidescrolling, but the classic stages don't have 3d so its a bit unbalanced.
Speaking of music, this game sounds wonderful. It includes a bunch of remixes of tracks in the series as well as complete remakes of them with the original artists returning! On top of that, you can use the unlocked music to change what plays in each level. Such a simple, but great feature.
Since we're talking about art, the visuals in this game are fantastic. The textures might not be the highest and a tad more anti-aliasing in the options wouldn't hurt, but I'm just nitpicking. This game looks absolutely gorgeous and I think they absolutely nailed the artstyle for a modern Sonic game.
The story.. umm. yeah, the story isn't good. Its just there. Don't expect a good story in this one. Considering this is an anniversary title, I don't think it even matters. The game is fun enough that I can look past this without considering it a flaw.
As for the PC side of things? This game is one of Sega's better ports and I'm glad to see them improving on that aspect. It runs quite well and I had no issues with it. Works flawlessly with the few gamepads I've used and performs without problem. Even when I had a weak PC, I could stay at 60 FPS pretty easily. Also has some leaderboards.
And of course there's mods. From your typical character swaps to music changes to new levels and even full blown expansions. The most popular one is the Unleashed project. It ports all of the day stages from Sonic Unleashed into this game. Tons of fun to play through and you don't have to suffer through those tedious werehog levels :) There's also all the acts from some of the zones in Sonic Colors and a million other different things. Great chance to play Colors and Unleashed levels if you never had the games on console and don't wanna emulate Colors.
Its definitely worth checking out the mods for this game, regardless of what you do :)
Overall this game is definitely a top favorite for the series and I'm a rather big Sonic fan. In fact, finding out the modern Sonic games were on PC now was a huge motivation to even get a proper gaming PC. This was my first game on Steam! and it still holds up 5 years later.
I really loved playing through Sonic Generations and can't recommend it enough. Its not something that'll get you hundreds of hours unless you're a completionist, speedrunner, or enjoy playing or even creating mods, but there's still plenty of content and replay-ability regardless. I really think its the best Sonic game out there! Give it a go.
Buy it.

While I've only just beaten the 4th level of this game, I can with very little doubt say that Freedom Planet is a masterpiece of platforming fun.
I'm so happy I decided to purchase this game, after seeing it sit quietly in my wishlist for a couple months.  What initially worried me about the game was that it would be too much of a Sonic clone, what with all those curved ramps, super dashes, and long rows of gems.  To be honest, I was never much of a Sonic fan, and I was worried the game would rely too much on that whizzing as fast as possible through the levels. And yes, this game can easily be played in a speed run style (you do have a timer in the right corner of the screen) where you simply dash, fly, hurl yourself through the gigantic levels.
But what I've found is that Freedom Planet also works wonderfully when played a little slower, taking your time to explore the various nooks, and rooms, and tunnels, etc. Because of this, each level I've played so far has taken me between 40 minutes and 1 hour to complete.  There is just SO MUCH detail in the levels that taking a more exploratory approach felt right to me, and is highly rewarding as well.  I've been savoring every moment of this game.
Yes, the cut scenes are a bit on the lengthy side, and yes they probably could be streamlined a bit, but this in no way detracted from my experience with the game.  From my perspective, 10-minute cut scenes were interpreted as generosity from the developers.  And if you don't like them, there is the "classic mode" which contains no cut scenes, only game play. There is a massive amount of content here, well worth even the full price, though I did purchase the game during a %50 off sale.
So, if you are in any way on the fence about Freedom Planet, may I suggest you hop off that fence and get ready to fall in love with one of the most beautiful, inventive, humorous, hear-warming, and incredibly fun games I've come across in quite some time.

Second off, the game is very, very polished.
