For a game that’s priced almost as much as its subgenre competitors (ABZÛ, Depth Hunter 2 and World of Diving), Infinite Scuba doesn’t have nearly as much content or polished details to compare itself or even stand out. Not to mention the chance of softening the blow from the premature implementation of microtransactions in an Early Access title that is obviously far from completion. The game’s developer made some amateurish mistakes which I will describe in detail below.
First and foremost among Infinite Scuba’s many sins, has to be the lack of proper diversity as far as the diving locations are concerned. You just have two such places and in a twisted sense of irony, one level has to be unlocked with “clams” (the game’s idea of currency). So indeed, you can visit just one stage if you choose to spend your initial and so far only amount of 500 clams on diving equipment instead of unlocking the Mesoamerican Reef level. Naturally, I had to make the only smart choice available in this case and I unlocked 50% more “content”. You cannot gain these pesky clams in any way during gameplay. So I think we can either expect the developer to proceed with his intention of selling the in-game currency at real world money value or take the decent way out of this mess and at least offer a way of gathering some of the clams through the activities you perfrom as a diver. But they probably won’t do that since the prospect of earning even more cash than the game’s price tag is too enticing to pass up, right? Bravo, gentlemen!
While the Belize level offers just the opportunity to explore a large coral reef, the game’s main location is the Chuuk Lagoon from Micronesia where you can delve into an actual historic shipwreck. Sadly, the Gosei Maru cannot be examined as thoroughly as you’d expect since Infinite Scuba’s interior exploration hasn’t been implemented yet. Just like its wonderful clam gesheft! So you may ask, just what exactly CAN you do in this simulator? Well dive, of course. I have to admit that the diving mechanics themselves as well as the information provided (and a pleasant amount of trivia also) gave the impression that the game tries to take itself seriously enough and I wouldn’t be able to rate it any lower than I did.
Honestly, I really gave it a fair chance and took nearly a dozen dives. It’s unfortunate that they have to last so little (not even 10 minutes per single dive) and the oxygen tanks seem to have the capacity of a plastic bag. If you don’t move a lot and your depth is just a few meters from the surface, I guess you could prolong the underwater trip but what’s the point of standing still, in a simulator about seafloor exploration? Infinite Scuba actually marked some of my dives as “unsuccessful” since I had less than 500 oxygen units left in the tank by the time I resurfaced. You start out all your dives with 3000 units which rapidly decrease if you swim below 30 meters. The grinding required in order to complete all your tasks, cannot be estimated at a number lower than 25 dives per location. Absurd.
The wildlife is nicely detailed and simulated, though there is never enough variety when it comes to larger cartilaginous fish (such as rays and sharks). And I’m certain that no one would risk deep dives just for the sake of fifty different coral shapes and sizes. At least there are also objects scattered on the seabed for you to collect or catalogue. You can take pictures of certain areas of interest on the shipwreck and get awarded with in-game achievements (which never result in actual Steam achievements or at least some wonderful clams to unlock new gear).
The simulation itself ain’t half-bad even with the mediocre oxygen tank capacity. You can enjoy the game and relax while swimming and exploring but I cannot tolerate this title’s particularly abhorrent form of microtransactions. A malicious practice to gaming in general, in Infinite Scuba this is only made worse since you can’t obtain the so-called clams through simply playing the game and thus there’s no real gain even from grinding the two areas (or just one, if you didn’t spend all the clams on the Belize level). This isn’t a reward system. Just pure greed!
+ Decent looking & sounding.

- Early Access with just two diving locations (one being initially locked until you “pay” for it).

So far, I'm really enjoying this game. I've always wanted to SCUBA dive, but I've not been able to. This game is realistic enough to give me a small taste of what it might be like. It simulates important effects of depth such as nitrogen narcosis and the need for a safety stop after a deep dive.
So far, the game includes two maps: Chuuk Lagoon and Belize. (The Belize map is 500 clams, but you start with that much at the beginning.) Chuuk Lagoon includes the wreck of the Gosei Maru, a Japanese ship that sank there in World War Two. Belize includes the Mesoamerican Reef. The player is given a list of "Things to Do" at each site, such as swimming to special areas, finding underwater caches, spotting different kinds of wildlife, finding artifacts, and, at Belize, cleaning up trash. I thought the activities were interesting, though some of the collections are very hard to complete.
The swimming feels natural, though it took me some time to get used to using the camera independently of the swim direction. The player can hit "N" to orient oneself, but I wish that there was also a button to just reset the camera. Also, the "H" key gives help for the keys but doesn't mention the ballast vest controls, CTL and SPC. A player would have a tougher time playing without that information.
A couple of nitpicks: The Belize map has water currents, but they seem to flow randomly and without a pattern. I could be mistaken, though. Also, a sudden surface from a very deep dive still counts as a "Successful dive" even though in real life it would cause decompression sickness.
The game does have microtransactions, but except for extra maps (in the future) it all seems to be cosmetic. There doesn't seem to be a noticeable difference in how the extra gear works. While some people hate microtransactions on principle, I personally have no problem with buying extra content.
For the price, I would recommend this.
Edit: My remarks to another review were deleted by the reviewer, so to answer those points again here:
"30 second unskippable warning screen every time during launch" and "Extremely long loading times accompanied by obnoxious music, even on an SSD." This is only the first time you play the game. The long loading time is because the maps are downloaded from the Internet when you first load it. The other reviewer must have just started the game a single time and then immediately deleted it.
"Only ONE map is included in the game price." It comes with one map and 500 "clams," and then you can get the second one for 500 clams. I have two maps, and I didn't buy anything except the base game.

Steer clear of this one unless you want to pay real money for game content which is already boring, dated and not a fun experience in any way.
Cons:
-  in-game purchases gates content despite already paying $13 for the game.
-  Low budget dated graphics.
-  30 second unskippable warning screen every time during launch.
- "Early" access to a game that's been worked on since 2010 and is a chore to experience.
-  Extremely long loading times accompanied by obnoxious music, even on an SSD.
-  Bare bones options.  A resolution and Quality setting.  Nothing else.
-  Extremely unrealistic underwater movement breaks any possibility of immersion.

PROS:

SimCity™ 4 Deluxe Edition offers the whole SimCity™ 4 experience, and in my opinion is the best SimCity™ game yet. It also allows you to export some of your creations and import them into The Sims™ 2, so if you also have that one installed you're in for a treat.

If you are looking for a city builder with extremely well designed mechanics and gameplay, Sim City 4 is the game, without question.
Cities XL, other generic clones, and even Sim City 5, shouldn't even be compared with Sim City 4. You may think like "Let's be honest, it's outdated.", and you would be so wrong. It is not, and probably won't be outdated, just like Mario Bros, Tetris, or Pac-Man.. Sim City is the very first initial applicaton of city building (both in terms of management mechanics and sandbox mode.), and Sim City 4 is the absolute peak of series. While even vanillia game is a very good experience, various mods which are still being created (After +10 years the game is released.)(Which on it's own is a proof of how well mechanics are made.) regularly, provides you anything you could ever wish for.
I almost can't find any possible upgrade ideas for Sim City 4 (While some mods are included.), except some graphical fidelity - and the fact that these 10 year old graphics are exceptionally good for its time (You can apply some recent HD texture packs, too!), it won't be bothering you at all. Actually, in my opinion, 2,5D graphics are pretty optimal for such game. There are some pretty obvious cases like Stronghold Crusader & Stronghold II / StarCraft:BW & StarCraft 2, where 2,5D to 3D transition actually killed the uniqueness of gameplay. Even in the case of SC, when I exclude the mechanical differences of SC5 with SC4, gameplay is also kind of degraded. With so much going on in terms of gameplay, you may, and probably will be looking for some simplicity in terms of graphics which lightens the load in your brain, and SC4 has that.
If you are someone who is looking for a top quality city building game, here is the absolute starting line.
If you are someone who is into that genre, and you didn't played SC4...well...better late than never!

Final Fantasy 9 is a game from my childhood. A game I have really fond memories of. In a lot of ways it's a game all about nostalgia.
Final Fantasy 9 takes place in a very cutesy chibi fantasy world where steampunk technologies like airships are just starting to become a thing. You play as Zidane, an amusing rogue who initially starts his quest on a mission to kidnap a princess. A far cry from the cold and distant protagonists of Cloud Strife and Squall Leonheart. However the plot gradually opens up into a very long quest as you eventually explore the world and encounter it's inhabitants.
The characters are where the game truly nails it. All of the party members in Final Fantasy 9 are memorable. Your black mage Vivi is insecure and always nervous. And Zidane and Vivi gradually grow into this almost brotherly bond with one another. Your princess Garnet yearns for adventure and over the course of the storyline develops a very pleasant romance with the protagonist. You eventually pick up her bodyguard Steiner, a perpetually aggravated knight sworn to protect her. And even more fantastical party members like Freya, an anthropomorphic rat clad in armor who joins the party looking for her long lost love. And Quina, a bizarre creature who has abilities based on enemies you allow him to consume. All of the party members in Final Fantasy 9 are great. I remembered all of them and the way they interact with each other and develop over the course of the story is a real treat.
The battle system in 9 takes from the previous games in numerous ways. The ATB system returns and they increased the amount of party members you can have in a single battle to 4 just like the pre-7 games. What I like about this release of the game in particular is it allows you to select elements of the user interface using the mouse. Which is very convenient and reduces the amount of fumbling through the menu that it usually would with the controller.
This is the first time Final Fantasy 9 has ever been released off the original Playstation so there are a few things to note if you've played Final Fantasy 7 or 8's PC ports. It doesn't let you use linear filtering like the original PS1 version, it uses a bilinear filter. For most people this won't be that big of a deal but it does look different compared to how you're used to. Otherwise it lets you play the game either with a controller or with a keyboard/mouse. And lets you control the user interface using the mouse which is a real treat to me. They also added an autosave feature and numerous little quirks into the game like allowing you to skip cutscenes.
One other thing to note is this isn't a full remake of Final Fantasy 9. The FMVs are the same, as are the 2D backgrounds and the 3D models. The only major differences I've noticed in the port compared to the original PS1 version are changes in the user interface. And like 7 and 8's PC ports it lets you optionally enable cheats to make you super powerful at the start of the game. So far the only major issue I've noticed is related to controller sensitivity so I hope that gets promptly fixed.
The entire game has this feeling of going back to something special. The soundtrack especially is full of very soft and somber themes that hearken back to childhood. It's a game that makes you feel like you're a kid again, and makes you want to return to old games you grew up with.

.

I have been a fan of the Company of Heroes series for many many years. From the very day that it first came out the new and exciting mechanics, the visuals, the visceral and extremely tactical gameplay, the sheer diversity of the units.. It all just took me away on a journey that would see me spend well over 10,000 hours. In the base game, in the expansions, even in the much-hated TOV mission pack. I had fun. The mods.. oh god the mods. So many, so diverse, so exciting.
Company of Heroes was a game that captured the attention and love of many people like me. It commanded our attention through it's gritty, yet tactical gameplay. It enjoyed our love through the excellent graphics and animation. We commited to it for years because of the excellent mod scene and thousands of tactics to try.
None of this exists in CoH 2. The graphics, although flashy, are rather ugly and difficult to keep track of. The sounds are less immersive than a shallow pool of acid. The gameplay.. stale, samey and fundamentally boring, with many a mechanic feeling like it was massively dumbed down for.. no real good reason. The lack of proper mod support from the outset meant that mods never took off like they did in vCoH, and now never will, further killing everything that was so loved about the original.
The ridiculous skinner box techniques? The laughable levelling system? The clunky UI and attrocious pathfinding - worse even that vCoH? The nails to the coffin are many.
I wish that, perhaps, with Company of Heroes 3 the series will return a bit to it's roots. That it won't continue down the path of simplicity, lame RPG-lite skinner boxes and a lack of interest in anything resembling tactics the way that Dawn of War 3 did. The direction taken by Relic by now is very clear, however. I do not hold out hope for I do not believe there is any to be had. CoH 2 is but the first death knell for the series. Both this one and the Dawn of War franchise. The two pillars of Relic crumbling to dust - this is where it started folks.

Solid platformer with cheerful music. Started as an homage to Sonic and evolved into something more original.

Each stage has a few levels and a boss at the end and some mini-bosses too. Bosses are diverse and range from pushovers to punishing. I either got them in one or two tries or died a bunch of times while figuring out their patterns. There is one uninspiring shooting stage but you can get through it almost entirely without moving.
You can play with three characters that each have their own tactics and some different stages. I suggest you check a guide or wiki to learn their moves, as the game doesn't tell you about them.
Lilac is a dragon with useful and powerful moves. She's strong and simple to control.
Carol is a cat with a motorcycle, can use teleporters, and she can wall-climb. Unfortunately you're often without the motorcycle, which diminishes her uniqueness. She has a harder time evading enemies, unless there's a handy wall available.
Milla is a dog that can fly, dig, and summon blocks and shields. She has less health than the others but doesn't need energy to power her moves. She's probably easiest to play once you get the hang of her. She isn't immediately available and has no story mode.
The story is simple and forgettable, but the presentation is endearing. You can play without the story parts if you like.
I didn't care for the pixelated art. If a sequel is made, I hope they try out high-resolution graphics.

First off this game feels amazing and satisfying, the looks are great, music  and sound is good, the attention to detail is there, quite really you can see that the developers of this game made it with love and care.

The gameplay of the 3 main characters is diferent from each other, Lilac is very mobile and has alot of ways to attack, and her dash is easly the best move in the game because of the invincibility it gives you, quite your balanced character, Carol is a very "in-your-face" character that you have to get in there to deal damage and avoid damage but its dangerous because its not as mobile and her double jump will get you killed more than it will help you on certain boss fights, quite literally her moveset yells: GET GOOD, also her motorcicle is awesome, honestly i dont know how they had the idea of having a motorcicle climb stairs, but y'know... videogames.

In terms of voice acting... well, i honestly am neutral, i dont mind is as much, because i feel that the voices do fit the characters greatly, but the execution on some scenes feel lacking, specially on Carol when she is crying, it just made me go: "Carol... you are sad.. why dont you sound sad, SOME EMOTION PLEASE" and Milla sounds very nasal to me, its almost there, but not quite, while Lilac, is the least flawed, but it does have some awkward lines where you can kinda notice that she is reading the lines but not getting 100% in it, but still her voice fits very well in my opinion.

Sega Fans:
Try and imagine that a Sega 32X game from the future suddenly arrived on a time-traveling motorcycle and said, inexplicably, "quick! Get on! There's no time to explain!" It then wisks you off to an alternate timeline where Gunstar Heroes, Ristar, and Sonic the Hedgehog were the top charting games of all time and the Sega Saturn somehow beat the Playstation and N64. This is the game that introduces you to that timeline. You owe it to yourself to buy and play this right now.
People with No Context for that:
Now that I'm done fanboying out, I'll tell you that if you played any of the Sonic games or any of the Mega Man games then Freedom Planet will feel familiar, but it's really its own thing. General controls and combat feel like a Mega Man game, but there's Sonic influences in that each level tends to have more than one path and there's a bit of emphasis on momentum, albeit not as much as in the actual Sonic games. There's a lot more margin of error, you have a health bar, and it isn't difficult to stop or change direction. You won't feel like you're controlling a pinball with legs so much as a very fast version of Mega Man who can cling to walls and run on ceilings.
In terms of production values, the game is influenced clearly from the best aspects of all of the above games, which all represent the finest platformers in the Sega Genesis catalogue. I mention the 32X because the presentation is a cut above those games, more in line with the 32-bit era of gaming than the 16-bit era, with more detail, more story, more color, voice acting, and a great soundtrack that goes beyond the indie chiptune status quo that you would expect from something like this.
Gameplay is a cut above the status quo as well. There's three playable characters with unique movesets and ways of navigating the environment. Each one is challenging and fun for different reasons and you'll have a blast taking apart enemies with their different blends of attacks. There are crazy-fun setpieces and tons of crazy-fun bosses galore. Every stage introduces unique enemies and obstacles, with very little being recycled between levels up until the end. Even then there's still new things being introduced as late as the last level. Everything sparkles, and EVERYTHING EXPLODES in the most satisfying way imaginable.
I will say it isn't without its rough edges. The physics are a bit odd, sometimes it feels like the characters are approaching top speed without ever reaching it, and the threshold for being able to cling to a wall with your speed seems a bit low -- which makes momentum-based obstacles easy to overcome, but they do feel a bit weird. There's some places where you can tell the designers were still "feeling out" what's fun and what's a fair challenge, particularly with some boss and enemy designs. Something you need to get through your head in later levels is that you don't really get points for killing most enemies, so a lot of them are better left ignored or treated as stage obstacles rather than opponents.
These aren't really "bugs" or marks against the game's fun factor so much as what you'd expect from "first iteration" growing pains from a polished, finished, new product. It's comparable to what Ratchet and Clank 1 was like before its sequels refined its formula, and I'll be excited to see how Galaxy Trail improves on this base. Relative to the platforming world the experience stays fresh and satisfying for a good, long time, and relative to indie platformers this showcases by FAR a higher level of polish, effort, and variety than I'm used to seeing. There are established companies that don't make platformers this good.

Troubleshooting I've attempted:
Using only KB/M with no controller or receiver plugged in - right turn only
KB/M with receiver plugged in - right turn only
KB/M with receiver and controller on - right turn only
Removed any unused HID devices in device manager - right turn only
Unplugged keyboard, used controller with mouse and reciever plugged in - right turn only
Unplugged mouse, used controller with keyboard and receiver plugged in - right turn only

Bit of Back Story
I encountered the original Company of Heroes many years ago and back then I recall just how incredible and immersive the original game was particularly compared to other strategy games at the time. This sequel to the original does not disappoint and having played this game for many hours ever since it was in beta I have had the pleasure to see it come a long way over the years.
The Question of Balance
Always when you win - SKILL but when you lose - BALANCE
This game has had its fair share of up and down commentry on balance but it is the case with competitive games that there is an issue with one side having some set combination that dominates for a while and then it goes back the other way when patches are made.
I would rate this developer quite highly mainly due to how they dealt with the balance issue, namely, through gathering community feedback and developing patches to address concerns often releasing those patches on a monthly basis which would often lead directly to some dramatic and noticable shifts in the balance of the game overnight but in the longer term this lead to some great stuff by this developer in terms of balance.
Other development of key components in game
A very good history of development of the game as well with the addition of the multiplayer setup interface which came almost a year after the initial release. Often it was particularly annoying that the old interface of the original version was not included originally but then when it was it was made particularly well.
A lot of superficial additions like skins but sometimes rarely you would get a treasure of something like a new commander or some special trait. This was good but then when they made it all for purchase it became a game of pay to win which was annoying but was a minor issue if you were decent enough at the game to win without the need for commanders.
The modding tools that were released for modding made the game particularly fun to play around with as you could experiement and share making historically accurate gameplay to incredible maps many of which would be incorporated into the vanilla game as an addition.
My Experience Playing
It should be noted that the campaigns and the challenges are fun but the real game begins with multiplayer but the campaigns act as good training fields to learn the mechanics of the game.
I mainly play as Soviets but have also played as every other faction and I have to say that there is something uniquely special about this series. You always have the feeling of being in the battle with the units you were controlling and even watching the game afterwards it is brilliant to watch games including those that you lose in almost a movie like experience. I particularly love starting with some small relatively peaceful looking village or town and then over the course of the game blowing it to bits.
Compared to other strategy games out there CoH2 is not necessarily the balance king that goes to SC2 but unlike SC2 the game COH2 is more forgiving and much more immersive. You can pull yourself back from the brink unlike other games which favour the victor of the intial battle and often just lead to the initial winner steam rolling their opponent in the late game. The mechanics of this game allows for multiple opportunities for each side to achieve dominance and even bounce back into the game even when hampered early on.
The terrain on maps forces more indepth strategies to develop for using obstacles such as bridges, buildings, real fog of war and natural barriers like rivers and mountains makes this game far more immersive than any other on the market today. The game is also centered around many hard counters such that players are forced to think more indepth regarding their unit combinations and how each unit relates to the overall company strategy.

An impuse buy during the Steam Summer Sale while I was picking up Sonic 2 and Sonic 3 & Knuckles. Over all, I think it's nice and a good buy.
The characters are fully voiced which is new to me in games like this, but I will say sometimes they don't sound like they're fully reaching the kind of emotion they are trying to convey but it's still pretty good voice acting in my opinion.
I'm not one for graphics but this game looks like it tried to emulate Sonic's early days on the Dreamcast and Megadrive (I later heard that this was origonally a Sonic Fan Game so it's no wonder) and it does a fairly good job of doing that.
The game itself plays a lot like a Sonic Game from the "Classic Era" especially when one plays as Lilac. As a result I keep trying to spindash when playing. However Lilac's ability that lets her bounce off the walls at high speeds is kind of hard to get a good sense on where you're going to go or even which direction you'll go as sometimes it seems like it doesn't matter.
The levels take me a fairly long time to beat but that's not nessicarily a bad thing, there's a fair amount of collectables I could go after if I so choosed and it's fairly liberal with it's checkpoints. Though I do wish there was a visual/audio cue letting me know that I hit a checkpoint, so that I don't have to worry about losing a signifigant amount of progress.
The boss battles are
fun. They are fast paced, straight forward, and give good visual cues when the boss is on it's last leg. However they are a tad unforgiving at times, the boss for Fortune Night has you dodging all many of lasers and explosives causing you to sometimes miss much needed health thrown to you by your allies. That being said I still enjoyed the battles greatly.
The music in the game is GREAT, I bought the soundtrack with this game and I'm glad I did. Each one is fitting for the area and tone of the level. As well as the boss music pumping you up for the battle at hand.
Freedom Planet is a overall fun game that might seem rough around the edges in some areas but is a good buy during a sale.

Freedom planet is a game that's caught my eye for quite some time now. Esentaly i see it as the genesis version of
Shovel Knight, taking bits and peices from some of the more popular franchises of a gameing era now past and meshing it together in a blender for a smoothie of wonderful nostalgia. Shovel Knight has that castlevanina/ducktails/megaman
classic vibe to it, where as Freedom Planet has more Gunstar Heroes/Sonic the hedgehog/Ristar/Rocket knight/Pulseman/megaman x feel. I think it's a great throwback to genesis games and i will even go so far as to say its a damn near perefect genesis game on its own. But that's not just good thing though, as many of the other games i listed above have some problems with them that really stand out.
Sonic the hedgehog has the fast-paced and fun green hill zone, then suddenly the speed takes a backseat to lavablock riding! Gunstar heroes has its op weapons that make using any other weapon useless, making the game stale because you're just waiting for the tracking beam to chunk the target before progressing. Pluseman has levels that drag on forever later on, becomes fairly time consuming and boring. Ristar's ONLY option for mobility can get a player killed really dang easily if they aren't carefull, Sparkster (rocket knight) has a DISGUSTING difficulty spike in bosses..every game thats great has some sort of blemish that keeps it from being 100% solid.
Freedom planet is no diffrent from these titles, which is why it's the perfect genesis game. The basic controls are only 3 buttons: a jump button, an attack button, and a special button. The characters handle like a faster Ristar, but that can quickly shift to being almost Sanic speed. Lilac's dragon boost is Rocket knight's dash meet's pulseman's voltecker. It her best option for mobility and regaining speed. but if you hit a wall, you better pray to the heavens that there's a floor below you. Carol's strongest single-hit attack, the wild claw, is great for chunking mini bosses, but insanly awkward to use on bosses that tower over her because you need to pounce before being able to use it. The command for Wild claw gets even more awkward when you're riding Carol's kickass motorcyle that can drive up walls, as the command for the attack shifts. The third playable character is slower than the other two and takes a while to be able to retailate with anything decent in terms of damage, at the cost of being the only one of the 3 that can pick up items and block projectiles. Every character has their ups and downs, the levels are challenging but fair, and the bosses range from
easy to hard. However the dip from easy to hard differs from which character your as they go though different sets of levels, and some characters make the AI really braindead because of the tools they have at their disposal.
The story is nothing special to write home about. It seems like not even the game knows what kind of story it wants to tell. It starts off with someone being decapitated. Yeah, dark as hell right off the bat, BEFORE THE TITLE POPS UP. Then suddenly its all upbeat and nice! and then it gets dark. and then its upbeat again. then its dark and-well the point should be made, it shifts tones dramaticly with barely any middle ground in sight.there's a wonderful thing that this game has that as much as i wish it was added into other games: the ability to play the levels back to back and completely ignore the story.Even if the voice acting in the cutscenes is fairly decent, being able to play this like
it's an old console game with zero explanation to whats going on because i didn't "read the manual for the story" is probably one of my favorite things about it.
Honestly i will say if you really have an urge to play a genesis game, this is a perfect title to pick up. its fun, plays extremely well and definitly scratches that blast-processing itch. To someone who didn't really grow up with the genesis though, this might as well be hit-or-miss with you. But i can definitly say it will not be a waste of your time, especialy with the game currently being on sale.

At a first glance, one would easily see this game as a poseur Sonic game. Trust me when I say that it's much better than pretty much any Sonic game in the franchise. Some will complain that it's a 'bit game', and to those people, I would like to remind that the current day and age is effectively a 'revival of the bit', so some humility to the undying style would be nice(though if you'll still complain, I will respect your opinions; this is the internet, after all...).
High points:
-A game whose fast-paced action style will invigorate fans of platformers and sidescrollers
-Well-balanced characters whose traits suit their styles of combat and exploration
-Immersive and catchy music
Tripping points:
-The story, admittedly, could have been better, but still keeps the feel of games in the Bit Console Wars(Sega vs. Nintendo)
-The final four levels come with a moderately steep learning curve, but by this point, the game will still be challenging you to develop accordingly, so you should be okay if you're playing well
With a free DLC coming within the next few months, at best, for Torque, Spade and Milla's story lines, this game's a good pick. It's colorful, it has a great soundtrack, and of course has its fair share of in-stage collectibles. If you want a good platformer, buy this. If you want to reminisce about the days of the Bit Console Wars, this game's great for that, too. And for those who really want the feel of a controller, there's ever-developing support for it. Galaxy Trail's flagship title is a good sign for the company, I'd say, and those who have played Strife's other works will be anticipating the next title in line.

Saints Row IV fully embraces the wackiness they experimented with in the third game and goes full on insane with it.
You are the head of the Saints street gang, then you get elected as the President of the United States (which all things considered might be the least ridiculous thing about this game), then aliens invade and you get superpowers and thats all within the first hour of the game.
Gameplay is similar to previous Saints Row games, a relatively big open world with a bunch of activities to do, ranging from racing through the city to murdering furries in a game show. These side-activities can get a bit repetitive over time, however the inclusion of superpowers should keep things interesting for the most part. Superpowers are just awesome, you can super-sprint, jump up to skyscrapers and glide through the city. In combat you have access to powers such as hurling geat balls of fire, telekinisis and just stomping thing really, really hard.
The story is a lot of fun, with the expected Saints Row humour nicely infused throughout it's quests and its cast of quirky characters. There's a lot of references to other games and video-game tropes sprinkled throughout the campaign, they even parody the mass effect romance system.
Overall a really fun experience not to be taken too seriously.

I've had this game for a good year now and I'll admit it was the first Saints Row game I picked up cause I was itching for super power mechanics late one night. Long story short, this game immediately made its way up to one of my favorites and is definitely climbing the ranks in what games I've replayed the most times.
The game is amazingly well rounded. It's mostly a shooter, yes, but there's so many different takes on the shooter mechanic, on top of literally every other mission you're given being something completely and utterly different and wacky to do. This game cleverly includes hilarious parodies on the text-based adventure, the stereotypical stealth game, kaiju battles, arcade side-scrollers, rhythm games, racing, platforming, and TONS of different ways to shake up the general format of shooting your guns and making stuff go boom.
On top of that, the story may be MUCH wackier than that of previous Saints Row games, but it's still scarily well-developed. It's got a really compelling story on top of a consistently hilarious script with really lovable characters, and while it's far fetched and obviously a joke, the game does well to take itself serious most of the time and keep the player enthralled in the story. If you're looking for the overall seriousness of the past games, even the Third, then I can see why this would disappoint.
In my opinion, all in all, it's a hilarious game filled with an overwhelming variability and has a real high replay value cause of just how fun the gameplay is. I've played it a few times now and I plan to play it much more.

This game is a rather interesting case. I would say that it's the best sonic game since Sonic 3 & Knuckles, but that's... not a very good saying, since every game before Generations and since 3&K has been a downright trainwreck, at least in my book. However, this game takes all of the most successful thematic and gameplay elements from the entire Sonic franchise, strips away the layers upon layers of marketing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, and works to celebrate the survival of Sonic the Hedgehog.
Before I get too far in, I just want to say that as a PC port, this is a strange one. The developers decided to integrate full mod support, and while the modding community doesn't compare to, say, Skyrim, the dedicated modders out there will be able to give this game life support and keep it fresh for months after initially completing the game. Yet, in a very unusual move, Sega chose not to put much development into optimizing their PC port, to the point that the game has a sporadic framerate, sometimes unreliable shaders depending on your GPU, and worst of all, no in-game graphics tweaking. You cannot tweak the gameplay on the fly.
PC controls got no thought from the word go, and instead of binding keys as is standard in PC games, Sega takes a very Ubisoft-esque approach to bind keys to Xbox controller buttons. A sub-par experience for those using mouse and keyboard, even if the controls remain very fluid.
I just found it odd that they threw in something like mod support, but completely neglected controls and optimization for the PC port. And that sets the precedent for Sega's approach to the game's design. This game does some fantastic things, but it still struggles with the bare basics of 3D level design, and the franchise still is coming to grips with its identity.
The dialogue is nails-on-chalkboard bad at times, and the story is lackluster in every concievable way. But honestly, that doesn't really matter, since unlike the likes of Sonic Adventure 2 or Sonic '06, the story is treated as a vehicle for the gameplay here.
And despite the aforementioned lacklustre level design and poor optimization, playing as Sonic in this game feels really good. Like really awesome. You'll love building up momentum and blasting through classic areas at high speeds. For those who have followed the series more well than I, memorable scenes like the GUN Truck, and the battle with Shadow from Adventure 2 are all here.
The developers clearly have a much better grasp of the franchise identity than they've ever had, producing a high-octane, incredibly enjoyable platformer, albeit, with its hiccups. But even if you're not a fan of the franchise, there's something beautiful here, especially for the perfectionist who will fight to S-rank every mission, and beat their scores. Not to mention the incredibly varied and interesting enviornments, and the fantastic music.
There is no shock in saying this game is flawed. Almost stupidly so. And I would perhaps be more willing to punish this game if it weren't so clear that it's doing everything in its power to give you, the player, a good time.
Hopefully later Sonic titles will learn from this one's critical success, and build on the formula that this has established. If Sega continues to go this route with the franchise, while giving their developers ample time to create a top quality product, I can see the Blue Hedgehog making a comeback in a big way in our future.

The legacy of both Dark Forces and Dark Forces II: Jedi Knight and the first person shooter action still remains alive in Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast. This game, despite being a tad old for it's age, deserves an award.
The epic, first-person shooter and lightsabering action combined with the amount of puzzles (to question your mind) and plot-twisting storyline allows for the most greatest game experience of the early 2000's era.
In your typical FPS shooter, you usually just aim and click at the enemy you want to kill, and watch it die slowly, gasping for life. Things in this however, are much different. Laser based weapons like the E-11 Blaster Rifle and Bryar Blaster Pistol shoot projectiles slowly from their barrels. (Based off an IGN review in their basics.) Now we can understand why people missed with their blasters in the Star Wars universe.
Force powers also must be used wisely. From a colossal force leap to the electricity of death of Force Lightning, to the Darth Vader enducing Force Grip, to the all forever mind trick, the force powers are unique. Kyle will recieve both light and dark force powers.
The lightsaber combat is great, although not as good as it's sequel, Jedi Academy. You must master both Fast, Medium and Strong Styles in order to be the Jedi Master. Along the way, you would also face Reborn warriors. Some are weak, and only use Force Speed and Fast Style, while others use all 3 styles and use Force Grip.
Even as of present day 2017-2018 as the year comes to a near close with Christmas, a website known as
still provides modifications.
also provides older mods, to compensate for JK3 Filefront. (It was closed in Mid-Summer 2015.)
All in all, the game holds up well for 2017, although graphics are a tad bit old for it's time. I recommend this game for the person who has enjoyed Star Wars, yet wants to revive an older generation. This and Jedi Academy still hold up for you and your friends to have a decent lightsaber battle. If you want a twist with Blasters as you command your squad, buy Republic Commando.
Yes, I recommend this game. (Mind tricks) You will buy this with your ten dollars, Jedi/Reborn!

While Jedi Academy was prabably the best swan song for the legendary Quake 3 Engine, Jedi Outcast is the better FPS. However, the first person shooting and environmental puzzles are actually quite fun. Jedi Outcast also has a better story than Jedi Academy. While Jedi Outcast has some good ideas, this game is just pretty frustrating to play. The worst part of the game is its level design. The levels seem like they are designed purely to irritate the player. Raven somehow didn't hear about how bad first person platforming is and included numerous platforming sections. I was often left confused on where to go and after watching a walkthrough the usual culprit was to destroy a barrel or some other inconspicuous object to progress. And who can forget the awful Nar Shadda streets. Raven tried to outdo the sewer level in the original dark forces with Nar Shadda streets. Snipers on very high rooftops hinder the player as they platform there way along, all at the constant risk of falling to your death.
The games shooting mechanics aren’t very good either. Projectiles just don’t move fast enough so you have to be as close as possible to the enemies to hit them. As well as this the enemies run around very unpredictably, so much so I have seen them accidently run off cliffs. These two factors make the shooting very irritating as it is such a crapshoot as to whether you will actually hit someone. The lightsabre combat is one of the games redeeming features. It is extremely fun and definitely the highlight of the game.  There are several styles of fighting to switch between and also numerous force powers.
The story is not amazing. It’s not terrible, but it isn’t very original either. Like the original Jedi Knight the story has dark jedi, the imperial remnant and the valley of the jedi. The games cutscenes aren’t good to watch, the way people show their teeth when they talk is absolutely hideous. The animations during the cutscnenes are very robotic and the voice actors sound a bit bored. The game shows off that Bill Dee William’s reprises his role as Lando but he sounded like he was phoning it in.
The biggest problem with this game is that it doesn’t do anything that Jedi Knight 1 didn’t do. Jedi Knight 1 is a better game than this, despite being older the level design is much better, the blasters handle much better and the story has more charm as the cutscenes are live action. The only thing Jedi Outcast has on Jedi Knight is the lightsabres, they are brilliant. But Jedi Academy has the same gameplay is this. While I haven’t played it yet, it looks like Jedi Outcast with a worse story but with better level design.
There is really no point in buying this game. If you want a better story play Jedi Knight 1. If you want Jedi Outcast’s gameplay minus the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t Jedi Academy is a better game. This game has some good ideas but is overall hampered by some really annoying issues. If you do want to play this game I suggest you noclip past the platforming sections and have a walkthrough handy for when you inevitably get lost. While some people tout this as one of the best Star Wars games ever I find the game difficult to enjoy. The wait is over, my favorite FF game is finally on Steam! I won't comment on the actual game since it came out 16 years ago and y'all should have a pretty good idea of what it is. I will however comment on the quality of the Steam release. Now I know that it's been out on Android for some time now, but having not played the mobile version, I cannot compare the two.
- After reading some reviews (both negative and positive) and the forums, I wasn't expecting my Xbox One controller to work without getting a Joy2Key and performing the "run the game, then connect the controller when you get to the options menu"
magic. To my surprise, the controller worked right away. No tweaking, assigning controls or any use of keyboard+mouse was involved while I was playing.
- Some said that they don't have an option to choose the 1080 resolution, I wouldn't know why that happens since I didn't encounter that issue.
- Reworked fonts and menus look crispy clean. I didn't think it would matter until I saw it!
- I'm not a fan of filters/other emulation enhancements and I took a moment to compare the standard emulation to the Steam release. The difference between the two is colossal. Yes, the static backgrounds haven't changed all that much but the new character models textures make more than enough difference.
- The new autosave feature is extremely useful and works flawlessly. For some of us who has gained real life responsibilities since the last time we played FF9 this is an actual lifesaver.
- Unlike FF7 and FF8, it was never ported to PC before so the MIDI sound issue 7 and 8 Steam releases had is not present.
To sum up my first impressions, I think the Steam version looks fantastic. This
feel like playing a remastered game. I know there's a lot of disagreement on what a remastered game should look like since the level of expectations goes from low to realistic to unrealistically high, but in my opinion this is a remaster worth playing.

Sim City is the all-time greatest version of the Sim City franchise, that holds up well in 2014.

Playtime (with mods such as Network Addon Mod, and Colossal Addon Mod (NAM and CAM), is absolutely limiteless.  As a testament, I am still playing this game 10-11 years after it's release.  I don't feel compelled to move to the always-gotta-be-online new simcity.  I don't need snazzy 3d for a casual game when I get all the feedback and playability this way.  There are so many different ways to set things up.  Totally flat worlds, or mountainous terrain, or even a city by the bay.  HUGE cities in this game, with proper modding as described above can support over FOUR MILLION people on a single CITY.  It's very reasonable to expect to have 50-100 million people in a large region if you devote time into this.
With the NAM mod mentioned above, you can build absolutely breathtaking realistic freeways just like you use on your commute to work or commuting to a shopping spree (heh).  With CAM mod, you can build huge skyscrapers and zone denser than ever before and really have a reason for all those highways.
Build Seawalls, Docks, Highways and Raised Road Viaduct/byways, Mass transportation suched as raised rail/monorail/subways/ground light rail and connecting all these together (mods may be required for some of these, but they are very worth it).  Build photo-realistic cities that you yourself wouldn't mind lodging up in.
The mods alone make this game easily worth it's 20 bucks (US $) without a doubt, and if it's on sale, you'd have to be a fool not to pick it up.  Simcity 2013 is like a graphically enhanced sample, of what this game is.  If you enjoy Simcity 2013 but would like to grow bigger, higher, more populous cities, and have complete control of the road network of your dreams, this game is for you!
You can spend hours just trying to mod this, there are thousands and thousands of different ones to choose from.  Start with NAM and CAM as stated and start looking around for what peaks your interest - with one caveat:  Watch those dependancies!
Simtropolis, Sc4Devotion, and Simpeg are all great places to go look for mods, free signup is available, may be required and is outside of Steam or EA service's control.

Yosumin!™ is a very simple puzzle game that requires you to connect four corners of a square or rectangle. It features clean, bright and colourful graphics. My wife and I played this game together taking turns at each level, and were at first put off by the simplicity of the game. I have only seen Adventure mode though, which does use a tutorial for each new section and game function. In the first levels, we both said, "Wow, really? This is too easy..." However, the speed and difficulty of the objectives ramped up quickly at points! This made us determined not to be outwitted, and we kept going. The game goes up and down in skill level quite often, and forces you to simply try harder when you lose. Despite this, we never really found the game to be unfair. It probably would have been more fun playing together if we were using a touchscreen, as we both really wanted to jump in and help each other when the game became frantic. Several times as the gameplay mechanics were revealed, we had to play the same puzzles over again, which is fine. We never were confused by the interface or objectives, once we figured out how each special piece is used. So far we have played the game only a few times, but I'm sure we will pick it up again. I'm interested to see how all the other pieces work, and want to finish Adventure mode, even though neither of us really care about the story. Give this game a try on sale maybe, and on these conditions: If you are in an easy-going mood, have patience for some of the slower paced parts, and want to play in either short bursts or longer sessions.

A cute puzzle game, yet it lacks the addicting nature that most matching games tend to. There's barely a semblance of story [though not most puzzle games have such], and it only progresses after you've played about... oh, 40 matches for each stage. Each stage has about 8 levels or so, and each level has 5 rounds to it. Because of this lack of progress being felt, it gets more tedious than other matching puzzle games do. It does have a bit of uniqueness to it, in that the matching gimmick is based off square or rectangular shapes; rather than moving pieces around to make a match nearby, you have to search for four corners in order to make a match. The music, while adding to the cute theme of the game, doesn't really have any memorable traits to it, and the music for when time is running out is kind of annoying more than adding to the rush factor. Transition between rounds is slow, for a matching game that includes a time limit. This adds to the feeling of slow progress, as well as the 40 rounds one must go through in order to see the next piece of the "story" that is meant to tie the game together. Since it's a puzzle game, I won't go on about the little bit of story that I've played through, other than that it's just there for show and doesn't add to the game experience.
There's just something missing from this game that makes it as addicting as other matching games. Perhaps the lack of a falling chain/combo, like other matching games have. Where more traditional matching puzzle games have new pieces fall in from above, this one just has them reappear. And since you have to click on the corners in order to make a match, there's some fun missing in having matches just suddenly cascade into a nice combo that completes the level.
Overall, if you don't care much about puzzle games and you find it on sale or in a Humble Bundle, I'd say go for it. But if you like the addicting nature of matching puzzle games, then I would pass on buying it unless you absolutely run out of other games to play or try.

Olivia wants to please her husband, Victor, with a nice vacation: that's how the Weather Lord and his wife find themselves repairing new lands or bringing more life after the demon that kidnapped Olivia last time came back. And in a twisted way, for the bonus levels unlocked with three stars, become the demon himself and disrup the peace!
Weather Lord: Royal Holidays is a continuation of the direction taken by the Legendary Hero, so allow me to copy paste some parts of the review for that opus, augmented with the new elements.
The gameplay brings back the deck of the three weather elements, which is better as you don't have to find them anymore on the level. While workers are still collecting ressources, now, you don't have trees or fields or mines. You have to build a grain mill to have fields to harvest, a sawmill for trees to chop and mines to get gold. Improving these buildings will allow you to increase your production. In other words, two gameplay mechanics from previous games were fusionned in one. However, you can still collect these ressources thanks to bushes or obstacles or shipwrecks or treasures. Besides, now, you don't have to build an house anymore for more workers, you can hire them from the wagon. As the game has also a seaside landscape, you'll get buildings to restore which will give... ressources: gold, food and wood. However, a new type of ressource appears and replaces the crystals: the fame, the only ressource that can't decrease. You can earn it by building arenas or fountains, defeating wild boars or even by speaking to natives (and restoring their houses). Also, you have traders to exchange ressources.
New buildings appeared: a textile house, jeweller's workshop or a forge to make elements needed like magic spheres or dresses or swords. The textile house is however just used for making textile that is a component for crafting, a new gameplay element that I will explain later.
The weather elements are these ones: wind (for mines, dissipating fogs or make trolls fly), rain (for flames, grain mills and sawmills), wave (for pushing vases with ressources to the ground, for leading aways turtles or shells, for fisherman's hut and archaeologist's tent), sun (for drying roads or puddles and for corral houses), thunder (for drying lava or destroying barricades), rainbow (for restoring portals, dissipating mirages and uncast a spell on fairies). A new one was added: the moon, used to scare ghosts or owls). These elements can also be used to drive away enemies, replacing the warriors from previous game, whether directly on them or by building a tower. Also, for some actions, like inflating balloons for trolls, you need a stronger element than given at the beginning of the level: you have to restore altars.
Also, you have also bonuses that you can use during the level: hire a temporary worker, stop time, more wood, food or gold, working faster.
The artifacts gameplay has also carried over: you can use three per level and they're varied: more wood, more food, more gold, longer bonus, elements getting resplenished faster, more ressources after using an element, etc..
And the new gameplay element? Well, it's crafting: for example, you'll need textile and wood to make beach chairs. Or for a dress, you need food and textile. Or even better, you need crystals (which is not a ressource like food, fame, wood or gold) from the fairies houses and food to craft... gold! Anyway, I'm letting you discover what you can craft. That element can be quite disconcerting because you're not always thinking about crafting what you need. And well, to reach now level 3 sawmills, forges or mills, you'll need to craft a piece of decoration...
That gameplay changes a little when you're the demon: you need to cast a spell on workers - every level begins by that if you want more of them. You need to destroy what was build though you're not really immune to the enemies like ghosts, which are really a common enemy between Victor and the demon. The moon is way more present when you're the demon than in the normal game.
Anyway, now, Olivia has a more active role and is even sometimes the sole heroin (at the beginning but also when the demon messes the couple up, with Victor on one side and Olivia on another). She has the same role as Victor: only needed for specific tasks.
The graphics are still cartoonish, which is nice and the soundtrack is fitting.
Weather Lord: Royal Holidays is a great game, though now more complex with the crafting side. I loved the demon's story and the fact that a new weather element was found: the moon. There is however a negative point: the last achievement is still bugged and I was victim of it, even if a patch was apparently released.
Really, now, I'm just waiting for Graduation to arrive on Steam, because it's the next generation of gifted people who will be featured...

This is a solid enough representative of its series and genre. I'm not quite sure what to call that genre heh... maybe the construction foreman genre? Anyway, it's the pretty common casual game genre where you order a bunch of workers to build, repair, collect resources, and generally terraform a bunch of one screen maps as quickly as possible. Lots of examples, no good name for it. This game is one of those, and it does that fine. It's part of a series, with the distinctive bits being you have weather related spells to clear certain obstacles and enemies, and to reload resources for your workers to collect. Some items also have to be crafted from menus while you're managing everything else. Anyway, solid enough, and the achievements all work now after a patch.
It's a quite divisive casual genre; some people utterly despise these, others like them. I'm in the latter group. This title won't change your mind either way, but it's a better than average example if you do like them.

Jedi Outcast is old, but it is absolute gold. Made from a modified version of the Quake engine by Raven Software, this first-person / third-person shooter is a blast.
The Single-Player campaign mode is very well done. You begin at an Imperial Outpost, fighting your way through hordes of stormtroopers and imperials.
The gameplay is smooth, the shooting mechanics are awesome, and it genuinely feels like you're a hero fresh out of a star wars movie.
As you progress through the game, you gain increasingly stronger and useful force powers which are hilarious to use on enemies.
The levels are designed amazingly; the puzzles can be frustratingly difficult, which I love. When you get your lightsaber, the fun definitely doubles!
The soundtrack is based off the OST for Star Wars by John Williams, and it is incorporated into the levels and cinematics smoothly.
Unfortunately, multiplayer is mostly dead. There are a few servers which spring to life every now and then, but don't expect to be able to take your blaster and lightsaber abilites to the online battlefield; you'll only be met with dissapointment and loads of bots.
Ultimately, this game is now only good for single player, but in its time, it was one of the best games you could play at the time.
I definitely recommend you play this, if you're up for a challenging single-player campaign with a reasonable story and a rewarding end.

This game has kind of a megaman/sonic (extremely sonic visuals wise) vibe to it.
It does a really good job of doing what it was meant to do, which is to be a 2D smash and bash platformer. To put it simply if you didn't like both Sonic AND megaman you WILL not like this because while it is an absolute blast of color and pixel art and drool worthy chip tune music, it has ALL the problems that both sonic and megaman have. If one of those games you could not stand for the problems, be warned that they are in this game.
With that warning out of the way I adored this game. The levels were juicy and filled with color, and you got to actually explore them because of how large and multi tiered they were. Part of this exploration is due to the fact that many of the levels required you to snatch keycards and push buttons in order to progress, like in megaman, while keeping a flowy pathway and physics ALMOST the same as Sonics. The difference being that unlike sonic you can still walk up those sloped walls without gathering a ton of momentum. A bit more like space physics than real life but considering that sliding down slopes was my biggest pet peeve at the original sonic, I still consider it an improvement because it makes your experience smoother with less having to run back just to get up speed. You also move much slower in this game than sonic, which is okay since the combat system is more out of megaman. No jump bopping enemies here, you'll be stopping to punch, kick, claw, or shoot the enemy unless you are able to bypass them.
The story was extremely cheesy, but in a nostalgic way, at least for me. Many of the actors were amateur voice actors with less than stellar recording equipment but it worked somehow, fitting in with the pixel art, and definitely adding to the stories cheese. If you aren't a fan of what amounts to a pajama sam story + the odd dark gory scene you may want to skip it and go right for the game however. Especially since the story scenes are unskippable if you choose story mode and some of them are loooooooong cutscenes.
Definitely extremely hard, the bosses start out easy letting you get a feel, but around midway through the game it decides you have figured it out and ups the difficulty by at least twice what it was before. This made things really fun for me but if you are a casual player, you might not enjoy it.
There are three different characters available to play at this time and each has completely different movesets. Two of them even get their own specialty maps. The strongest and easiest to play is Lilac, the medium difficulty being Carol, and the hardest player being Millia. Each are fully voice acted as well.
All in all this game is pretty fun, It took me about seven or eight hours to finish a single storyline playthrough without stopping for collectibles. The replay value is high with multiple characters and a generous amount of collectibles as well as a good amount of acheivements to get.

This is a ridiculously good Sonic game.  After playing all of these recent Sonic games that kinda suck, I didn't really think there could be another good Sonic game.  I'm really glad this game proved me wrong, because this is Sonic at his best.
You play through the game as “classic” Sonic and “new” Sonic.  There are many different stages that are all based on classic sonic levels.  The look and music will make you super nostalgic if you played Sonic on the Genesis back in the day.  When you are classic Sonic, you go through the level just like in the original game as a 2D side scroller.  The graphics are great, and the gameplay in these sections is pure classic Sonic.  When you are new Sonic, you play through the game in a racing style.  It almost reminds me of Sonic R on the Sega Saturn but a million times better, because Sonic R SUCKED.  Anyway, these sections are just as fun.  You get to run through the level as quickly as possible and you lock onto enemies more like the new sonic games.  These different game modes go together better then you'd expect it is super fun.
The game is pretty short, especially if you don't care about getting a high score.  There are challenges after you have beaten the classic and new Sonic levels, and most of these are fun.   A couple are pretty tedious, but luckily most of these are optional.  There are some pretty fun boss fights in the game too, but don't expect anything too challenging.  The game is very easy to complete, but you can always go back to the levels and try and beat your score which is where the developers obviously hoped you'd spend a lot of time.  If you are the kind of person that likes getting high scores and short times, then you will be obsessed with trying to beat your old scores.
The bad part about this game is the port.  The port is pretty awful.  There are no graphics options, and on my machine which has specs that are way higher than the recommended setting it took me a lot of time to figure out how to get this game going at a decent framerate.  It took me a couple hours and a lot of google searches to get this game running at a playable framerate, and if your computer is below the recommended specs and closer to the minimum specs, you may have some issues getting this game into a playable state.  I ended up having to download some 3rd party software to even get the game to run at around 30 FPS.  30 FPS is a bit low, but I don't mind it on this game.  The game was actually designed to be run at 30 FPS from what I can tell, so if you can get it higher that is great but 30 works just fine.
Even though the port of this game sucks, I still would recommend this game especially if you can get it on sale.  Since the game is short, it might be a really good deal to wait for the sale.  I got it for 7.49 and it is definitely worth the price.  If you are an old school Sonic fan, you owe it to yourself to get this game because it truly is the best sonic game to come out this decade.

Since Sonic Adventure on the dreamcast I haven't enjoyed a single Sonic game thats been released, until now...
This is a true fan service game featuring remastered versions of some of the best levels from the entire series while playing as 2 different versions of Sonic.
Each level lets you play as either classic or modern Sonic, classic plays as a side scroller while modern plays like Sonic unleashed (without the silly werehog sections). The game runs at an eye watering pace (especially modern Sonic) and theres multiple routes and secret tokens hidden throughout each stage, getting them all will take some time.
Aside from the main story, which should take the average player 6+ hours to complete, theres over 100 challenges to complete too. Beating these challenges unlocks bonus content such as character models, classic music and artwork.
If your a fan of the Sonic series then this is a must buy, its simply the best Sonic game in years by far.

Something old and something new; you get the best of both worlds in Sonic Generations. SEGA proves that Sonic the Hedgehog can still remain relevant in the platforming genre that has been mostly dominated by fat Italian plumbers. With decade’s worth of nostalgia and fan service being crammed inside the title of “Generations” is truly fitting. The game focuses on playing as both a side scrolling “Classic” Sonic that plays like Sonic from the Sega Genesis and then 2D/3D style “Modern” Sonic which plays like Sonic Colors or Sonic Unleashed. The game offers some of the finest platforming (both 2D and 3D) that you’ll be able to find on the PC.
Many often criticize sonic games by complaining about the “speed” of Sonic the Hedgehog and that when playing he doesn’t feel fast enough, or that they make him too fast and the platforming isn’t enjoyable, Sonic Generations finds that perfectly happy medium between speed and platforming, It is incredibly fast paced but it doesn’t force you to go insanely fast if you don’t want to, if you want to take your time and try to gather all the collectibles it gives you the option to do so. If you’ve ever played any of the games from either era of Sonic then you will be right at home with the combat system, either jumping on heads or using a spin attack as “Classic” Sonic, or flying through the air using homing attacks as “Modern” Sonic. Both the combat and platforming controls feel tight, fast, and fluid, it handles just the way a sonic game should. The game also periodically shakes things up by adding in fairly interesting boss battles that are each centered on a different type of combat component that you haven’t previously experienced in the game prior.
Sonic Generations is quite the visually stunning game, the game looks absolutely gorgeous, especially the redesigned HD versions of classic Sonic levels. And the 60 FPS of the PC version makes the game feel and run buttery smooth, which is an absolute must for game that revolves around moving at such a high level of speed. The game also boasts an impressive soundtrack featuring a plethora of some of the greatest hits from Sonic games.
The main story sadly only takes around 5-6 hours to complete, However despite the fairly short campaign, Sonic Generations is crammed to the brim with unlockables, collectibles, game modes and challenges that will easily put your play time into the double digits if you tried to 100%. Don’t let the short campaign scare you off, even if you’re the type of gamer who likes to do a single play through and be “one and done” ,Sonic Generations is a high enough quality game to warrant spending at that type of price to gameplay hours ratio
Overall the game shows that Sonic still has what it takes to be a powerhouse of the platforming genre, offering fast fluid controls, amazing level design, beautiful visuals, an incredible soundtrack and enough fan service to make any devote Sonic worshipper cry tears of joy. The only downside of the game is that by the time you beat it you’ll still want more.

This game, how best to describe it? A game highly reminiscent of the games of yesteryear with flairs from modern design. Playing FTL brought me back to my days as a fledging gamer playing such classics as Oregon Trail and Adventure. There is very little hand holding, FTL will teach you the basics but after it has shown you the way forward it will throw you straight to the wolves without remorse.
The visuals are very clean 2D sprites, that remind me of some of the better flash games of the early 2000's very colorful and well fitted to the sci-fi theme of the game. You really couldn't ask for more.
The gameplay itself is divided into a few parts, first there is the star map. A nicely shown overmap to guide you through your adventure and give you a bit of a heads up onto what will kill you in the future. This is procedurally generated and keeps the game feeling fresh. Next is your ship menu, here you will be able to designate which room your various crew members will die in. Speaking of death, oh it happens in so many wonderous ways. Most common will be suffocation, followed by burning to death and being left in the vacuum of space after your ship is destroyed. If you are lucky your crew will die in glorius combat fighting the giant Mantis people or the Rock people or maybe just to another human. Ship to ship combat is managed through a very nice real time but pausable battle system, this keeps the already intense gameplay from becoming overwhelming.
The sound is also very well done the ambient music when not in combat is soothing and the various themes you hear while encountering the various adversaries and alien spieces are all very nice. If you enjoy listening to "video game" music I suggest buying the soundtrack to listen to at your leisure.
Finally the flaws, the game can get stale after a couple dozen attempted playthroughs, there are many items in the game to obtain but few have a definitive impact as much as your starting equiment. The RNG can leave you high and dry with an unwinnable campaign from the start.
All in all though I will say this, FTL: Faster Than Light is an exceptional game in all regards and I only wish there were more games that achieved this quality. The development team obviously love this game and it shows in the final product.

tl;dr: Fantastic game, great port, 9/10.
I can't give this game enough props. Everyone speaks about that one game that defined them, or their childhood. This is THAT game for me. Everyone who has played this game sings the same tune: you can't beat FFIX. It's so charming and the story is so intriguing. The charcters are relatable and engaging, and you'll find yourself engrossed in the whole FFIX world from the off.
As a port - I can't fault it. It runs smoothly and flawlessly. I was curious as to why the game needed the Android SDK before release. I can now see that it's so you can click the mouse on the screen to make your charcter move in that direction - smart. I imagine this adds touchscreen functionality too, but can't confirm due to my lack of touchscreen.
The original soundtrack is in this game which is a big plus for me personally: this soundtrack was easily Uematsu's finest work.
The upscaled and retextured character models look great, and the new battle/text interface looks really nice as well. The cutscenes have also clearly been remastered but not so much to the extent of the models.
However, having played the original PS1 game, and then again (several tens of times) on an emulator - I would not say this is the definitive version. Though the new charcter models look nice - the pre-rendered backgrounds have not been changed, and the two graphics fidelities do clash sometimes. Not only that, but some sounds effects that weren't there in the original game have been added (one in a cutscene, which I won't spoil but it does kind of ruin the mood a bit).
That said, these are only very minor issues which for me only detract from the game slightly. I am throughly looking forward to playing this one through again, and strongly recommend it for those who have not yet played it.

SimCity 4, the last Maxis SimCity, remains the best of its genre to this day. Although it lacks the speculative technology of SimCity 2000 or the beautiful slit-scan rendering of the (perhaps unfairly infamous) 2013 revision, SC4 is thorough and rigorous in its realism and level of simulated detail.
For example, to check the operation of the simulation at the individual level, you can create and follow sims (and their dynasties) as they travel around from home to work and back, finding jobs appropriate to their social class/level of education, to test your city's transportation grid down to the individual level of detail.
This Deluxe Edition comes with the Rush Hour expansion which adds even more detail and control options to transportation simulation. The only significant drawback is that, like previous SimCities, roads cannot truly bend or angle properly; cities consequently must be laid out more or less in a grid pattern. Of course, as Atlanta just demonstrated in Half-Inchopocalypse 2014, there are excellent reasons to avoid curving and angling roads all over the place in city planning, so this is a "feature" that you most likely won't miss.

COH 1 is one of my favorite games.  COH 2 isn't, in fact I'd say it is a dud.  The gameplay just isn't the same and the graphics are worse.  I hoped to see a bigger, better COH game but it's just dumb.  There is an old adage in software development that says " if it isn't broken, don't try to fix it (because you'll just end up breaking it)" and that is what happened.
I have been playing the Bulge campaign.  It's just dumb capture the flag.  The units don't behave like real units, they just charge around like kids playing chasey.  Armored vehicles in towns are king of the battle field whereas in reality they were extremely vulnerable.  A PzJg IV is just as strong attacked from the rear with bazookas or above by infantry as fron the front.  Paratrooopers and supplies drop into towns in the middle of bad weather.  The 10th Armored doesn't get a mention.  One scenario is won by capturing abandoned vehicles with your infantry.  It's just a glorified easter egg hunt.  German rifle infantry squads can walk up to stone buildings defended by airborne with 50 cal mg's and wipe them out with impunity. It's just garbage.
The Russian Campaign is worse.  It's just a collection of scenarios with the usual infantry running around like headless chickens.  Many scenarios enforce co-op play with the AI as a partner.
There is little if any opportunity to use real-world tactics in the game or vehicles that actually appeared at that point in the historical timeline.
Regarding graphics, everything seems murkier and harder to see.  So the visual appearance of COH2 is worse than COH1.
Luckily I waited for a sale because full price would be way over-priced for this game.

I guess this was supposed to be an expansion to Gothic 3, but it fails in so many aspects.
To start, all the♥♥♥♥♥♥that happens in the normal game doesn't count here. The game world is just a chunk of the standard Gothic 3 map; It's not small, but it's still kind of disappointing, especially considering how Gothic 2 and other open-world RPGs have handled expansions.
The combat is fairer than in normal Gothic 3, as blocking actually works for the enemies. The visuals are more efficient, but this is to be expected, seeing as how the size of the game world has been drastically reduced. I would have figured that this would also lend more depth to the actual gameplay and variety, but most of the unique NPCs are now just replaced with generic stand-ins who give fewer quests but otherwise perform the same functions.
There are also so many things that simply don't have a reason to exist. For example, in Gothic 2, it's possible to escape from the map into the void, but it does require some going out of the way. In Gothic 3: Forsaken Gods, all I have to do is jump around the little boulder blocking the path to Nordmar. My question is, "Why bother including Nordmar on the map if I'm not even supposed to go there?" I can see the location when I bring up the map on my interface, but it has no reason to be present in the game.
My biggest gripes are in the general sloppy execution of the whole thing, resulting in problems not even too plentiful in vanilla Gothic 3. Models are poorly placed, the AI doesn't know how to follow, many NPCs have multiple voices, the crime system is gutted to the point that I can steal entire towns without consequence, and I could go on and on. Some of the bad changes can sometimes be helpful, such as how I can use transformation potions to morph into animals in front of hostile guards and just walk past them, but doing the same in front of allies is asking for suicide.
But none of that matters, because all that it really took to kill it for me was the broken quests. When a main story quest irreparably ♥♥♥♥s up without explanation, that just ruins everything. This is an expansion only in the loosest sense of the word. It might as well just be mod, and a rushed one at that.
