Tl;dr the combat in this game is an embarrassment to it's predecessors.
I had hoped that this game offered a fresh, modern take on the Ys combat feel, but they made a game that I don't feel should belong in the Ys line of games. They only added variance and artificial difficulty through their poorly implemented combat system, exceedingly poor combat AI, and the nightmare of a game experience when these completely separate things with little cohesion get stuck together. They added a blocking system to Ys 7 that the tutorial doesn't even tell you about, I only figured out about it when I died to the first boss a few times and I looked into my button settings for a jump command, which they took out in favor of a dash command that you'll be spamming just to avoid walking at a snails pace literally everywhere. When I looked for a tutorial of the third boss there were people that at that point in the game didn't even know that blocking was a mechanic.
Specifics on the combat system:
They basically added rock paper scissors to the game with Slash/Impact/Pierce damage. In the game, Adol with his sword is Slashing, Dogi is Impact damage with his fists, and so on. Now alone this system is fresh, added complexity to a wonderful game series. Almost every cluster of enemies is varied, so it rewards you for switching between who you're piloting.
Right from the get go you have access to an ability for each character, even as you unlock different abilities for characters, they're all only able to be used in combat, none of them seem to give invincibility frames, and the abilities are the only shared command on the entire control scheme, if you use an ability as Adol, the rest of your party will follow with their ability that they have bound to that button/key. From the get go I absolutely hated this, and actually purposefully bound the first abilities that I got on Adol/Dogi to different buttons so that I could micromanage more and not worry about the AI missing the ability, however this approach ended up becoming cumbersome when Adol and Dogi got second abilities that I had to bind to my two remaining buttons for ability use, and my control scheme for the abilities became completely invalidated when a third character was introduced.
The final nail in the coffin is the AI that pilots the other characters in your party during combat. There is personalization (that ultimately has to be changed if you want to try to do things optimally). These settings are having them Gang up on targets with you, having them Split up, and having them attack the Weakest target. This personalization doesn't mean much, because the AI still follows the same flow chart and will behave inconsistently no matter what setting they're on. While on Gang they'll split up almost every time they get the chance because they calculate a weaker target than the one you're attacking, because they'll get bored and assume they have to restart the fight during the wind down animation of your right click combo even if the enemy unit hasn't entered combat yet, and even if they are two screens distance away from Adol. (literally they will aggro to things outside of their tether, and will snap back to you only to try running at them agian) while on split they'll calculate that you're done fighting because of the inactivity during Adols or Dogi's right click wind down animation, and dash directly towards you and then recalculate quickly to just attack whatever you're right on top of. On weakest target, they'll almost always split, because they register equally weak targets, and due to part of the flowchart seeming to be splitting up when possible, they will do that at random, consequently leaving it to random if they're even using the correct type of damage on the correct type of target. Often times there is a solution that would have them all dealing bonus dps, but they all randomly decide to attack the wrong type and they stay that way until you switch characters, making the AI think that you're out of combat, making them jump directly on top of you, only to realize that there are enemies around, so they'll aggro randomly again. This sort of thing also happens when you have the AI set to Split, or they'll do it when they split when you're set to Gang.
add mid combat looting to this, when you fight one thing and kill it, your AI's will exit combat and pick up the loot for you, but in extended fights they'll whip around all over the place not killing anything properly, leaving ample time for the loot to disappear, leaving you to focus on a single target and hope your AI will help, then pick up the loot yourself as your ally AI recalculates to try to fight more enemies, then you have to properly dps something else, and pick up the loot while your ally AI recalculates separately to try to fight something else/ other things, rinse and repeat through every encounter in every area.

I will say up front that I really wanted to like this game. I played Gothic 2 and, though I found the game difficult, ended up enjoying it greatly. I anticipated Gothic 3 would be another open-world fantasy game with better graphics that would, like the prior game, rise above its flaws. I was mistaken in my anticipation. Unlike Gothic 2, which was greater than the sum of its parts, Gothic 3 is merely the sum of its parts, some good, many flawed.
The graphics are nice, but the animation is bizarre. The game writing and voice work is poor, resulting in real problems with immersion. The game doesn't telegraph well what you are supposed to be doing and how to interact with the world and the various items you'll pick up. These are all forgivable and leftovers from the previous game. Worst of all, however, is the combat mechanic. Gothic 2 was a little wonky in combat, but it all worked out. Gothic 3 does not work out. Combat is how you advance your character and interact with the world, and it is the most distancing and alienating part of the game.
Also, I didn't read well enough and picked up both Gothic 3 AND the Forsaken Gods Enhanced Edition. That was pointless. They're both pretty much the same game, with the latter being slightly upgraded. Thank goodness for massive sales. I would otherwise have been pretty angry.
If you like open-world fantasy games and have run out of entries from Bethesda, this game might be worth trying on a major sale, but chances are you'll end up disappointed. Sure, the lack of polish is annoying, but the actual gameplay mechanics themselves are just not there, leading, ultimately, to little desire to keep playing.

With the possible exception of UNDERTALE, this is an absolutely peerless PC RPG that cleverly and interestingly explores toxic masculinity. It questions a broad range of topics including: How abuse can beget more abuse despite good intentions, whether you can be selfish in a world without order, and how many porn magazines is enough, exactly?

Lisa the Painful is a 2D side scrolling JRPG with a crushing difficulty level featuring a narrative centered on exceedingly taboo subjects. A game that forces you to make challenging choices and shoots hot jets of man themes such as: masculine and sexual identity, child rearing, role expectation, sacrifice, redemption and failure. It gleefully indulges in the darkest depths humanity has to offer and pulls you down to hell with it. I don’t believe Lisa the Painful was intended to be a fun or enjoyable experience, but rather to say something. To force the player to participate in a twisted world, To look at content you may not like and experience unknown feelings you can’t easily explain.
Despite its Super Mario Bros. 2 over world, Earthbound style combat and quirky indie humor, the content of this story is intended for adults. And it’s ♥♥♥♥ing awful, I’ll say it. It’s an incredibly upsetting and dreadful experience. But it’s also overwhelmingly satisfying, deeply rewarding and my personal favorite kind of story. The less you know going in, the better it is. The gameplay and story muddles player expectations, conventions and morality, thus will have more of an impact if you can’t predict what’s about to happen.

The second episode of the Blackwell series shifts focus to Lauren, the aunt of the previous protagonist, Rosangela.  A stark contrast to the timid bookworm we're used to, Lauren is a chainsmoking toughgirl with a sharp wit and a bit of a mean streak.  She is joined by Joey, and the player gets to experience what Rosa's aunt was really like in her prime.
Like in Legacy, Unbound focuses on finding ghosts stuck in the world and helping them move to the next.  The more historical setting works fairly well; things like researching on the computer is replaced with typing terms into a phonebook to find numbers and addresses, which feels fairly interactive and rewarding.  While there's still a lot of running from place to place to unlock topics, there are more interactive puzzles this time around, and overall the game feels more freeform, if only just a little.
An interesting gameplay change is that you can now directly control Joey in addition to Lauren, letting you investigate through walls and observe things Lauren can't.  This adds a lot to the gameplay potential and was a welcome change for me.
The talking portraits disappeared for this installment, which I honestly didn't mind.  The art is mostly the same as before, though the Google Maps screen was replaced with a lovely skyline of New York.  I'm not entirely sure, but I think Joey's sprites might have been updated as well, which is a nice touch.
The voices of Lauren and Joey are pretty good this time around, though several of the supporting roles suffered.  Several of the supporting roles (two black men, and two old ladies, in particular) sounded more like someone doing a (bad) voice rather than actually fitting the part.  One of the old ladies was very clearly a much younger woman doing her best "old lady" voice and it fell spectacularly flat.  But like I said with Legacy, I got used to it fairly quickly so I can't say that it detracted terribly from the experience for me.  It's almost turning into a sort of charm.
I finished this game in 3 hours, and like Legacy, I paid $1.25 for it.  I feel pretty good about the game given that price, but I don't think I would if I'd paid full price.  If you've read this far and still find yourself interested, I'd encourage you to give it a shot for yourself, but I can't say I can recommend this unless it's on sale.

This is an interesting and unusual game. It has things that are lovely and things that could be improved (note that it is in early access).
It has a lovely atmosphere and graphics/music, and an interesting and novel concept. It can be rewarding and relaxing to play, and it is very satisfying when one manages to get a five star wine. However, there is not enough feedback for players in some cases, which can be frustrating at times.
In more detail - one starts as a small time wine producer with one plot of "loam" soil, on which one can grow one or two varieties (or "veritals") of grape: cabernet sauvignon or sauvignon  blanc. The former is cheaper to buy and maintain, and is easier to get good wines out of it.
One plants the vines and tends them depending on the weather, which is random, Rain makes the foliage grow, and sun ripens the grapes; too much foliage can stop the grapes from ripening and too little foliage can over-ripen the grapes in the sunshine. Too much foliage in wet conditions can cause rot, which can be cured by exposing the grapes to the sun - but being careful not to over-ripen them.
One then harvests the grapes, crushes them, processes the crushed juice and barrels the resulting wine. The idea is to produce a wine that has the right characteristics to make reviewers happy. Some relationships are very clearly explained (e.g., fermenting by x time reduces sweetness by y), but some is not explained at all (e.g. how the "body" score is calculated). Perfecting the wine is done by trial and error, and ideal wines for one type of grape have totally different numbers to ideal wines from other types of grape. Also, some wines will be treated as being moderately good if they are close to the ideal range, whereas other wines will be rejected as undrinkable if they are only a slight amount off their ideal range (and those wines will sell for more money if they are ideal).
After bottling the wine, one must submit it to reviews before it can be sold. There are different ranks of reviewers, from one to five stars. At the beginning, one can only attract one star reviewers. Reviews by one star reviewers are less harsh on the wine than by higher star reviewers, but carry less weight. The higher the quality of the review (i.e., the higher the number of stars and the higher the star rating of the reviewers), the higher the price for which one can sell the wine. Some types of wine are inherently more expensive than others (but those tend to be the ones that are harder to grow).
For every 5 star review that one's wine gets, one attracts one new reviewer of a higher star rating. One then often finds out that the wine that would cause lower ranked reviewers to give it five stars will only get four star reviews from higher ranked reviewers, so more trial and error adjustment is necessary.
The reviewers will occasionally give a clue as to what they like about a wine (e.g. "this has just the sort of thing that a cabernet sauvignon should have - tanins and acidity"), but will rarely do so, and will never do so for a bad review ("Ew" is the totality of what one gets on occasions). This can be frustrating as it gives no clue as to the direction in which one should be taking the wine. Perhaps somebody with more knowledge of wine would be better at this than I, as I suspect that the game is quite realistic.
As one gains more money, one can buy more land and grow more vines - but the more vines that one grows, the greater the risk of pests, which need treatment with expensive pesticides - and as each vine needs to be trimmed by hand (i.e., the player must click manually on a vine with the game un-paused and hold the mouse button for a set time before the vine will be trimmed), managing vines quickly becomes challenging as more are added, and requires upgrades, such as pesticide treatment and the ability to cut all vines of the same type at the same time, which can be researched and purchased (I do not understand for the life of me why an individual farm should be researching its own pesticides).
Money management can be challenging - at times, too challenging: one can take a loan, but there is no overdraft facility, and if one misses three payments, the game is brought to an abrupt end, even if one could have borrowed more to start with (one cannot add to a loan once taken out before it is repaid, which is arbitrary and silly), and there are long periods of time when no income is being generated as the previous year's bottles have all sold and the next year's grapes have not been harvested. I advise avoiding loans all together.
There is an element of strategy in deciding what to do with poorly reviewed wine, but there is a simple all case right answer that detracts from the "interesting decisions" as Sid Mier would have it: wine with a 3* or better rating should be sold to the three main distributors; wine with a 2* or lower rating should be sold to the bulk-buyer, "Kruppe". This is because the main distributors will not allow one to sell more wine to them when they still have unsold bottles, and poorly reviewed wine will sell very slowly. Kruppe buys wine at a very low price, but pays instantly (unlike the main distributors, which pay only when the wine is sold), and will take endless vats of the worst possible quality wine without any penalty whatsoever. There is an option to destroy the wine, but there is no reason for a player ever to do this when it can be sold to "Kruppe". ("Kruppe" is a new addition to the game, so there would have been a reason to destroy wine in the past). Selling awful wine through "Kruppe" does not seem to have any adverse reputational effect.
The early part of the game can be very rewarding and satisfying, although if one grows more than one type of grape, it can be very hard to keep up with what works for each variety, and I found myself getting cognitive overload. The trouble is that one almost inevitably starts with one specific variety of grape, cabernet sauvignon, meaning that, if one wants to plumb the game's interesting depths, one has to end up with a multi-grape vinyard, which, for my multi-tasking unfriendly mind, is rather overwhelming. I ended up having to make detailed lists in Notepad of what characteristics worked best for what types of wine (with one type of wine, this can be memorised without difficulty), and this makes the game rather too much like hard work. This would be alleviated considerably if there were a way of looking back at previous wine reviews and the statistics of those wines so that one can deduce from that what reviewers liked: having to write this down outside the game in order to do well is just silly.
There are also lots of features with which one can decorate one's wine farm and purchase for in-game money, but I have still not worked out whether any of these things have any actual function or not.
The graphics and sound are lovely, and the game concept is refreshing and delightful. The game can be quite fun despite its flaws, and, given that this is an early access game, there is a possibility (but of course not a certainty) that some of the flaws will be fixed. Given the game's low price, it is worth having a go with, I think.

As a person who likes both wine and tycoon games, I'm already hooked on the early access version, and I anticipate spending even more time on Terroir once the devs roll out additional updates.
It took several tries to get my vineyard going at first. There's an element of luck in surviving the first few years: the random weather events, the size of your harvest, the quality of your wine, and the amount of time it takes to produce a wine (among other things) all determine how much money you'll have for the next year, if you have any at all. Bottling a wine takes cash, and unless you have a few good wines out already, you can't apply for a loan. If you're in the red before your wine is bottled, you're pretty much done. Reroll and start over.
Luckily, once you've had a few good years, it gets easier to stay afloat and to build up more money to buy more plots of land and upgrades like taverns. The game gives precious few hints about making good wine, and it may take several restarts and several harvests before you come up with something that the critics like, and that will make money in the marketplace. This trial-and-error approach isn't to everyone's taste, but I found the lack of hand-holding refreshing. There isn't much to lose in starting over when you only have a few tiles, and you can use what you learned to do better on your next try.
tl;dr I like it already, eagerly anticipating future updates, it's a bit difficult to get started but very rewarding.

Straight to the point; is this good? Yes.  Is it worth buying?  No.  Well, maybe.  If it's on sale for five bucks or less, then I'd say go ahead and buy it, since this game only has about five bucks worth of content.
Right then.  Sonic Generations is a game in which a giant plot device tears a hole in space time because who bloody cares.  I personally skipped the story because I knew that it existed only to justify the gameplay.  You play as both old and new Sonic, both of which have different physics and controls.  As old Sonic, you play in 2D levels, and as new Sonic, you still play in 2D levels, because apparently Sega just gave up.  There are some 3D parts sprinkled into new Sonic's levels, but it's maybe 50% at most, which I found kind of disappointing, because I thought those parts were a lot of fun.  What was there reminded me of either SA2 or Sonic Unleashed, if Sonic Unleashed had actually been well-designed.  So I was disappointed to see that I was basically playing the same kind of level twice, one with 3D elements begrudgingly thrown in.
That being said, the gameplay was very fun, at least at first.  Maybe I just have a massive hardon for the older Sonic games, but I found that once we got into newer territory (Unleashed and thenceforth), gameplay got a bit stale and boring.  The game is divided into three segments; each segment consists of three stages, and each stage is played through once by both Sonics.  After that is the final boss.  Generations is a lot like the Genesis games, in that it is about as long as one - I finished this whole thing in about five hours, though to be fair, that was only what I had to do to actually complete the story.  After that, the game tries coaxing you to play through the levels about thirty times while adding mundane stipulations, most of which can be summed up as, "Beat the time limit whilst utilizing one of our pointless gameplay mechanics.  Maybe you'd like one of your annoying friends to join you so they can feel like they're actually being useful."  Your reward for playing these extra "challenges" is unlocking extra concept art and music, which I suppose is nice, but I personally don't think it's worth it.  And of course, they bring back the horrible mechanic of tracking down five shiny things hidden in each level to unlock even more concept stuff.  I suppose if you're really just that into Sonic, you might find it worth going through all that to look at some pretty pictures, but I don't think I can be arsed.
Bottom line, this game was a disappointment.  A tiny bit of enjoyable gameplay that quickly tapered out to a massive letdown that left me empty and with a void unfilled.  If you want your Sonic fix, stick to Genesis and Dreamcast.  Clearly, as this game demonstrates, that's where it all was anyway.

It's a Ys game, first of the "modern"-style ones: Party-based combat, crafting, and true 3D graphics.
The good:
-The upscaling from the PSP original is surprisingly good. Some of the textures aren't great, and the polygon counts are noticably low, but it looks more like a PS2 game than a PSP one.
-The combat is the same fun Ys standard: fast-paced, big on combos, with difficult bosses.
-Less reliance on levelling up than other Ys titles. Traditionally a Ys game requires you to level grind, since every level of difference between you and enemies makes a huge different in your combat ability, this is much less emphasized here.
-Nice nods to the series history.
-Stellar music. It's a Falcom game, of course the music is amazing!
The Bad:
-The plot stays pretty thin, as is standard for Ys games. More depth than most Ys titles, but still not going to win awards.
-...that's about it, really.
Overall: An excellent Zelda-esque ARPG that shines through its somewhat-dated graphics due to its excellent combat mechanics and music.

Buying a console port on day one isn't necessarily a smart decision. In this case however I haven't encountered any crash, bug or otherwise unintended behavior after playing for 8 hours. For anyone who cares: Yes, it does run with stable 60 fps at least on my non-high-end computer.
The controls are smooth and the combat system offers this overall satisfying feeling almost exclusive to the Ys-series. However, a gamepad is highly recommended.
As far as I can tell, it is a direct port of the PSP version, no added content, no change to animations or cutscenes (fortunately no horrible 3D models like in some other ports from a well-known Japanese publisher...). The game does look a lot better than on the PSP thanks to higher resolution textures, but it is still a game from 2009. That said, the graphics are well aged and look beautiful in full HD.
The story isn't bad at all, although not too complex either. Some dialogue -> go somewhere -> fight something -> some more dialogue or event, that kind of pattern. Don't expect something like Planescape: Torment, but for an action-RPG it's pretty solid.
Four difficulty settings unlocked right from the start should be enough to entertain everyone from casual gamer to Ys- veteran. The learning curve isn't too steep, bosses can be a bit difficult if your level isn't high enough, but they aren't unfair. I'd say most if not all of them are possible without even getting damage, if you learn their patterns and can react to them. It helps that the game lets you retry lost fights and even gives you back the items you used in your last run.
If you like grinding, you should probably choose a higher difficulty setting. Besides character levels it's also possible to raise the level of different skills for each character.
Buying this game should be a no-brainer for fans of the Ys series. If you like action-RPGs with great and responsive controls, you should definitely give this game a try.

Do you like arcade flight simulators? Think back to the great games in the genre: Ace Combat, Crimson Skies, Fury 3, Lylat Wars, YAGER; what would you like in a game like that?
Do you want pretty? Pretty you'll have. While explosions don't have the best effects by far and environment textures could use some work, AX:EL is one of the prettiest flight games out there in light, colors and environment. The camera and the moving planes give also a great sense of action alongside with non-annoying but very nice touches like lens flares, glows, refraction and lots of tiny details like some destructible structures, flora and waves.
Do you want campaign? The "Mercenary missions" mode currently offers 10 missions that need to be unlocked progressively, with objectives varying from destroying squadrons, running search and rescue operations, transporting sensitive cargo through storms, and fighting huge boss-like enemies. While the number might seem a bit small, they are highly replayable, fairly long, include their selection of music (also composed by the author, really nice music, too.) and feature no lives, meaning you'll have to do them on one try, which adds to the difficulty but doesn't make them especially frustrating.
Do you just want to shoot stuff down? The Arena mode features deathmatch and team deathmatch, both with customizable bots. It also has multiplayer support, but only ip-to-ip or LAN modes. AI can get pretty intense on the higher levels.
Do you want customization? Every kill in either game mode, Arena or Mercenary, or Mercenary Mission completion, will earn you MsM. You can use that MsM to purchase a variety of body, weapon, wing or tail modules, with specific bonuses to each one.
Do you want spectacle? Not only AX:EL's visuals will keep you engaged, the planes control really nicely, and the combat soon gets close and personal, with planes struggling to shake missiles while avoiding explosions and pulling insane-G maneuvers. It would be safe to say it's a game one will want to come to time and time again.
Did I mention the planes can go underwater at any time? And that once there they switch to an underwater configuration? And that there's underwater missions, as well? And that there's sonic booms, working in-cockpit first person view and different atmospheric densities?
Now, while still weak at the finer points of the game and control (I feel like the weapon system should be more fleshed out and general presentation is still a bit lacking), if what you want is to fly planes and shoot stuff up, I couldn't recommend a better game to do so with. Easily over War Thunder if you don't mind the limited multiplayer, and easily over Ace Combat Assault Horizon, period.

One of the best 2D platformers I've played since the 16-bit era. Definitely deserves a place of honor alongside other more high-profile indie games like Shovel Knight and the Shantae series. While this game looks sort of like a mere Sonic the Hedgehog clone, it's more of a tribute to the Genesis as a whole. Taking elements from games like Gunstar Heroes and the Rocket Knight games (and yes, a healthy dose of Sonic), Freedom Planet delivers a satisfying experience overall.
At present, you're able to choose between three characters, with two more planned for a future release. Sash Lilac is most similar to Sonic in terms of gameplay, due to her super speed. But instead of somersaults and spin dashes, Lilac can perform a hair whip (not unlike Tails' tail whip from the Sonic Advance games), twirl in mid-air to attack and slow her decline and even perform a powerful Cyclone attack (which reminds me of Sparkster's charge attack from the Rocket Knight games). Carol Tea is a bit different, using her claws for various slash attacks and to scale walls (like MegaMan X, not Knuckles). Carol can also collect gas cans to ride her motorcycle, which increases her speed, gives her some new attacks and allows her to drive up walls. Finally, there's Milla Basset, who can fly for a short time (which kind of acts like a cross between Tails' flight from the Sonic games and Yoshi's flutter jump), form an energy shield which can reflect enemy fire, toss energy blocks to attack enemies, and even combine the latter two for a powerful energy beam attack.
The diversity in play styles between the various characters gives the game a lot of replayability. You've also got the choice of playing the game with its story intact (only available for Lilac and Carol at the time this review was written) or without. There's also a Time Attack mode where you can replay any stages you've already cleared, a set of challenge stages and even a Mahjong solitaire mini-game. There are also 10 collectables in most stages, which also adds to the replay value as well.
TL;DR - if you're a fan of the classic Genesis Sonic games, Genesis-era platformers or just 2D platformers in general, do yourself a favor and pick up Freedom Planet. It's well worth the $15.

This gem is easily one of my favorite games ever. From the soundtrack to the gameplay to the art, this game is definitely worth your time.
The soundtrack is
! It's got to be my favorite soundtrack of anything, ever. Seriously, go buy it.
The art style is gorgeous too. The characters' animations are all lifelike and colorful, and the bosses are awe-inspiring. Clearly a lot of work went into all the sprites. There's even a neat little easter egg in the third level where the characters dance!
The gameplay is incredibly fun. The levels are huge, with lots of room to explore. This was inspired by Sonic, so expect loop-de-loops and running on walls, but the overall pace isn't as "go-go-go" as Sonic is. There are multiple ways to get through any given level, too - so replaying one level can actually feel like exploring a whole new one at times.
There are three characters at time of writing, with two more on the way, and all of them have vastly different playstyles. For example, Lilac is speedy and strong, with a double-jump and a speed-boost attack; on the other hand, Carol trades all-out speed for the capability to scale walls, smash enemies with her Wild Kick move, and even
The bosses are quite interesting - early on, they're pretty simple, but later on, they get crushingly hard. You have to pay close attention to their attack patterns if you're ever going to survive. The final boss smashed me 25 times before I eventually conquered it - but I enjoyed every second.
On the subject of difficulty, there are four modes - Casual, Easy, Normal, and Hard. Casual is easier than easy - you take scarcely any damage, even from the most powerful foes, and your health regenerates to boot. Easy keeps the regenerating health, but you take the same damage as usual; but Hard is brutal at times. If you're looking for a challenge, that'll satisfy alright.
While the story is not one of its strong points, with some pacing issues in the cutscenes, there is a "Classic Mode" that lets you play through the levels in order without a single cutscene to be seen, if you prefer it that way. Nonetheless, I actually enjoyed the story, despite its cheesy bits.
All things considered, Freedom Planet is not without its flaws, but they're few and far between. For a mere $15, it is definitely worth your time and money. What are you doing still reading this?! Go play it and see!

Lilac reminded me of Twilight Sparkle from My Little Pony
Carol seemed to be a mild mix of Buttercup from the PowerPuff Girls and Rainbow Dash.
Milla makes me think of Fluttershy, but more brave.
Either way, the characters are lovable and are in my opinion the only thing in making a good game good.
The characters control really well with an XBox 360 controller. I didn't try the keyboard, but I'd rather use the controller.

Overall, do I reccomend this game? Well if you're into Sonic games of the classic era then this game is right up your alley.

A great sequel to The Blackwell Legacy. There are a few improvements in the interface and it has a more polished feel. The game features Lauren, Rosa's Aunt, as the main character and also introduces the ability to switch between both Lauren and Joey, which certainly adds a lot of scope to the gameplay. Ultimately, it's a short, quite straightforward, but entertaining and engaging point-and-click mystery adventure with some interesting characters, decent writing, and a satisfying story arc. It wraps up in about 2.5 hours, and is well worth the $5 it sells for.

Blackwell Unbound flashes back before the setting of The Blackwell Legacy, building the story up while tuning the gameplay with new mechanics.  However, the less linear story mixed with those new mechanics and the same flaws that were present in the previous game can make this game a pixel hunting back and forth drudge at times.
The production quality is the same as the previous game. Pixel art and voice acting get a passing grade but no high marks. What has changed is new game play mechanics.  You can now switch control of between Joey and Lauren. It is an interesting concept, Joey, being a ghost, can pass through walls and explore places unencumbered by privacy concerns. But the previous limitation where Joey cannot stray far from his medium is still present, so it does not add as much freedom as you might think. Moreover, inventory items can now be used with the environment, a standard feature of point and clicks that was missing in the previous game.
Aside from the additions to the mechanics the gameplay is largely the same; find clues, interview people, and draw conclusions.  This time around though the pixel hunting gets worse as, on multiple occasions, objects that I needed to interact with were sandwiched between two other large objects.  This is not good game design. Needing to click the 12 pixel cluster between two things is just annoying.  That aside the overall gameplay is still pretty solid. The detective work is well suited for the point and click genre.
Story also improves a bit. It removes linearity giving you two cases to work in tandem.  However, in my play through, I did not notice that Joey could enter another area until after I completed one of the cases. So, for me, the play through was more akin to having 2 consecutive cases.  As the cases build, there is more teasing to the fate mediums, building up tension for future games in the series.
All in all, Blackwell Unbound still gets a recommendation. The annoyances with pixel hunting were not so great as to hinder the gameplay.  If you are looking for a detective genre gameplay, this might be up your ally.

My review is about the entire Blackwell series, not about a specific episode.
TL;DR - highly recommended if you're looking for good quest games.
Although being quest series, the Blackwell series isn't difficult comparing to other games in that genre as there aren't logic puzzles to solve. However, the games don't suffer from one flaw that exists in many quests, and that is excessive use of items. In some quest games you usually stack up a lot of items and end up trying every combination of item and something clickable on the screen until you find that absurd combination that makes you progress. The Blackwell series doesn't have that flaw as items aren't the main part of the game. Also, when places become irrelevant you can't access them anymore, which also prevents having to go back and try to find something useful in every place that you've been through at the endgame.
The progression in the game is made by combining the abilities of Rosa (or Lauren in Blackwell Unbound) and Joey, which complete each other. Joey can enter locked rooms but cannot interact with anything, and Rosa can do the opposite. Only by combining their abilities you will make progress. There's also a built in search engine inside a game in which you have to use in order to progress, which makes you feel that you're doing detective work and not just trying to figure out how to use your inventory.
The plot becomes "bigger" in each episode and ends with a grand finale in Blackwell Epiphany, so you don't feel like you're doing that same thing in each game.
I really enjoyed the series and I highly recommend it.

There are three ways to look at Ys Seven: As an Action RPG, as a PSP port, and as an entry in the Ys series.
As an Action RPG, Ys Seven is stellar.  The combat is smooth, and the learning curve is very forgiving.  You acquire new gear and learn new skills at an even pace, so you're never going long periods without an upgrade of some sort.  There are 7 different characters to choose from with their own weapon styles and skill set, and you can have three in your active party at any given point in time, controlling one while the AI controls the other two.  The ability to switch between characters at the press of a button makes the rock-paper-scissors style of weapon resistances work well rather than become a hindrance, and gives the player plenty of options in boss fights.  Becoming accustomed to the dodge roll and mastering flash guard will allow a skilled player to excel even at the higher difficulty levels.
The boss fights are where Ys Seven really shines, all that training and work you did with the regular monsters really pays off.  You can get by with a minimal amount of grinding (I really only do enough to buy all the weapons and learn the skills at each town as I visit), but it pays to be prepared for the boss encounters.  The first time I faced down the two headed turtle and the boss track started got my heart pumping, and I knew this was a great game when I pulled off my first super move and just annihilated it!
Since Ys Seven is a port of an 8 year old PSP game, there are some minor nuances.  First, the game runs extremely smooth, even at max resolution and settings in borderless window mode; no pixelated lines, all crisp and smooth.  The colors are crisp and much more vibrant than on the PSP port, and the controls work just fine (although I would recommend a controller for the best experience).  Now for the elephant in the room: the graphics are a little blocky, and the big bug eyes the characters have contrast sharply from the gorgeous anime-style character art.  I'm willing to grant this a pass since it is an 8 year old game, and the standards for a small screen (and an underpowered device like the PSP was) were a lot different back then.  I have absolutely no complaints in how the game performs, and it's still a joy to tuck in.
As an entry in the Ys series, Ys Seven is one of the best there is.  This was the first game in the series to introduce the party concept (now implemented as well in Memories of Celceta and Lacrimosa of Dana), and being able to play Dogi and deliver that wall crushing punch was INCREDIBLY satisfying!  The game picks up where Ark of Napishtim left off, with Adol and Dogi finally arriving in Althago, and the red haired adventurer immediately tucks in to solve all the world's problems.  As expected of Falcom, the music is amazing, from the animated intro to the final credits, and I had no qualms buying the soundtrack and keeping it in regular rotation.  My only wish was that this release had a boss rush mode like other entries in the series (like Origin and Oath of Felghana), but with the level of customization in gear and party composition I can see how this would be difficult to implement.
The "TL;DR" line is that Ys Seven is amazing, one of the best entries in the series, and the Steam release is a welcome addition and very well done!  If Falcom is the king of action RPGs, then Xseed is it's herald, and they once again deliver a game that is a must have for any library!

I used to look at this game and see the very bland graphics, and equated it to all the other bland graphic roguelike games I see on steam.  So I overlooked this game forever.  I tend to not like roguelikes, and I tend to prefer games that look fancy.  I wish I hadn't let those things deter me for so long.  This game is outstanding.
So the basics.  You pick your starting ship (you start with only one option, with more unlocked as you play a couple of times).  You explore the universe, while running from the ever-encroaching rebel fleet.  The game offers events that have different outcomes, with some outcomes in blue that are only available if you have a certain race of crew member, or if you have upgraded a system to a certain point.  Some events only have no non-blue positive outcomes.  It adds a lot of decision making and a bit of a roleplaying element to the game, and it's nice.
The graphics look basic, but that actually works in the game's favor.  If there were a lot of things going on, it would be harder to keep track of the important details.  As it is, the game's simple design and straightforward controls allow you to react almost instantly to things.  And there are enough ways to respond to a situation that "mastering" the game takes a lot of time.  For example, it's better to kill the entire enemy crew, so you can get more scrap from their intact ship.  But that's very hard to do if you don't know what you're doing, and sometimes it might be worth it to just blow them up before they shred through half your hit points.
The game is the best kind of repetitive.  It's repetitive in the same way an Elder Scrolls game is repetitive.  You know to expect the same type of experience, and you don't care because that's exactly what you want.  There isn't a part of this game I had to "tolerate" in order to enjoy it.  I just... enjoyed it.  And that's rare.

Let's start with the good thing. Company of Heroes has (according to me) the best concept of a strategy game with constant back and forth thanks to the Victory point system, RNG and squad management. It's fundamentally different from games like AoE or Starcraft. Games can also last up to 1 hour (or in some rare cases even longer) with incredible thrilling action and close standoffs. 5 unique factions offer a wide variety of ways to play this game ("cancer", "cheese"). It could be the perfect strategy game... if it wasn't for Relic....
Relic has managed to disappoint the playerbase since launch. From P2W commanders("windustry", "I-win-button") and factions ("OPKW") to questionable stability/performance, limited mod support (none at first) and a talent for applying balance changes with a sledge.
The lack of support is astonishing despite this game being Relics biggest success. Support practically ended in march 2016 (when they fired the balance team) even though it's supposed to end in 2018. Promised performance patches were never issued (game tends to crash constantly after about 2-4 games, massive performance drops on snow maps). The last attempt to cooperate with the community to issue balance patches was eventually canceled shortly before the patch was going to be live "due to unforeseen circumstances" (AoE4 was announced at the same time).
With an unsatisfying state of balance and no changes in sight this game is doomed to die with a decline of the playerbase.

I used to play the crap out of this game as a kid in the early 2000's. There is certainly fun to be had here, but players used to modern game design, be warned. Objectives are clear, but how you're supposed to get there is NOT. Pathways that lead to where you're supposed to go are often blended right into the scenery, and you'll most likely find youself walking in and out rooms looking frantically for a button to press or a doorway you may have missed, it can often even lead to the point of frustration, since it's so easy to walk right past something important.
But the good news is that this game's controls are very solid, and shooting is fun, followed by some of the best lightsaber gameplay in any star wars game to date. The graphics are dated but certainly aren't dreadful. It's the atrocious lip-syncing and wonky animations that will take the most getting used to, but if you can get passed that, this is not only a great star wars game, but a great shooter in general.

You play as Kyle Katarn, a name that carries as much weight in the legacy universe of Star Wars as Luke Skywalker or Han Solo or Gartogg.
Sent out to investigate the Imperial Remnants of several planets, Kyle, and his partner, Jan, get caught up in a plan by the Remnants that leads to pain, adventure, mystery, and cool lightsaber fights.
Jedi Outcast came out in 2002 when it was hip to make everything on the Quake III engine. And when it came out it looked really good. It still does, though you need to fiddle with the options just to not make it look all wonky on your new intergalactic space computer.
As Kyle, the coolest guy with the lamest name, you get a variety of weapons. Outside of the lightsaber that even the original game box advertised back in the day, you also get blasters, bowcasters, rocket launchers, space shotguns, space sniper rifles, thermo detonators, trip mines, and even that little orb thing that shot look in the original movie.
The shooting is nice, all of the blasters have the iconic Star Wars sound effects. They're crunchy, fun to fire, and since most of them have a delay like before hitting their target like a blaster in Star Wars would, you usually have to predict where your opponent is going to move before you fire.
While the shooting is fun, the lightsaber begins to take center stage as your powers grow and you become one of those intergalactic murder hobos known as a Jeddy. Not only can you murder fools with the space knife but you can also block incoming attacks and throw it like a very dangerous boomerang. Like the one from Road Warrior but not thrown by that kid with autism.
There's a big power trip in just clearing a room with your blue stick, dodging or deflecting incoming blasters, throwing people around with force powers, and leaping over fools before cutting them down.
The levels in single player are impressively large. Each area is unique considering most places you go to are in different parts of the galaxy from the last. “Abandoned” outposts, mining facilities, crime city, and Lando's crib are places you will visit on your journey to hit people with your laser sword.
“That's fine and all.” You tell me as you kick me in the junk. “But tell me about the really cool stuff.”
That was very rude of you.
Well if a really tight first person shooter with cool third person combat and sword fighting doesn't appeal to you then check this out. Jedi Outcast was released at a time when Modding was at a all time high. I remember about a year after it's release someone made a total conversion mod that was a single level where you play as a Gladiator in Rome. Not only was it kind of neat, but it was actually pretty educational as well.
Not only that, but there are skin packs, like one that returns Kyle to his original appearance in Dark Forces that was released in 1995. Fan made gameplay tweaks exist as well. If that doesn't tickle your pickle then there are also an assortment of console commands that can add replay value or just flat out break your game.
One console command that stands out actually increases dismemberment from your lightsaber swings, adding things such as cutting off heads or flat out bisecting people depending on high you set the value. I feel like the original idea was to always be able to dismember people, but maybe Lucas Arts didn't allow anything other than hands or arms? I don't know, I don't actually have any info on that.
But how friggin cool is that? You just type out a console command, slap in a few numbers, and suddenly you have the most brutal Star Wars game ever made.
So what else is there to cover?
Multiplayer, duh. Pay attention.
So I went into multiplayer with the intent of screwing around with some bots and covering the game modes. But to my surprise I actually found a few people still playing?
Back when I first played in 2004, I went into multiplayer ready to smash heads and immediately found a bunch of people just kind of standing around and chatting while other people fought in makeshift arenas around the map.
There were a handful of servers that focused on deathmatch, team deathmatch, etc, but a good majority of them were about dueling. Jedi Outcast's lightsaber combat, which was mostly about positioning, movement, and timing, was just complex enough to gather a cult following for dueling.
I remember challenging someone to a duel, then bowing before the fight begins, predating a certain other games dueling community by a few years. But back then it was fun to just sometimes sit around and chat with others, or jump and flip around the map.
There were clan wars that would break out on servers, rivalries that got pretty intense at some points. Jedi Outcast's multiplayer back in the day was something special, and finding it so empty actually made me feel...Sad, I guess.
I got a chance to talk to the 5 or so people that were actually playing at the time, with one person saying that he has been playing since 2004. I didn't stay around to duel, but I did ask a few questions.
They said it was weird to be part of a such a super niche community, remnants of what was a rather large nation back in the day. But the dedication of who was left was something to admire.
It's sad to see the multiplayer the way it is now. The last members of the Jedi Outcast community are an endangered species of true fans, even if there's only a few of them left. But hey, Jedi Outcast had it's run, it had a few years of fame and countless hours of good memories between thousands of players. And all good things have to come to an end, right?
The single player still holds up, coming out at a time before Disney decided to throw away thousands of stories in the galaxy far far away. The combat and exploration are still fun, even though you may get so lost in the early levels that you may as well set up camp and play campfire songs.
But Jedi Outcast's multiplayer was one of it's big draws in the early 00s. It was special and stood out from many of the other games that were out at the time. But hey, I know a lot of you still have Jedi Outcast sitting around, either in a jewel case or on your Steam library. It's never going to revive, I'm not that optimistic. But if you ever feel like just reinstalling, if just for a little bit, maybe stop by one of the servers and say hi to who's left, maybe stop for a duel or two. While you still can.

You can choose between three modes, Advendure, Classic and Time Attack. Adventure will allow you to proceed through the complete story with cool cutscenes and fully voice acted dialogs as Lilac or Carol. Milla can not be played in Adventure mode. Classic mode is the same as Adventure, except that there will not be any cutscenes or dialogs. Time Attack... I think this is obvious.
You can set the difficulty from Casual to Hard, which is... REALLY hard. I completed my Hard playthrough as Carol today, now that I understand the bosses patterns, it was a bit easier, but keep in mind that each characters has their different gameplay experience. ... Voice acting ranges from amateur to decent.
... The overall plot.

Nothing stands out as bad to me.

Freedom Planet is an absolute gem that just happened to appear as recommended to me on Steam one day.  After trying the demo, it more than warranted the purchase.  The game got better from there and has since become my favorite game on Steam, and also my favorite game of 2015 so far.  While the game does have some troubles with finding a consistent tone with it's story, the characters are still well designed and very likable across the board.  Ultimately what pushed this game past Shovel Knight in terms of overall enjoyment is it's difficulty, which allowed me to play on a difficult setting from the get go.  That said, for people newer to games, there are easier difficulties as well, so everyone wins.  The gameplay feels like a mix between Sonic and Mega Man Zero/ZX.  If you're a Sonic fan looking for this to PLAY like Sonic, it's actually quite a bit different... actually more like Mega Man Zero/ZX in my eyes.  In conclusion, I cannot recommend this game more for fans of platformers or retro games, and anyone with a passing interest should definitely try the demo.  My only question is, when will Freedom Planet 2 come out?

The second episode of the Blackwell point&cilck adventure series is a prequel. It takes place in the 1973, starring Lauren — the woman whose ashes Rosa scattered at the beginning of the first game. Together with Joey the ghost detective she helps undead spirits find peace by solving mysteries of their lives and deaths. This episode feels very intimate, taking place in a single night and focusing mostly on Lauren's feelings about being a medium and her relationships with Joey. The mood and atmosphere are great — the game is melancholic and tender, dealing with human emotion and regrets about wasted lives. I'd suggest it's a better introduction to the Blackwell series than the first game, which had less polishing and didn't always get the tone right. Great both as a part of the series and a standalone game, Blackwell Unbound is a great experience for any classic-style point&cilck adventure fan.

TLDR: If you liked Legacy then you'll like Unbound as well. If you like point n' click adventure then you'll like this game no doubt.
The game offers new mechanics that are in my opinion a nice addition. You can alternate between Lauren ( Rosa's aunt) and Joey, as well as use an in-game phone directory to progress forward. Joey and Lauren can do their own respective things when playing as them. For example Joey can move through walls. The story this time is set several years prior to Legacy, so much so that Rosa is either not yet born, or she's just a baby. Your task is to help two ghosts depart while trying to find a connection between the two. Sounds simple, but let me tell you: "It ain't". Unbound's puzzles require a bit more thinking than Legacy, which is great in my opinion. Graphics are about the same with some changes to character design on Joey, but nothing terrible.
Love the Blackwell games! This is a game I played through and couldn't stop. The others in the series are just as good.

This to me is exactly what a good sequel should be: It elaborates on the first by adding a couple of new mechanics (switching between characters and having more item interaction is great), and it also adds to the world.
In Blackwell Legacy we dealt with Rosa's acceptance of being a medium following the death of her aunt, and solving her first case. With Blackwell Unbound, we step a few years into the past to visit the aunt for what may be her last case, and we learn why she took the time to help raise Rosa.
The game itself is great - an interesting mystery that really adds more to building the world, with mechanics that feel improved over the first game. The storyline and characters are where this shines, though. I was hesitant to play as Lauren after it took me a while to connect with Rosa, but Lauren hooked me immediately. Without spoiling anything, as the ending approached it filled me with pretty legitimate anxiety with what may happen to her.

I'm still partial to Blackwell Legacy, but I'm in it for the story--so wanted to check this prequel out. I find the artwork a bit (and only a bit) lacking as compared to the original game's art, except for the area inside the main character's mind (I love how Lauren's mind place looks as compared to Rosa's). The "quest/case" menu definitely lacked the first game's case menu originality. The music is still pretty good (although for the sax music, it sounds synthesized.. because it didn't quite sound like the fully body of an alto or a tenor [appearance varied depending on perspective... ghost sax looked alto, portrait sax looked tenor... but the sound was closer to alto] sax sound like I was expecting (I played for several years, as long as I could), Joey's vocals and lines are still by far the best, and the story is... well, it is what it is. I know this isn't a raving review, but it's not necessarily negative either. I feel like this part of the story was meant more for the creator than the fans.
There are a lot of little nuances that don't necessarily appeal to me--Joseph Mitchell and his vocals irritate the snot out of me, the Shivah achievement is purely a nod to the creator's previous work and therefore comes across self-aggrandizing, the commentary achievement (ack, again?!) is still annoying (but thank goodness he told us about being able to skip over them), and the two different smoking achievements... not clever forcing the people to replay the game more than they may want just to get an achievement. If I'm getting all of these other achievements, I might as well have all of them... right? Ha.
Overall, the story--worth it. The addition of the Countess was a brilliant idea and I can see where this might go in the next three games. At least, I hope some form of this character is revisited somehow (hopefully, no spoilers here). Most of what doesn't appeal to me wouldn't bother others.

This game is great.  Don't let the graphics fool you- this game is quite a lot of fun.  The first time you play through a level it's just like any 16 bit sidescrolling shooter.
However, the second you die, you're forced to rewind time,  When you do, the second time you play, you're playing alongside a shadow of your first playthrough.  Every time you rewind, you don't eliminate your previous efforts, but all of your efforts become cumulative.
For example, need to kill a boss in 6 seconds, but it normally takes 60?  Rewind time 10 times to split your character into 10 characters, all gunning the boss down in 6 seconds.
The concept of teaming up with yourself and blasting enemies away with a small army limited only by your own skill at a run 'n' gun game is brilliant. It's fun to play and offers a unique challenge.

After disposing of all my old CDs in favour of copies on Steam, I recently bought JK2 and found the game to be just as enjoyable as it was all those years ago. Okay, so naysayers may moan about the graphics not being up to modern standards, but I don’t think that matters – at least not to me, anyway, because hey, it’s Star Wars and the opportunity to leap around the room hacking and slashing with a light-sabre is always going to be fun, no matter how pixelated it may be.

Cheap at twice the price.
Great combat action.
Great atmosphere that really feels STAR WARS!
Good immersion factor.
Good light-sabre action compared to JK1.
Good selection of weapons, although you rarely use them once you get your hands on a light-sabre.

Cons:
Too many jumping puzzles.

Jedi Knight II - Jedi Outcast came out almost 15 years ago, and it's still one of the best Star Wars games ever made.

Even now, in 2017, this game holds up as a fantastic action experience. 'The Force Unleashed' may have been more visually ambitious and 'Battlefront II' may have been a more grandiose idea, but I've rarely found a more exhilarating game experience than the deadly lightsaber duels of 'Jedi Outcast'. In this game, you play as Kyle Katarn. You'll be familiar with him if you've already played earlier 'Jedi Knight' games, but your gaming experience won't be diminished if you haven't. The early scenes of 'Jedi Outcast' show Kyle and his partner Jan attacked by a formidable Dark Jedi called Desann. Desann is one of the most well-designed villains in 'Star Wars' game history, and is certainly one of the most menacing, rivalled only in my opinion by Darth Malgus (SWTOR) and the various Dark Lords of the 'KOTOR' games. Kyle soon realises that he must reawaken his Jedi powers and, as Anakin Skywalker once said, this is where the fun begins. Over the course of 'Jedi Outcast' you'll battle hordes of Imperial Stormtroopers and Dark Jedi whilst closing the distance between you and your ultimate enemy. The levels are very enjoyable, and I don't recall a dull moment in the game. Overall, an excellent title.

This game has great lightsaber combat.
At least that's what they say. I gave up on the game before I ever got a lightsaber.
The only real reason for this is because I couldn't get past level two, not because of the enemies, but instead because of the terrible level design. Maybe people who grew up in the days of layberinth-like first-person shooters will like this game, but people who are new enough to gaming to not play through this era will find a lot of difficulty. A lot of things don't make sense, like requiring you to find areas and paths that are so well hidden they would be too much even for a secret area. sometimes you'll see little bits of architecture that turn out to be REQUIRED to go through in order to finish the level. And if that wasn't bad enough, there was at least one time I can remember that following this logic led me to a death trap.
Speaking of which, there are death traps EVERYWHERE! You need to quicksave constantly, since the checkpoints aren't very well laid out. I once spent around an hour stumbling through level one, when I came across an elevator. I pressed the button to send it up, but it wasn't going up. A few seconds later I realized it was above me because I was crushed to death by it, and sent back to the first five minutes of the level because that was the last checkpoint and I hadn't saved.
I've heard this game has some great lightsaber combat, and a pretty decent story, I've heard it gets better at some point, but why bother slogging through all this terrible design when you can get Jedi Academy which has slightly better graphics, improved design in nearly every aspect, and lets you wield a lightsaber and force powers from the very start? This game has not aged as well as many other reviews will tell you, and if you don't have nostalgic feelings for this game from playing it when it came out, you will have a very difficult time enjoying it today.

As someone who works in the wine industry, I was understandably intrigued by this game, but was a little surprised by how... poorly researched the game seems to be. Before I get into the nerdy wine stuff, I will reiterate what other reviewers have commented on: there is very little to do at this stage in the game's development. You basically sit there watching the clouds go by, then a button pops up allowing you to plant your first vineyard; you choose from 2 grapes, then wait until another button pops up over your Chateau that allows you to harvest. There are a few decisions to make regarding how to ferment, barrel, and bottle your wine, but it doesn't matter for the first several vintages: you're basically going to be making the same decisions over and over, because you really don't get many options, and the options you have don't really make a lot of difference.
Now for the nerdy wine critiques: the game is curiously inaccurate. We're supposed to be in Bordeaux, but I'm allowed to plant Chardonnay? When choosing the length of fermentation, the only intervals are represented in months which "decrease sweetness," but a wine can be (and typically is) fermented completely dry in a few weeks, not months. A long fermentation has more to do with the type of yeast used and the kind of flavor profile you want from the wine, not "getting the sweetness down." And when pressing the wine, you can choose the ratio of free-run to pressed juice, which is cool in theory, but the game says adding pressed juice "increases acidity," when pressing will typically extract more tannin than acid from the grapes. Vineyard management is also extremely simple, boiling down to just pruning the vines with a mouseclick whenever the canopy gets too dense. The game has a weather system, but it doesn't measure temperature, an extremely important factor in the development of wine grapes.
This doesn't need to be an educational game with hyper-realistic viticultural simulations, and I recognize that the game is still early in development and will no doubt have way more features in the future, but at this stage it's really not worth picking up. In my eyes, the whole point of a game like this is to take all the little nuances of vineyard management and winemaking and translate them into fun mechanics. Currently, the game is neither fun, nor accurate, so until they fix that, what's the point?

I played Actual Sunlight for my dissertation in Uni and there are a few things I feel that need to be pointed out.
* as a person not being influenced by mental illness this was a good insight of a depressed mind
* it gives you ONE (maybe quite stereotypical) view of depression and how it feels (It might even be impossible to provide EVERYTHING that depression is for everyone in one game anyway)
* it is very linear and more a graphic novel
* nothing you do will change the story
I actually found this quite believable especially because after a short while you find out that your character might not retell everything the way it actually is but the way he sees and experiences it ( like the letter from his absent boss).
It shows how mental illness influences your view on yourself and the world.
I would say it is a good game to play if you are interested in the topic but I would recommend a careful approach if you might suffer from mental illness yourself, especially if you're not in a good place right now.
The writing is good, if you want to play a book.

This game is a slice-of-life albeit the focus is on perceiving the world view as hopeless.  This game has a few unique concepts that differ from most games.
1.  The story touches on sensitive issues such as depression.  The developers do a pretty decent job on telling a story of one man's life that isn't going anywhere (or for most people in the story for that matter).  The execution was done well due to relatability and even understanding some of the view point of developers.
2.  The game focuses on a lot of reading but each text by Evan Winters (also other writers, I think), holds a deeper understanding about life or what's "actually" going on.  This may be just one view-point but its good to have additional perspective.
3.  I can't speak for the developers of its purpose of the game but the game is interesting enough to give gamers mix feelings on the purpose.  Is the game meant to give perspective of modern day life?  Is it meant to teach us something?  Is it just telling a biography of one person's life?  Is it meant to give us hope or despair?
Although I lean towards a thumbs up, I will hold off recommending/not recommending.  Any gamer should view the features (about the game), and several player's reviews prior to buying the game to get an idea if this is for them or not.

If you don't understand or suffer from depression but want to, this game might be worthwhile. If you DO have depression, or if you're looking for a good game, I'd recommend skipping it.
There is not a single uplifting thing about this game and it ends on the bleakest possible note. This might be a simple forgivable arthouse game, if not for an early block of text that breaks the fourth wall and talks to the player. It says "Hey, if you're young, don't kill yourself! This game is for people feeling this way in their late 20s and early 30s."
Wait, what? So yeah, the game essentially tells you early on, in a fourth-wall breaking moment, that he's going to kill himself, and you can't do anything about it. And it makes a deliberate point of saying "if you're in this situation, I'm not going to tell you not to kill yourself". As someone who's struggled with depression and suicidal thoughts for years, I found the game insulting, and I'm guessing most of the acclaim comes from people going "wow, cynicism, mental health, that's deep", and games journalists falling over themselves to lavish praise on a game that tackles anything deeper than a stab wound.
The game also goes out of its way to say that it hates romanticizing depression and suicide. It doesn't do that. But it DOES go halfway there, though, by saying "but hey, maybe it's not so bad".
It grasps for connections to the reader like a fortune teller - "You play videogames? You masturbate? You have a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ 9-5?" and halfway blames these things for the protagonist's depression, having him smash all of his possessions to 'start fresh', but then has him decide to kill himself anyway. Ultimately, from the perspective of this game, there is no hope, no way out - and appreciators of this game might say that's the point. Personally I just feel like this game had nothing to offer. No comfort, no solace, no advice - just bleakness.
The writing quality is actually really good, and the writer clearly has experience, but I assume from making this game that he DIDN'T kill himself. He found a reason to live. Maybe share some of that, rather than the Tommy Wiseau-esque self-indulgent suicide fantasy.
Ultimately, you can choose how to react to this game, what to take from it, like any fiction. But if you suffer from depression, this game is just a walk through familiar territory and there is absolutely no reason to play it. We play games to escape to something better; to have fun, to discover something new. Unlike what the cynical creator of this game may believe, games can bring joy to people's lives - hell, they can be the source of it. So play something that does that. Not this.

The descendent is an adventure game in 5 episodes. It uses the Telltale adventure system (The Walking Dead series of games), which means that the game is closer to an interactive book than a game, with QTEs during dialogues or during some action sequences.  It’s also very linear, the spaces you’re exploring are small and simple – and the only time it got a bit more complex the game provided a map. The story is a sci-fi classic: you’re sent to explore a space compound where everything went of course horribly wrong and you’ll slowly discover what happened. The story is very well told, the characters very solid, the graphics are comics style, sharp and colorful, the voice over are top notch and the music perfectly sets the eerie ambiance.  There are quite a lot of puzzle games, extremely easy at first and becoming a tiny bit challenging toward the second half of the game. The bad? Well I often cursed at the camera system which makes walking to a given point sometimes hard due to all the camera angles changes. Another bad is the story predictability where you jump from a cliché to another cliché, but the whole game experience is very good, solid and fun, it’s hard to put it down before the end. You do have some surprises here and there, some ‘Oh Really?’ moments. The whole game lasted 6 hours, which is a bit short for the genre. But I still recommend it, even at full price. Don’t hesitate to buy it, grab your controller and your headphones and play it in the dark!

Winged Sakura: Demon Civil War is a first-person jRPG dungeon crawler. While we've seen a resurgence in this genre, with many well-made localisations on the PS Vita, e.g.
,
, there's a startling lack of Vita ports on Steam at present.
is the only port that I'm aware of, all other games (e.g.
) are PC exclusive.
In terms of art, Winged Sakura: Demon Civil War strikes a happy medium between that of
and
. The artwork is mellow and cute, without being too overt on fanservice as the Sakura series is infamous for. Those who are not as into moe, or who desire artwork of hot-blooded male characters, would probably find
to be more suited to their tastes. If you're familiar with Winged Sakura's previous work
, you'll find that the artstyle has completely changed (in my subjective opinion, for the better) - it reminds me more of
.
The gameplay formula is pretty generic and similar to the other first-person jRPG dungeon crawlers out there. You can customise and command a party of up to five members, augment their stats, skills and equipment, and progressively explore monster/treasure-filled dungeons in first person, one step at a time. There are adjustable difficulty settings, so you could set it on Newbie if you're just interested in a story playthrough with minimal grind, or Permadeath if you're feeling masochistic. A cool thing to note is that the dungeons' layout, loot and mobs are random and procedurally generated, adding an element of replayability and some sort of "roguelite" factor into the game. While you can mess around with customising your party members' skills and stats, I found the build variability to not be particularlly extensive. Most of the time, speed is king - you want to hit hard and fast before your enemies can move.
The plot retains the cheesiness factor from
, but overall it isn't too bad. Similar to plenty of fantasy anime shows out there, you are a human transported into a alternate world where factions of demons are embroiled in civil war. It's up to you to form contracts with various demons personified into beautiful ladies, and put a stop to the bloodshed!
*Speaking of
, as a perk for people who own the other Winged Sakura title, they gain access to the unique characters Mindy and Minzy!
really won me over on its price. It's the cheapest among the first-person jRPG dungeon crawlers on Steam by more than half the price, at only ten dollars. You could definitely get more than $1/hour's worth of entertainment from this title.
Overall, this title is well worth a try for anyone on the fence about getting into this subgenre of RPGs.

(THIS REVIEW IS SPOILER FREE)
While I could tell you about the cute pixel art, atmospheric music or mysterious story, all of which are great, they are also things which I kind of expected to be great from a point and click adventure game.
What I didn't expect is the direction the game took with actual gameplay and problem solving. Forget L.A. Noire, this game makes you feel like a true detective. This can be kind of said about all of the Blackwell series games, but for some reason I felt like it shone the most in this one. (maybe its the chain smoking of the main character)
First of all, important events get written down in your notebook, but instead of your character reaching conclusions on their own, you have to actually connect important notes yourself, to either make educated guesses, figure out if characters are lying or just notice that two cases might be connected. I have never seen such mechanic in a point and click adventure game before. Some people felt like it was annoying so they took it out in the next game, but it has since made a return in the fourth.
Something which they have improved from the first game is the way you do research. In that game, you would use your clues in the notebook to research things, which meant that it would sometimes come down to you trying all the options to progress. In this one however, you need to actually type in the thing you want to search for, which means that you actually have to notice clues in things like letters, photos or the enviroment, which the playable characters won't even mention. This is actually the first time a game made me draw a mindmap on a piece of paper to note down all the suspicions I had and important figures and their interactions with oneanother.
Another addition from the first game is having control over your little ghost partner, this leads to some clever puzzle solutions where you have to send him to scout out areas which you don't have access to, or create distractions for you to take advantage of, something which has since been much refined in the later games.
The only issue I had with the game stems from it being made out of material cut from the next game Blackwell Convergence. You see all of this game was originally supposed to be a flashback in the next game. While this hasn't hurt the games length, it does kind of create a problem with the order youre supposed to play the games in. If you play this before Convergence, it will kind of....ruin the mystery a bit (I'm trying not to spoil anything). Whereas if you play Convergence first and then this one, you will already know how everything will play out. Best way would be to play Convergence up to a certain point, then switch to this, then switch back, and so on, and so on. But the issue with this is that you won't know the moments when to switch without knowing the whole story, so you would need someone to tell you when to switch, and I can't really write the moments when to switch here, because the moments themselves would be a spoiler.....
It might be just something bugging me personally, and it definitely doesn't hurt the game as a whole.

I thoroughly enjoyed the entire Blackwell series. The interesting story and characters and the great music and voices overcome the so-so graphics. Joey is a joy. The puzzles and story progression are generally logical. I found I needed to refer to a walkthrough only a few times. If you like adventure games with a good story, I can recommend playing the Blackwell series. Play them in sequence one after the other to get the full effect. This series is now in my Top 5 Adventure Games list.

Bllackwell Unbound is the second game in the Blackwell adventure series. If you're not familiar with this series, I'd suggest you just start off with the first game, the Blackwell Legacy.
Anyway, here we are back in the 1970's as Lauren Blackwell, Rosangela's aunt and her medium predecessor. I have to say this game has a much more involved story line, and it's a wonderful step forward for the series. I really enjoyed the prequel angle, jumping in time and seeing what it is like being a medium from another perspective. Lauren is a more interesting character in my opinion, though I may grow to really like Rosa in the later games.
Unbound has a very noir feel to it, it taking place all in one single night. You investigate two deaths, one of a saxophone player and the other of a woman who shut herself in her own apartment for years. These two stories are written quite confidently, and I especially enjoyed the one about the musician. There's something really compelling about investigating the deaths of these characters. You're digging into the past, step by step you learn about people and their issues.
But the real highlight was the end. Obviously I won't spoil it for you here, but just know that this game isn't just about two random cases without any more personal connection to Lauren. When the credits rolled, I found myself empathising with her a whole lot, and it really cast a spotlight on Rosangela and the things that lay in wait for her.
Blackwell Unbound is an excellent continuation in the series, offers the usual great banter between Joey and the main character, has interesting cases to solve and above all raises the stakes for our heroine(s). A big recommendation from me!
