A portrait of despair.
What you need to know:
This is one of those games created using RPG Maker.
This is not an RPG. There is no combat, no leveling system, and you are unable to affect the outcome on anything. The story is linear and presented in a relatively straightforward fashion. It’s much closer to a visual novel than anything else.
This title is about depression.
No matter how much you might not want to,
The creator of this game calls it a snapshot. Of himself at one point in time perhaps? I couldn’t tell you and it’s impossible to infer that from the work alone.
It’s very short, it’s well written, and it encapsulates themes that will likely make you uncomfortable, sad, or unhappy. If you struggle with depression, playing this might actually just make you more depressed.
It’s difficult to recommend/not recommend the game. I really wish I could just leave a neutral review. Nevertheless, I am tentatively giving it a recommendation, so long as you know what you are and are not getting.
Wait for a sale, if you feel you absolutely must support endeavors like this. It was a different sort of experience for me from most of the things I play.

That being said, it is extremely complex varying between 5 different characters with 3 (or 4) stances/movesets, 5 unique weapons, and a specific playstyle for each individual. No matter how you come about this game, your form of strategy will ultimately be true to you by the end of the match. Bringing with it, a "rock, paper, scissors!" attitude to a 3-D sword game involving finesse and aim, Blade Symphony can quickly turn into a game of wits rather than strats.

If your looking for a special community, don't get your hopes up too high. Take this community with a grain of salt. The "devs" had walked out quite some time ago due to controversial aspects of the game (as so its said); however they are seemingly making a return. Despite all this, if you invest 10+ hours into this game, you will more than likely develop a sort of crack addiction that can make Lindsey Lohan's meth induced third chin flinch. It's the Sonic Game you've always wanted. Story is a bit cliche, but nothing too dull to bore you.
If you really hate stories and want to get into the action, there is a 'Classic' mode, where you don't have to watch the cutscenes.
In my play-through of the game, I chose Lilac. Here is an overview of her character;
Lilac (the purple one) is a dragon-girl (don't ask me why, I don't know either).
Playing as her is fast-paced. You'll be relying on her special ability; 'Dragon Boost' (think Sonic Dash) to gain maximum speed and fly past enemies. Double-jumping gives you a helicopter-like hover/spin, allowing you to jump further, fall slower and deal lots of damage if you time the attack right. Holding 'down' as you perform this attack will have Lilac spin downwards (or along the ground), this can be used more for combat. Lilac also has close-melee attacks, like an upper-cut, downwards kick and a hair whip.
Carol (the green one) is a wild-cat.
Carol plays slower than Lilac, expect more fighting than running. Her attacks deal more damage, but, once again, you'll have to play completely different compared to Lilac. I haven't had as much play-time as Carol, but I'll give you a quick run-down;
Carol's special is a 'Wild Claw' attack. Simply holding the special button will shred anything in her path, easily taking out all. Double jumping will instead of gaining height, perform a 'pounce'. Time it right and you can do a quite bit of damage. This also leads on to Carol's wall-jumping ability, as well as the jumping pads scattered around the map. Standing on one of these pads will let Carol defy gravity, jumping from pad-to-pad, often upside-down. These pads will let Carol access areas Lilac couldn't, or maybe even provide short-cuts if you're into speedrunning.
There IS a special third character, although I haven't had any playtime as her so I can't say much.
If you're a platformer, I HIGHLY recommend this game. Like, it's REALLY good. REALLY, REALLY, good.
Just go buy it already.

I will be honest and say that as much as I love Sonic the Hedgehog, I am not really a big fan of his classic games. I have played all of them (Sonic 1-3), but find them too frustrating, especially when losing all those rings I painstakingly gathered for those special stages from one hit. I know it all comes down to skill in the end, but still...
So I was surprised when I bought Freedom Planet and have found myself coming back to play it over and over again.
Freedom Planet is unquestionably inspired by Sonic the Hedgehog. It even started out as a fan game but evolved into its own unique experience. I saw this game through a review on YouTube and was really curious from the start, downloading the demo and later buying the full thing. I spoiled nothing save for looking at one stage not included in the demo, but that was it. Everything was a complete blank until I began playing.
So with that said, is this game worth the price tag it comes along with? Absolutely!! If you are a fan of Sonic the Hedgehog, then you will most likely enjoy this game. Don't mistake it for a clone, because it is not. Freedom Planet is it's own unique game, adopting sonic mechanics such as high-speed platforming while adding combat, intense boss fights that will have your reflexes tested throughout, and unique play styles that, while subtlety different, don't change your overall experience of the game. The story is fun in my personal opinion, but plays a lot with its tone and pacing, so keep that in mind when you choose story mode. The graphics are really pretty to look at, and the music beautifully captures the atmosphere of the stage you are in.
Freedom Planet is definitely a game worth picking up if you are into the 2D platformers, especially if you are a Sonic fan.
Also, motorbikes that defy physics altogether. Have fun!!

A very solid adventure game/interactive story.  There are a couple things that really distinguished this game:
+ Story
+ Ambiance/Setting/Environment
+ Voice acting
Overall the game is 60-70% story and the rest filled with puzzles and exploration.
The game was lacking in the puzzles department...yes there are a handful and some well designed puzzles but nothing challenging.  As for the positives I mentioned above, I feel the game is well worth playing just for those pieces.
I love experiencing graphically rich adventure games and I think this game was a huge win because it was done with Unity.  Yes there were some camera and control glitches here and there...but overall, the environments were very well detailed and designed.  If more traditional adventure game elements (like deep inventory management) were a part, I could see exploring these environments would be an awesome puzzle in of itself.  Instead, the objects to find are very easy and often highlighted, which takes the hidden object challenge away from those that like that sort of thing.
I liked the multiple dialogue selections and thought the narrative flowed well...but I never really saw any impact to the choices I made.  Not to spoil anything but the endings that are available are solely based on a final decision.  I would have like to see more impact throughout the story based on the choices as there was definite tension throughout the episodes as to the mystery behind everything going on.
All in all...I applaud the team for making a very solid episodic adventure with modern flavor and employing a game engine to a level that deserves it.  Recommended for fans of recent Telltale-style games likeWalking Dead and Wolf Among Us.  What's coming for round two?

Just beat the season last night, here are my thoughts:
Story: 8/10
Fairly solid story, I found it engaging and I was interested the whole time.  The ending was a bit abrupt, but I'm hoping there'll be a second season at some point.  If you don't mind a bit of an open ended finale, it's all good stuff.
Voice Acting: 8/10
I was impressed for the most part, there were a few awkward lines but for the most part all of the voice acting was pretty good.
Gameplay: 6/10
The gameplay itself is fairly linear, and mostly consists of walking around and fixing every broken computer in the building.  (Who designed this place to have a different style of fuse box in every room??)  The gameplay is mostly a vehicle for the story, but the controls for moving around were really touchy, and lining yourself up to investigate something could be tricky.
Overall: 7.5/10
Despite being rough around the edges, The Descendant is a solid interactive story.  I still need to replay and see how much your choices really change things, but I'm satisfied overall.  Hope to see a second season, and I recommend this for anyone who's a fan of post-apocalyptic stories or Telltale-style games.

The Descedant is largely a point and click adventure game set in the post apchalypse.  The "Descendants" of the title are  surviors, cyrogenically preseved in undergrund bunkers called Arks.  Descendandts and Arks are maintained by "Janitors", which comprise the playable chrecters.  The story switches between two of these charecters arcoss 5 episodes.  I found each episode took about an hour to play, so I felt I was getting plenty of entertainment for my money.
I may have to replay this title, just to see if the many choices the game gives you actually make much of a difference to the outcome.
The gameplay is mostly long scripted sequences and point and click adventure, with a fixed 3rd person camera.  The collectable items to solve problems make sence and are not too hard to find (one of the classic adventure game sins avoided).  There are some mini-games to break up the sameness of the point and click and a some quick time events to add a sense of urgency oh and that "tap button E quickly" to climb a ledge mechanic.
If that sounds like your kind of thing then I recommend this game.
This game has loads of very easy achievements.  Seriously you get an achivement just for sitting though the opening scripted sequence, making arbitrary choices etc.
Had a couple of glitches where the game presented me with no-options.  Exiting and reloading fixed it both times.
I'm really sorry for the game.  I respect the ambitions etc., but the execution simply ruins everything. The more the game wants to be move- or TellTale-like, the more uncanny it gets.

As a player of Winged Sakura Games' previous release, Mindy's Ark, I've been hyped up for their next release for quite a while now, and I definitely wasn't disappointed with this game.
Art / Graphics: Everything is pretty good here, you can definitely see the improvements to the character designs the most and that's the best part. The area's and enemies designs are just as good, but there isn't enough of it. Like you go into the dungeon, and you see similar looking walls throughout the game so it always feels like you're in the same area rather than other dungeon crawlers' "You're in the same dungeon, but this area is Watery / Fiery / Earthy / ect." This isn't a huge disappointment, but what's there still looks nice.
Sounds / music: The sounds are good, but the previous issue still stands, there isn't enough variance here. As for the music, it's amazing. It fits the given situations perfectly and it's all really nice.
Gameplay: The gameplay is what really stands out to me here. You have your average characters, but they're extremely customizable with their stats and spells / skills. At any point in the game if you're having trouble with enemies / bosses, you can just fiddle with your party's stats and see how it goes. While this can get somewhat tedious, it also makes for many interesting combinations like "How much strength can I dump on this character before I get 1 hit by enemies".
Randomly generated dungeons are nice as always. You move on a grid-like area and enter rooms, what you find inside is random. Enemies, Chests, Healing Fountains, or the door to the next area. There isn't much to say here, it's pretty good.
Another thing to note is that the game has difficulty levels, which can be changed at any time in the game.
Story: There's not much I can say here without spoilers and I also haven't quite finished the game yet, the game is heavily story driven. It's a decent story and ties in well with the previous game. If you've played it, knowledge from that game will help you here, but it's still beginner friendly :)
Overall: 7/10
What's holding it back from higher ratings is that there's not too many varied things, and it get's somewhat tedious after a while.
TL;DR - It's good, especially if you've played the previous Winged Sakura game. Worth the money you pay for sure.

This game is outrageous.  Your commander wears two eye patches, and at one point sends you into the future to download plugins so you can watch a cat video.  The developers really went all out to fill this game with humor and style.
The gameplay is also outrageous.  Think like Contra, it is a platformer run n' gun through large, detailed stages.  When your character dies, you can rewind, and send another character (and there are plenty of characters to choose from) to go through the stage again, but with your previous character's ghost replaying its actions, killing things for you.  You can do this upwards of THIRTY TIMES in one stage, allowing you to create a gigantic posse of whirling death.  You oftentimes won't, as you have no reason to add more ghosts if you're already destroying everything, but the game is filled with all sorts of 100% completion stuff.  Collectibles and time attacks (not the kind you are used to!)  It really is a full experience, and I recommend it for any action fan.

After suffering a series of migraines, New York native Rosa Blackwell finds she has inherited a family heirloom in the form of a spirit guide named Joey Mallone whom, with her assistance, helps losts ghosts travel to the afterlife. Choosing to embrace this as a gift instead of a curse opens her life up to new opportunity and new dangers, both in the form of a secret cult with desires of their own and the possibility of her following in her family footsteps and losing her mind.
PROS:
CONS:
This is just a great series with excellent, emotional writing. Such progression as well! Going from a lonely girl living in an apartment to a medium with her own business is laid out on screen perfectly. The progression of the games interface (going from writing notes on a notepad and using a desktop computer to doing everything on her smartphone) helps you, the player, feel like you are growing and evolving with these characters as well. It's all about the characters. So many great moments in this series. Can't recommend it enough!

LISA is, without a doubt, one of the best video games I have ever played. I wish only that more people could play this game. It surprises me that this game did not recieve the same acclaim that UNDERTALE recieved, considering they are both heavily inspired by Earthbound.
I wanna talk about the music first and foremost, because it's still in my head to this day. I'll whistle the tune of iconic moments and feel that same feeling I felt whilst doing it, This game not only incorperates a completely unique soundtrack but it also ties its pieces in well with what is actually happening on screen to make it impact that much more. It's the only soundtrack I have ever purchased for game. it is so zanny and fun.
The story literally depressed me for a day and a half. Which is not a bad thing, many people praise Earthbound for being a game that is not exactly fun to play, but makes you feel something. LISA is similar, there are moment you don't want to continue your path, you don't want to be forced to do this but you have to. And it's brillant.
The humor is an excellent balance to the heavy heartedness of the main heros journey. This whole time you are beating dudes literal brains in, and then it'll make a goofy joke about a guy pooping and you having to kill a little spider to save him by stepping on it. I honestly can't do it justice.
Much of this sounds like bias, and a lot of it probably is, but I really do believe this game is worth playing. It's a unique thing found amongst the gaming world. And it does it well.

It's not very often that media presents a realistic view of depression. In
depression isn't romanticized, the protagonist has no sudden solutions, and the game's world just does not care.
Instead, we are given a story that takes place mostly in a man's head. He tries to make his feelings seem unique, when they're anything but. He tries to play himself off as a tragic soul, when in reality he failed due to his own shortcomings. In this aspect, the game is entirely self-aware and while such a viewpoint offers no alternatives - no solutions - I think that the documentation of this sort of experience is valuable.
isn't a pleasant or fun game. It's a visual novel more than anything. Regardless, it's message is unique and worth being exposed to.

I cautiously recommend this point-and-click story. If you play this game, know that it's a solid 7/10 and, for the first four episodes, will be just intriguing enough to click a few more times.
Pros:
+Episode 5: It's worth pushing through the first four episodes. The game finally figures it out. If all the episodes were like Episode 5, the game would be an 8 or 9 out of 10.
+The environments and character models are quite beautiful.
+The concept is fascinating, and the storyline took some unexpected and fun turns. I'd gladly read the book.
+Some of the choices you make will be difficult.
Cons:
-Gameplay: The greatest point-and-click games let you explore the environments and click on different objects to hear your character's perspective of them. It's the tiny details like this that add life to your avatar, but this is almost completely overlooked until Episode 5. In the first few episodes, you're going to just click on the next objective to advance the story. Fortunately, that also makes the episodes less of a drag.
-Voice acting: It ranges from fair to atrocious. Emotional sequences are squandered by jarring inflection and substellar writing.
-Music and sound effects: Sometimes the music is great, but often the game is just too quiet. This game would be much better if there was more background ambience. Sound effects are canned; in fact I think they're just using the stock Unity sound effects for footsteps and the like. Perhaps this is a consequence of low budget, in which case I look forward to seeing this improved in the sequel.
-Price: Too expensive. Buy it on sale.
Overall, yes, I recommend this game. It won't knock your socks off, but it'll be a fun and relatively short experience. And if the developers make a sequel (which I hope they do!), this story has a LOT of potential.

The descendant is an overall decent episodic adventure game with very minor decision making. The first season has a lot of potential to set up for a much better continuation (if there will ever be one). In the descendant you play as two characters who are in charge of the lives of those left in a destroyed world. One character is in the present while another is several years into the past. Unfortunately not much is done with the differences as both characters play identical.
EPISODE 1 - 5/10
PROS
+ good ending
+ decent voice acting
+ interesting world build up
CONS
- Boring start
- Terribly paced
- Like 5 dialogue options in the whole episode
- Short (45 mins)
EPISODE 2 - 6.5/10
PROS
+ Better pacing
+ plot gets interesting
+ some unique puzzles
+ Tough decision (despite it not even mattering)
CONS
- Most of the puzzles are repetitive
- Areas can get way too large (Mia's section)
- Still hardly any choices to make
- Where are the dialogue options?
EPISODE 3 - 6/10
+ Great story beats
+ Much needed character development
+ Strong ending
- BACKTRACKING for 40% of the hour long episode
- Obtuse puzzles
- tries to hard to make you think your choices matter
EPISODE 4 - 8.5/10
PROS
+ Beautifully paced
+ actual decisions (they don't mean much, but that's nice)
+ Surprisingly intense
+ all the Puzzles aren't terrible for once
+ much needed character interactions
CONS
- crashed twice
- Wouldn't let me play the episode for a week despite it being out (Biased)
- Decisions still don't mean anything
EPISODE 5 - 6/10
PROS
+ Good set up for a second season
+ Well written
+ A decision (GASP!)
+ Neat arcade-like segment
CONS
- What happen to SIlas?!
- Feels very underwhelming
- 90% of the episode is just one location
- Mia being wasted
- Choices never amounted to anything except for trying to guilt trip me for a few seconds.
Overall - 6.4/10 (Get it on sale)

After hundreds of years in cryostasis the few thousand remaining humans awake in the aftermath of the global apocalypse. Two men set out to investigate the fate of ARK-01 - a bunker somewhere in Alaska - which didn't respond to the wake up signal given by the ARK network.
Narrated in episodes each lasting about one hour the whole season contains five episodes with four of them already released at the time of this review.
The story is told in two timelines. You play as Mia a 'janitor' of ARK-01 in the past and as Donnie one of the two investigators in the present.
Voice acting and and soundtrack are on par with the nice visuals which make good use of the Unity engine.
The puzzles you have to solve are of the casual sort and shouldn't pose a problem.
I played all available four episodes and the story kept me interested from beginning to end. As the structure of the game is similar to a tv series there is a short summary of previous events at the beginning of each episode which is handy if you haven't got the time to play the game in one go.
Although the game officially only supports up to 1080p resolution I had no technical problems running it at 4k with a R9 390 X 8 GB in Win10_64. The only problem I encountered playing this point and click game with a mouse were the hotspots showing very late which may be related to the resolution. I soon changed to a XBox controller and had a much better experience.
While the game isn't groundbreaking in any way it will keep you entertained for a few hours and is worth your money.
I would buy it in the coming holiday sale if you can wait a few weeks.
The game has achievements and trading cards and you can buy the first episode separately to try the game.
Developers respond to forum posts and seem to be dedicated to fulfill their promised release schedule.
For me it's a solid 7/10 and I hope The Descendant gets enough attention to justify the production of a second season.

TL:DR;
Half content and half story of TWD: Michonne. I cannot recommend it to everyone - read on to find why.
Review:
The Descendant is a tell-tale type of visual novel with multiple choices along the way.
You will get this feeling right away from the start and yes this is clearly what this title was supposed to be.
However.
- the story is badly written and very inconsistent. I could name numerous examples, like technical specialists not having a toolset on them, but going to visit a high tech bunker.
- the game is very short. it's actually 8h at maximum at slow pace, I got more because I was idling on start screen.
- it costs a bit too much for what is offered
- episode 1 contains most of non-plot points of interests like posters etc. they are almost gone in the rest of the episodes and very rarely you can click something that is not story relevant. This adds to the picture of empty world full of nothing.
- characters are basically cliche to the point where it hurts. Oh and suprisingly all white people in the game are evil or insane.
- puzzles are insulting.
- quick time events are insulting as well.
- game breaking bugs!
- controls! with mouse clicks your character walks slowly, but with gamepad they always run
- no access to options in game except sound. Not even the control which you cannot remap anyway!
Don't get me wrong. This game can be played, can be finished, except of few stupid achievements (you need to fail to get them, wtf?), but unless you are a fan of this particular game type, you will be better off getting The Walkind Dead 1 & 2 for a story.
This one here? I purchased it on sale and have mixed feeling about it, so it is not worth it's full price for sure.

UPDATE: Some of my criticisms of the story were rendered moot by plot twists in later episodes, but this doesn't negate them being worthy of criticism IMO...just warranting a different form of criticism. Namely, that significant information about player characters is not known to the player early on, when it is relevant...which is just a cheat from a storytelling perspective.
------
There are some good ideas and intriguing plot details here, but some gameplay mechanic elements are immensely frustrating. This game makes me wish that Steam had a less binary review system, but as it is, I can't recommend this game.
For starters, one of the two playable characters is supposed to be a hand-picked expert who is responsible for the survival of a large portion of the remaining population of the human race, but the game treats the player assuming her role like a moron that needs to be handheld by dialogue catered to the lowest denominator. In spite of being one of only 4,000 people specifically selected to survive an apolocalype that wiped out the rest of humanity (you'd think the powers that be would be able to pick some competent people with that ratio), she has no idea what her job is or how to get around the facilty. The other "janitor" (term for the caretakers of the cryo bunker facilities) talks to her like she's an idiot, which turns out to be completely justified as almost all of the dialogue options available to the player make her seem like some random person who walked in off the street with no context of what is going on (the game tries to excuse this by her being a last minute rushed replacement, but it doesn't really work for a position so important). And the puzzles the player needs to complete as her are laughably simple in spite of her supposedly being some mechanical and/or engineering expert (there is a dialogue choice that even lets the player select what her specialty is, since it matters so little because nothing she does requires any technical knowledge).
The first crisis you must resolve as this character involves extremely simple puzzles, but also a lot of nonsense and logical problems that are disorientingly glaring. There is a problem. You look at the computer and it has the word "critical" clearly displayed. You go to solve the problem. Your partner gets on the radio and says "IT'S GONE CRITICAL!"
It said that from the goddamn outset.
Then for some reason even though you are the one person tasked with rectifying technical problems in the facility, you have no idea of the basic layout of the facility and need to get directions, and there are keycode-locked doors that you were apparently never provided the codes for. Fortunately because this is a video game, those are just left lying around right beside the door (what the hell was even the point of that, from either a story or gameplay perspective?).
The storyline is divided between two characters, centuries apart, and the experience with the other character is equally illogical. You are performing a recovery/salvage mission and apparently brought NO TOOLS whatsoever, resulting in the need to pick up random tools off the ground along the way (how convenient that the right tool is always just lying around). The gameplay in that section is mind-numbing: you find one item after another and ALWAYS get messages along the lines of "its battery is missing," "it is out of fuel," "it is missing a part," etc, over and over and over and walk around finding the appropriate item three feet away to make the other item work.
But the frustrating gameplay mechanics are actually worse than the internal logic that leaves the player baffled by stupidity. You are given time-sensitve critical tasks and...
1.) You can't interact with objects during dialogue, and characters chat away like idiots.
2.) You run into scripted cutscenes that are unskippable and in which characters take far longer to realize something than a remotely intelligent player would.
3.) Movement is clunky at best. You left click to move and sometimes the character goes well away from where you want them to and you need to direct them to the right place repeatedly.
4.) Camera angles change jarringly and further complicate movement and cause misclicks.
5.) Characters don't act with any sense of urgency in respects that the player doesn't have control over (talking, taking forever to process things, inspecting things for excessive amounts of time and thinking through pointless commentary to themselves, dropping things, walking briskly instead of sprinting when they have seconds to spare to prevent people from dying, etc).
6.) If you click the wrong thing during a puzzle it usually delays you by several seconds while you hear your character say something along the lines of "that won't work." You can't interact with anything while this happens.
7.) You can't interact with objects unless you are positioned in the "right place," which is always guesswork and complicated by the bad movement and camera angles.
8.) You have to pointlessly stare at objects for several seconds after interacting with them before backing away from them, even after deducing they are useless.
The cumulative impact of all this clunky nonsense is that even though puzzle sections are not intellectually challenging whatsoever, 80% of the time you spend on them are wasted dealing with this frustrating BS (yes, I still completed the relevant sections within the alloted time limit, but it was not fun).
Oh also, you get achievements for everything. Including just starting the game. What an "achievement."
I like the basic story idea in broad strokes and there were moments that intrigued me (the computer selecting descendants to terminate at the end of the chapter was a highly that reinforced the "choices matter" gameplay), but it's unfortunately badly executed.

Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast marks the second time that LucasArts' Dark Forces series of first-person shooters has been released for a console--the first time being the mediocre port of Dark Forces for the PlayStation. The game was released in 1996, and it was plagued by sloppy controls and graphics that were, to put it bluntly, ugly.
As far as the single-player component of Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast is concerned, the game is unchanged from its PC cousin. You are cast in the role of Kyle Katarn, a gruff mercenary who lends his smuggling skills to the Rebellion during its uprising against the Empire.
In your quest to put a stop to this army of cybernetic soldiers, you'll fight your way through 25 single-player levels that span eight different environments, one more than the PC game. The Xbox version of Jedi Knight II includes the level that was found in the PC demo but wasn't available in the actual PC game itself. The single-player campaign is relatively long compared with the single-player modes in recent shooters, and it's also quite tough at the default difficulty level.
If you can weather the first few hours of Jedi Outcast, you'll note that it takes a sharp turn for the better. Suffice it to say that Kyle regains his force powers and lightsaber, the combination of which makes for some very satisfying and original action.

text:
is a game (a visual novel to idiots insisting on this not being a game) about a depression patient Evan Winters. Personalities and inner world are revealed by the character's interaction with things around him.
The game brought me desolation more than anything else, stronger than any other emotions any other games ever brought to me. I have some of the very thoughts of the protagonist: like how other people are more successful, how I consider myself a loser about once every 10 hours on average, how I rarely got around to doing anything i wanted to, how I feel like I am not loved, how I feel worthless, etc. etc. etc. etc. etc.
I related strongly to the game.
But fortunately I am not nearly as hopeless as Evan. I am not 300 pounds, I am still quite young, I have close friends of both sexes even though I never had a girlfriend, I have things that I excel in doing, relatively speaking. I do have a depressing personality, but I can usually get over the downs, and I am far, far from needing a treatment.
I guess that is something for me to feel fortunate about, but it also reminds me how Evan in the story is very aware of the fact that there are people suffering much worse, but still can't get around to feeling better. I cannot blame him. When I have my downs, it is hard (ok, impossible) to think straight.
This game depicts a depression patient. I do not personally known anybody like this, but I have read about the things written by them on the internet, and I feel for them strongly due to my personality. But, you don't need to be a depression patient to relate to the game. If you are like me, or like anybody who has a insecure personality, you can relate to this. The game encaptures all the thoughts we had at some point.
Evan felt like he is worthless, and sometimes so do I.
For us insecure, anxious people, recognition is everything. We long to be considered important. We desparately try to get ahead, because if we don't we feel like we don't have value. We have all this wonderful vision for our future selves, and then we commit to doing it, and then we inevitably fail due to our innate qualities as animals. And we berate ourselves for being incapable. We compare ourselves to others, the shiny, successful people around us or on the other side of the screen. We see them with the qualities we desire, with the life we crave, with the happiness we lack.
We want to be loved.
My favorite movie is
, a story about an actor who fell from fame and could not ever climb back up.
To me,
is a game about self-esteem and personal value. The protagonist struggled for this in the movie and this game.
I see all these people in the review section downvoting this game for reasons like it isn't fun, it is too pessimistic, it's just whining like a teenager. On one hand I don't like this. Do people today have so little empathy and sympathy that they just don't care about people as such? But on the other hand, I guess it's a good thing that people can't relate to this, because it shows that they are secure, maybe even happy, at least not depressed in the way that Evan is.
Whether or not the developers intended for this to happen, I don't know; but once I got over the residual of the depression brought by the game, I actually felt less burdened and more positive. I came to realize that even though sometimes I think I am messed up, I really am not. I have friends and family who care about me. I have failed but I can start again. I may not be as good as some, but I am better than the vast majority; I only need to be more content with it. I have not lost my passion for life.
If you think what I wrote fits you ok, I recommend give this game a try. It is extremely emotional, but it does have something to offer.
If you don't want to be depressed because of a game, or you don't find anything above relatable, you probably shouldn't play this.

This review is slightly biased as I am a 28 year old Canadian suffering from major depressive disorder.
Being someone who has had severe major depressive disorder all of my life I could relate to bits and peices of what the protagonist of this peice went through. Although, for me personaly our outlooks and how the issue effects us are very different. His struggles are of that in conflict with his life and choices where mine are dealing with the very poor health side of things.
If you are interested in a loose defined late onset depression as apposed to what would probably be classified as early onset depression this game is very interesting. A lot of people seem to be afraid that someone with depression or going through something will do something drastic but in reality it would probably give them something to relate to / might help them process. If not than they are probably already in a level of trouble that the contents of this game wont be the swaying factor. Individuals with depression are usually some of the absolute strongest people I know who are usually geared towards survival. They do not need to be protected they need to be supported.
The game treats the subject matter in an adult way and doesn't shy away from subject matter too much.
Depression, both early and late onset is a very serious subject and needs more light and treatment options available.
So I am glad this exists.  As a game it isn't really anything special,  but as an art peice it stands well enough.
If the subject interests you or you like the psychology it is worth the hour or so to play through it.

The difficulty is fair, and dying isn't frustrating because even if you get a Game Over, you'll still respawn from the last checkpoint, just like a regular death.

Overall this is a great trip down the nostalgia lane, and a must-play for anyone who likes 2D Sonic games.

A MUST HAVE for all Sonic fans new and old. But keep in mind: It's NOT a Sonic clone. This game is a real gem  and there are many reasons why. I'll only cover a few things as to not give away any spoilers.
Gameplay: In short, Freedom Planet is Sonic 1, 2, or 3&K but different by the addition of combat and health as well as enemies needing to actively attack instead of run into you to damage you. The physics is also slightly different to accomodate each character's playstyle.
Controls: The controls change for each of the different characters that you can select. The main controls are meant for a Mega Drive or Genesis controller but can work for any controller with 4+ buttons and just a Keyboard. The controls can be changed in the Options to suit your liking and feel totally responsive. There's even an Analog Stick Sensitivity Option.
Story: To keep from any spoilers I'll only say this: The story is a fairly typical "save the world from aliens" story and has a hard time pacing itself with lighthearted moments intermingling with dark ones. However, if you aren't interested in the story and only want to play the game, then you can select the Classic mode at the beginning to completely eliminate post-stage cutscenes.
Characters: Lilac is the main protagonist and is the most fun to play with. Lilac is the fastest of the characters and has a double-jump, a wide variety of attacks, and a boost that can fire in any direction except for straight up or down.
Carol is Lilac's best friend and is also fun to play with. Carol isn't as fast as Lilac unless she acquires a gas canister to power up her motercycle. Without her motercycle, Carol has a simple attack that can be performed really quickly, a kick attack that makes her invincible, wall-jumping capability, a pounce-dash, a rolling ability, and a power-slash attack. With her motercycle, she gets a boost while on the ground and can run up walls with ease.
Milla is unlocked after completing the second stage in the Story mode. Milla has less health than Carol and Lilac and has no way of gaining great speed. However, to accomadate for this, she has a shield that can block or even deflect certain attacks that also attacks upon releasing the button, a block that takes time to generate, a super-attack achieved by mixing the block with the shield, a flutter-jump, digging ability, and she can also mount certain enemies to control them.
I've heard that two more characters will be added later on as well.

After playing the Blackwell Legacy, I was totally amazed with its storytelling regardless of its somewhat simple graphics. The game certainly took me by surprised and when I saw the next game in this saga, Blackwell Unbound, I didn’t want to play it as I thought it couldn’t live up to its standards. Well I simply caved in and installed the game. Once completed, this one moved me more than the first (Blackwell Legacy) with even better character development. There were also slightly more technical improvements however the puzzle elements were the same; that is wasn’t challenging enough and lack thereof.
Blackwell Unbound takes place in 1973, meaning it served as a prequel to Legacy. The game assumes the player’s knowledge of the main character Joey and introduces a new one, Lauren. Lauren is the aunt for Rosa from Legacy and her demeanour is considerably different as Lauren is more confident in her abilities as a medium. Then again, it didn’t explain at all of how Lauren was introduced to Joey in the first place. Nevertheless it’s a refreshing outlook of Lauren’s more assertive personality considering she is a chain smoker from hell. I guess that’s the 70s for ya.
The gameplay is in the style of a point and click variety – that is you literally just do that, point at a hotspot like an item or person and it will interact. Right click the mouse for the character to analyse and left click to interact. There is some inventory management where only Lauren can access (as after all, Joey is a ghost) and the neat notebook feature is here again. What this feature does, once it gets an update prompt, you can join sentences together to form another. Yet to those who’d played Legacy, there’s a new feature where you get to control both Joey and Lauren individually. This is pretty neat considering some puzzles requires swapping between characters.
Speaking of which, there are only a handful of puzzles to solve yet thankfully, they are all logical so they are no mind-bending at all. For some, this maybe a put-off however the plotline and game’s pacing hits the spot as there’s momentum instead of having a difficult puzzle to bottleneck the tempo. Also the storyline is so well written with realistic problems that’s very welcoming. The general mood is sombre yet well fitted for the plotline.
Thankfully to enhance the sombre mood, the musical scores by Thomas Regin is nothing short but exceptional. All the scores are well suited for this game and has that jazz feel. Not overdone however very welcoming and professionally composed. It’s that good I purchased the soundtrack in iTunes for USD $10. Graphically it is powered by the Adventure Game Studio (AGS), graphic artist Erin Robinson made some alterations, mainly with the characters and done a wonderful job at it. They are all dressed up as if it was the 70s and there’s little to be said about pixel hunting. Yet the opening screen where is shows the Statue of Liberty overlooking the Manhattan skyline at night is lovely to see.
It’s pretty rare that an adventure game sucks me in as well as Unbound did. The game’s length, depending upon your detective skills I guess, could take around the five hours mark. However I really cannot let go of this game until completion as mentioned before, the game’s pacing and storytelling is simply fantastic. Granted there’s a couple of bugs where the written text and spoken words differ and at one occasion, the text is there however the voice is muted however, and thankfully so, didn’t ruin the game. There’s obvious love and care poured into this game and the game’s ending, as much as I did actually panic, feels like I need to perform a standing ovation! A definite must play.

Blackwell Unbound, the second in the Blackwell series by Wadjet Eye Games reverberates some of he more in-depth adventure games that used to be around; Even though it can be a bit short in playtime.
The solid storyline and good voice-acting from the first epidode (The Blackwell Legacy) is continued as we pick up the Blackwell family history with Lauren Blackwell in 1973. The family legacy is a 'spirit guide' in the form of the ever present, but ghostly, Joey.
The scriptwriter(s) get the relationship between Joey and Lauren just right and the fine voice-cast excels in making the most of the dialogues. The game also gets the music just right. Never intrusive, but flowing and sometimes catchy. The atmosphere of seventies New York is is quietly blended in the background to give room to the characters which are key in the game.
This all results in a immersed gameplay experience even though the graphics are retro (similar to most Lucasarts and other adventure titles from the early nineties).
Like in those games, lots of questions and interaction with all the protagonists are required if you want to make headway, and even the most experienced adventurers sometimes will have a hard time making the next step. Because the game is so engrossing this never really irritates. I found myself curious about the next part of the story for almost every part of the game.
A nice feature is the bonus content that can be unlocked which provides for some re-playability (ofcourse this takes the form of "Achievements" if you play under Steam). All in all another solid title from Wadjet Eye.

This is one of the best adventure games I ever played. Very good storyline and game mechanics. It kept me up late at night several times because I just wanted to know how the story ended. The only bad thing I can say about it, is that the story ended after part five. But that is probably a good thing because you do not want to ruin a good story by stretching it thin.
You play this adventure with two main characters: Rosangela Blackwell and Joey Malone. Part two is kind of a prequel in which Rosangela is replaced by her Aunt Lauren Blackwell.
Rosangela and Lauren are mediums and Joey Malone is their spirit guide. Together they help the souls of dead people (ghosts) that are stuck in this world to move on. Doing so they encounter a number of persons/ghosts who play an important role in the story later on.
Joey is a ghost himself so he can reach places that Rosangela cannot, but he cannot wander off too far because he is bound to Rosangela. He also cannot touch anything so he needs Rosangela for this. This poses some interesting situations in which Joey needs to get Rosangela into locked rooms/buildings.
A very interesting game mechanic is that you have to cross-reference pieces of information. By cross-referencing the right information you will learn new things which will help you to further progress into the game. Some information you have to lookup on the internet (in game) and emails play an important role too in this game.
The Blackwell series consists of five separate parts:
1. The Blackwell Legacy
2. Blackwell Unbound
3. Blackwell Convergence
4. Blackwell Deception
5. Blackwell Epiphany
Be sure to play them in that order because it is in fact one big story divided over five parts.

My experience with Blackwell Unbound was completely different than my experience with The Blackwell Legacy, which is both a good thing and a bad thing. Some of the problems I had with the first entry were remedied in Blackwell Unbound, while some of the shining points in the first game were surprisingly absent from this game.
The story premise has really started to interest me. I think it has the same kind of longevity as some template-based TV serials like X-Files or Star Trek. In his commentary track, Dave Gilbert discusses the "lingering ghost" trope and why it's interesting, and he's right--it is interesting. As far as the story goes, I am now "on-board" with the Blackwell games (although the final scene of Blackwell Unbound posed a huge moral problem for me). It was really cool to play as Lauren; she is an interesting character, especially alongside Joey. I wish I could have seen more interaction between them.
The gameplay of Blackwell Unbound differs from its predecessor by allowing the player to switch between playing as Joey and playing as Lauren. I think this is and always has been a cool mechanic. Unfortunately, unlike some other successful adventure games who have used this mechanic, like Maniac Mansion and The Cave, Blackwell Unbound doesn't really make good use of the ability to switch characters. Joey is only necessary for a couple of small actions, and he is otherwise unnecessary. However, Gilbert does explain in the commentary track that Blackwell Unbound was meant to be a short project to tide players over until the more ambitious Blackwell Convergence was finished, so I assume that the character-switching will be put to better use in the next game in the series.
The graphics and voice acting are other pieces of evidence that Blackwell Unbound seems to have been given less thought and attention than the first game (I have not yet played Convergence, so I can't compare). I was really impressed with The Blackwell Legacy's graphics and voice acting; everything looked really painstakingly drawn, and the voice actors gave great performances. Although some of the environments in Blackwell Unbound look really great (Jambalaya Records, Lauren's apartment) some of the environments looked pretty rushed (the map screen, the construction site), and there were a couple times I turned down my speakers because I was embarrassed that someone might hear the terrible voice acting. The problem with the voice acting seems to be that the actors were not very well-matched for the roles they played. Three of the characters (The Countess, Harriet Sherman, and Joseph Mitchell) are 50+ years old but are voiced by young people trying to imitate "old" voices, which makes for some really cringe-worthy moments. Another character, Dwayne, has a pretty embarrassing Jamaican accent and in the credits he appears to be voiced by a white guy. I hate to criticize peoples' acting abilities, especially since I'm certain I'd be absolutely terrible at it, but I feel like the voice performances in Blackwell Unbound really got in the way of my enjoying the game.
The puzzle logic in Blackwell Unbound really irked me, too. Obviously, in a series like Blackwell, the player needs to discover clues to progress. In Blackwell Unbound, there's a really cool mechanic that tasks the player with remembering and manually entering into a phonebook names that other characters mention in dialogue. I love it when games make me pull out a pad of paper and a pencil to solve a puzzle. My problem is that most of the "clues" seem really obvious and unnaturally forced into the dialogue ("That's how we treat your kind at
!"), so it felt like Gilbert left a really obvious trail of breadcrumbs for me to follow.
The commentary track this time features Gilbert alongside one of the game's artists. It is sometimes interesting to hear about the processes they went through in designing the game. Dave Gilbert wasn't as annoying to me as he was in the commentary for The Blackwell Legacy; maybe he's growing on me.
In summary, Blackwell Unbound was a much more interesting game than The Blackwell Legacy, but I think The Blackwell Legacy had a greater level of polish and seemed more like a complete game. I'm excited to play Blackwell Convergence, and I hope it has some decent voice-acting.

One of the best WW2 games I've ever played. CoH2 allows the player to play as 5 different factions: Soviet Union, United States, British Forces, The Wehrmacht Ostheer, and The German Oberkommando West. Each of which has access to a variety of infanty and vehicles, all of which have unique abilities, strenghts, and weaknesses. Heres a rundown of each faction:
Soviet Union: The "starter" faction of the game, Soviet infantry and vehicles are cheap to produce compared to other factions, at the sacrifice of battle preformance. Infantry are inacurate and dont have much heath, tanks have weak armour and mediocre guns. But you can make a sh*t ton of them to swarm the evemy.
United States: Heavily versitile. The United States specializes in infanty. Thier riflemen are acurate have have decent health, the MG squad carries a .50 cal, perfect for shreading infantry and light vehicles. However the vehicles are mediocre at best, not much health or amour, and guns are lacking. Infantry is the United States' specialty.
British Forces: The British are excellent at defending points or a crutial area. The British have access to trenches, mortar emplacements, artillary strikes, anti aircraft emplacements, etc. The tanks are adequate, the churchill is perfect for defending, as it has VERY thick frontal armour, at the cost of speed and a powerful cannon. The British lack on offense, the infantry are lightly armed, and the MGs arn't very powerful.
Wehrmacht Ostheer/Oberkommando West: Both German factions are powerful in all areas. Infantry are highly skilled and efficient in combat. Vehicles are powerful and able to crush the enemy if used correctly. However great power comes at a great price, literally. The german units are expencive compared to other factions. Tanks take up lots of reasorces and are slow to construct. The German forces are incredibly strong late game, but in order for German forces to be effective, it requires a lot of skill from the player. What comes with late game comes more powerful opponents. The Soviets get access to IS-2 heavy tanks, US gets Pershing heavy tanks and swarms of shermans, British get the mighty Churchill and powerful defensive emplacements. German players have to know the strenghts and weaknesses of thier opponents in order to make a difference on the battlefield.
Overall this game is great. I recommend waiting for a sale on the master pack, you can get the game along with all DLC for around $20. 9/10, great game.

This game is a love letter to Sonic fans. It very self-aware in the aspect that they acknowledge the campiness of the series with a wink and a nod. Classic Sonic will mime actions and make bouncing noises as he gleefully jumps around, and (current) Sonic will make comments about déjà vu as he progresses through past stages.

The game moves along quickly, especially the first few stages, but the last few are actually fairly tricky in execution, with a lot of “HAH! Gotcha!” moments with enemies and spikes sprinkled in. That started to annoy me in the later stages – I felt as if I was punished for trying to go fast. I would speed along, find a clear path, and then spikes would suddenly appear out of the wall because they had KNOWN I wouldn’t be able to react fast enough to stop myself from running into them.

The boss battles are non-intuitive, you have to decode hints dropped from a helper character when the encounter begins and hope you’re doing things right. My battle with Shadow lasted almost twenty minutes because I had no idea what I was doing to harm him, and the final battle took a few attempts as well as I tried to discern just what exactly I was supposed to do. Once I figured it out, however, the fight itself was done in less than five minutes.

Voice acting is just fine, but the music and sound effects are wonderfully nostalgic. I would keep hanging around City Escape just to listen to “Escape From the City” one more time.

The game is surprisingly short – I clocked in five hours, and even then that was going long and wasting some time dinking around doing nothing progressive. Still, I felt this was one of the best Sonic games I had played in years.

Ah, Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast. I have fond memories of this game from when it was first released. I was entering my teen years and I remember playing the demo of this game at my local Best Buy. I remember how floored I was at how awesome the gunplay, lightsaber and Force mechanics were. It made me eager to play the full version. While I wasn't able to play the PC version of it, I eventually was able to play it on my old Xbox.
Now, full disclosure, back then, I was quite the cheating little ****. If the game had cheats for it, more often than not, I would use them. I had no interest in being challenged, and I didn't want to lose, ever. So it was the same with this game. Despite my cheating ways, however, I remember having a ton of fun with the game. The lightsaber and Force mechanics were amazing, and it had a great story to go with it.
A decade and a half later, I, now older, wiser, and more willing to challenge myself when it comes to video games, come across it being offered here on Steam, and nostalgically, I decided to purchase it and give it another whirl, without cheats this time. Play it as it was meant to be played.
However, within a couple hours of playing, I found myself coming to a stark, unanimous realization: This game is one
son of a *****, especially the first couple of levels before you get the lightsaber and Force powers and all you have to rely on are blasters to kill enemies who maddeningly never seem to stop moving for long enough for you to get a bead on them, and there are often several of them at a time, and they tend to swarm you and shoot at you from multiple angles. If you get into a huge firefight, you have to constantly be on the move to avoid the hail of gunfire coming at you, while at the same time straining to target your enemies who, like I said, are also moving around constantly. And God help you if there are any officer-type enemies among them, or ones firing rapid shot blasters. You will end up dying quite a lot on these first two levels, I guarantee it. And I was playing on
difficulty! Oh, and also, the checkpoint system in this game is atrocious, so you'd better make sure to manually save your game a lot, or you will find yourself losing a ton of progress when you inevitably die.
Once you get the lightsaber and access to the Force powers, though, the pressure eases up a bit, as you're able to deflect all the annoying blaster fire, and you'll eventually get the Heal Force power to let you regain heath. But you'll still have to watch to make sure enemies are not flanking you from behind when using your lightsaber. And there's the all new challenge of lightsaber duels. There's a whole lot of strategy involved in lightsaber dueling; you will die quickly if you're not careful in engaging your opponent.
Despite the tough difficulty curve, and the admittedly outdated graphics, I still find Jedi Outcast (and its sequel, Jedi Academy, for that matter) a really good game. The lightsaber and Force mechanics in this game still have no equal compared to other Star Wars games, in my opinion. They are just as fun and thrilling to use now as when I first played it. The story is also very good. And hey, you get to play as Kyle Katarn, the legendary bearded badass himself. If you're looking for a great Star Wars game and do not mind a tough challenge, then I heartily recommend you check out Jedi Outcast.

This is the first review I've ever written on Steam! How many "funny" votes do I get?!
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
------- THERE WILL BE NO SPOILERS TO THE PLOT THIS REVIEW -------
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Freedom Planet is a 2D, side-scrolling platformer that wastes no time foraying into the realm of Genesis-style masterpieces.  Did you like Sonic & Knuckles?  Cool.  Did you like Rocket Knight Adventures? Great!  Do you appreciate a game taking those similarities and still adopting a unique identity?
Oh boy buddy-ro, you're in for a treat!
The game starts up with a lovely opening that sheds some light on the story: aliens invade Not-China, kidnap a prince, slay a ruler, and on top of all that, war is being waged between three kingdoms as a result of an energy crisis.  Yeah, it's basically a Sonic-like plot where the villain of the day wants the Master Emerald, but you then add a tiiiiny pinch of convoluted world-building!
Just before starting the first level, you make the decision to take up the role of one of two characters, Lilac and Carol.  The two seem to act as a vigilante duo, bringing justice to where it's needed, and it's through impulsiveness like this that the plot leads us through their stories and how it intertwines with those evil alien guys from earlier.
The STORY is nothing special, I'll be honest.  It's cute and gets the job done.  I was left wanting a little bit more from the story, but at the same time, it doesn't overstay its welcome.  There's a lot of weird implicit storytelling that I think was supposed to happen.  I guess I didn't catch all of it.  Characters move to and from certain locations without explanation or motivation.  Does the world take place on a one-way road?  Nothing important was discussed between?  Who are all these characters?
I'll admit that I've not yet completed the story mode with both characters either, so perhaps more of the questions get answered from seeing the other character's (in my case, Carol's) perspective of events.  That's a Sonic Adventure-ey thing to do, so I wouldn't be surprised if it ends up being that way!
But overall, the story's adequate: it's there if you want it, or you can play the game through "Classic" mode if you just wanna go stage-by-stage.  It's a nice compromise!
Freedom Planet is no slouch when it comes to GAMEPLAY.  It's a well-endowed woman in slow-motion: the assets run and bounce like a dream and it all looks gorgeous as it happens.
...I'll work on that analogy.  It implies that the characters run slow, and they definitely don't! If you're looking for the high-octane action that my comparison to Genesis-era Sonic and Rocket Knight promised, you're on the right track.  The two characters control differently, and yet both play through the same ten levels.  The ways they get around completely change how you're getting through each level, and it's pretty amazing.  A lot of developers don't try to do stuff like that anymore, y'know?
Correction: a lot of developers aren't talented or clever enough to make a level play out unconventionally between two slightly varied characters.  That takes a lot of planning, and I commend the dev team for such fantastic thinking.
Lilac takes Sonic's speediness, Blaze the Cat's spinny...tornado thing, and Sparkster's jet boosters to create a fun, vanilla approach to how the game is played.  Lilac can run and move fast, but has some strategic edges in her melee attacks.  Throw on some invincibility frames from soaring through the air like a rocket and the player will soon start to notice a fun formula, especially in later levels: run fast and hop around during the levels, and coordinate your melee skills and time your rocket beautifully during boss fights.  It's a winning combo, and in the higher difficulties, this is expected to be a mastered concept less than halfway through the game.
Lilac's sidekick, Carol, provides a slightly slower, more exploration-based style of play.  There are many collectibles waiting to be found in this romp, and I assure you Lilac can't collect them all by herself.  With Carol's ability to cling to and climb up walls as well as a speedy motorcycle at her side, she seems to be the character you play as second to go around all the levels and pick up the stuff you couldn't get as Lilac.  Her melee attacks are less varied but much faster, and while she's not as speedy, her ability to cover a lot of ground makes for a fun, fresh take during a second playthrough.
The game looks incredible.  Just when I thought I was getting sick of pixel GRAPHICS, Freedom Planet comes along with some of the most ambitious spritework I've ever seen.  The boss fights and spectacle portrayed by them is notably impressive.  I won't spoil anything, but there's a specific boss you fight where you'll be so awe-struck at what you're fighting you'll barely be able to react.
Character designs are cute and colourful, always reminding me of old 80's cartoons and 90's company mascots; levels are equally dynamic and vibrant...do I really have to say anything?  You see the screenshots and you know it's THAT good!
MUSIC is always a pleasure in this game as well.  A lot of ambient electronic tunes, appropriate boss music, and a main theme you won't get out of your head until weeks after.  Music helps establish how players feel, and a testament to that is something as simple as getting an invincibility powerup in this game and hearing its jingle.  SEGA always nails that with their Sonic games, and I'm happy GalaxyTrail took note of implementing something so subtle yet so drastic.  Oh, and there's a level where you can walk on a keyboard and play an eight-note musical scale.  Man, I just love stuff like that.
The voice talent, while not shining as brightly as the soundtrack or the graphics, still managed to keep my attention.  My only gripe with the cast is not in their own talents, but from a technological standpoint, you could tell it's all done on an amateur scale.  Actors and actresses clearly use different recording equipment, and most importantly, you can blatantly hear the varying acoustics among different speaking roles.
It's too much to expect the developers to have rented out a recording booth and fly in their cast to do their lines, don't think I'm expecting that!  It's the simple matter of, if I were in a developer position, I would've compromised my current choices of voice talent in exchange for audition demos that sounded consistent.  Purely a personal qualm that in no way harms the game!
Have I covered everything?  Nah, probably not.  There's so much more to this game that could be explained, like some extra powerups available to collect, some of the enemies being really annoying, an extra playable character(!), and some other twists and turns in both the story and gameplay itself.  For the skeptics out there, I DID run into a few bugs, glitches, and hiccups in the game here and there.  Note that none of the quirks I confronted hindered my gameplay.  If anything, watching a random enemy wheel itself into the physical geometry of a quarterpipe and continued into the void of neverending wall was pretty funny to sit and watch for a moment.
The game isn't perfect.  Some of the story elements seem questionable, some of the later levels got too lengthy/weirdly cheap and I lost steam, and most important to note is that there's a roller coaster of difficulty to ride with the bosses.  But it's all so, so worth it.  GalaxyTrail nailed to a tee what makes a Sonic game good, how to marry extra mechanics to that existing concept, and how to shape it all into an original adventure that they can call their own.

This game is amazing. It has a wide variety of character, some fairly good pixel art, a stellar sense of humor (at least for my horrible standards), and it's challenging, down right brutal at some points.
STFU's greatest part has to be it's main mechanic, the ability to travel backwards in time. It works as if the multiverse theory is true, that you can have multiple versions of yourself working for a single goal all at once. Say there was a barrier that you needed to destroy in a certain amount of time, but you couldn't break it fast enough in one time. You could get another you to help you destroy it faster, and thus allowing you to continue with the same amount of time left over. It uses this mechanic amazingly and explains it much better than I can.
The game has two levels however, that, at least for me, were not fun what so ever. They both are the jet pack levels from the Jurassic Period and the other from the Medieval Age. The controls are super floaty and is difficult to control. Combine that with cramped corridors and constantly being swarmed by enemies and it's just a mess. Luckily, because of all the lives the game gives you, it's not too bad.
Over all, I'd say if you enjoy strategy and plat-former games, you should get the game.

I felt compelled to write a review on this game because it was an iffy title on my wishlist for quite a while. Eventually, it went on sale and I got it. It was on my wishlist simply because it was a retro style 2d platformer, which I love but to my surprise- it was so much more.
The game starts off with the tutorial. It is a bit overwhelming and I almost quit because I had other games that I wanted to play instead. I decided to get through the first world before quitting. By the time I finished the first boss, I couldn't quit. I knew it was going to be one of those 'Finish in One Sitting Games'.
As a lot of people with my taste realize, if you like 2d platformers... you will download 20 bad/mediocre games before finding that 1 gem. This is one of those elusive gems.
First thing you need to know is that if you watched gameplay footage or the trailers, you cannot truly appreciate what this game is. After you finish a run, you can watch the replay. The replays are (somewhat) boring, just as watching someone else play the game would be. The fun in this game comes from developing a strategy, learning which characters you play best with and then working your way through seemingly impossible scenarios with ease.
This game is extremely fun, extremely satisfying and extremely re-playable. It is clear that a lot of time and work went into developing the engine. It isn't like other time manipulation games, this game truly plays by the rules of time manipulation with no paradox unaccounted for without being an awesome game mechanic.
I don't like time restraints personally but as you will come to find in this game, nothing about it feels rushed. The time restraints are even a positive feature in the game. You can only understand by playing. Long story short, this game is groundbreaking in my opinion and everything is exactly as it should be.
If this game looks even slightly appealing to you, it will exceed all of your expectations if you don't let the tutorial trick you into thinking it's going to be overwhelmingly complicated; because it's not. This game is a masterpiece and when it comes to 2d platformers, there are only a very select few games I will say that about.
In fact, just talking about it made me want to play it again. I'm ending this review to go play it again now.

This follow-up to The Blackwell Legacy actually happens to be a prequel, which does a nice job of explaining where the legacy came from in the first place. Jumping back to 1973, you're placed in the shoes of Rosa Blackwell's "Auntie" Lauren, Joey's previous partner back in the 70s before things went... not so great.
Most of the elements from The Blackwell Legacy return this time around, minus the search engine given the lack of consumer internet access at the time, obviously. Once again, real New York scenery and elements are intertwined with the Blackwell fiction, creating a perfect hybrid that feels like it could have happened were there more ghosts hanging around. Lauren is a nice change of pace from Rosa as well; their personalities differ enough to provide a change of pace, but at the same time, you can see where Rosa gets some of her sass. Also changed this time around is the in-game art style, having been handed off to a different artist this time around. The visual shift is also a nice change, and further cements the differences between Rosa and her aunt. Personally, I think Unbound's representation of the door before the afterlife is my favorite in the entire series.
Despite it being a jump back from the series' start, Blackwell Unbound is still worth playing, both for the context it provides and some of the groundwork it lays later on. Really, there's no reason to avoid playing any of the games in the series, so get to it.

First off, I played some Sonic Adventure (1 and 2), Sonic Heroes and Shadow The Hedgehog and loved all of those (Yes even shadow) when I was little. I thought they were amazing, but I never really played the old ones so I wasn't that much of a Sonic fan. Just recently I got this and played this, and HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥
I thought this was more than anything Just a lot of fan service disguised of a game. And yes, maybe it is, but I have to say this game is AMAZING. I didn't even play the classic Sonic games, so I can't really say the nostalgia applies to me. Even so, the 2D levels, which I was kinda afraid of at first, are extremely fun and work wonderfully with the playstyle. They blend with some 3D sections, which are also great. Controlling Sonic in those feels tighter than in any other Sonic game I played.
Gameplay aside, the presentation in this game is mind blowing, both music wise and visually. The visuals are stunning, everything is moving, changing; it feels great. The music is also really good. The song of City Escape is still on my mind.
And, for the story, well, don't expect one. Is really simple. Is mostly an excuse for remastering levels and having the two Sonics. But it works wonders, so hey, this is not a problem in my book.
Another bad thing I could say, is that the game is short. I played only 3 hours (didn't finish it yet), and you can blaze through the stages. However there are a lot of side missions and stuff to do. Also, I heard that there are mods. So I'm not really worried for that.
Anyway, in conclusion, this game is Just great. There's a lot of Sonic games I didn't play, but I think it'll be hard to top this one. The game is a blast to play, to look at, to hear. Is pretty much perfect for what it is: a celebration for having Sonic around for so long. I have no doubt that if you played other games on the franchise first you will enjoy it A LOT more (City Escape, GOD), but even if you're not a die hard fan, this is probably one of the best Sonic games you can get. So yeah, buy it.

tldr - Don't let the DLCs and Microtransactions turn you away, the game is the gem of the RTS genre. Wait for sales if you want, the price of CoH2 + DLCs is ridiculous.
Seeing all the Negative Reviews here, I felt like I really have to give my own opinion about this.
So yes, there are plenty of Microtransactions, DLCs and stuff and Yes, you can pay a lot of money after buying the base game for getting them all. But the keyword here is the 'can pay' and not 'have to pay'.
You can always see the bad side of the game and write a 5 liner review saying you are being milked, and Sega should extinct and that "it's not what it used to be". You can, and if you wish, don't buy the game, but you are losing a gem here because of some salt over the DLCs.
Those DLCs have been in PLENTY of Sales, you can buy all of the DLCs including the base game for a real tiny price, and not buy it mid-year when the prices are normal. I myself to this day don't have the British DLC, or the Ardennes Assault DLC and I am doing just fine - Those DLCs are NOT pay-to-win, they just offer a different arsenal of factions, playstyles and more. Don't let this decide whether you want or don't want this game.
The Microtransactions in-game are nothing but consmetics and small boosts, which some you can get by a little bit of grind. Let me tell you that - You are not going to be "1337 Hax0r" if you're going to buy all those commanders, boosts and other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, it's RTS, a bad player will still be bad.
I myself played both CoH1 & 2 for a lot of time, the game is a quality RTS which you can't see much following the same formula in today's market. CoH2 had a tough launch, balance issues and more, but now the game is much more absolute, and updates are still being made, even though a lot of time has already passed.
CoH2 is being sold real cheap, and in sales the price is ridiculous - If the RTS is not burning in your bones but you want to try out this game and maybe stay for long, go ahead and wait for sale. But don't give up on this because of the DLCs and stuff.

If you are suffering from depression, this is not a good game to play.
If you wish to understand people with depression, this is not a good game to play.
Depression can be a difficult subject to approach as a topic in media for a variety of reasons. The two main issues that I tend to have issue with is that they tend to retread the same ground we've seen over before or they're overly angsty. Unfortunately Actual Sunlight retreads the same ground while having some of the most angsty material I've read in a product.
We're shown the life of a man filled with extreme self-loathing and hopelessness. He's in a job he hates and his time spent outside of that doesn't fulfil him spending it mostly on drinking and video games. This is a pretty cookie-cutter approach to it and is certainly a setup that is fairly common to the point it feels somewhat snotty, especially when it's such a focus as it is here. However not everything has to be original in concept of course, if it's executed well enough it can still be an extremely interesting piece of media. I have to say Actual Sunlight is a letdown in this aspect too as the game does nothing but beat you over the head with how much the character hates himself when doing anything and while that is obviously an aspect of depression that I can attest to when it's handled in this manner it just comes off as obnoxious and forced, there's no nuance to it and you could get about as much insight into what it's like by simply reading an angsty teens blog and if you're suffering from depression you're unlikely to have any realisation that'll help you cope with it only acting as a reinforcer for that extremely crushing mindset.
If you're going into this game you're not going into it for the gameplay obviously. While I'm personally more in the camp that would rather have games properly used to explore the theme via actual gameplay mechanics I can still enjoy a game that's light on that assuming it's executed well. Unfortunately Actual Sunlight uses its interactivity to have you interact with objects in the rooms which just transitions you into text screens informing you how self-loathing the character is, with no clever use of it being a game until closer to the end. The art is very basic too and not pleasing to look at aside from the little original pieces that popup on occasion which I wish was more frequent.
Due to the games poor writing and lack of point in it being interactive instead of just a blog I can't recommend this title to anyone.

Rating 8/10
Overview: 2D action
The Good:
+ The games primary feature is that you can rewind time if you die and choose a new character while your original character still fights for you in ghost form. You can do this up to 30 times thus creating lots of clones to fight for you. It is a game mechanic that has been used before, primarily in puzzle games so it isn’t a unique concept but one that works really well for an 2d action game. You also have a time limit which adds to the challenge, luckily there are tokens throughout the level that extend the time limit.
+ You start with 3 characters but can unlock more as you play. Each character has its own attack and special ability
+ Awesome boss battles
+ Funny dialogue
+ Each level features a different time period
+ 50 puzzles levels
The Average:
Sometimes it can be very hard to see what is going on when you have a ton of clones fighting and there is gun fire and explosions happening all around you.
The difficulty seems a bit off balanced. While you can play any level in any order you wish, some levels feel a lot harder than others.
Conclusion:
Its hard not to love this game. It has a solid game mechanic that is implemented really well, the variety of characters, funny dialogue and crazy boss battles makes for a fun time.  Your enjoyment of the game will be largely based on how much you enjoy the rewind-time mechanic.
Difficult games usually inspire rage instead of joy, but what we have here is something special. Thanks for making me smile, devs.
