The second Blackwell game, a prequel, builds well on the strengths of the first game - strong story and characters, easy interface and connection of clues through a notebook. You also have a few new gadgets to use, which help make a logical and clever way to move the story on. The relationship between the two leads is just as strong, but Lauren is much more world-weary than Rosa (the female lead in the first game in the series). This suits the darker tone of the stories and serves well to show how living with a spirit guide and dealing with unresolved death could take its toll. I love the Blackwell series.  It's a collection of relatively short, story-rich mystery games.  The voice acting is excellent, and, except for the first game, the ambience is so deliciously noir with a great smooth-jazz soundtrack.  While the actual graphics are, obviously, old-school adventure-game pixelly, the game is still beautiful.
Regarding Blackwell Unbound specifically: I found the female protagonist - Lauren Blackwell - to be a pleasure. A young-yet-jaded, snarky, chain-smoking pleasure.  The relationship between Lauren and Joey is... hard to describe... but it works so well that this may be my favourite of the series.

Blackwell is a great series, and this game is where it really comes into its own. It's got a great 1970s ambience that feels fittingly both tacky and lush, and a smokey jazz soundtrack. These both perfectly compliment the chain-smoking protagonist who just can't bring herself to care about much anymore. The game does a good job of telling its own story, and of adding great background and depth to the Blackwell series.

While Sonic The Hedgehog is now little more than an online joke, Freedom Planet's Lilac and Carol are (or should be) taking the spotlight for retro-esque fast-paced platformer. The game's great in some areas and poor in others, while not being as  memorable as the 8-bit wonder of Shovel Knight or as popular as Five Nights at Freddie's, this is one of those underrated gems that's just a little too overlooked.
Gameplay: 9/10: If you're familiar with classic Sonic The Hedgehog, you'll be fairly familiar with Freedom Planet. A fast-paced platformer with multiple characters to choose from with their own unique talents to add more versatility in the game. The controls themselves are fluent for the most part, only having a minor issue with the ends of jumps (Though this is only really apparent in a level outside of the main game itself). The difficulty itself isn't too bad, though the difficulty spike really ramps up specifically at the Stage 8 midboss, onwards. The bosses are cleverly designed and get rightfully more difficult as the game progresses, requiring you to use different strategies with your character. My only real complaint are the powerups, consisting nothing but shields, shields, and more shields.
Graphics 7/10: The visuals in the game are very appealing, especially for a 16-bitish game, and most of the character designs are great. Not just the characters, but the stages are also designed very well, which is where a majority of my praise comes from, going through temples in one instance only to be traveling through a supermarket filled with baddies the next. Admittedly though, Quite a few instances feel very oriental, which throws me off of the otherworldly experiance. Knowing this is taking place on a whole seperate planet and I can't think that these sentient species decide to have their culture similar to that of Earth's Asian cultures. Call it a nitpick as well, but I can't see an alien culture heavily similar to our own.
Story 5/10:The worst thing about Freedom Planet is the story, voice acting, and character developement... Respectively. While there are a couple good voices and originality put into the story, it's overshadowed by the sub-par voices and Clichés. Your characters don't go too far from being tokens, the main 3 playable characters being a good example (Lilac=levelheaded heroin, Carol=hot-temptered but a softy on the inside, Milla=heavily shy and emotional, opening up to previously mentioned characters). The story itself is passable, and you're free to select "classic" mode to ignore most of it.
As for the voice acting, a majority is tolerable with the exception of Spade, who's... Cringeworthy for having the "edgy emo kid" tone, similar to Shadow the Hedgehog but a little more "amateur-ish". Torgue's doesn't fair well either simply for having little emotion for a vast majority of the game along with a slight scottish accent, subtle to the point where can't really tell if he's got one or not. I can't ignore the voices that aren't bad at all, like the Magister's, Lord Brevon's, and the Dragon Scientist's.

Sound 8/10: The game's soundtrack is great overall, with a few hiccups here and there. While most tracks are great like Relic Maze's, Dragon Valley, Thermal Base and more, there are few duds like half the Dreadnaught themes that I'm not a fan of. The main theme of the game however is one of the best in it, which just amps you up to hear more of what the soundtrack has to offer. By no means is this the sound quality of Shovel Knight, it's still worth a good listen!
The game's flawed, yes, but even if you're not much of a fan of Sonic, you'd probably still like Freedom planet. It's not as fast-paced as Sonic, but that's easily countered by the special traits each character has within their abilities. As for the Sonic fans themselves: If you've wanted some resurrection in the series, Freedom Planet isn't that- It's a reincarnation.

A fun and well-made game, one of the best platformers I've seen in a while. Every aspect of this game is excellent.
Great level design is its best feature. Levels are all huge (when you feel like you should be getting close to the end of the level in a normal game, you're probably near the halfway point), nonlinear and secret-filled. They also all have unique hazards and features you can interact with, from platforms that move when you touch them to slot machines and giant dandelion seeds. Level design virtually never punishes you for going fast in an area that looks like you're meant to go fast except by making you miss items (you'll never barrel into spikes or fire or enemies), which is important with all the inspiration it takes from Sonic.
The soundtrack is also top-notch, and both the bosses and regular enemies are well designed. Each character plays differently with their own attacks and abilities, and there's a few levels you'll only see with one character with extra focus on their abilities. All three characters feel versatile and fun. There's a level select once you've beaten the game, and an option to skip all the story cutscenes (which is a good thing, since the story is the one thing in this game that's not especially good). Difficulty can be adjusted as needed.
To sum up: This game is excellent in every way a game can be excellent, and FUN. Buy it!

I own several of these little pixel based, platforming, dungeon exploring roguelites.   There is something really special though about Catacomb Kids that I can't quite place my finger on.  Not sure if it's the fun physics, superior combat, interesting magic, complex items, tense exploring, or cool soundtrack.  Perhaps just the overall feel of the game pushes CK above and beyond the rest in its class.  Armor and wearable items actually changing the appearance of your pixel character, torch stands falling over and igniting enemies, throwing potions on baddies to learn their effects, and the ability to flavor a dead rat with hot sauce for some extra flavor are just a few prime examples of developer inguinity.  It's these small details and great mechanics that show the love the developer is putting into this game.
CK is a great rougelike cake with plenty of frosting and I'm excited to see how the entire game pans out.  My only warning would be if you are a casual gamers and don't enjoy extremely challenging games you may want to rethink or watch some let's play videos first! Personally I love a challenge and it keeps me highly entertained.
P.S.  Caveblazers, Spelunky, Towerclimb, and Vagante are similar titles you should check out as well if you haven't already done so.   Happy Gaming! :-)

Sonic Generations is a blend of two games. The old school original Genesis 2D platformers that have you speeding through winding labyrinths. The other half has more modern Sonic games that are not only 2D platformers, but 3D platformers and straightaway running in 3D. After completing the first level as old school (classic) Sonic, you're treated to a story cut scene. The game then game opens up to the platforming hub level. The hub level lets you switch between the two versions of Sonic. Levels are full of loops, straightaways, platforms, rails to grind on, tubes to shoot down like Sonic 2's bonus round, spikes, death pits, water, red rings that will launch Sonic and many paths here and there. While Sonic can't swim, he just jumps higher underwater when he used to just move slow in previous games. The levels are throwbacks to previous Sonic games. Consider it a best of collection.
The game consists of three major chapters. Every chapter has 3 zones. Each zone has two levels (acts), the first level is that straight up 2D platformer and the second level is the more modern 3D version. You can tackle them in any order that you like. Once an act is complete, you rescue one of Sonic's many friends. After you complete the 6 levels of each chapter, then challenges become unlocked. Each zone has 5 challenges for each version of Sonic. 3 keys will also appear in each chapter and unlock when you complete one challenge from a zone. Then if you have 3 keys in one chapter, you can use them to unlock the boss for that chapter.
The challenges offer some variety with objectives. For the most part you're just running through the same levels you had to get through to unlock them. There are a few unique levels in the challenges. The challenges range from beat the clock, racing tails in a plane, racing your own doppelganger (ghost), timed drifts, enemies moving at double speed and completing a level with only one ring. Since you rescue Sonic's many friends, there are special levels that make use of them to help Sonic. Amy Rose has a hammer that if you time it correctly you can do a mega jump. Knuckles will dig up medals for levels that you need X number of medals to complete the challenge. Rogue will charm armored enemies so Sonic can defeat them. Every enemy that gets defeated in her level makes hollow blocks into solid ones. It feels like a way to make a 4 hour game into an 8 hour game.
Not only does every chapter have a boss, but there are also mini bosses. Basically you walk up to them in the hub level and challenge them. Once they're defeated, you get yourself a chaos emerald since there are no bonus levels like previous Sonic games. Each boss is original and unique, since Sonic has so many characters, you'll never fight the same one twice. The main bosses are gigantic. To take them down, its not just hitting a boss, but its timing the attacks when bosses are vulnerable and the way you'll need to make them vulnerable.
Since it is like two games in one, there are two sets of controls. The old school sonic that has just a jump button. Who can duck and hit the button to start a spin dash that he'll release when you let go of down. Then there's the modern sonic that has the same controls for the most part. Modern Sonic has a homing attack that will lock onto an enemy, springboard or claw and dart to them in mid air. This helps with traversing the land as its a lot quicker than loading up a spin dash. Sonic can now slide under objects as he runs, but it feels more like a quick time event than anything. There are even level specific controls like wall jumping back and forth. Sonic will even find a way to make him stick to walls and ceilings.
There is also a boost button that will send Sonic instantly dashing. The boost has a meter that decreases over time. To get boost you will need to collect rings. You can also get boost from drifting around corners when you're in a straightaway by holding the L or R when you go into turns. On top of that, you can gain boost by jumping through rainbow rings that will let you do mid air tricks by hitting the left thumbstick. Comparing the two control types feels like old school Sonic is one dimensional. This could be a subtle way of proving which character is better.
The Sonics also have skills that you can use to customize them. Things like stopping on a dime no matter how fast you're going. Getting an extra life when you run out. Not taking fall damage and so on. There are even skills just for classic Sonic and others just for modern Sonic. Each skill you unlock uses points. You have 100 points to assign the skills. So the better the skill, the less others you can assign. There are loadouts too for quick assigning.
As always rings are like Sonic's health. If you have a ring, Sonic can take a hit from an enemy or spikes. That will send the rings spraying from his body. If you don't have a ring when Sonic gets hit, he loses a life. The game's helper even announces it.  The game's helper is a big help, especially with the challenges. The helper will explain everything as you play including how to defeat the bosses. You can of course turn the helper off.
Sonic Generations puts a real emphasis on speed more than the original Genesis games. The boosts, the loops, the bosses chasing you, a semmi truck trying to ram you, competing against doppelgangers. It all goes to prove that Sonic is fast if not parkour with his homing attack. At the end of each level and challenge, you get graded with par times. It almost feels like a racing game disguised as a platformer.
The game is beautiful, but it feels like a beast on my system, causing me to lower resolution. Every blade of grass gets rendered and everything is colorful. The only problem is Sonic is super small on the screen. He gets dwarfed by how gigantic the world is around him and the camera never really being tight up on him. As everything blurs from the speed its easy to lose sight of him in 2D. Because of this, some of the game felt to me like it was playing itself. Even the quick time slides still made Sonic slide when I failed to push a button. Not holding the thubstick still made him move. Some of it gets relegated to timing homing attacks to get over areas. Is that a bad thing? No its visually impressive even if I don't feel like I have complete control.
Another problem in the 3D worlds is no camera control. You're stuck looking at what the game wants you to. While that's not always a bad thing, it can be problematic. Sometimes I lost sight of Sonic or couldn't see a gap between areas sending into death pits. There were plenty of times in 3D terrain I jumped to my death. Often from misjudging where I was or from Sonic's slippery turnarounds. Often times Sonic would stop in mid air to fall to his death even having full momentum into a jump. Using boost to run over water is treacherous. Even in what looks like ankle deep water can send Sonic to his doom if you get clipped by a platform and stopped.
There are plenty of extras to unlock including artwork, music that you can select to replace the current level music. It is a lot of content with 18 levels, skills, 90 challenges. For me it felt like the fun didn't last as long as the challenge. The death pits and water deaths seemed too constant. Even with a few glitches here and there, the game is by no means bad. It is just trying to be everything at once. Playing the classic Sonic feels forced when modern Sonic has so much diversity. I'd rather play one or the other.  To get to a destination, I can drive a car. Then I can flatten the tires and drive for 5 minutes. After that I can fill up the tires again. Then flatten the tires again after 10 minutes and fill up the tires again. I'll still get to my destination, but I'd rather not have flat tires from level to level. I would have appreciated if the game had two halves. If only you could complete a classic half and a modern half, without completing them both at the same time.

This is practically a sonic game that allows you to relive some of the best moments of the sonic franchise.

Old school is where you play as classic sonic and remember the good old days of a simple(...ish) 2D platformer with the occassional jumping and dashing into robots, and going up against the evil nefarious Dr. Robotn--ahem, Eggman.
And new school is practically taking the mechanics of current gen Sonic and playing through a 3D environment, using your boost, rails and homing attacks to get past the zones.
Maybe I'm a little too old school, but I much prefer the classic Sonic if anything. It feels well paced.

I'm not gonna lie, I downloaded this game without almost any expectations for it.
Well, I'm happy to announce that this game surpased my almost non-existing expectations. Just you look at how much I spent playing this game, and you'll understand what I'm saying.
Let's review it for parts, so it's a bit easier both for me and you (or at least I hope so)
As the description of the game already tells you, the main characters are jerks, each one of them. You see that cute boy there? Jerk. See that sexy dude? Jerk. But each one of them has a very unique personality, and that's one of the great things of this game! Each of them is different from the other, and you'll notice that when you date, in the meetings, and the random events, and I find they very funny! Each of the characters have also very unique styles, and you can see that in their clothes.
Well, it's not like it has a super deep story. You're a girl that goes to a boarding school and find yourself in the after school group of people that nobody wants in their group. There are a lot of events (but I have the free version, so I haven't seen them all), where you can have a really good time reading the conversations of the characters. As I said before, I think is really funny and, if you like comedy, you'll enjoy this a lot!
The MC is hilarious! Her hobby seems to be looking at hot dudes and she won't even hide what she does. She's carefree, fun and easy-going, and tends to annoy the main characters a lot, but that's part of her charm. Is good to see she's not your typical innocent and naive MC, I really like her.
The art for the sprites is
good. It's really pleasant to the eyes, and I love that they have so many outfits! I haven't yet seem them all! As of the CGs...I personally was a little disappointed, as I was expecting art like the sprites. I have seen games that have CGs like that and also super good drawn ones, so I waited to see more...but all of them were the same way. It's not all bad, though!
Overall, I really recommend this game! Not only the main characters are unique, but the side characters are really interesting as well and you will want to get every event possible! If you want a good laughs and a good time, this is your game.
I would probably have liked if there were halloween events, St. Valentine events, Christmas events, and something like that. It was weird to see our "always seeking romance" heroine not even mentioning them.
I hope my review can help some of you make a decision!

EPISODE 1 REVIEW
It's quite simple really. If you like Telltale style of gameplay, you will most likely enjoy this. The graphics are just OK and the animation is not going to win any awards. However, the voice acting and music on the other hand are top quality.
The opening of the story is most likely nothing new to many and the overall setting will definitely feel familiar. But if you're like me, the post apocalyptic setting just never gets old (I thoroughly enjoy experiencing one developers vision over another). I do appreciate the way the game tells it's story, which I don't want to spoil for those planning on giving the game a whirl.
The Descendants reflects HEAVY inspiration from the Fallout series and the movie Air (starring Norman Reedus), which is totally not a bad thing for us post apocalyptic junkies.
Of course, the game is episodic, so there's no way to truly tell exactly where this is headed. All I can say is that so far I am absolutely hooked and bought the rest of the episodes immediately after finishing the first one.
The puzzles won't require much thinking as it's really just a matter of finding item "x" or very easily determining a simplistic order of operations. But trust me, you're not playing this for the puzzles or the gameplay. You're playing this for the expertly presented drama and the "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥" moments set in a great looking science fiction environment.
Overall, there's not a whole lot here, but what is here is absolutely worth the asking price. $2.99 for 1 hour seems fair to me.
I'll update this review as I play each episode. I truly hope the game can keep this  level of tension and intrigue in it's story, but only time will tell.

Okay, boss, real talk time!
Its an exceptional game, with exceptional effort put into exceptional gameplay, with an underwhelmingly and almost saddeningly small community that is (despite what too many people say) somewhat xenophobic, however its not hard to blend well even if you're new/bad.
Obvious outstanding Pros:
+Awesome sord-fitan
+Cool, somewhat unique character roster, each having their own moveset
+Community content can be enabled in settings, allowing you to see someone elses workshop weapon! (Honestly best!)
+Legitimately skillful (supposing you dont have higher than 60 ms ping) gameplay revolving around your reaction times, planning, strategy, and ability to think on your fingers.
+Custom servers with unique content enabled change the design of the game, lowgrav makes aircombos (with some ground stances) available midair, creating more intricate and unique ways of play, though lowgrav is dead now.
+Character combos are honestly as depthy as it can get, and unless you're fighting a one trick pony, you will need to adapt and switch into different tactics to win the fight, I garuntee it, boss!
The sad cons, that we should all understand are NOT REALLY THE DEVELOPER'S FAULT
-It sometimes feels like you might be the one and only person who plays this game.
-If you are easily stressed/find yourself mad a lot, this game will make you angry. You will lose a lot, it is to be expected.
-Weapon types are somewhat lacking, and should change more than just damage values, interval rates, and such. I always feel as though the katana is useless, scimitar is hyper situational, Jian is for pure, and only longsword/rapier work out in the end for stable gameplay. If you're like me and you fashion souls, you wont worry, and will just have a beautiful tool swinging at those nasty little runts!
-Perhaps a hidden ranking system, or the ability to not show your rank on some servers. Its jarring when you're oak/iron, and all you see is masters, because you dont want to lose, its a possible reason why our community is so small.
-Community is TINY. Even on our recent peaks, we will only see around 100 people at most on servers, whereas mostly its 20-10, its that bad. However, whoever is there is strangely always someone different.
-Any lag whatsoever kills the fidelity of the game, on either end. No matter which side is lagging, you're going to lose, because for some reason, this game cannot handle even the minutest change in ping, you will notice that your parries are useless, your gaurd always broken, your back always being stabbed, ranged always hitting, lights parrying balanced, and worst of all, they will almost always disappear when you swing. Its bad, its so bad, but its source, and thats source's horrid issue, best you can do is hope to lead where they're going and always use light/air to keep quick.
Some nitpicky issues now.
-Characters are all asian, its the game's design style, but its just edgy and silly, boss.
-(Weapon) feels weak unless used on (character), every type, every character.
-Weapons should be better diversified, and the ability to possibly use a customized, point based weapon type with the only change being a skin might actually seem better than the current system. For example...
---
Lets say, you just want to make a sword thats good for comboing. You have around 100 points to spam into various attributes, those attributes could be divided into some divisions like
Base damage
Side damage
Air damage
Combo interval
Combo speed
Can guard/(whatever rapier's gaurd is)/Feint/no gaurd (for increased points or easier charge)
Charge speed/damage mods
While veterans of the community are K with what we have, this change would bring more uniquity to the gameplay as less cut and paste styles would be present. We're looking at you, JianPure/ScimitarPhalanx.

It might even be a rad idea, to do something like this with characters, mixing and matching combo patterns to weave your own intricate web of butt-touchingly awesome combos that will make everyone on the server mad!

Overall, its a great game, boss! But it has its flaws, and they can get a little jarring if you're not very prepared to face them. I think if more people played it, more love would be seen all around, while I would prefer to see the game change drastically, most people don't and are comfortable with what we have, but I feel that appropriate changes would see a more unique crowd enter to join in on our fun.

Honestly? The game is awesome. The community is great, the gameplay is fun, and the characters are diverse.
The problems?
There is a huge lack of players in Blade. New players are always welcomed, but they wont have an easy time. If you're new and trying to get into the game, you will be destroyed over and over, for hours on end, until you eventually start to get good enough to compete with the community that's left in the game.
There are five different classes in the game to choose from:
The Judge
The Phalanx
The Ryoku
The Pure
The Vanguard
Each of them have their own pros and cons, and learning how to play your selected class will take a lot of time. There are a multitude of sword types in the game and they all offer their own benefits, so learning which one is best for you is key when working on your class.
The game works off of a ranking system:
Oak
Iron
Steel
Diamond
Master
You get promoted through the leagues by beating opponents of your league. This isn't a great ranking system, as you could be an oak leaguer who consistently beats masters, yet gains no elo points so you dont progress; you would need to wait until an oak leaguer faces you and then defeat him to advance for instance.
The game will test your ability in every fight. You will have masters who have over a thousand hours and they will beat you over and over, but you'll take a lesson in each fight and those lessons will eventually shape how you play the game.
If you're willing to put in enough time to learn how to compete against the majority of the players who are still on Blade, then this game is very rewarding and very fun. There are a lot of players who are interested in teaching newcomers, and the community in general is very nice and are a lot of fun. However, if you don't want to lose over and over again whilst you learn the game, then this game isnt for you.
I give this game a solid 8/10. There are issues with the gameplay such as dodgy tracers sometimes and ping can play a large part in the combat, but the game has an amazing community and the game itself is a lot of fun if you invest enough time into it. I reccomend bringing in a friend with you if you want to buy the game to not be completely alone whilst you learn.

+ Relaxing, contemplative soundtrack; it's the kind of soft music that helps one to focus
+ Each selectable character has a different play-style that can be accentuated with the right weapons and use of fighting stances
+ Can chain various stances together for combos during combat; can be quite fluid and practiced after enough time in the ring
+ Dueling servers make for very focused, civil engagements between players; there is an overall atmosphere of respect surrounding the player-base
+ Heavily skill-dependent; gameplay is generally very well balanced and, save for practice and dedication, there is little that another player can do to hold a significant advantage over others
+ Exceptionally friendly and inviting in-game community
+ Very mod-friendly; this feature can actually supplement the act of unlocking in-game weapons and appearances
+ Character emotes (such as bowing) help to keep duels expressive; these are gratuitously used to show respect to other players, and this keeps the experiences generally positive
+ Combat mechanics feel solid and are well-implemented
+ Plenty of aesthetically pleasing unlockables available
+ No microtransactions
+ Crisp, minimalist UI
+ Throwing items, feints, and grab mechanics do well to keep gameplay feeling fresh
+ Game heavily rewards strategy, timing, and finesse
+ Interesting environmental designs and character models
- Some animation sets are stiff and awkward
- Moderately small active player base (only 2-3 active servers during the making of this review)
- Fairly steep (though rewarding) learning curve; while I don't necessarily consider this a bad thing, I recognize that it may be enough to turn away more casual players

I received a coupon for this game, after reading the description I decided to buy it and play it for one of those days. The story was short and felt linear, but it did touch on difficult subjects. It started off with humor and relatable concepts, that began subtle then revealed for what it was towards the end. The majority of it is reading transcripts of what the protagonist has done with some interaction with his coworkers and people in his life. The protagonist's relationship with his coworkers, how they view themselves and how he views himself through them were a central focus to the narrative.
It was described to be profound, a deep narrative on the troubles of depression. While it did provide the struggles, the things we often tell ourselves "I'll start tomorrow", it was one person's experience. An experience to say, don't let it consume you because by the time you realize it was not worth troubling yourself over, it will be too late. There are more concepts I wish this story did deal with rather than forward time and let it be another day, which is still a concept of itself to how life will seem to move even if you don't.
I recommend this for the messages it has, there is a lot to pull out directly and subjectively with the most important one I believe: if you're still young then don't act like your life is over otherwise your choices will make sure of it.

It wasn't until I noticed I needed to clock more time in this game to unlock all the available cards that I realized how much I hated playing this game.  The main character was both unbelievably boring and unimaginably irritating and I didn't want to spend more time with him.  And that's what makes this game so good, and why you should play it.
It isn't meant to be fun, or happy.  It isn't meant to leave you with a sense of accomplishment.  This is a game that gives you a virtual experience of what depression can be for some people.   This game is hard to play, and I don't mean in a Dark Souls way, I mean in an emotionally draining, exhausting way.
I'd suggest, if/when you play this game, to consider how the game makes you feel.  The anger and frustration with the character is completely valid.  The boredom is completely valid.  Now imagine that instead of those feelings being directed at a game, it's directed at your life.  That infuriating character with the dialog that drives you crazy is your own internal dialog.  Yep, you absolutely know better than to do the stupid things he keeps doing. Yup, you can see how things are going to unfold from the moment you start playing,and eventually you're rushing though everything just to finish the damn game with the obvious ending. Yup, everything would be better if he would just stop whining for a moment.  But he won't.  Welcome to what depression is for some people.
What makes this game so good isn't the gameplay.  It's how much it makes you dislike it that makes it good.  If you have never experienced severe depression, this might give you an idea so you can understand what a friend/family member is experiencing.  If you have experienced it, consider this a window into someone else's experience, so you can see how things are similar and completely different all at the same time.  But most of all, please don't play this game if you aren't safe right now...take care of yourself.  Come back to this when you're in a good place - depression isn't easy at the best of times, and double dipping the depression can't be a good thing.

I don't think this game deserves a negative review, but neither do I think it deserves a positive one. I chose to give Actual Sunlight a "thumbs-up" because it's well made, not because I had a good experience playing it. At any rate, I think it's best to look at what I will say below as a warning or observation rather than a review.
First of all, this isn't really a game. It's a narrative experience centered on Evan Winter, a man who thinks he's worthless. The only things to do in Actual Sunlight are examine objects and talk to NPCs. The only choice you have is in which order to do them. Each interaction you perform presents a written vignette that will gradually lead you deeper into Evan Winter's troubled life. Through talking to a limited cast of characters and examining Evan's home and work environments, you will learn about how his life has gone stagnant and gain insight into exactly what Evan thinks of himself, his culture, and his circumstances. These vignettes are sometimes humorous (in a cynical way) or sad, but they always seek to illustrate the profound loneliness of Evan. It took me about an hour and a half from start to finish.
The writing is good. That, almost exclusively, is what will carry you through the experience. But when you finish reading the last sentence of Actual Sunlight, you're not going to be smiling. You might not even feel the satisfaction of having read a well-told story... even though the writing does deserve praise. Here's the catch: if you suffer from depression or social anxiety, like I do, reading through Actual Sunlight can be triggering. If you play this game, you are going to stand in the shoes of a man who has no hope and thus no future. If you think (mistakenly) that you are even remotely in the same situation, then please consider firing up some zombie-killing simulator instead. It'll make you feel better than following Evan Winter around.
Actual Sunlight is unrelentingly, brutally harsh and dark. There is no redemption to be found here and certainly no happy ending. This game seeks to embrace the old idiom: "sometimes the light at the end of the tunnel is a train." It's like witnessing a horrendous car wreck and trying to make sense of it. Can you? Is there any meaning or purpose in something like this? Why did I play this game? I appreciated the quality of most of the writing, but I certainly didn't have fun. In fact, I feel pretty bummed out.
So there. There's your warning, and I got something off my chest. Now where's that shortcut for Plants vs. Zombies? <click-click>

Blackwell Unbound, the second game of the five part Blackwell series is a minor masterpiece in adventure gaming.
I just played the first game, Blackwell Legacy, yesterday.  Having known very little about the series going in, I have to say I enjoyed it, while not being particularly overwhelmed by it.  Before tackling this second game, I did a little bit of reading on it.  The general gist I got was that most people felt this second game was inferior to the first, and that it might be a little to short or too slight in content.
I could not disagree more.  Whereas the first game was a nice enjoyable story, I found this second one leaps and bounds superior.  I did not find it too short (and really, what does "too short" mean when you're only paying a few bucks for a game?).  And the ending was pretty darn clever from a plot standpoint.  Unlike the first game, there is a consistent tone to Unbound, helped tremendously by the excellent jazz-tinged music score.  Unbound takes place in the span of one night--and the everpresent night scenes coupled with the themes of loss and regret gives Unbound a wonderful sense of poetry, of sadness.  And considering that this is a low-resolution game in the graphical spirit of early LucasArts games, it's somewhat miraculous that such a tone could be achieved.
Another criticism I've come across (and also disagree with) is that the game doesn't "help you" enough in terms of the notebook feature.  Some people have gone really overboard and called the notebook "broken."  The complaint seems to center around the idea that you as a player in real life shouldn't have to make any logical deductions on your own, but rather have the game itself spell it all out for you in Lauren's notebook.  It's ironic.  On the one hand people complain that the game is too short, on the other, they don't seem to want to take the time to ponder puzzles or be stuck on them.  I think in this modern age some people don't remember that adventure games traditionally had "being stuck on a puzzle" time factored INTO their play time.  So when you'd read descriptions of old King's Quest games and they claim to have 30 hours of game time, that's assuming the players don't just read from a walkthrough like some digital version of paint by numbers.  You're kind of supposed to have to think over things and figure things out in adventure games.
Besides, it's all rather moot.  I mostly found it pretty self-evident when the game wanted you to write down specific names that came up and look them up on your own.  The one (rather clever) puzzle, that I indeed was stuck on for a time, had to do with making observations about a photograph in Lauren's inventory.  I think some people honestly wanted the game to make this observation for the player and spell it out in Lauren's notebook without any intuitive thinking required..  But frankly, if the game had done such things, it would've robbed the player of so much of the point of experiences like this.
In Unbound there is a different protagonist than the rest of the Blackwell games.  And that proves to be a double-edged sword in a way, as I actually liked this character (Lauren) better than Rosa, the other lead.  I will say that it does make for some mixed feelings regarding Lauren given that she--SPOILER ALERT--apparently spends the last 25 years of her life a miserable vegetable in a mental hospital.  (That's what we learned about her in the first game.)  So the bittersweet ending of this has that extra edge to it.
I'm curious if the subsequent games ever bring some kind of satisfying resolution--impossible as it may seem--to Lauren's fate.
So to sum up:  Blackwell Unbound is a great throwback to point and click, low-resolution, plot-centric adventure gaming.  And frankly, given the strength of its writing and the richness of tone (again, gotta love that jazz), in many ways it's better than a lot of the games that came from the so-called "golden" era.  If you are a lover of adventure games, then you really need to check this series out.  These games are selling for a song these days, so there's no excuse not to reward the developers for their talent and hard work.

Honestly, this is one of the greatest games I've ever played. I could give many reasons why this game is so great. For one, the visuals in the levels are fantastic. Additionally, there's a great variety of levels, with each being different from the last. The character designs are incredible, and the sprites are VERY well done.
Every character in this game plays differently, so there's no copy-pasta when it comes to the characters. Lilac is fast, generally ideal for speedruns. Carol is more combat oriented, and has this amazing gravity defying motorcycle she can use to go faster. Milla can use a shield which can deflect projectiles, and she can also fly. With three characters to play as, each with her own set of levels, there's plenty of replay value. Also, there are achievements, which add even more replay value.
The levels are well done, the distribution of enemies, health, crystal shards, and other gimmicks is reasonable. Sometimes, there will be areas that are more difficult than others to get through, but what fun is a game if there's no challenges to overcome? The bosses are great as well. They can be a challenge, especially when first playing through the game, but if you keep fighting the bosses, it can become easier to defeat them.
Overall, I think this is a fun fast-paced platformer, with a fair difficulty, great visual design, plenty of replay value, and a great soundtrack too. If you like fast-paced platformers (like Sonic), I recommend this game. Or if you have any concerns or doubts that it's for you, at least check out the demo. The demo will give you a good idea of what the game is like.

So, when first buying this game I thought it would be your standard rogue-like game. It turns out that this game is so much more. Usually games of this genre are extremely frustrating and give little user-satisfaction. I love the fact that with every play through you learn something new which eliminates that feeling of "why am I still playing this game?" you know that feeling if your a fan of the genre, these mechanics and little details have you constantly think "omg the developer thought of that?!?". This is a game where the learning curve is extremely steep and will have you stuck. At the moment there are 3 classes and 5 weapon types, also your character's stats and equipment are randomly generated each time. Combat is amazing for a rogue-like and the AI is very well designed, as your enemies will dodge/roll and strike you making their fighting pattern very hard to read, this enables a very fluid style of playing where you have to roll with the punches and not get too complacent when it comes to battling enemies. This game is still in Alpha and I hope that this game gets 100% polished off asap as games of this genre have a very short shelf life.
If the developer is reading this comment I would like to say you have done a spectacular job at creating such a refreshing spin on the genre. Local Co-op makes this game one of my favourite of all time, however I WOULD LOVE TO SEE 4 PLAYER LOCAL CO-OP.
If you are reading this, do you have any plans in expanding local co-op to 4 player in the future?
I understand it would be tricky as things would be hard to follow with 4 players bouncing around, but due to the pace you are able to play this game at (because of all the booby traps) it would work fantastically with 4 players who knew what they were doing. Also it could add another component to gameplay as a group of friends would plan team compositions. This 4 player local co-op could even be split via LAN with 2 players on each computer.
Still haven't managed to "git good" yet... :/

It's like a platforming action game, but with roguelike elements. Death is the end of your run, putting you back at the beginning with a brand-new character. It's really hard- enemies are tough and deadly, and the traps are even deadlier.
However, the name of the game is taking advantage of your environment. For example, if a pond full of piranhas is in your way, there's a couple solutions- you could find a pair of boots that lets you walk on water, you could swim really fast and hope you get to the other side, you could kick an orc in there and let him fight the fish for you... or if you found a way to heat up a boulder, you could boil the fish alive and get a tasty meal.
You'll die a lot in the early levels before you figure out how things work, but that's just part of the game. Every death is another lesson, which you can use in your next run.

XOXO Droplets (XOD) is a fun visual novel with unique personality.  Though it has a few small areas to improve on, XOXO Droplets gives massive value for its cost (including the retail dlc for the extra routes), and is a game almost any otome game player would enjoy.  With the low, low starting price of free, there's really no reason to not give XOXO Droplets a shot.  Just be prepared to lose the next 10+ hours of your free time to this game!
XOD is a stat-builder type visual novel, where the player must maintain a certain level of reputation with different cliques while building affection with their love interest of choices.  I found the stat building system somewhat difficult to juggle the one route I played with the stat building.  It was a constant struggle to keep the cliques happy with me and actually having time to go on dates with my chosen love interest. Furthermore, it's pretty difficult to unlock all the date locations this way.  I suspect that to reasonably be able to see all of the love interest's content you'd need to play their route multiple times this way.  Overall, the stat-building aspect of the game is pretty standard for the genre.
The developers have helpfully pinned a post with cheat codes that let the players decide whether to skip the stat building aspect of the game or not.  So, if you dislike stat-building VNs as I do, worry not: use of these cheat codes mostly negate the need to stat-build for the main love interests.  I ended up doing this for the other routes and was much happier.
I have 22 hours of game time in this game.  This is, for the most part, real game play time and not idle time.  I am a fast reader, but here's what I accomplished in those 22 hours:
- All 6 main love interest routes (friendship and boyfriend endings)
-- 1 route without any cheat codes / pure stat-building
-- All other routes with the use of cheat codes to skip the stat-building
- All 2 side boyfriend routes
- All friendship routes
As you can see, there's a lot of content here.  Your time with the game would likely be double or triple mine if you choose to complete more routes without the use of cheat codes.
The game's writing is top notch and is some of the most fun I've had with a visual novel in quite some time.  I have to admit that the you-are-a-jerk-dating-jerks approach is not prevalent in the genre and is really refreshing, especially when pulled off this well.  Before playing the game, I was worried that the main character (MC) and love interests (LI) would be so much towards the jerk end of the spectrum that I would find them unlikable and that would ruin the game for me.  And I think a game like this could have easily crossed the line into that, but the great writing keeps everything charming, entertaining, and engaging.
Pros:
* Dialogue in the game is almost universally brilliant, with just the right amount of humor.
* All love interests are lovable and likeable in their own ways.  This may be a game about romancing jerks, but unlike many other visual novels, the love interests don't focus on being jerks to the main character.
* Relationship building feels, for the most part, natural and smooth, and are built up over a number of in-game years, which gives each relationship weight.
* Diverse cast
* Strong main character with a definitive personality
Cons:
* If you are looking for a bunch of romantic gestures and love confessions, this isn't the game for you.
* QA of this game missed some bugs (mostly missing expressions) and many typos.  The dev team have promised to try to fix these, so this point may be moot in a few weeks.  However, right now, if you find your immersion broken by typos (like me) you may want to wait as there are still quite a few.
* This may be a minor nitpick, but I found that I would have liked to see more commas in the writing.  It's pretty hcommon to have dialogue that takes up most of the text box with hardly any commas.  If you read that dialogue as I do, it becomes somewhat exhausting to read that without a mental "break" that a comma represents in the dialogue.
[Art]
The faces on the sprites are really good.  There's a lot of subtle expression work done with them that ties in really nicely to the dialogue and allows the game developers to express a broad range of emotion as well as slight shifts for different characters.  There's also quite a few (5+) outfits for each character, which gives a nice visual break to the player.  The proportion of some of the sprite bodies can be a little strange (such as Shiloh's), but it's pretty minor and mostly just noticeable when you hide the UI.
All the CGs have the characters in chibi form.  The CGs are pretty cute and the artist does a good job of expressing interactions between the characters in them.  That said, this came as a slight surprise to me and I do wish we also had fullbody CGs in this game.
[UI]
The UI is pretty standard for what you'd expect from Ren'py games.  Happily, there is an outfit and CG gallery for each character, and there are separate options to skip different types of events that are helpful for completionist players.  On the other hand, there are a few missed opportunities where the devs cou ld have added some quality-of-life improvements to help the player:
- Event gallery / replay
-- This would especially help completionists make sure they've seen all content
- Put your current boyfriend on the top of all UI lists in the game to make them easier to access (Cala's menu, daily events, phone UIs, etc.)
-- Scrolling down takes up a lot of time when you are on the route of one of the latter 3 boyfriends
- When presenting options for daily events, show stat effects on the main UI rather than in a popup that the user has to click away from because they accidentally chose the wrong option.
-- It is pretty difficult to remember which person is in which clique, especially in the first couple playthroughs.
Overall, most of the areas of improvement I've listed here are minor and are heavily outweighed by the sheer force of charisma this game brings to the table.

I started playing the free version of this game out of morbid curiosity. I ended up loving it so much that I paid for the full version while I was still only partly finished with my first playthrough.
The things that first attracted me to this game: the amusing trailer and good-looking character designs. The trailer was a bit of a lie, though - the characters turned out to not be nearly as terrible as I was expecting. Yes, they each had their own issues and quirks, but they were all more annoying and/or frustrating than truly terrible. That said, it’d take a thick skin and a good deal of patience to put up with most of them for more than for a few minutes. Thankfully, the heroine seemed to be completely invulnerable to insults and found their quirks more entertaining than anything.
The heroine was part of what made this game so enjoyable. Yes, she was shallow, but her shallowness allowed her to deal with the guys without taking anything they said or did personally, and she could give as good as she got when she had to. Also, just like the guys weren’t as terrible as they made themselves out to be, she wasn’t quite as shallow as she seemed, or she probably wouldn’t have been as interested in getting to know everybody. She was just…more likely to want to get to know the good-looking guys.
I highly recommend trying the free version of the game if you’re not sure whether the full version is for you. There are some areas of the game where things are noticeably locked down (limits on who you can text and date, no way to buy stuff in the accessories store, etc.), but you can still do a full playthrough with Nate, Everett, or Shiloh, give the Reputation system a shot, go on dates, make use of a few cheat codes, etc. There was enough there for me to decide that 1) I was actually intrigued by these “terrible” guys and 2) I could put up with the Reputation system.
I normally prefer less complicated dating sims and visual novels: “choose your own adventure” style rather than stat-building games. I was very concerned about the Reputation system, at first, and the game’s tutorial section was so lengthy and complicated-sounding that it almost scared me off. Once I started playing, I found the Reputation system easier to manage than I expected, but I later learned that there were aspects I’d completely missed.
That’s where the cheat codes come in. For the first few hours of my first playthrough, I was determined not to use any cheat codes. But then I started to have fun during the various dates with Nate (the guy I opted to focus on), looked into why a few date locations hadn’t unlocked, and realized that there were a whole bunch of dates I likely wouldn’t manage to go on if I kept on playing the way I had been. I also realized that the main character and Nate weren’t actually a couple yet. Whoops. (I totally missed the icon on the “dates” screen that you have to click to officially start dating someone.)
So I broke down and used a couple of the cheat codes. I wish more stat-building visual novels and dating sims included this feature. It gives people the option to focus on what they’re most interested in - folks who want more game-like features can worry about the stats, while folks who are just interested in the story can focus on that. Suddenly I went from constantly checking Reputation stats to just relaxing and enjoying getting to know Nate and various other characters.
So far I’ve finished one full playthrough with Nate and a partial one with Nate to track down some of the things I missed during my first playthrough. I haven’t decided which character I’ll focus on next, but I’m sure I’ll continue to enjoy myself.
Pros:
+ Gorgeous sprites and background artwork, and cute CG artwork.
+ Lots of features (cheat codes, "skip read text," special candies that make the weekdays go by faster) designed to make things easier on folks who are more interested in the characters and dates than they are in the more game-like Reputation system. These features also make future playthroughs easier.
+ Appealingly thick-skinned heroine.
+ The guys are surprisingly intriguing/appealing, despite their more annoying personality aspects.
+ Quite a few interesting minor dateable/friendable guys, and several interesting friendable characters.
+ The teenage heroine cannot date any of the game's adult guys, no matter how much she flirts with them. YAY for the lack of grossness. (I was a little worried after the first scene with Lynn.)
+ There are some incredibly cute moments during the dates and group meetings. I was not expecting this game to be nearly as sweet and cute as it turned out to be.
+ It's overall just light and fluffy fun, with occasional humor. Dating and flirting are treated as fun activities, rather than super important things that will for sure lead to marriage and other life-changing events. Date a guy all the way through to graduation and things will end well, or dump him and graduate without a boyfriend and things still end well.
Cons:
- Fully understanding and working with the Reputation system is difficult. Thank goodness for cheat codes.
- Could have used a little more proofreading - the first few hours were pretty error-free, but I noticed more and more typos, missing words, and incorrectly used words as time went on.
- Several of the icons weren't self-explanatory. When I first started playing I kept thinking that the wallet was what I needed to click on to go to work, rather than the piggy bank. Also, it took hours of gameplay time for me 1) to realize that I wasn't officially dating Nate and 2) to notice the "ask him to be your boyfriend" icon.
- A greater variety of mini-games in the arcade would have been nice. The one game that was available wasn't really all that much fun.
And that's pretty much it for cons because, honestly, I had more things I loved than things I didn't. If the cheat codes didn't exist, I might feel differently (all those date locations I'd never manage to unlock, and all that effort required to earn enough affection points to go on all those dates, ugh). However, they do and they're extremely helpful.

This game is bloody brilliant.
A few words of explanation first: I backed "XOXO Droplets" on Kickstarter, because it reminded me about "Heartstring Bugs"- free, extremely lengthy dating sim, with outdated art and rather silly, light-hearted story, but with  lovable jerks and so much freedom that no other dating simulator ever offered me. With promise of random events, befriending characters and even breaking up, it looked very similar so it immediately got me interested.
It turned out, it's not really that similar, which is fine. "XOXO Droplets" is a great game on its own and even though it does not offer you as much freedom as I hoped, it's one of my favorite games in dating sim/otome genre.
I love the protagonist, she's amazing. I love every single one of dateable guys (including two side options) and most of friends options. Characters are great, realistic, different, hilarious and pretty twisted, in their own way. Each one of main guys annoyed me at some point, but I still adore them and I enjoy how well this game portraits people with certain... issues. I'm talking especially about Shiloh here. I don't think I've ever seen character like that in otome game. I expected something cliche, some sudden change or something like that, so the ending was very nice surprise. Humor is the strongest point of this game. Some scenes are a bit over-talked for my taste, but besides that, most of them let you learn something new about characters. I loved special events (I wish there were more of those, like Halloween parties, Valentines or more school trips), work event and random events, especially with characters that hated each other.
There are few things I wasn't fond of, but those are minor offenders. First of all - censored swear-words. I would get it, if there were few during entire game, that were "fitting" the situation, because then I would assume, creators didn't feel comfortable with language like that. But there are so many of them and it just looks weird, especially with words like "prick" (even Steam doesn't censor that!). I just don't get what the point is and as non-native English speaker, it threw me out of reading rhythm more than few times, since I needed to stop and think about what characters are trying to say. If swearing is such a big deal, you can just skip it completely, it wouldn't made any of this characters any less of a jerk.
Also, I disliked gameplay mechanics. I usually like mini-games and stat raising, so keeping track of popularity levels with cliques seemed like a decent idea. It isn't terrible. A little too boring and not rewarding enough for my taste, but still, I could live with that, but I just HATE raising affection with members of cliques. I know it's not a necessity, but it kind of flows well with the game narrative (since protagonist tries to be on good terms with people, or at least, better terms than so far) and it's disappointing to see that it's much less difficult to befriend the biggest jerks in school than just some regular folks. Also, I really freaking hate the situation where you "buy" friendships with gifts, so that mechanic only made things worst. If sitting with certain people and interacting with them (maybe not by random, but by giving player a choice?) would give bigger affections boost, it would worked better, but right now this whole mechanic is an unreasonable chore (not to mention, I don't think it quite work well). Also, because you need to constantly raise affinity with character you want to date, there are pretty long periods of time when you two don't see each other and that also feels weird. It makes forming of relationship very weirdly paced. I'm not a fan of "buying" date scenarios with affection points. Because of all that, the game is the best with cheats, which is kind of sad, because I really had high hopes for this mechanic.
To sum it up: Very unique game with great protagonist, cast of lovable jerks and clever humor, crippled a bit by dull and repetitive gameplay mechanics.

A lot of people are reviewing episode 1 and mentioning Fallout and TellTale games and I think that is a fair assessment. I, personally get strong vibes of Stanley Kubricks 2001: A Space Odyssey. It also reminds me of Zero Escape, a puzzle visual novel on 3DS and Vita. Anyways, on to the review.
Episode 1 is relatively short and introductory, it took me 50-55 minutes to complete, I felt I was relatively observant, I looked around each room, examined everything I thought I could before progressing so expect about that playtime for you, give or take 10 minutes.
You play as two characters, one from the past who is tasked with making sure that the survivors who were cryogenically frozen are all okay. These people are called janitors, they themselves get frozen as well and only wake up if there are issues. The other character you play is in the present, their job is to wake up all these sleeping survivors who for reasons unbeknownst to them, haven't woken up yet despite the surface being safe to live in again.
The controls are super easy, you click on where you want to move to and what you want to interact with. The only keyboard control I remember inputting was the 'E' button for certain basic QTE's. There are some relative basic puzzles featured but nothing that will have you scratching your head or maybe I've just been playing The Witness too much! Also at certain points you can choose what your character has to say, I'm not entirely sure how much influence these have on your playthrough yet but you see the typical "character x will remember that" text during certain decisions so I'm assuming we'll see the outcomes as we progress into later episodes. If you enjoy the gameplay approach of the TellTale games and Life is Strange then you'll also enjoy the game very much.
The story for me is where it shines, alongside the atmosphere. Even though it's very much an introduction, there are very subtle hints as to what is going on. For the first episode, it does all the right things, presents you with loads of questions as to what is going wrong and leaves you wanting for more. It's hard for me to talk too much about story without giving spoilers, especially as the first episode is relatively short, so I'll just say if you're familiar with and enjoyed the premise of  2001: A Space Odyssey, Fallout or Zero Escape then the story of this game will interest you.
If I were to criticise it for anything, I guess it would be the length of the first episode. It is a tad short, I'm hoping future episodes will be a bit longer. I think there were a few minor camera angle issues as well, but nothing that negatively affected the experience.
All in all, I'd recommend giving the game a try at the current price. It's hard to say how much your decisions influence the game at this point, but if the 'premise' at least has you interested. I find it very hard to believe after playing episode 1 you won't want to, no, need to play more. I hope these episodes arrive rather quickly!

Pretty fun!  I say 'pretty' fun because it seems this game was made to compare Old Sonic to New Sonic- glorifying how far the gameplay has adapted.  Old Sonic's stages were annoying to me because of the difference in gameplay. (no homing attack / running boost / etc)
I once described Sonic as a 'thrill ride' and this game is no different.  Sonic games are all about speed!  It's based largely on trial and error.  The first time you play any stage, you WILL make mistakes- things will go past you faster than you can react to them.  This turns some people off; the kind of people that are only playing for the story or 'the end'.  This isn't how Sonic Generations should be played.  Think of it as a racing game.  You play for time, improving it with every run.
Old Sonic is pretty easy.  You boost, you run, you jump.  The stages do have a flow to them after you've learned where you should do what.  There are special stages where your friends will assist you using their special move.  These are fun in their own way...but I play for the races and these stages are probably more suited to children that don't understand the need to GO FAST!
New Sonic has a number of unique moves that you'll have to absorb over time. Here are the basics: you should be boosting every chance you get, homing every time you see the icon, side dodging obstacles, and drifting around turns.  Drifting takes some getting used to, but helps immensely once mastered.  Red rings mark the fastest path- and using the right moves in the right places improves your time.
One thing I dislike about this game is the restart option.  I feel like it should be free...but it's not.  Every time you pause and restart, you lose a life.  This eventually gets you to zero lives- so you can't restart until you get either more lives or a game over.  In a normal racing game (Mario Kart for example), the life system doesn't exist and restarting is WHAT YOU DO when you make a mistake during ghost runs and whatnot.  It bugs me.
Overall, I'd rate this game an 8.  They put a lot of work into New Sonic making Old Sonic feel a bit empty.  This made me just a little sad...but I can ignore those stages.  They do make you play through everything at least once but it's really easy to ignore either half of the gameplay once you've unlocked everything.  Pressing Y switches between Old and New Sonic- so once you're playing for sng's, you pick the one you like better and never press Y again!
That's all I've got for now.  Can't wait for Sonic BOOM!  *high hopes*  Thanks for reading~

A nice little third-/first-person romp from back when Raven Software did something other than porting previous Call of Duty maps to whichever one just came out. Jedi Academy is technically a better game by virtue of giving you the lightsaber right away and not punishing you with a level filled with five-hundred snipers before you actually get to enjoy using it, as well as the ability to pick your own powers and play the missions how you want. From a story standpoint, though, I like this one better mostly for that it actually gets pretty grim for a Star Wars game that's not KOTOR II - from a mining colony that's been hijacked by the Remnant and had all its workers imprisoned, to any given day on Nar Shaddaa, to essentially a battalion of mercenaries stealing Cloud City right under Lando's nose, basically every situation you come in on has been ♥♥♥♥ed from the get-go, and there's not a whole lot you're able to do about it until you get strong enough to take the fight to the enemy. I mean, there's also that goddamned stealth section, but you get to throw a hangar full of stormtroopers out a couple airlocks a few minutes beforehand, so it all works out.
Another year, another nomination for "Best Unintentional Use of Shadows". If you're not playing this with the ill-fitting volumetric shadows that float high in the air half the time and make the game look like killer7 the other half, then you're not playing this correctly. If all else fails, maybe it'll convince someone to rerelease killer7.

The best melee gameplay experience in any game. It doesn't have the variety added in Academy, but the simplicity leads to a more elegant skill based experience.

The game becomes a solid masterpiece about 4-5 hours in, once the lightsaber combat sequences begin. They are amazing acrobatic encounters. A flurry of leaps and hops, both side attempting to knock the other off balance or off a ledge. These are unlike anything in any other game, and capture the feeling of using the force in a duel better than any other depiction of the Lightsaber.
The story is much more solid than Academy, and while it never reaches the heights of Dark Forces II, it stand as an excellent Star Wars adventure.
To this day still the best Star Wars game ever, especially the Lightsaber combat.

Unintuitive, clunky, poor interface, boring, lack of personality, just plain not fun. Any one of these things would spell the death knoll for a game, but SimCity nails them all. To make matters even worse, it doesn't like windows 7 or 8, and will fight you to the death on anything past XP. And it will win.
See, the sad part here is I actually *LIKE* city-builder games. Tycoon series? Pretty good! Tropico 4? Awesome! SimCity 1? Win. Afterlife? Epix Win. Sim City 4? Eh... mediocre at best?
So what went wrong? How did SC4 fail it up so badly?
I think the biggest problem was they lost sight of what made sim city games fun... the city building and the balancing of economy against people's desires. These things all exist in Sim City, and they've been inflated to a status of excessive grandeur, but that may be where the problem is: too much of a good thing.
Yes, there's lots of buildings, tons of them in fact... but it mostly just turns into a bogged down mess of junk to sort through if you want to have even a minimally running city at all. Instead of having a reasonable juggling act of a few major things your people need to be happy, tempered by a limited economy, Sim City 4 just throws all caution to the wind and piles on heaps of useless busywork. It's not even interesting construction; a good chunk of it's underground where you'll never even see it anyway. It's just there to waste money and make building the city more "realistic" but less interesting.
If I wanted "real" I wouldn't be playing a game.
Tropico 4... is a nice balance. It tosses the balls at you one at a time, slowly ramping up the difficulty and keeping the game entertaining and interesting the whole way. Sim City 4 piles too much needless crap on all at once that provides a remarkably harsh learning curve, for a minimal reward at the end.
Sim games have typically struck a wonderful balance in the past between the work and reward aspects, and gave you the tools needed to quickly and efficiently manage your little slice of heaven (or both heaven and hell if playing afterlife =P ). SC4 just kinda drops the ball (to maintain the juggling metaphor from the previous paragraph) by giving slow, irritating, clunky tools which technically "get the job done", but are a pain to use and not very fun.
Toss in the severe glitches, and absolute, seething hatred SC4 has for pretty much anything above WinXP, and you may as well not even bother considering it. There's simply better games out there... Cities XL for the obsessive compulsive "realistic" city builder, Tropico 4 for those who want a great storyline and awesome gameplay with proper balance of being "just right" a la goldilocks... and afterlife or sim city classic if you're nostalgic.
Final Verdict:
SC4 really just doesn't have a place in the city builder market. Anything it does, other games do better. Much, much better. Game-breaking glitches don't help it's argument, either.
Overall Score: About 40%. If you can get it to run, it's not really BAD... it's just not particularly good, and you can do better for lower cost, anyway. The music's pretty epic, though.

It was way past 2 AM and sleep was certainly not an option anymore. It was one of those days when Dunkalunk had an inspirational trip to do and boy what a trip it has been today.
Everything around him felt like it was a dream. He had blurry vision and he felt like he was somehow misplaced. He was not sure if that was because of 21 cups of coffee he killed today or the sheer fact of what he was about to publish on Steam.
Back when he was in school the cool kids always laughed at him, called him Loser and made jokes about him having crazy ideas, being fat and generally being a target of humiliation. His dad was dead and his mom was exceptionally good at drinking a very huge amount of alcohol per hour to keep her liver busy.
Still, he had this one dream he had to fulfill one day. That dream was building the perfect project, finishing what the first humans started after they started to think and questioning the world 5000 years ago. As a reference for his school experiences he called it Loser. That wouldn't sell well, so let's build some random♥♥♥♥♥♥story about a girl around it so he could make that Lisa.
The real background behind this though was not the name or the history behind the person making it. The message lies deep down, borrowed below a community that tends to overthink everything and compares it to other projects like Under the Sharktail, bigger than anything you can imagine and more important than anything the game seem to say over the course of playing it.
You probably think this game is just a joke, some sort of meta humor about video games itself like Understory and Dingedunk has nothing special to say.
You probably think this game covers the nature of humans thinking solely of themselves, drawing connections between things that don't have one for their own good.
You probably think this game is actually about the relationship of a man, whose sister commited suicide after being sexually assaulted for years by her own dad, because by the way this game is a sequel from LISA: The First where exactly that happens, and a girl that he defines as his daughter.
You probably think it's about forgiving people that make mistakes (or not doing so) and the terrible depth of where drug addiction can lead you to.
Maybe you are right with one of those and maybe all of those assumptions. Maybe there is no more than this obvious surface scratching of story that I just listed. Maybe this is all just a game and there is nothing behind it.
However, that seems unlikely. This game centers around a special scene. One scene that covers up everything and drills you down to the real story of the story, the meta level of the meta level, the loser behind Lisa. Far beyond anything that terrible film quotes about the name Lisa could ever include.
It's the scene where a guy wants to take a dumb and a spider crawls inside his butt.
Believe me, I have done my research. More than 15000 hours of game time on Steam alone, twenty four years of active studying on academic level, a bachelor and master degree, a doctor degree and one hundred and two lectures held about this topic.
This game all comes full circle when this scene hits.
The spider is not just crawling up his♥♥♥♥♥ it's slowly coming closer to him while he is actively trying to calm himself to a level where his hole can let loose. A symbol of a treacherous history combined with eight legs that obviously stand for the volatile nature of nature itself? Probably not, but what if it is such a symbol?
The guy then begs you to help him and you have no option but to walk towards the spider and kill it by stepping on it. The guy is then so thankful that he joins your team forever.
This scene represents everything dunkalenk stands for. It's his legacy and it's what not only LISA but the entire LISA Series - LISA: The First, LISA: The RPG and LISA: The Joyful is about. The message is crystal clear.
The ethics, the morality, the philosophy, the history, the science, the art, everything comes together at this scene. The past, the present and the future are all within there. It all comes full circle at this scene, this very point of the game.
If you ever want to take a dumb outside in the woods and you see a spider coming close to you, you know what to do now. You will be ready for it and you and your life can become a unity of peace.
Open your eyes and be ready for that moment. Your spider is waiting for you.

"It's cool to be sad"
"No, it isn't. It's just sad."
Actual Sunlight is best described as an interactive short story portraying a man fighting a losing battle with depression; as the protagonist's dark thoughts get the best of him his hate for himself and his own life send him down an ever darker spiral.
There's not much of a game here but its strong narrative, great writing and rarely touched subject matter make Actual Sunlight an experience worth considering for those strong enough to face its bleak, hopeless nature.
-top notch writing creates a great, mature narrative
-the few artwork pieces used in the game are simple yet beautiful
-good soundtrack
-holds no punches when it comes to subjects such as depression, suicide, self-hatred, abuse etc...
-will easily evoke strong emotions and/ or provide some food for thought
-the themes presented will be too much for some, the game is crude and bleak and could easily cause discomfort to gamers who are either too sensitive or too close to the subject matter
-some phrases can feel a tad too stereotypical
-very short, you'll be done in an hour
-little to no player input is required
Actual Sunlight is an experience...a bleak, raw, thought-provoking, emotional journey that is sure to stir strong emotions in its audience. There's basically no light or hope here, the story goes on and meticulously chronicles the feel of desperation, self-loathing and hopelessness that many people fightning with depression face every day. There can be a few bitter laughs here and there though, if you're a cynic like yours truly, when the game provides some social commentary on how relationships or job seeking work nowadays.
Evan Winter, the game's protagonist, is on the far end of the depression spectrum but there's no denying that many people will feel familiar with at least a few of his thoughts, actions and feelings: hereby lies Actual Sunlight's true strength as the game lets you project your own uncertainty and discomfort onto the tale being told.
Is this story one for you? It's honestly hard to say...I was deeply touched by Actual Sunlight and personally feel it'd be experienced by basically everyone at least once, provided you won't be upset or disgusted by its themes. I must also warn you though, just as the dev does ingame, that this story could also push you further down a dark path if you're having issues yourself so tread accordingly.
Don't play it, after you've just broke up with a girlfriend.
