Overall SR4 is a pretty decent game you can have lots of fun with. However, there's a ton of wasted potential and various issues that annoyed the sh** out of me. So far I'd consider it the weakest part of the SR series.
Why is that? Well, first, the whole thing feels like an addon of SR3. The city of Steelport is exactly the same. Nothing has changed. They just added some alien invasion backstory, which feels very generic and cheaply made. There's barely any new content and the whole story part's taking place on a boring space ship with nothing much to do but fu** your crew. I know that the franchise is known for its humor, over the top action and unexpected story development, but just recycling SR3's sandbox and making it a simulation, where you're basically a living god with super powers, isn't really what I was hoping for. The premise of the player character becoming POTUS at the beginning is pretty neat, but again they wasted most of the potential as it's just the intro to being stuck on a dull, non-customizable space ship for the rest of the game.
But back to the main part of the game: The Steelport simulation. It might be a matter of personal taste, but concerning the visuals, I really hated the fact that it's always night in the simulation and the permanent glitch effects in your environment felt somewhat annoying, too. The super powers were entertaining at first, but made the game way too easy. Guns became less important and cars don't serve any real purpose in SR4 – they're just moving objects you can make explode. You're always faster than any vehicle using your super sprint or gliding ability. Guess that's why there are less car types compared to earlier SR games (at least that's what it seems like). Don't get too excited about the arsenal of super powers, though. You'll realize that you only use one or two at best throughout the entire game. Some of them are just useless and you'll find yourself wondering why they included them in the first place.
Apart from countless mini games and collecting the usual stuff there's nothing much to do in the simluation. Most missions are composed of doing more mini games or feel like recycled SR3 objectives. Take over shops (yes, even more minigames), wait for the money to come in and upgrade your weapons (and super powers). Do some additional mini games. Beat the final boss. Uninstall. It feels like such a waste to have an open world, where there's absolutely nothing to do after you've got yourself all the collectible objects.
The character creation still is one of SR's strongest features. That's why I was getting really excited seeing that in SR4 you can customize your weapons' looks, too. Sadly, there aren't many skins to choose from, especially for some of the more powerful weapons. Also, the selection of available clothes is very similar to SR3, which I found very disappointing. Especially because the graphics didn't improve at all either. Textures look extremely outdated and are 100% the same as in SR3 – another reason why this game feels like it's just a big DLC of its predecessor.
All in all, SR4 is much too meta, repetitive and forced in terms of silliness. I'd have preferred a less "insane" story, taking place in an entirely new city, where you can explore things and maybe even interact with your surroundings. It feels like the developers got somewhat lazy here. I won't even mention the many bugs, but why not upgrade the mechanics, the graphics, etc. and make this technically outdated franchise evolve a bit? I still have to undergo plastic surgery to get a new haircut? Really? It's like they didn't even try.
For the reasons mentioned above I can't really recommend this game to fans of the first three SR games. Haven't played Gat out of Hell yet, but it seems like we're not getting any down to earth SR games anymore.

Second game of the Blackwell saga, and actually a prequel to The Blackwell Legacy, The Blackwell Unbound is one charming point and click adventure. Featuring Lauren Blackwell, Rosa's aunt, the game is full of little details that will help us understand that part of Lauren's past we just had a glimpse of in the first game, and her connection with Joey. New York in the seventies is so freaking cool in this game, and so are the strange and funny characters (and ghosts) that Lauren and Joey will find on their journey.
As always with the Balckwell games we're not talking about a game hard to beat, the puzzles are pretty easy, but even if I don't like it very much I'm inclined to think that it is a specific design choice to make the story flow freely at any time. The narrative aspect of the Blackwell games is prominent, the story is very well written and it always feels that the player can identify with the characters and some of their problems, and choices. Plus, Joey. Joey's awesome. So, essentially, the Blackwell Unbound is a good game "per se", a very cool second chapter of the saga, and a great prequel.

Blackwell Unbound is a prequel to The Blackwell Legacy. It is a point and click adventure, and sticks to the usual control scheme and playstyle of the genre.
In Blackwell Unbound, you play the aunt of the protagonist of Blackwell Legacy. Since this game sort of jumps in to the middle of a relationship between a medium and spirit guide, it is helpful to play the original game first to get some explanation on what is going on. With the help of Joey Malone, a ghost from the 1940's, you must solve mysteries and help lost ghosts find their way to the spirit world. It is a nice shake up of the usual detective story dynamic. While you still must look for clues and interrogate witnesses, you are doing so with the help of a ghost. You can switch from time to time between Lauren and Joey, the ghost, to help you advance. Certain things can only be done by Joey, such as moving through walls or talking to other ghosts in the real world.
Blackwell Unbound runs a good bit shorter than The Blackwell Legacy. I really enjoyed the notebook functionality in the first game, but found it a little lacking in this one just due to the overall shortness of the game. This may be because while there is one overarching story, there are two distinct mysteries to solve. The first game just had one mystery that kind of led to another and so on, but the clues really built off each other and involved a lot more using the notebook to combine clues and interrogate witnesses.
The graphic style is pretty much unchanged from the first game. It is reminiscent of early 90's adventure games, which in my opinion have aged better than games from the late 90's and early 00's that begin using 3D. They look well enough, but they are really lacking in detail. It's ok to use that style, but I'd like to see it sharpened up a bit with some more detail added overall.
The voice acting is much improved, with only small complaints. The main character in particular sounds so much better. She sounds engaged in the story, while her predecessor sounded a little bored. Joey sounds the same, which is neither great nor bad. The main villain sounds pretty terrible in Blackwell Unbound. It really kind of removed me from the story. I think you will understand when you hear it.
Overall, I actually enjoyed this more than Blackwell Legacy. While it was a little shorter, and I missed using the notebook as much as the original, I found the overall improvement of the story and voice acting won out. I really like this main character more, although I'm not expecting to see much more of her. I will definitely try out the next game in the series, and recommend you give this game a look.
Grade: B+
Even if Lauren is not nearly as interesting as Rosa, Blackwell Unbound is a solid prequel to one of the most interesting adventure games in a while. 7.5/10.

The Blackwell Series. I'm starting to like these games more and more. I gave the thumbs down to the first game Blackwell Legacy with a question mark, since it wasn't altogether that bad (see full review on my profile). I've come to realize that these games are not your typical point and click adventure. Let me explain. Most point and click adventure games (at least the ones I have played) are puzzle based. This game on the other hand is more dialog/clue based. There are a couple of puzzles in the game, but the game stays true to what it should be a murder mystery (Don't worry the game is not graphic at all, just a bunch of cartoon looking ghosts).
I still give the first game about 6/10. The main reason being too much storyline setup, a couple of really annoying puzzles (the director apologized for these), and super short game. While not the best game, it accomplished something important. It is like the introduction to a very good book. You can not only see that the director learned from some of the mistakes made in this game to make Unbound much better. It also helped in being able to jump right into this one, as characters were already set up. If you want to play this game, it is important to play Blackwell Legacy (Hey, its short! Maybe that was a good thing). You can definitely put this on the buy list. Here are my Pro's and Con's.
Pro's: Great Storyline for three different characters. Lauren Blackwell and the ghost she helps. The character interaction between Lauren and Joey is very good, you'll love these two characters and their relationship. No ridiculous puzzles in this one. Some hard one's, but nothing way out in left field. And the game is also longer too. Most of the stuff that was good or bad from the last game was improved on.
Con's: Art is still not the best, but that is the style. Although the music music in this game probably did a better job at setting the right mood, there just weren't really any toe tapping tunes that the first game had.
I'm working on Blackwell Convergance right now and it is going good thus far.
Check out my other point and click adventure reviews on my page!

The second in the Blackwell series of point-and-click supernatural adventures, prequel to the Blackwell Legacy, where you get to control Lauren and Joey.
Unlike some other adventure games the mysteries are largely solved by gathering clues and combining pieces of information, so it's less puzzle-based and more like detective work, with a methodical process and moments of insight, which grounds the experience - yes, one of the main characters is a ghost, but the problem-solving is built on real-world logic, not magic.
Another thing I love about the series is the way the relationship between the two main characters develops and matures, and the characters get fleshed out as we learn more about them and their backstories. You can also see the art style and character design mature with each installment.

The CD-player in my car is busted, the disc won't eject. So, imagine having to listen to Jamiroquai's "Traveling Without Moving" constantly. It's a good album though, came out in 1996, had classics like "Seven Days in Sunny June", "Canned Heat" and "Supersonic". Speaking of Super Sonic, the lack of a certain hedgehog on the Sega Saturn was very strange. There were a couple spin-offs and Sonic X-treme (which was never released), but no Sonic 4. In fact, Sega still hasn't released a Sonic 4, I can't understand it.
During the 16 and 32-bit days, the mascot-platformer was the most over-stuffed genre on store shelves. These games were mostly garbage like Bubsy & Awesome Possum. Anytime there was an actual hit (like Earthworm Jim), publishers would run it into the ground through a combination of uninspired sequels and marketing. Still, there were a lot of good games released during this time: Rocket Knight Adventures, Socket, Pulseman, High Seas Havoc, Adventures of Little Ralph, Keio Flying Squadron 2, Tryrush Deppy, Ristar, DoReMi Fantasy, Super Tempo Popful Mail, Astal, Clockwork Knight, etc.
It was a rough transitional period for the platformer. Due to the popularity of Mario 64, most developers went 3D (or at least 2.5D) with varying levels of success. The 2D platformers released around the time were by small teams, and unless you read Diehard GameFan, you didn't know of their existence. Freedom Planet could have been one of those games. If it had released in 1996, it would have toiled in obscurity for nearly a decade, until it was purchased by somebody in a random ebay auction. This guy played through the game, thought "Wow this is really good!", and told everyone in his gaming forum about it. I'd wager that by 2008, Freedom Planet achieved some mid/high-level of notoriety, and commanded about $80 per disc through online auctions.
Freedom Planet follows the adventures of Lilac, Carol, and Millia. Three heroines, three kingdoms, one war, an alien menace, and that's the short version. There are a lot of cut-scenes in this game, and the story takes some unexpectedly dark turns. Saying anything else is liable to turn this review into spoiler-central, but I'll say this much: there's at least one scene in this game that I'd be perfectly content with never seeing again.
But enough about that mess, let's talk about the actual game. There are three playable characters, and they have a variety of unique skills. This is a fast-moving platformer, not unlike the Sonic games, so expect loops, ramps, and so on. The stages are all fairly large, with numerous optional paths, secrets, traps. and enemy robots. This is also a combat-oriented platformer, and the later stages throw a lot of baddies at the player. Freedom Planet certainly isn't lacking in boss-fights either, you can expect two or more in every stage.
How you deal with adversity depends on the character. Lilac soars with her various aerial maneuvers (including a flying dash-attack & a shoryuken), Carol has her claws, Chun-Li kicks, and a motorcycle, while Millia creates blocks and shields to frustrate anything capable of firing bullets. These skills are also necessary for getting around the stages, whether it's flying over massive cliffs, driving up walls, or even subtle tricks such as using a phantom block shield blast to propel Millia a few feet. The controls are exceptionally fluid, and the mechanics are very solid. While the levels are fun to explore, they're even more entertaining, when using every ability to its fullest extent to speed through them. Also, unlike some platformers that emphasize speed, there's no worry over taking damage from simple enemy contact.
As I mentioned earlier, Freedom Planet has a lot of boss-fights, and they can be pretty tough. Most of the challenge is in reading their patterns. They move quickly, and while you might see this as a sign to move fast yourself, it's all a smokescreen. What's liable to happen is that you'll bump into their attacks and get yourself killed. Instead, you want to stop, wait, and see what happens. They'll jump from one of the screen to the next, present some opening, and that's when you attack. Each character has a move that gives them some invincibility, such as Lilac's flying, Carol's kicks, or Millia's shield. Using those moves, even in last-ditch situations, could save your life. All that said, even the easy setting will lead to some boss-related deaths. The most devastating attacks tend to juggle you, which eats through a ton of life. Also, Millia has half the health of the other heroines, but she tends to kill bosses faster so it balances out.
Where this game really excels is in level-design variety. All too often, variety is a double-edged sword. Yeah it's fun to see something new and different, but when you're flying from one set-piece to the next, you never really get a feel for how the game actually plays. You buy a game, expecting a third-person shooter, but every other level involves turrets, vehicles, flying, swimming, sex QTEs, and so on. Each stage in Freedom Planet is different from one another, but not so different that you feel like you're playing another game. It's also important to note that the level-design never completely shifts gears. One stage might feature more enemies, another probably has some extra puzzles, but it never feels like "this is a puzzle stage" or "this is the stage where you fight all the time". Everything comes together naturally, and you're always in complete control.
Although, yes there is a 2D shooter stage. Of course there would be a 2D shooter stage. I've been a platformer-fan for decades and this happens every time...EVERY SINGLE TIME. Apparently, there's always someone out there that thinks "Our game is too good, we should throw in a really weak section to give reviewers something to complain about". Towards the end of Freedom Planet, there is a 2D shooter stage. It's not particularly bad, but it's just...there. All told, I guess I can deal with a few minutes out of a 2+ hour game being merely passable.
Freedom Planet is a relic, and I mean that in the most affectionate way. It's a mid-90s platformer that has all the elements of a forgotten classic, but it was released in 2014. It's unfortunate that more games aren't released that emulate this style. It seems that for most indie-developers, their favorite system growing up was the NES. That's cool and all but eh, I prefer the days of the Genesis/SNES/Saturn/PSX. I'd rather see more games that prey upon my nostalgia, and if they turned out to be half as good as Freedom Planet, then I'd be in for a treat.

Telltale Games certainly made a splash when they released The Walking Dead: The Game. It seemed to be the best way to bring the point-and-click adventure genre to modern gaming. It allowed the developers to tell an emotional story that still gave the player a feeling of agency. It’s surprising how rarely that formula has been copied, with Life is Strange being the closest comparison.
The Descendant is now the closest thing to a straight copy-paste of the formula Telltale has mastered, but it’s boring characters, boring plot, boring… everything make it a chore to get through it’s first episode.
The premise is simple enough. Global Warming caused wars between the world’s superpowers, ending in nuclear war. Sanctuaries known as Arks were built to house some of the world’s elite in cryosleep until… well that’s unclear. These Arks are maintained by engineers known as Janitors, who are automatically awoken at key times to work on things like water heaters.
The Descendant’s first episode is split between three time periods, following two characters. In the past, Mia is the “new guy” on Ark-01, who works alongside one of the most poorly voice-acted characters I’ve ever come across. There’s a weird moment where it feels like the game is interested in building some level of distrust between the characters. “Who are you?” asks Mia’s partner, “You’re not the guy I expected.” Oddly, this tension between the characters is never suggested again.
In the future (“Centuries later...”), you’ll take control of Donnie, a one-time Janitor who is now partnered with a cranky, old Senator, tasked with investigating what happened at Ark-01. The Descendant jumps around periodically between Donnie and Mia, unravelling more of the mystery as the game goes on.
The basic premise of learning what occurred on Ark-01 is admittedly intriguing. Even though we’ve seen this idea done to death (waking up years after the Apocalypse), The Descendant’s idea of turning it into a mystery is something that I haven’t seen done a million times. It’s unfortunate that the game is so bad at communicating exactly what the mystery is. Upon Donnie’s arrival, we don’t know anything that’s happened at Ark-01, so immediately, tension drops. Donnie makes a suggestion that the senator should stay behind (and you’re given 4 options of reasons why he should stay behind) because presumably there’s danger afoot. It’s unclear why Donnie feels this way. Is the world inhabited by mutants now? Was there signs of distress? Couldn’t the Ark have simply had a mechanical failure and everyone died in cryosleep?
There’s no reason to feel tension other than the fact that the developers lay on the thriller movie music. Even in the moments that feel like they should be tense, they aren’t because the controls don’t allow you to move your characters quickly. With the exception of one scene, the characters crawl along at an alarmingly slow pace considering meltdown seems to be occurring. Then these moments feature puzzles that require you to find a thing to make another thing work, so that you can get another thing to work. There’s no urgency and thus no tension. Then the episode - which took me all of 40 minutes to complete - ends with what I can only assume was intended to be an intense cliffhanger, but because I’d been so bored until that point, I couldn’t find it in me to care at all.
Everything about The Descendant’s first episode feels like a really boring SyFy original series, while Telltale’s games, while not perfect, tend to feel more like an AMC or HBO production in comparison. The Descendant’s low budget shows at every seam. The voice acting is bad to terrible, the writing is unsure of itself and never knows where to go, and the gamiest aspects are okay at best. The puzzles are simplistic, and the camera lingers in places that force your character to constantly walk into walls or get stuck in awkward positions.
The Descendant's first episode is a mess from beginning to end. It's near-interesting plot is brought down by bad execution (bad voice acting, bad pacing, bad animation). Thankfully it's only a briefly painful experience at 40 minutes.

Actual Sunlight is a bleak look at a broken man slowly destroying himself.
Expecting the worst of himself, misreading everyone, and seeing no hope. It is a somber story that certainly does not start in a happy place, but it only sinks lower from there. Depression is not an easy thing to talk about, and Actual Sunlight does not attempt to shy away from every thought that comes from a dark place. The protagonist expects a stranger to try to strike up a conversation with him as he gets on the bus, getting annoyed that some stranger would try to talk to him in a pathetic attempt to make friends, but then the stranger simply tells him something mundane, like his shoes are untied. The protagonist feels stupid for hoping that someone would talk to him, just so he could reject them, but only finds out that he was the one who was pathetic enough to want human contact with a stanger on a bus. He uses videogames and material things to drive away the emptiness he feels inside. He thinks his co-workers are terrible, but he envies them. Nearly everything sends him into a feeling of bitterness and defeat.
Finishing Actual Sunlight is not so much rewarding as it is sobering. The gameplay aspect has you interacting with objects and people as you walk around in an oldschool JRPG perspective. There is little to be done besides exploring the environment and talking to other characters, which just peels away more layers of melancholy. It is a different experience, and for better or worse, it is a moving one.

Buyer be advised: "Actual Sunlight" is basically a visual novel... and I don't mean the kind with fan-service cheesecake tossed in (unless you're into flabby white guys). There's almost no traditional gameplay in it. You play it not for "fun", but rather for an emotional experience and perhaps for some insight into the psychology of depression.
If you're still reading, then maybe you're open-minded enough to get something out of this game. You play as Evan Winter, an overweight white-collar drone who tries to bury his loneliness in video games, daydreams, and misanthropy. Gameplay consists of guiding Evan through a few days in his overly routinized life, interacting with other characters and environmental objects in order to trigger Evan's dark and sardonic commentary (the game is
text-heavy). As the game progresses through its roughly hour-length, Evan's depression becomes increasingly severe. There is only one possible ending no matter what choices the player makes along the way. And with a name like "Evan Winter" ... brace yourself.
One of the things I liked the most about "Actual Sunlight" was how the developer took advantage of the unique features of video games as a medium in order to convey Evan's psychology in a visceral way. The graphics are mostly flat, basic, and bland; environments are constricted; and the narrative choices given to the player are ultimately illusions -- exactly how Evan feels about his own life. Which is not to say that "Actual Sunlight" asks you to
with Evan's worldview, but rather to take a walk in his shoes as a cautionary tale. When the game is over, the player must do something that Evan also does every day: put down his/her own controller, return to "real life," and ponder the choices that they may not have even been aware that they were making. The difference is that we have Evan's example to learn from.
Sounds like a party, right? ;) Buy "Actual Sunlight" if you are looking to think and feel more than to "play," and if you are capable of handling dark subject matter. It took me a couple tries to get into it, but ultimately I'm glad that I did.

The relevance to the twentysomething of 2015 and wit works on its own, but strong prose and a commitment to the core message pushed this past an 'oh, okay' for me. This is a work that could easily have been on paper, but the O'Neill's choice of RPG Maker and Steam targets Actual Sunlight towards those that can benefit most from his experience.
If you're upset with its length or lack of interactivity, log back into Maplestory. For everyone else, this game has something to say and is worth the five bucks to hear it.

Actual Sunlight is an interactive text based short game that talks about depression. Depression is not an easy subject to discuss nor is it easy to relate to in our case. I've been exposed to the topic and have few people in my life with Clinical Depression, It was tough for me to deal with them and support them but there is no way I can imagine what they are going through. Actual Sunlight has one of these cases and from what I've been through, you know you hit rock bottom when you start contemplating suicide. That is probably the intention behind this game, to bring awareness to the whole topic.
I've been torn on whether I would recommend this game or not. There are many reasons for both in my own opinion. For example, I'd recommend it if it would raise awareness to depression and familiarize people with the topic so they can find a way to support someone before it is too late. I'd not recommend it because it is not a very engaging experience, however, that would be quite offensive to the experience on "Evan Winters". I decided I'd go with recommending it only because it is not a simple topic and I'd be happy knowing this game could spark a feeling for someone.

I'm rather torn about Blade Symphony.
You probably already know by now that it's a pretty in-depth melee duelling game with a vaguely Asian theme. The game plays a lot closer to fighting games than other melee-heavy ones like Chivalry or Mount and Blade, which are mostly about directional control and that is where it lost me a little. I do prefer the more intuitive "what you see is what you get" type of directional attacks and Blade Symphony is instead heavily focused on learning combos and their animations. If you like fighting games you might be right at home but I'm mixed about it.
The mechanics though are deep, innovative and balanced. Combos here are built between strings which represent stances, fast, heavy, balanced & air. You can change stances at the touch of a key and a good deal of the gameplay is changing stances between attacks to be one step ahead of your opponent. Attacks unlock the next tier on any string so, for example, if you attack balanced once and then switch to heavy, you will use heavy attack tier 2, and thus you have a myriad of possibilities to reach your character's favorite and appropriate attack, thus creating the "symphony" of your blade.
The game is quite deep and takes a lot of practice to withstand even bots. There are innovative mechanics such as two simultaneous attacks leading to swords clashing and the heavier stance wins the attack, recovering faster and opening the opponent, different attacks having different recovery rates etc. It is quite complex and whereas a fighting game has 2 control input parts, directional moves and attacks, here you have the extra input dimension of switching between strings. To my mind, this game would benefit from a slightly slower pace to gain a more tactical feel, yet I am a mere newb.
The content is also decent, there are currently 5 characters each with their own unique attacks and stance-biases, and 6 or so weapons that play very differently(katana, rapier, scimitar etc). If you want to play competitively, you will have to learn a character builds' every intricate combo, their precise animations, and then do this for each other character and weapon combination because you need to be able to discern what stance the opponent is in and what attacks they are trying to string. Again, very much like a fighting game.
As you can see, there is a lot of depth and flow to the combat, and overall it is a game that I would recommend to people showing an interest. The strongest point and also biggest weakness of Blade Symphony is not really about its quality, nor about the hard work of the devs. It is the fact that it has a small community of very talented and experienced players and not much for a new player.
As a new player, you will play the tutorials, spend a few hours learning the movesets against bots and then search for a game and proceed to have someone mop the floor with you. You will have a hard time getting into it. Tis an unfortunate circumstance that befalls smaller online games with steep learning curves and past their popularity peak, through no fault of the developers or of the dedicated community.
If you truly think you might get into this tight-knit competitive scene and understand that it will take you possibly hundreds of hours to match these players who know the game with their eyes shut, I wholly recommend Blade Symphony. In truth, though it saddens me, I do not consider the majority of buyers or of my acquaintances would find satisfaction here unless they pour a lot of dedication in it. Myself, I do not think I have it in me.

I love this game. It's incredible. It seems on the surface like it might be fairly simple and straight-forward, but that is not the case at all. It's one of those games that is deceptively deep, and steeped in possibility.
What do I mean by that? Well let me give you an example:
I came upon a goblin who surprised me, and I was at low health with a damaged weapon. I ran out of the hallway into the room I had just been in. I didn't have many options so I used a spell called "Push" (basically a jedi force push) to buy myself some time. The spell actually picked up a ball of slime off the floor and flung it in his face, blinding him and giving me the upper hand. I quickly took my opportunity and slew him. As I picked up his corpse to loot it, what I failed to notice is that the potion he was holding had rolled onto the nearby campfire. It vaporized into the room, and I freaked out trying to get away. It turned out to be a potion of might, so it actually helped me. Or it would have if I hadn't been freaking out and ran into the spike pit in the other corner of the room. DED.
There are so many random, totally one-of-a-kind moments in this game that you can run into, or even consciously create. It baffles the mind. If you see a treasure chest at the bottom of a pirhana-filled pond, and you happen to have the Chain Lightning spell, you can electrocute the entire pool and have the spoils. Or throw in a skeleton as a distraction and hope you can swim down and get your loot before they pick it clean.
It has a well-balanced leveling system, interesting weapon enchantments, dastardly traps...I mean, you can even bake potatoes, or put hot sauce on a goblin corpse you're about to eat to get a better benefit out of it. It balances action, exploration, tactics and all-around cute♥♥♥♥♥♥very well.
Not only that, but it has local co-op which absolutely does not disappoint. My girlfriend isn't much of a gamer, but we've been jamming this game together, and she loves it too, even though most of what we do is get ourselves (and each other) killed.
And it's only in Alpha! For the love of god, buy this game.

Sonic Generations is the ultimate love letter to any fan of Sonic the Hedgehog, new and old. The game is composed entirely of levels and music from 1991's Sonic the Hedgehog, to 2010's Sonic Colors, all redone and beautifully recreated. It's both a 2D and 3D platformer, and that's the gimmick here. You can play as "Classic Sonic" in Act 1 who's play style is exactly like a traditional 2D Platformer, and as "Modern Sonic" who's levels are 3D. Modern also has the boosting feature from Sonic Rush, and the Homing Attack, whilst Classic can just utilize the Spin Dash.
As stated, all stages and music are completely re-done from the ground up to make up pretty interesting levels. But it's not just an HD makeover, every one of the levels have been edited to where it's different from the original game, while it still has those familiar bits here and there.
The soundtrack is also beautiful. Every piece (Save 2 or 3 exceptions) is remixed Sonic music from the past, fitting with the old stages you play. Actually, it's remixed twice. Classic has more retro sounding music, and Modern has, well, you can put two and two together.
Now where the problems lie, there are a couple. This one is pretty obvious, but if you're not the biggest fan of Sonic, this game might be pretty average to you. Don't get me wrong, the game is still a spectacular platformer, but the entire purpose was to celebrate Sonic's 20th anniversary, therefore it was made for the fans. Another issue is the game is really easy compared to most Sonic games, and platformers in general, and it doesn't take much effort to get an S rank on every mission, so that could also be a problem.
In short, Generations is a wonderfully crafted Sonic game for the fans. If you love the hedgehog, definitely get this game, you won't regret it. If you're not a Sonic fan, it's still a good platformer for what it is, I think you'll still like it.

Blackwell Unbound is the second instalment in the Blackwell series, and interestingly, it’s a prequel to the first game, The Blackwell Legacy, set almost 30 years prior to the events of the first one.
Unbound is where the series really kicks off and start the format of introducing more than one separate cases (ghost you need to save) in one game that in the end tie into a bigger plot. This episodic format restricts puzzle elements somewhat but it also removes the frustration that comes with most adventure games, especially the indie title where finding the solution to one puzzle requires you to explore a dozen or more maps for that elusive clue.
The overall quality of the game is a step up from Legacy, the writing and the dialogues are improved by quite a lot, and puzzle solving still requires finding clues and combining them instead of the classic use Item A on Item B type, unrealistic adventure game method.
Overall this is a very good follow-up on a promising first game, paving the path for the future instalments.

LISA wasn't made with anything fancy, and it doesn't try to make you think it was. It's objectively a very simple game, but subjectively it's everything but simple.
There's so much to say here:
This game was made so unique because of its sheer creativity, and its willingness to share human qualities. Everything in this game felt either insanely ♥♥♥♥ed up, funny as hell, or both. Just the writing itself felt so real to me that each and every character I came across felt like they had some sort of secret backstory that has been locked away for only the developer to know, and a lot of games just don't do this anymore. It's refreshing. There are so many tiny details added to this game that could easily be skipped over, but they're so worth it if you find them, because they add so greatly to the amazing personality this game has. The combat is meaningful and brutal. Every area feels unique. The game has replay value out the♥♥♥♥♥ It doesn't hold your hand. It ♥♥♥♥s with you just because it can. The way the party system is balanced with rng helps weigh down on the difficulty in an actual unique way, and it also adds to the general aesthetic and uniqueness of this game. Everything you see in this game is exactly what you get. It's incredibly flexible as well in terms of how you wish to play the game, and there are varying difficulties based purely upon how you choose to play it. There clearly was a huge amount of time and love put into this game. Pretty much every aspect of the game was planned with a level of intellect that you really just don't see much anymore.
TL;DR? This is a damn good game for many reasons.
I don't think I could recommend this to a child, because the developer paid no mind to cencorship here, and most of the meaning of this game couldn't properly be appreciated by a child. To pretty much everyone else though, I would highly recommend getting this game. It's definitely a nice addition to your favorite's list.
P.S. The soundtrack is amazing.

Whow, this was not at all what I wanted. I really wanted to love this game for so many reasons. Please read full review (ESPECIALLY the end).
The good:

The bad:

However, the most important piece of fact is most likely this:
This game was funded by investors, who purchased stocks in Gaming Corps. I was one of these investors. We did not get to see this game until two days ago. Upon playing the game, most investors were horrified and sold the shares, resulting in -30% stock value. However, a bunch of investors still want this game to sell; therefore, many positive reviews will be the result of biased reviewers. Moreover, critical reviews will most likely get downvoted.
So be careful when buying this game. If you are into Grim Fandango and have the money to spend, maybe this is for you. But please read all positive reviews with critical eyes.

The Descendant (Episode 1-3) is a casual, story rich, point and click adventure game that takes place on 2 different timelines.
Check out my
here:
In The Descendant, you play as two different characters, one from the past timeline, and one from the present. So far, the game is a user-friendly point and click adventure, where you can only interact with objects in the proper sequence. The objectives are fairly straightforward. You can inspect various objects, but you can’t pick up anything that isn’t your current objective. The game has a few puzzles, but so far, nothing too complex. In between the point and click gameplay, there are choices in dialog selection, and other things that require you to react.
The story starts after a near-human extinction event, with what’s left of humanity trying to wake the survivors and rebuild. You don’t really know what exactly happened, but the mystery very intriguing.  When the episode ends, you probably won’t want to stop playing.
For the most part, your decisions in episode 1 seem to have the same or very similar outcome, but decisions made in previous episodes are acknowledged in Episode 3.
Both Episode 1, 2 & 3 each take 30-60 minutes to complete, depending on the player, and what decisions are made. You can replay the game to try making other decisions, but you can’t skip any of the cut scenes, so it is repetitive. Also, there was one part in episode 2 that I didn't agree with, and I would have liked to have had a choice to let me choose otherwise, but it doesn't change my review.
I don’t know exactly how long the next three episodes will be, but if they last about the same as the first episode, I can see waiting for a slight sale even though it’s priced similarly to some other Telltale adventure games. I am looking forward to finding out what happened, I hope the following episodes don’t take too long to release. You might want to wait for all the episodes to release because you will most likely be left wanting more story immediately.

I thought that the time control mechanics would be really gimicky, a crutch for mediocre gameplay. I was wrong. On its own, the platforming and combat are satisfying, thanks to great audio design and animations. The time control mechanics adds unique puzzle and strategy elements to the combat that are unlike anything I've seen before.
It clicked for me in a mission where I had to protect the platform I was on from being destroyed. Enemies are coming from all sides and they hit the platform so fast that the only way to shoot them down before they hit you is to know that they are coming, and they come from all sides. With time control and the "cloning" mechanics, I could put myself where I'm needed before the events happen to handle them perfectly. Even the pickups throughout the game will vanish before you can reach them, meaning you have to know about them in advance and put someone there to catch them.
You also get unique teamplay, like having one character cloned twice provide AoE cover at a lot of incoming objects while other characters that can do heavy damage take down the target. The game ends up being a dance through time, as one character goes to save another's life and others go to position themselves perfectly to cover each other. Watching the replays can be a treat, just to see impossible saves happen with perfect coordination.
It seems complicated, but actually is very fluid and understandable in gameplay. And just to help you get better with time travel, there are trial rooms that act as small puzzles.
My only gripe is the LOL INTERNET HUMORZ dialogue. If you like that kind of thing, this is perfect for you. I think it's a poor attempt at being funny and doesn't work. I do like that the game doesn't take itself seriously, though, and gives the characters very punny names.

Background: Don't be turned away by my hours played. I remember spending entire evenings of my childhood playing this on Windows XP. I bought it on Steam because hey, its a classic, oldie with Kyle Katarn (Someone who needs to be on the Silver Screen).
Story: The story is great and holds up against the $60 Big Studio and Assorted Indie Games of 2016.  You contend with all the classic enemies like Stormtroopers, AT-ST, Imp Officers, and Bounty Hunters. You even meet Luke Skywalker!
Lightsaber Mechanics: A Few levels into the game you go through Jedi Training...Again. Lightsaber Combat has 3 forms. A quick low damage striking form, single hits can still off Stormtroopers. A Medium speed balanced form, and a Heavy hitting Slow form that strangely enough throws off lightsaber wielding opponents. You also pick up your Basic Push, Pull, Jump, Speed Skills. These evolve as the game progresses.
All other Combat Mechanics: It becomes your generic shooter with weapons from the Star Wars Universe. Stormtrooper E-11 blaster, Wookie Bowcaster, Thermal Detonators, Trip Mines. It is also challenging and has some puzzles that you have to work your way through.
Final Thoughts:  Its a great nostalgic game from years past. I love it because of Star Wars.

I got this game for almost nothing in some Star Wars Humble Bundle that i bought for other games a few year back, that's why i'm considering i got the game for free (probably for less than 0.25€)
I hadn't played this game for more than 10 years... A friend lent me the game back then, but i never finished it. When i noticed it in my Steam library this week-end so i decided to give it another try.
The game is a blend of FPS and third person lightsaber combat. Weapons feel responsive, sound great, and carry the nostalgia of these early-2000s Star Wars games. The graphics are not bad, they aged well in my opinion and i'm genuinely still amazed by the marks left by lightsabers on walls.
Now for the cons :
* First it's clearly not worth 10€ in 2016.
* Some game mechanics are NOT introduced, i discovered that i could use objects, after being stuck for half an hour in the only part of the game that really require using them (The nightvision goggles in the hangar level). Moreover, i only discovered during the final level that i could heal myself using a force power. (Explaining why the last levels were so hard, since medipacs were not provided anymore as i was supposed to use the force...)
* Talking about levels, they seem well designed at first glance, but they are a labyrinthic mess. Prepare to run around levels you just cleared for hours before finding out an utterly hidden ventilation grid on the ceiling of a random room that will lead to the next part of it. This happens in every level and i wasn't prepared for that. I still can't believe some levels of this game made it through QA and play-testing, as half of them require you to perform jumps that would have been considered as glitch/skips in any decently-designed game.
TL;DR : This is overall a good experience, but kinda frustrating if you are used to modern games that have corrected the youthful errors of this one over a decade.

I have a bit of a love-hate relationship with this game every time I play it. It's the kind of game that's not afraid to tear you in half and beat you upside the head with your own rear end, ESPECIALLY at the start. The first few levels are a first person shooter hellscape, but memorize the quick save and quick load keys, suffer through those, and once you get the lightsaber and force powers, that's when the real game starts. Suddenly you're zipping around, hacking and slashing, force pushing people's grenades back at themselves, dueling other lightsaber chaps for those one or two good hits that settle the fight, and just all around having an insanely much more entertaining time. Keep in mind the game never gets "easy," but having the lightsaber and force powers suddenly nets you the ability to actually deal with their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. You'll find yourself screaming at the screen one moment, and patting yourself on the back feeling like a badass for some particularly acrobatic and amazing room clear or lightsaber duel the next.
All in all, my synopsis is once you clear the game up to the lightsaber, I HIGHLY recommend this game. You'll laugh, you'll cry, you'll pull all the guns out of the hands of a room full of stormtroopers and feel yourself release your inner dark side as one by one you use the force choke power to drop them all off the nearby ledge into the infinite death pit.

Sonic Generations. A title that is really good, and has a lot of replay value, but it really... understates its welcome? It has a (slightly) diverse range of remade levels from past games, and both Sonics control beautifully, but it's pretty damn short, and $50 is honestly just overpriced. But when I say replay value, I MEAN IT. It has lots of stuff to collect, including concept art for Sonic games from the past, and even MUSIC from Sonic games from the past! The levels always leave something new for every playthrough, first or not, and keep you playing over and over again. The remixes used for levels are downright AWESOME, and the bosses provide a fair challenge while not being too overly frustrating- very rarely do I ever rage-quit because of a boss. Overall, it makes its place well in the Sonic franchise, and it's an amazing 20th anniversary title. However, the story is so simplistic that it's almost bland, and it just screams missed opportunities. But it does have, yep, a modding community! You can download and play a diverse range of mods that can have new stages, characters, bosses... anything, really! Overall, it's a good game, but a bit overpriced. I recommend it to Sonic fans old and new. Heck, even if you're not a fan of Sonic, just give this game a go. You might end up loving it!

Beat the main three characters playtroughs so doing a more overall review of the game.
I went into this game seeing JessieCox playing this and it seemed really cool so I decided play it myself. Several hours later I can without a doubt say this is one of the best games I've played in a very long time, if not one of the best I've played of all time.
As a person who grew up playing platformers like these, I already went in knowing I'd like it, but its not a cakewalk at all which some may take as a bad thing, but to have a game that actually is challenging is a nice thing compared to easy games that tend to be prevailant now. Many say its like a Sonic platformer, but I wouldn't really call it that alone. It's more of a combination of other platformers like Sparkster, Mega Man, Sonic, Rinstar, and others mixed into its own unique flavor. Game starts off decently easy letting you get to know how to use the characters, then it kicks it into overdrive and gets challenging (there are difficulty modes so those who don't want it to be as hard can have it this way). Level design is well done and interesting. Bosses get progressivly harder along with stages. There are three characters to play as who each play very differently than each other and each are sastifying to play as. Gameplay is pretty damn solid with nothing to say other than its really fun. You get to go fast and there aren't many momentum killing enemies. Nothing to gripe and its really damn fun to play. Story is actually pretty interesting too which I wasn't expecting since most of the time platformer games have minimal story that you tend to just put to the side if its even followable. Even playing classic mode (level to level with no story elements) its easy to catch on the story and follow along. I liked it a lot and wasn't too hard to follow in the midst of playing the game.
Visuals and the soundtrack are great as well. The graphics are a throwback to stuff back in the early/mid 90s which look really nice and run smoothly. The only thing one could gripe about visuals would be the slowdowns at a bosses defeat, but that is very minor and has no effect on actual gameplay.  The soundtrack is well beyond what I was expecting. From start the start I was instantly in love with it and it only got better the more I played. The boss music is easily in my top ever of just overall game music. The stage musics are also really great too. It was the one time I didn't even hesistate to buy the ost for it. I had to have it and support it. The only thing I could find some people could have a problem with in the audio department is the voice acting (cheesy), but then again, thats not a nack on the game at all. It didnt bother me (I actually liked some of them a lot)
Overall I'd have to say if you loved playing platformers back in the 90s or you just like good games, I highly recommend getting this. If you buy the British forces as a standalone then it comes dangerously close to being propaganda for those with an unhealthy interest in Austrian gentlemen of historical interest. Since release no-one uses the British forces in competitive gameplay, barring a very occasionl diehard. Which should tell you all you need to know.
Basically the British forces ties you down to building immobile emplacements, or using tanks with paper thin armour against much more durable German ones. Don't expect any historical accuracy, the norotiously thin skinned Panzer 4 is just as well armoured as the Brit's Churchill! Yeah...
Overall I like a challenge but on reflection would rather like 900 hours of my life back instead.
Supposedly it's set in 1944 but you'd think from the gameplay that you're trying to hold back a technically superior German army earlier in the war. Relic claims that the Brits early game is weak but they get stronger. Except that the Germans get stronger still. And of course you have to be able to get to the late game without serious losses. Good luck.
For instance once you've collected every intel bulletin which give small buffs to specific troops you'll have 38 of them. Ten of which might on a good day be useful and the vast majority just utterly pointless, like a 5% boost to the armour of something with no armour. The two German factions get 100 and 108 to choose from respectively. The community provides feedback designed purely to enable the Germans to win quicker, as that is effectively what their player base wants, that is what Relic does.
The standard of coder support is woeful. Balance patches generally introduced an array of bugs, which oddly tend to favour the German side ( and the game is no longer supported). Meanwhile the core mechanic in the game, infantry veterency, didn't even work until late last year for the British forces. Hence your highly prized veteran infantry were no better than newly created German ones. When they fixed it the games got longer, which gave the Britis a chance, so they nerfed them into the ground.
You can win, but it takes you half an hour to an hour to do so. Most of which you're holding on by the tip of your fingernails. Axis forces on the other hand are likely to run over you in 15 minutes or less.
It can be fun playing 4v4 as the Brits as long as you have a couple of more aggressively set up Russian or American allies. But only really with one commander ( who you have to pay extra for) and only in a stodgy slow grinding sort of a way. The game effectively forces you to build a sim city where the other factions are mobile. Basically to hold on long enough and soak up enough axis pressure, artillery and manpower for the Americans or Soviets to win.
So if you want free wheeling combined arms attacks and strategy look elsewhere. If you want to be reminded that the Axis forces won WW2 with their superhuman men and superior tanks then consider it.

First the summary; Don't buy this game unless you have money to waste! Read why below..
I got it as part of a paid for bundle and would never have specifically chose this game on its own based on the video on the sales page.
#Well, it's not a SIM, (I knew that from the video on the sales page. More about that later).
Here's why I'm punching this game in the face! Mission 20 = Black - not night - just black holes of nothing visible to see or click on. There was one mission like it earlier, I don't know the number, but it was totally stupid.
I tried to brighten the game graphics and my PC screen but there was still nothing visible. I guess the devs must have made it this way, like you can click something, but you won't know if it's worked or not until you drive your train.
Reverse the engine up to the wagon, hitch it up. Nothing - no click sound and no visible clue as to if it is connected. Pull the engine forward, the carriage didn't move.. Did this over and over and over again, Arrrrrrggggggg, how stupid this is..
Pools of light under the streetlamp-esk floodlights along the trackside on the shunting bays, but on the approach track where the train-carriages are to be shunted from, are totally in the dark, there was nothing - you couldn't select anything because there was nothing to click, nothing showed up.  I spent ages clicking in the black areas, not knowing if I had got it or not. Reverse the train up to the carriages, nothing to click in the black areas.
You'd never work 'blind' like this.  It's just stupid, totally stupid. Its no fun and what's more it is totally boring, what the heck were the devs thinking when they made this mission?
I was peaved with this game after the first few missions because of the direction controls changing all the time, (see later); but I gave the game (and the devs), more opportunity to try and entertain me. I don't like to hammer nails into coffins before the person inside is actually dead. But this 'SIM' ha ha, needs burying...
I wanted to give this game a real good chance as I love train type games. That's all it is 'Just a game'. But after 3 hours of playing it, (I think I've given it a good chance to impress me in some way), but it fails to amuse me and actually p's me off- on most of the missions. Like: every mission is basically the same!
For example: I've had a firman on standby in many missions yet after 20 missions I still have seen no-use for him, no fires or smoking wagons etc. Don't even know why he's in the game?
Next: You start with breaking carriages from the main line 3 - onto lines 1 and 2 - later its lines 1 and 3 all the time. By mission 19 you are still just breaking a train of carriages down onto lines 1 and 3. Man, that's gets old real quick.. What the heck were the devs thinking? A little research into what goes on in a shunting yard would have helped them.
Next; there is an issue to take up with the developer' Look - forwards and reverse does not change! A train has a front and a rear - and whilst it can usually push or pull equally well in either direction, forwards and reverse still remains the same.. Don't the devs know how to do research?
'W' is accepted by most keyboard driving games as being forwards - and 'S' would be reverse. - The most annoying thing about this game, (although there were several things), was the fact that the forwards and reverse keys kept changing their function, depending upon which direction you were facing!
Like most people, logically I think if I am looking backwards from the vehicle and want to reverse, that I will naturally press the 'S' key.. But, if I decide to spin the view, suddenly 'W' becomes the reverse key? How stupid is that?  That's the main reason why I am going to say and recommend that you don't waste your money on this game.
It becomes more of a pain when you realise that you can drive the train from wherever you are on foot. So you decide to bring the train to you, waiting for it to appear through a foggy morning mist, by the wagons you need to shunt around.. . Then you realise it had gone in the wrong direction because of the direction you were facing when you tapped 'W' four times.
There are other things too, like there was a dark-black mission, NOT JUST NIGHT TIME! I mean total black! It was meant to represent night time I guess, but there were areas where total non-visibility. I struggled for 40 minutes on the mission that should have taken me 5 minutes, if only I could have seen what I was doing!
There are usually green track markers that light up the track selection - there were none in the dark-black missions. There was also no-visible wagon connecting spots, in the dark-black missions, yet in normal daylight there were big yellow, and green glowing spots. What's that about?
Finally : I could see it was just a 'game' game and not a real simulator, from the video on the main sales page, so I didn't really expect much by way of simulation. My point here though is, devs should stop calling their games  'simulation', especially in this day and age when we expect a little more from a game that calls itself a 'SIM'.
If you don't already understand that concept of 'SIM' over 'just a game'. then I ain't going to bother trying to explain it to you, because if you don't already understand it you won't agree anyway. I'm just annoyed that devs call their games 'SIM' when it is clearly just a game. Not even a good game!
The concept of making a train shunting yard game, is a good idea, but the way the devs have done it, means the game makes no progress. Career Mode? What career?  Its just the same mission over and over again with random track and wagon breakdowns.
I won't be playing it any further. Sorry devs.

This game was a pleasant surprise. What plot that exists is completely ridiculous and is just a bunch of odd excuses to have levels in varied interesting settings (e.g. Atlantis, age of dinosaurs, Mad Max's Thunderdome, a medieval castle, and more). The gameplay is unique and interesting, though. It is a 2D run 'n gun game where you can rewind time and play alongside ghost versions of yourself through levels. Levels are timed and you need to work together with other versions of yourself to beat them in time. I found it to be pretty clever. The level replays are fun. When you beat a level, you get to watch a replay with all your lives/runs playing together to beat it. Normal difficulty was pretty forgiving; you unlock hardcore hard mode when you beat the game (you keep all characters you have unlocked for hard mode), and it has an interesting twist; if a character dies on hard, you cannot play that character any more during that level, unless you save the character from death with a different character.
Recommended if you like unique games and 2D run and gun platformers.

Any game that can actually bring physical tears to my eyes is an automatic 10/10.
LISA is an automatic 10/10.
More detail below.
The story is where LISA shines.  You play as a man haunted by drug addiction and a troubled past, wondering how he can redeem himself in his own eyes.  Then, one day, the answer presents itself...
Or,
self.
As much as I'd like to get into the story, for your convenience and enjoyment, I can't.  I recommend going into the story as blind as you possibly can.  The only complaint I have about the story is I feel some characters got the short end of the stick from a narrative perspective.  I would've loved to know a bit more about some of the characters, but after looking into the developer's reasoning, I can forgive it.
The aesthetics of the game are rather unique.  A fun, expressive art style accompanies your adventure throughout the game.  If you aren't a fan of pixel art, this game likely won't change your mind, though.
The music, my GOD the music.  There are SO MANY JAMS on this soundtrack.  It's worth buying alongside the game.
The game is full of personality, and carries a heavy atmosphere and storyline, but also knows when it's appropriate to be funny, something that's very hard to master.
You can bump this up or down to whatever you want depending on your opinion on turn-based RPGs.  I love me a good RPG, and I love the feeling of progression they give you.  However, it's a double-edged sword.  There is such a thing as 'too much of a good thing'.  Thankfully, LISA's gameplay wasn't just cut and paste despite being an RPGMaker game.  The DLC adds a bit of freshness to the combat.
If I hadn't played the DLC, this category would probably get a 5/10 instead.
This game is $15 base price.  You get around that same amount of gameplay in hours.  I think that's a fair trade.  I would go so far as to mandate you get the Joyful DLC in addition to the main game.  It picks up immediately after the base game ends and wraps the story up nicely.
LISA is one of the few remarkable RPGMaker games I've seen.  If this puts you off, bear in mind that I didn't even know it WAS an RPGMaker game until I started playing.  It's got a homely pixelated art style that expresses just enough of the characters but still leaves the details to the imagination.  The gameplay is your standard turn-based RPG battle fare.  It's nothing you haven't seen before, but it's serviceable enough.  It never got boring for me.
I adored the characters and the final act of the story brought me to tears.  Actual, physical tears.  The Last of Us didn't do that.  Life is Strange didn't do that.  Mass Effect didn't do that.
LISA did.
That's why LISA and its DLC has undisputedly earned its:
If this game goes on sale for below $10, you are doing yourself a disservice if you do not buy it.

First of all I'd just like to say that this game is amazing and a ton of fun. If you like competitive games similar to this then you have no excuse but to buy it; especially at such a reasonable price. From what I've played the community has been nice and very helpful, in fact someone volunteired to teach me some of the more advanced mechanics of the game. I've not gotten to an extremely high level within the game, but I can with reasonable confidence say that the game is skill based and has quite the skill ceiling.
A warning however is that before you understand the game it could be frusterating for some people since you may not know what you did wrong. Actually I have one tip for people that are just getting into the game, keep in mind that there are three difference staces and an arial state for when you're jumping. Someone can break your stance with an attack from a superior stance, thus breaking through your attack and cancelling it. Fast stance beats arial, medium beats fast, heavy beats medium, and arial beats heavy. Though just because you're using a superior stance than the enemy doesn't mean that they might not hit you first or attack faster, so get used to timing your attacks just right.
One more thing about the game is that everyone seems to develop their own unique style of sword play, and by no means are any of them better or worse than others apart from the skill of the swordsman. Not only can you develop your own style of play, but you can compliment it by selecting what character/sword combination you want to use. If you want to be big and hard hitting character and slow but satisfying attacks you can pick Judgement with the Longsword as a devestating conbination. Or if you'd rather deal your damage with speed, then try Pure with the Scimitar. Either way the game will be super fun with lots of variety. (One last tip, I'd reccomend when you first start to pick Phalanx with the Longsword and once you get used to him try other characters with the Longsword. Once you feel ready and are starting to develop your style then try experimenting with differnent conbinations. This is how I was advised to learn and it worked out very well for me.)
Past that though, the game is a blast; especially with friends. I'd highly reccomend it to any hardcore or competitive gamer that thinks they'll be interested in the game, and even if you're a casual gamer I think it's worth a try on a sale. Otherwise you're only out 10 bucks (Not the deer).
***I apologize for any mispelling or improper grammar, but I hope that this review was a fun and helpful read reguardless.***

This game is amazing. It celebrates the highs of the Sonic franchise and acknowledges the lows. ('06). It features both Classic and Modern Sonic. Aside from the Final Boss, (and a few of Modern Sonic's missions: Vector's Rooftop Run and Charmy's Planet Wisp), every game stage, normal and mission is excellent.
One of my favorite parts of this game is that they provide a whole bunch of iconic Sonic tunes for you to unlock and use as the music to the stage.
The only drawback this game has is: the plot (I know) feels unfinished. They needed more cutscenes featuring character commentary on stages. (Presumably, they were cut for time.) There are nine stages: Green Hill, Chemical Plant, Sky Sanctuary, Speed Highway, City Escape, Seaside Hill, Crisis City, Rooftop Run, and Planet Wisp. Each level has a Classic and Modern level, each accompanied by five missions. (You only have to do a grand total of 9, one per unique level.) There are three bosses, and three rival fights, and your typical Super Sonic final boss at the end.
The format is good. But honestly, without ANY Eggman base levels, it feels like it's the first half of a game that immediately skips to the final boss. Small Nitpick to avoid a repeat of '06.
My personal picks would have been:
Scrap Brain Zone (1), Metropolis Zone (2), Launch Base Zone (3), and then Aquatic Base ('06) that segways into Final Egg (Adventure).
After that you get the flying ship levels, Winged Fortress, Flying Battery, and Skydeck. And then you get the Final Base.
I also would have liked that they included levels with scrapped ideas from classic games like Sonic 2's Winter Zone and Rock Zone and Dust Hill Zone or Sonic CD's 8th level. (more commonly known as R2 due to CD's missing level slot.)
But time constraints, I suppose cut prospective ideas like that out, I guess making it a 21st anniversary game with the slogan 'He's legally an adult now.' probably wouldn't have worked.

Imagine the graphics of Rayman 1 with the speed of Sonic 3 and Knuckles, the control of Sonic CD mixed with Rocket Knight and Shantae, the explosive boss battles of Gunstar Heroes, and the kickass soundtrack of a beloved 90's action game all wrapped up into one nice, beautiful little indie game package and you have yourself Freedom Planet. Much like Shovel Knight, this game is a throwback to all the kickass platformers back in the simpler days that focused more on high-speed fun and enjoyable level design that keeps you wanting to play, rather than the modern day stuff where developers find what sells the most and rehash it until the once perky mounds of enjoyment become saggy and undesirable. Whereas Shovel Knight catered more to the Nintendo side of the old days, Freedom Planet caters more to the SEGA side of things, and I love it for that.
The controls are tight and responsive, the visuals are amazing and unlike most other throwback indie games, don't rely on pseudo 8-bit to give a feeling of nostalgia, the sound effects and music are spot on and really drive the sense of atmosphere home, the voice acting (yes there is voice acting in this) is especially good despite the small development team, and though the story may seem a bit...basic and random, it develops the characters quite nicely and makes you think more of the characters as actual living beings instead of merely icons that exist only to save the day. If there's one thing I have to complain about, it's that the collectible cards for the gallery in each level don't really do anything other than serve as a means to get an achievement. It comes off as more of a nitpick though, as older games had plenty of collectibles that only existed for bragging rights, but it could've doubled replay value if the cards let you view concept art or something after collecting them, as even people who aren't completionists by normal standards would have a reason to seek them.
I highly encourage anyone looking for a good action platformer to pick up this game; it's well worth the $15.

The music, the graphics, and the atmospheres from level to level all come together perfectly to make for an endearing experience. The story is very cute, and most of the voice acting is fantastic… There may have been a grammatical mistake or two (if memory serves), but that was entirely overshadowed by everything else.
Just about my only problem with the game is how short it was. It has so much potential to be drawn out into a much longer game, or perhaps a series (I’m not sure if a sequel is even being discussed, but, in my opinion, it should be seriously considered – perhaps with the protagonist being the young girl, now grown woman, telling her child about one of her adventures). The only improvements I can think of besides elongating the narrative would be the ability to further upgrade the grappling ability, adding an optional compass, adding some (more?) Easter eggs, and *maybe* adding some sort of dialogue option which could result in changing the story (perhaps giving the game more replay value).
Bottom line: this game is fun. It’s a lot of fun. At the end of the day, that’s really the whole point of a video game. I am happy to give it somewhere in the range of an 8/10 or 9/10 – but with some small improvements, I could easily have given it a 10/10.

Obligatory header to the review: I focus on four primary areas whenever I review a game: gameplay, story, graphics, and sound/audio/general things that go into your earholes. Gameplay and Story get a rating scale from 1 to 10, and the AV stuff gets a rating from 1 to 5. My philosophy on this is that there are some instances in which a game may not necessarily have that much in the way of gameplay (take Amnesia for example), but the story/atmosphere/whatever it may be is reason enough to pick it up. Also, take the cumulative score with a grain of salt; it's just a numerical feeling about the game as a whole. That's part of why I do these subscores. Also, keep in mind that I'm not going off of school grade based rankings. A 5/10 denotes what I feel to be an average game. Likewise, 7/10 is a game that I think is pretty cool, and something that gets a 2/10 is near-abomination level. Pinning scores to an even further obfuscated rating scale is kinda senseless, but for the sake of my backloggery, I'll repeat again that 1.0-2.7 is a one-star game, 3.0-4.7 is a two-star game, 5.0-6.7, 7.0-8.7, and 9.0-10 are three, four, and five stars, respectively.
Additional note: This review will be shorter and will be written in respect to the first in the series (Blackwell Legacy), since this is an episodic sort of series.
Gameplay: The biggest addition is the ability to use Joey and Lauren (Rosangela isn't the protagonist to this game, much to my surprise) independently. This is used fairly often throughout the game. If you're coming from the first game, I'd still recommend leaving hints on, as otherwise this mechanic may blindside you (as it did me, wondering when Lauren was gonna finish her dang cig). Puzzles are a little bit more logical this time around, although one issue I had was that both my solution and the game's solution made sense (I thought of recording the song with my dictaphone and letting C hear it so he could get the ball rolling on what happened). It's better enough to show a marked improvement from the first game. 7/10.
Story: Again, the big surprise for me was that we weren't playing as Rosangela this time around. I called one of the big twists early, which was kinda disappointing to me.  Hopefully the Countess isn't who I think it is, since that would be disappointingly easy to figure out. I enjoyed the slightly non-linear story, since you could do either case first. In terms of writing, it is a bit of a step down from Legacy, but it's still enjoyable nonetheless. 7/10.
Graphics: It seems like we've gotten a consistent art style now, which is great. Plus, all the art is OC this time around, and it's all quite good. 4/5.
Sound: Decidedly jazzy to fit the scenario; still quite good. Still a bit of issues with the recording quality of Joey's lines (popping every now and then). 4/5.
Overall scores are: 7/7/4/4; cumulative score of 7.3/10.

Despite the fact that I'm giving it a thumbs up, I do not recommend this game. But it IS a great work of fiction (or maybe not so fictional?) and THIS is why I will never recommend it to anyone whose mental stability I am not 100% confident in.
This story is about a simple man, suffering from a severe case of depression, and it is everything you think it could be, and yes, it ends exactly how you sucpect it to end - in a grim, but realistic way. The thing that makes this not so original story great is the bluntness and intimacy it is told with. The author honestly tells in your face a lot of well expressed thoughts you will definitely not like to read without being afraid to call a spade a bloody shovel.
The thing that makes this exceptional is that it will most likely cause you, the player, to pick out parts of these thoughts that you truly can relate to (hopefully not all of them), and you involuntarily start to remember all the related stuff from your life, and believe me, it's not the the stuff you want to remember, like, ever.
I am not qualified in psychiatry, so I can not make predictions of how this story can influence a person, who is undergoing a struggle with depression. Will it show you that while it is bad, it is not as bad as it can get if you don't turn for help to somebody? Or will it instead worsen the situation to an extreme extent?
That is why I will not recommend this game to anyone with such problems, or even the hints of the like. Even if you're just a person with a sensitive emotional state like I am, think thrice before playing it, for it can mess up your day for good.
If it can cause such feelings though, ain't that a great piece of art?

why didnt i read any revieiws
*After I Calmed Down
First of all, I want to say that I understand Evan, I identify with him so freaking strongly that it hurts. It's so hard to overcome, when everything seems hopeless and worthless and everything is screaming that you'd be better off dead- you believe it, because nothing seems to say otherwise. Those thoughts that won't go away, always telling you to give up, that you're nothing, you'll never be anything, you just take up space and time and inconvience people. You can't think of people who love you; you can't think that you can be helped; you can't think that things could ever get better; you can only think of how much it /hurts/, and how much you want it to stop.
But, I don't understand the purpose of this game, to be honest. There's no saving Evan, there's no message that you should get help if you're suicidal; hell, it says that a therapist won't help you, that nobody will help you. There's nothing that says that this is the reality of a suicidal person, and that's why mental health perception and care need to change, or there's nothing that suggests this is just an insight into someone who's depressed- for all intents and purposes, it paints suicide in a positive light. It says that suicide was really Evan's only option to be happy, that it's everyone's only option.
It is just asking for someone to finally do it. If someone played this while they were suicidal, it's very hard to believe that they wouldn't do it. It's not a bad game, per say, but the content was a mistake- not in how it was presented, as putting people into someone's mind is a very effective way to get something across- but in how it was portrayed, the ending. I've seen talk of romantisizing suicide, and if there ever was an example of that, it would be this game.
If you don't have depression, and you want a heart-breaking look into what it's like to have it, then sure, play it, If you want.
If you are depressed and/or suicidal, or even used to be, do not play this game. It will comprimise your safety; It puts
into your head. I couldn't be alone after playing this, in case I did something I would regret, like trying to follow Evan's footsteps.

Those of you who got the game very early on (early 2014) remember that there was a single achievement for B.S. called 'Initiate'. For some reason, the developers decided to remove this single, FULLY FUNCTIONAL, achievement with the excuse that it was simply a test achievement. This was a big mistake because   a) there's no benefit to removing something that works just fine and   b) it broke my achievement showcase. If you want an idea of how it's broken, either check out my profile or search the term 'achievements' in the Blade Symphony discussion board.
By doing something SOOO UNNECESSARY, Blade Symphony created a yearlong problem for people such as myself. The showcase's calculation of average game completion is also partly to blame but the game developers are easier to reach in order to obtain a quick fix.
With this in mind, I have been (for the last year) trying to suggest that Blade Symphony reincorporate any  single achievement so that we can get a bandaid solution for our profile issues (which they are partly to blame for). In response, the community manager/moderator has made several replies that have either been excuses, empty promises, more excuses, and other disappointments.
Recently (February 2015), a few other games have caused other players' profile showcases to become 0%. One of them was Midnight Mysteries. In less than a week, the developers of that game FIXED the issue with ease. This begs the question, why has Blade Symphony taken so long to provide assistance to those of us they have affected? I have come to the realization that all of the suggestions and points I made over the last year have fallen under deaf ears.
