I'll start by saying that I am a big fan of Jason Statham. I really liked his performance in The Transporter. Took notice of him from then on, from films such as Cellular, The Bank Job, and then there's this film, Crank. I saw it in theaters and have the DVD, but gave it a rental viewing here for convenience sake (and to try out watching movies with Steam...bizarre to think that a game app outlet has come this far, that they are offering films for purchase now). When I did grab it, it was only available for rental. Now I see there's an offer to buy. Anyway I'm getting off-track here.
To summarize, Crank is an adrenaline-pumping, action-packed, crazy and comedic film. It's over the top silly, with Statham running around town like a madman, causing havoc and killing plenty of men to stay alive. At the beginning of the film, we see him get injected with some kind of poison. The poison is meant to slow down his heart until it gives out and he dies. To counter this, Statham's character, Chev Chelios, has to keep his adrenaline pumping. In doing that, he can prolong the effects of the drug that was given to him and he does so with one goal in mind: To kill the men who backstabbed him.
It's hysterical, to see this actor who is typcasted into usual tough-guy agent-like roles, usually silent and bad♥♥♥♥♥ to this more wild and curse-happy individual, screaming at the top of his lungs and be percieved as psychotic. Even better, it's done well! It's a little gore-y and very over-the-top, the idea is rather silly to begin with so it's not for everyone, but I'm recommending it. High entertainment value, no holds-barred action flick. It's got cliches thrown in like a car chase, but the focal point of the movie is always in the lead, never losing focus. It's actually brilliant how many ways the writers thought up how to keep the flow of adrenaline running in someomen. Don't try this at home, though, plenty of feats on here would kill.
If you're looking for a good popcorn flick (that's rated R), look no further!

Probably my most favorite rogue-like on the market. Whether it's pure action or tactical gameplay, Catacomb Kids is here to deliver it well. As you venture forth through multiple procedurally generated levels, you'll find yourself facing the brutal challenges of traps, relentless enemies, poisonous mushrooms, and.. fire ( surprisingly my worst enemy in this game ). You will spend your time exploring and scavenging for better equipment to make your character stronger. And... if you choose to.. you can eat stuff to gain beneficial stats for your character. See that annoying bat fluttering about above your head? You can eat that. See that weird gooey slime making its way across the ceiling? You can eat that. See that ugly goblin that tried to kill you a few seconds ago that's also lying on the ground right now because you decapitated his head? You can eat that. Oh, what's that? You lost your leg? Well, you can ♥♥♥♥in eat it OR you can smolder it with a torch and attach it back on as sort of a peg leg. You're a monster in this game if you choose to be, and I love it.
The enjoyment I get from playing this game is the interactive elements of the environment around you. This means that there are multiple ways of dealing with certain situations. In example, if you see an angry goblin rushing at you with a weapon at hand, what would be your first instinct? You have options. Fight him head-on. Run away and lure him into a trap. Pounce him and continously bash his head in with a rock or any other small, portable object. Pick him up, throw him into a pool of piranhas and watch him get shred to pieces. Goomba stomp him. Cast a spell that can either manipulate the situation to give you a higher advantage or completely obliterate him. Dip your weapon in a fire potion and burn him to death with your mighty weapon blows of destruction. Throw a slimeball in his face to blind him, then stand back as he swings his weapon around at nothing like an idiot ( Then kill him, of course ). This is just ONE of many situations that can occur. There are endless possiblities.
I can't even imagine what this game has to offer at full release. It already shows so much promise in its current state as an early access game.
Is it worth the $16? For me, personally, YES. I'm having a blast with this game. If you're unsure about the early access content, by all means, wait for a sale.
Who am I kidding... just buy the game. It's awesome.

Second in the Blackwell series, Unbound is unique in that it focuses on Lauren Blackwell, the aunt of Rosangela Blackwell who is the protagonist in the other titles in the series. Lauren is a world-weary, lonely, chain-smoking smartass and is therefore one of my favorite characters ever, Unbound continues the retro point-and-click style, while adding a few new features to the game. As sharp and lovely as ever are the writing and music, and the humor is second to none.

Blackwell Unbound is the second chapter in the Blackwell series, where you once again use your point-and-click adventure skills to put wandering souls to rest. Unlike the Blackwell Legacy, which took place in modern times, Unbound takes place in the 1970's, which is why the New York skyline features the World Trade Center.
This is a solid and retro-styled game with an excellent sense of storytelling. As you progress through the story, you develop an understanding of the tragedy in the victims lives and what keeps them anchored to the world. Plus, the steps you need to go through in order to advance provide quite a bit of challenge.
If you find yourself experiencing a glitch where it doesn't register your Steam achievements, remember to verify the game's file cache.

The second game in an adventure series, with excellent writing and an amazing twist here and there that kept me fascinated the whole way through.  Good stuff!
This is a prequel to Blackwell Legacy; and its protagonist is a young adult Lauren Blackwell, Rosangela's aunt.  She and Joey investigate a number of deaths that were written about in the New Yorker, and deal with a strange old woman.
The next in the series is Blackwell Convergence.

Story is perhaps more hardboiled and rather more interesting after playing both the prequel and the sequel.
Even though they took out some fancy stuff like the nice avatars system and the pixelart was odd, Unbound sure has some of the fanciest art on the entire series, JUST LOOK AT THE DAMN COVER. I wonder why they changed it so much on Convergence.
In term of game mechanics, us being able to control Joe for the first time was in fact a pretty good and solid development that was needed to make this franchise once again stand out.
Unlike Convergence character development is small if not laughable, but that seems to be on purpose, since this one seems more like a setup for the last game in the story line.
First title in the series in which I found no bugs too!
Just like the others, get it if you find the bundle at a cheap price and in need for some noir settings and Convergence is worth playing the others to understand it fully.
Edit from the future: There's in fact one more game to this series but I'm waiting to get it on sale before changing this review.

I'm not sure where to begin with this game.  I had recently discovered it from a video created by a popular content creator.  After a grueling tale of heartbreak and suffering...
I can say that without a doubt this is one of my favorite RPGs.
Sounds melodramatic?  Probably.  Regardless I wholeheartedly recommend this game.
The gameplay offered is very in tune with the events within the story.  The battle system combines a blend of strategy and attention, similar to Earthbound's, with varying status effects.  Some characters are capable of utilizing combos using the WASD keys that when used correctly can result in powerful moves you can use to annihilate your enemies.  Others rely on inflicting status effects.  Each attack, even some with the same name used by different characters, feel well thought out and look flashy when used.  Martial arts look awesome when you're using them to beat the pulp out of some dirtbag who just rushed you with a lead pipe.
Of course then there's the part where everyone and their grandfather seems to always ambush you.  Literally every step of the way there's going to be some jerkwad sitting behind the wall waiting for you to skeddadle past.  The game's gameplay has a strange sense of humor much like the characters, the story, and the backdrop of the world has itself.  This game is practically out for your blood with a saucer at the ready and a dainty straw.
There's also a "Hard Mode" in the game.  You know, for anyone who didn't want to tear their arms off, scream in their house, and toss their computer out the window using their teeth after playing this game in the first place.
The world combines a blend of post-apocalyptic dark humor and adventure to it.  You have a stark contrast between dark, grimy, dangerous caverns with eerie music that makes you afraid someone or something will strike out at you.  Then you have literal Power Ranger stand-offs back to back with WWE plotlines and other nonsensical humor.  Then it promptly takes a break to disturb you with gruesome images of death, decay, and destruction.  The three D's of doomsday.
...If we ignore doom, day, and duck.
The story itself is best experienced by yourself.  In combination with the rest of the dark humor surrounding the world of Olathe.  It tells the tale of a man and his suffering throughout his own journey for his second chance.
That's essentially all I can say.  Delving into this game is important as spoiling all of the shock, the horror, the pain, the heartbreak, the terror, the ultimate disgust of it all...
It doesn't make things as fun.  I highly recommend you play LISA.

Story:
LISA is a game that offers what it says on the tin "A life-ruining experience". Now, when I first saw this, I was skeptical about buying it as most games nowadays seem to try and offer deep storylines but end up being convoluted or just plain boring. LISA is none of these. Every new place you explore has its own backstory and if you explore, you will not be disappointed by what you uncover. I can't say much else due to this game being best when played blind and no spoilers are known.
Music:
The music is...unique to say the least, it is nothing like I have heard before but it creates an appropriate atmosphere for the right places, whether it be the eerie tunes of the caves or the calm but sombre BGM to the resting places, you will be immersed.
Gameplay:
Now, this is where I think most of the flaws lie, as someone who prefers Action-RPGs such as Dark Souls, the turn-based strategy of the game worried me as I get bored by them if there isn't enough variety in movesets and characters - LISA has both of these. Despite this, I still felt that having the levelling system reward players for keeping the same party forced you to keep them later in the game and I only switched when desperate for a stronger character with super-effective abilities for certain bosses. Needless to say, if you enjoy games such as Pokemon's battle system, you should be fine with LISA's.
Overall I'd rate it:

Anarcute is a game that involves leading critter rioters against the Brainwash Patrol, who have dominated the world and rule through broadcasting propoganda and I guess sleep-signals (hence the sleeping rioters, and the ones who are attached to the side of buildings).  The game has a cute aesthetic based on chibi models, simplified yet interactive backgrounds, and catchy + cute electronica soundtracks.  It involves massing up rioters to gain abilities (which can also be lost if you lose rioters at certain thresholds), some of which you need to traverse, but the game works well in that you can find other routes and means to get through the level with what is given.  New abilities range from improving speed or stomping, to bouncing and endless projectles, as well as ludicrous ones like enamoring cops with cuteness or grabbing buildings and throwing them on your enemies.  Though I see the most usage out of the molotovs one.
While the game itself is short, that is only if you intend to breeze through it without engaging it's ranking system.  Getting S ranks in cities can earn you cosmetics, from kimonos to tuxedos.  Also getting more critters unlocks special gliterry eyed exclusive animals that can only be gained if you gather all the critters of the city they are tied to.  But it takes alot of practice to get those S ranks, especially with how the crowd controls.  A bit wonky, seems to follow an invisible actor of sorts that they use to rally around judging by how they may crowd and circle at some times.  They also seem to be averse to bunching up to walls, so you may have difficulty trying to grab props to throw if they are in corners.  That said, it's not all that hard to get used to and once you get the hang of it the means to avoid danger is much easier than it initially seems, good reflexes help with reactionary stuff like mines and shock towers.
Since this game runs in Unity, it could use a level designer function so people can make levels, and with steam workshop functionality they could effectively give this game more life.  But I can understand if that is off the table considering it's been out for a year.
All in all, it's a good game and I recommend it.  Heck, I even 100% it and I don't typically go for achievements and I did those while I was at it.

Blade Symphony is those games that have great idea, very original. But suffer heavily on the execution.
First of all, the game is multiplayer only. It isn't a bad thing in intself, but it's pretty bad when the netcoding isn't well made.  Any game with more than 50 ms is unplayable, you'll take damage without even seeing the attack animation. There were some pros and some cons I thought of this game, but what made my mind about not reccomending is this. Blade Symphony is a fighting game, like Tekken, Soul Calibur or Virtua Fighter. And even though it runs on completely different rules, reaction time is everything about these games. How quickly you dodge, defend or counter-attack is what defines most of the matches.
The second great sin of this game, it's terrible in explaining itself, and there's no matchmaking. Meaning you'll have to play to understand the game and you'll always end up in matches where your opponent plays the game for far longer than you, meaning you'll learn nothing and get perfected all the time. There IS a tutorial telling the game's commands, but that's not what we need to know to actually jump in multiplayer battles. Imagine if Street Fighter had a tutorial like this "this button punches, this button kickes, this one is used to move character". And playing with bots will warrant you no real experience of the game either. The bot will just run in a straight line and attack you.
So, TL;DR
The bad:
-Lag issues
-Lacking tutorial
-Very steep learning curve
It might be a good idea to get this game to play with friends only, maybe after a while you might learn something. Unfortunately it wasn't an opportunity I had, so I can't tell.
It'd be unfair to let out the good of this game though.
It has a great idea, of all games that advertised "swordfighting" as a selling point, I've never saw one that came this close before. It really feels fresh and original.
The community is pretty good for an online game. Although most of them will not actually give you a good help of understanding the game (90% percent of the time I got "playing is the best thing to do", the other 10% were gimmicks that didn't worked on higher level players), Blade Symphony isn't the kind of multiplayer experience that seems like a Tourette Syndrome training camp (or Coprolalia if you're nitpicky). The players are most of the times cordial, there's almost no one trying to troll around, and the user-created content is great (I've even had a Keyblade skin).
Maybe if this game had a Single-Player mode or mabe even the "coaching" option like TF2, I could recommend it, but in 4 hours of gameplay I've had 3 and a half of frustrations. Not exactly what I'm looking for when buying a game. Frankly speaking, Blade Symphony never really left Early Access. It's still unfinished.

As a deppressivem person, I can say that this is the best telling of depression I have ever seen on any medium.
Though, a word of warning: this story basically says that if you are like the main character by the age of 30-ish, all hope is lost. That's simply not true. It may be harder to change your career, especially if you've already begun to climb the ladder, so to speak, but depression is something that can be fought and challeged at every stage in life, not just the begining of adulthood.

Actual Sunlight is the story of a man named Evan Winter, a man who is coming to terms with depression. It is not a game for the faint of heart, but in its dialogue and dramatic scenes lies a tale of understandable sorrow. The sorrow of never quite knowing one's self or one's worth is a burden that can truly drive one to the brink, and for Evan, the brink is always on his horizon. Dreaming of a better life with a better job, better coworkers, better relationships, and better hobbies eventually cuts into Evan's comprehension of reality and what it means to truly be alive. In this narrative, the player and Evan will discover what life is, its meaning, and what it is to have the power to overcome the obstacles one faces with that knowledge. Sometimes the knowledge, the freedom from the surrounding obstacles, comes at a terrible price; but Evan, trapped in a world of constant fluorescence, truly, honestly, and simply wants the feeling of Actual Sunlight.

STAR WARS™ Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast once again puts you in control of the famous Kyle Katarn, a former Jedi who now operates as a mercenary for the New Republic together with Jan Ors, a female pilot.
The game takes place after the events of Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II, but before the events of Jedi Knight: Mysteries of the Sith.
At the start of the game, Kyle & Jan have to investigate some leads to the presence of the Imperial Remnant on a supposedly abandoned Imperial outpost on the planet Kejim.
They later find out that the Imperials are trying to find the Valley of the Jedi, and use its powers for themselves.
Kyle progressively realises that without his Jedi powers, he is unable to protect the ones that he loves.
Along Kyle's journey, he meets a variety of legendary Star Wars characters like Luke Skywalker & Lando Calrissian, but you also meet some new enemies like the Dark Jedi Desann.
Besides this, Kyle also visits iconic places like Bespin (Cloud City) & Yavin IV.
This installment of the Jedi Knight series no longer features the RPG-like system that the previous games possesed (the ability to distribute points for certain force powers).
This time around the game just gives you certain force abilities overtime, which gradually upgrade as you progress in the story.
Most of these force powers however are very well done, and they add a lot of diversity to your combat and play style.
A handfull of levels require you to use your newly learned powers to overcome its puzzles.
The game also features a wide array of weapons and items that allow you to develop your own playstyle.
The only significant problem that I have with the combat, are the hitboxes.
In my opinion, the hitboxes are way too small, and often times it is very hard to hit an enemy, even when they are standing still or crouching down right in front of you, let alone an enemy that is running at or away from you.
Lastly, I believe that the game has a very decent overall length, and depending on the difficulty that you play on, the game will take you over 10 hours to complete, which is around the same length as the other Jedi Knight games (in my case).
The game ran very smoothly on my end, with a stable 60 fps and no crashes or freezes.
The only technical downside of this game is the resolution.
The game does not allow fullscreen playing on modern systems, and some of the preset resolutions do not work, but with a few workarounds, this is easily fixed.
The game also features a very neat quick save and quick load system, which allows you to save at any point in the game, and load that save whenever you like at the press of a single button.
The controls are highly customizable and the standard preset works very well in my opinion.

All in all, Jedi Outcast is one of those overlooked Star Wars games that is actually really good and enjoyable, and it is definitely a significant (technical) improvement over the previous games in the Jedi Knight series.
If you are a fan of the Jedi Knight series, or just a fan of good shooters set in the Star Wars universe, then you should definitely give this hidden gem a go!

There are a couple reasons why I recommend this game;
It's smart- what I mean by that is the game doesn't baby you or hold your hand. You're dropped into the action from the start and left to figure out where to go and what to do on your own in relatively large, somewhat non-linear levels. I could almost compare it in that respect to a game like Half-Life.
It holds up well- This game is 13 years old, and while it shows through in some places, like widesreen resolutions not being supported in the options menu (although this is easily fixed by tweaking a config file), the visuals and physics are still solid at worst (generally they're fantastic), and the sound quality is absolutely amazing, unlike a lot of other older games which I find the sound quality is really scratchy a lot of the time. It feels like a game that came out maybe in the early 2010s, and not '03.
Low price- while $11 may be a slight stretch, the price often drops to less than $2 during sales, so you'll be getting a lot of bang for your buck.
Fun as hell- a game could have the best graphics, biggest maps, most sophisticated ai, etc etc, but if it isn't fun I see no point in playing it. This game has quickly skyrocketed into my favorite games list.
For one thing, yes. I know it seems like a sonic ripoff, but I assure you, it's much more than that. What I mean is that while it DOES have elements from the Sonic series, i.e: Sonic 1, 2, 3, and "Sonic and Knuckles" it also borrows elements from other SNES and Sega Genesis titles. Those elements combined make for one of the best games I've played recently.
Diving in one by one, in terms of playable characters, Sash Lilac, to me, derives from Classic Sonic. Hair whips, her Dragon Cyclone, and Dragon Boost make her ideal for blazing through stages with practically no reason to stop. Her personality is very similar to Sonic's with a strong sense of justice and compassion.
Carol Tea, with her various claw attacks, her Wild Kick, and her wall jumping abilities, make her unique for close combat. She seems to me, more laid back, a lot like Tails to some extent, but these are just comparisons. Carol is a major tomboy, if it wasn't already obvious.
Milla Basset... She's actually one of the more interesting characters to me. Her nature, makes her very likeable. Her abilities, with her Phantom Block and laser make for quite an experience, especially when you combine her moves. That and the upcoming update I've heard about, I can see how Milla came to be. I'm honestly excited for that.
The soundtrack, oh man, I love this thing, special mention going to Prince Dail's boss theme, Aqua Tunnel 2, and Fortune Night 2. It's got quite the variety in terms of music genres, and I like that. The bloopers in the cutscenes were pretty funny too, especially the segment where Spade's like "G****** my coolness." The level design is really cool too. To me, it follows Sonic 3's formula in terms of act transition. The levels themselves are awesome. and near the end of the game, things get REALLY hectic.
Overall, Freedom Planet made for an awesome experience from beginning to end, and I'd love to see more content come out soon. Anyway, I highly recommend this game.

Mafia II is a strange anamoly as far as open-world action games go, it has all the hallmarks of a GTA-esque open world game while possessing none of the open-worldness.
That isn't a cut at its merit, rather a literality; the game doesn't possess an open-world mode that can be accessed by players between missions, instead, the open-world is only accessable during missions. Missions in which the player is dragged into immediately upon the completion of the previous one.
It's for this reason why this game is an anamoly; it's a Grand Theft Auto without the freedom to spend your time to yourself between missions doing whatever you want in the sprawling world provided. While this is easily ignorable by the player once they realize the nature of the game, it's bound to take you back for a second when there's a vast world which is completed and stuffed to the brim with activities for the player to partake in, yet is only accessable in missions that constantly impose a direction to the player.
For the reasons alone I provide, the lack of an open-world detracts from the game to a major extent. While the strong plot and characters, which I rate highly, keep things going, the nature of the game makes me think that it aspired to be much more. I can't help but think that Mafia II aspired to be a giant like Grand Theft Auto IV, but instead decided to settle on being an railroad imposed on the player, with tracks placed in a world that was developed more than the bullet train of a ride speeding the player through the chapters.
The plot, while good, seems to rush itself in some areas, and early in the game (I won't spoil anything), the game gives the player a jetlag-like feeling after throwing them into opposing situations in a manner that I'll just describe as being odd. The game's plot gets better as you go through, but maintains minor issues throughout.
I don't like to rate games on a number scale, but if I had to give it a grade, Mafia II would be a flat C student who is just trying his best but keeps turning in papers that consist of fragmented ideas that could've been that just aren't included in the final draft.
In the end, I personally like Mafia II, it's not by far my favorite game on Steam, it's not even my favorite third-person shooter game. The best I can say about it is that it's a fun romp, and the worst I can say about it is that it's a discount Grand Theft Auto IV that can run smoothly even on your grandmother's rusty toaster.
If you enjoy (albeit, limited) third person shooters that have basis in historical precedent, you might get a nice time out of this. If you can get around the limitations of the game, I'm sure you can find
that keeps you coming back to it, even if it's a course of just a few weeks before you ditch it. For me, it's mods.

Consider all the best parts of of organizing an attack team from things like Pikmin, and the madness of snowballing destruction from something like Katamari, and wrap that all around a ball of adorible characters and a soundtrack that is much catchier than it needs to be; and you'd get Anarcute.
Now admittedly, the game is very short if you're not going for 100%, and the graphics aren't anything too complex; but the simplicity really adds to the charm. Which makes this a good game for maybe killing an afternoon or burning off some stress after a hard day.
All in all, Anarcute is a very simple game, but it uses that simplicity to it's advantage, and I'm happy to keep it on my Favorites list and will definately consider coming back to it again if I ever feel the need to tear down a few buildings.

Anarcute is a mix of Pikmin and Katamari that focuses on creating violent riots with adorable human-like animals that fight against evil capitalists that threaten the freedom of us all! It combines a very cute art style that is minimalistic but very effective, almost completely destroyable levels, and a fresh take on crowd-based combat.
Each level starts with just a couple of people but you quickly build up an horde of charming rioters who are then used to fight the corrupt police. There are four different countries to liberate and each of them is divided in five to eight levels and one boss.
Unlock skills as you grow in numbers and tear down even buildings or collect cars and everything else around you to throw it at the enemy! You collect coins from completing levels to unlock and swap skills outside of missions. Free new animal species and customize your army to your heart’s desire and pick only the animals you are interested in. You can even change their costume if you get an S on every level of a country.
The game can be pretty challenging at times, but you get used to it real quick. Stealth levels for example feel a bit overwhelming at times since you barely have any rioters, but it's manageable after you get the hang of it. Skipping difficult sections is also an option, if you simply don't care about the cosmetic unlocks. The controls and the camera movement feel a bit wacky at times, but it's not too bad.
The soundtrack is definitely one of the strongest, if not the strongest point of this game and it's fitting the theme of the game so well; they just nailed it. Each song is bound to make you smile and feel good, and it even makes you care for these little critters. Especially within the main menu, the music is so awesome that I stayed in there for far longer than I was supposed to.
The game’s length is about 5-10 hours which might be too little for the price asked. I recommend getting it with a discount of under $10 which I feel is just the right price.
Regardless of the price, I recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed Pikmin, Katamari, or just wants to have a good time with a very passionate and cute little game.

Anarcute is one of those games that slipped through the cracks. I have very little to say about it negatively beyond wishing that there was more stages, but I’ll address that in a bit.
The premise of the game is as follows: the world is under the boot of a gas-masked dictator and his riot-geared police force and it's up to /you/ to rally your own forces--never mind that you’re all cutesy, big-eyed critters of the land and sea -- and fight back!
You begin every map with a base group and to fill out your ranks you simply need to walk into other groups of protesters, which can be found on the map. Some will require you to liberate them from cages by smashing “A” or and others can only be accessed by traversing laser and/or minefields. You get a bonus to your rating at the end of a map based on how large your remaining group is, so it would behoove you to take extra care with your riotous cuties.
You also get a bonus for completing your objectives quickly and for beating up the fuzz (haha, get it?)
These objectives includes sabotaging enemy communications, surviving waves of enemies, rallying at predetermined points, and whatever else a good riot committee does nowadays. There are a total of four major cities you’ll rampage through - Tokyo, Paris, Miami, and Reykjavik- and each has its own aesthetic theme and soundtrack. The soundtrack is really, really good. Did I mention that?
Throughout your rampage from node to node on the map, you’ll also see dialogue-less cutscenes during which your masked oppressors will behave nefariously. You’ll also encounter boss fights--one per city--which consist of mechanical giants. Like any good boss, these have attack patterns and stages, during which they’ll change up those patterns. Taking down an entity that big and hulking is satisfying.
After you complete a node, you are graded for your performance and rewarded with a single token. These token can be used on the customization screen to buy powers from the vending machine. There are three tiers of powers, each of which require a certain mob size before you can use them in combat. These powers are a mixture of passive stat increases and special attacks, so find the right combination to suit your play style and sometimes the stage.
There is a bonus to completing each stage with the highest rank (S) so that adds a bit of replayability. There are also different animal types to discover, meaning you’ll need to play stages perfectly or play them twice - once to discover hidden animals and once to get through as quickly as possible - in order to reach 100%

After playing over 100 hours I feel like I got enough of a grasp on this game and wether I could recommend it or not. Please keep in mind that I'm not a native english speaker and typos could happen.
So, do I recommend this game to you? In short: Yes! In long: Kinda.
Obviously the game belongs to the strategy-genre, but in comparison to most other strategic games, like for example Age of Empires II, Age of Mythology, Sid Meier's Civilization V it's a lot more fast paced, without the need of putting so much time into building and for example advancing to the next age. There is also not as much economical strategies involved, as in most other strategy games I've played so far. The game is mostly built around fighting strategies, and countering enemies, and of course map control, since the main part of your economical ressources is conquering rally points.
I won't go too much into detail with the campaign mode, since for me, most of the strategy games will sooner or later end with me playing in multiplayer. The campaign is nicely made and you can learn a bit about history and interesting things like for example the russian order 227, which basically meant that every retreating soldier should be shot by his own men.
Anyways, now let's go onto the bad parts about this game: It is basically a grindfest to get a new commander. Those commanders mean different tactics and more variation for your playstyle, and while you obviously don't mean them, they do make the game more fun, because they increase replay value. You can obviously by those commanders with real money, but I bought the game already, including all of it's DLC, which are needed for more campaign missions and most importantly a whole new fraction (Oberkommando West). Grinding is too much, because for each lootdrop you need to win three times and most games take around 40 minutes. While that wouldn't be a problem, most drops are ugly skins, bad minor skillincreases for units, if you are lucky 500 gold, and if you are really lucky a commander. In my 140 hours of playtime I got exactly one commander, so good luck with that. You can also buy them with gold, but they cost around 10k-15k.
So let's summarize this:
Pros:
- Fast-paced
- Interesting setting
- Light focus on economy
- Lots of different units with different strengths and weaknesses
- Different factions with different playstyles
- Well made PvE
- PvP (if you like)
- Nicely done campaign
Cons:
- Lots of micromanagement (I personally don't see this as a flaw, but it can be sometimes annoying)
- Too much of a grind
- Too much microtransactions
As you can see, most of the cons aren't about the gameplay itself, but rather the developers policy, and while I am not one to hate on DLC, I do consider the grind to be a bit too hefty.

Do not buy any game (particularly strategy games) published by Sega unless you are prepared to pay an additional two to three times the base price of the game in DLC and microtransactions before you have what can be qualified as an entire game.

This is a review for the ARDENNES ASSAULT stand alone DLC.  No choice but to place it here since Steam won't allow the DLC itself to be reviewed.
This campaign is head and shoulders above the rest of the game's single player offerings (the ridiculously historically inaccurate Soviet campaign and the mission packs).  It feels like playing the CoH1 single player campaigns, actually, except you also have a strategic layer where you coordinate three companies, upgrade their (interesting and varied) abilities and take on a mix of scripted missions and pseudo-random encounters with the AI.
It's a great way to play for those of us who do not like multiplayer RTS (because we're old and slow ... or for whatever other reasons).  This is much more interesting than mere skirmish but isn't as constraining as the main campaign or as bland as the mission packs.  Admittedly the audience for this may be quite small, since everyone seems to talk about the multiplayer.
I paid a measly 7 bucks for it on sale, but I feel like it's worth three times that, so do yourself a favour and pick it up when it's on sale again if you love CoH single player.  Because there's little more satisfying than watching a Panzer IV explode from a volley of AT gun fire, or a Sherman Bulldozer wiping out three enemy infantry squads with a single well-placed shell, and you don't have to rely on and deal with other pesky humans to experience this joy. :)

Oh and you do not need to even buy the main game since this is a standalone expansion.  Do not get the Rangers DLC for this (the fourth company) firstly because they aren't as interesting as the other three companies, and second, because they are ludicrously overpowered and therefore offer little challenge.

This is pretty much the same review I wrote for each of the two previous episodes of Space Pilgrim, so if you've already read either one of them, don't waste your time with this one.
Space Pilgrim is a cute and short point & click adventure game, which kind of reminded me of the old Sierra quests from the 1990s, except it took me couple of hours to beat. The graphics are nothing special, there's hardly any music or sound effects, but the story is nice and funny, just enough for this game to be worth it, considering its price.
The only aspect of the game that really got me annoyed was the user interface. It took me way too much time to figure out where and how many times I needed to click to use or combine items. Also, whenever there's a dialog box open, it seems like the mouse cursor doesn't need to actually be inside the box to choose an option. Too many times I ended up clicking somewhere outside the dialog box (for whatever reason), just to accidently choose something to do or say.
TL;DR - A nice low-budget point & click adventure. You can enjoy it as long as you don't expect too much.

Gail Pilgrim and her co-pilot Sabina White set course to Leto, in Delta Pavonis. After ousting the police out of their spaceship and helping the rebellion, they need to stay low. Leto is a planet with many retired rebels or pilots and Gail's dad is living there. So, while Sabina will try to get Emet out of the space port and make sure that the android isn't spotted, Gail will try to find her dad as he disappeared and help friends of his... Seems to be easy, eh?
This third game continues the plot from the second episode. As usual, it's full of humor, of Gail putting herself in impossible situations, though Sabina is now joining her in that field. True, the ending wasn't the one I was expecting and I'm eager to discover the final episode but it's nice to have a story that isn't revolving around space ships.
The gameplay is still the same, you discuss with people, you take items, you use them or combine them and you try to make people happy so that you can reach your goal. The fact that you can go where you want is nice too, mainly in Gail's part of the story, where she's using a map to reach each district of the town.
The game is made with RPG Maker. It didn't change. However, what changed mainly is Gail and Sabina's appearance. No more long hair, no more nice haircut. Nope, you're under the impression that they're coming back from a huge rain. I can understand the need to make Gail look like an adult as she was looking like a teen in the previous games. However, while I don't mind the removal of freckles, I do think that her new look isn't the best. Also, I loved the goggles too from the first game. Anyway, the fact that you're leaving finally space and the Quicksilver, Gail's ship, is a good change. You're now on a planet, even if the first act is only in the space port. Gail is in the city and you even have a beach, so...
The soundtrack is good too: when you enter the café, it's like you're into an old one, with classic songs. However in Club Venom, it's loud beats.
Finally, this game is longer than 1 hour. I've played nearly four hours, only because I didn't save my game and that I exited with a wrong move. So, I must say that in 3 hours, you can finish the game.
The price is still interesting, despite the game being longer. So, yeah, while Space Pilgrim isn't the most innovative game in terms of gameplay, it's getting better each time (apart for Gail losing more and more of her appearance each time). So when is the fourth and final episode released? Because I'm really eager to discover what will happen to Sabina and Gail!

The first time I played this game, I was at one of my lowest emotional points I'd been in a while. I searched, "suicide" here on Steam and found this.
This game is all about a guy who is struggling to live his monotonous, seemingly irrelevant day-to-day life. If you're playing this in hopes of some kind of story of triumph or something similar, you will not find it here. At least, not in the traditional sense. Still, I would recommend this game. Maybe don't play it when you're super depressed though, as I did. Made me feel a little worse. Would have probably made me feel some sense of pride, etc., if I'd played it at a happier time.
My one major complaint about this game is its subtle self-righteousness. There is one element where you can click on an item, and all said item proves to be is a diatribe of how you can't possibly relate to the main character and to think you do is wrong. Why would the game developer do this? Just because the player isn't in the EXACT same circumstances as the main character does not, by any means, equate to having nothing of value to compare. Really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off and took me out of the game's reality. It was a one-time instance, but its jarring appearance stuck with me throughout the rest of the game.
So I'd give it a 6/10. Would probably give it an 8/10 if it not for that.

Never before has a game sparked such a huge emotional reaction. Evan Winters is just your everyday guy, but what makes him special is that theres something of him in everyone of us. The worthlessness and misery that Evan feels every day is something that everyone has felt at least once in their lives. You not only feel for him, you feel what he feels as he goes about his day-to-day life, basking in his miserable and meaningless existence.
Thats what makes this game so special. You feel such a sense of hopelessness and misery, but you just want things to work out for Evan and no matter how much he tells himself or you wish it for him, hes doomed to be stuck in his cycle of misery forever and ever. You as the player just want to help him and pull him out of the darkness, but in reality this isnt a game where you are the brave hero. You aren't some noble protector, saving the people from villainy. You are just a man living out your doomed existence.
Actual Sunlight deals with some really heavy themes relating to depression and suicide, so if you are suffering from one of these issues, I wouldn't reccomend immersing yourself into this world too much. If you feel like you need to talk to someone, contact lifeline on 13 11 14

Actual Sunlight is an ambitious project, it strives to illustrate depression and is particularly effective at doing just that; creating a sense of despair in the participant. It presents an array of characters, one is incapable of having any sense of meaningful connection to. The narrative flits around inside our protagonist's internal space, supplanting a stylized life in lieu of the world about.
It is in this space, of having illustrated such a bleak mental space that this game could have reached something deeper, where the title could stand as a metaphor for finding meaning; and if this was the intent, then an epilogue is desperately required to solidify that experience.

In my opinion, the best SimCity of them all, for the pc. For consoles, the very first SimCity on the SNES was the best before that.

Probably the best city building, management and simulator ever made. Extremely detailed, with lots and lots of well done prerendered graphics (the world, cars and some objects are 3D though, so it doesn't ruin the presentation at all). It's the deepest SimCity, and it's also the hardest: you'll really need to grow your city slowly and watch the taxes, or else you'll be bankrupt in no time. There are some problems though. For example, no widescreen support and flawed transit (both can be fixed by mods). Also the game has some compatibility issues with newer systems and 64 bit Windows, so you'll have to use software mode and put some graphics options on medium and low.
Other small flaws are: the driving minigames (you can drive cars, helicopters, planes and even a tank on missions around the city), which are a bit annoying, and can become frustrating due to city traffic and sudden failures. Nowhere near as good as what Streets of SImCity did with SC2000's maps. And the other small problem is that  it tries to mimic the graphic style of The Sims, so most cities will look the same. Still, it's good that they didn't casualize the game to the max back then in 2003, trying to appeal to The Sims audience. Instead, we got the most complex SimCity to date, and I recommend it.

This is a good game. This is what you want from a game. There are a lot of games on Steam. A lot of them are alike one another. This is not like them.
Maybe it's just 'cause this game feels like a good night out on the town with your adorable friends fighting the hostile overlords that operate from the shadows and fund what overtly commercialist dreck millennials sobbingly think passes for musical "art". Maybe this game hits too close to home. Or maybe it's because somebody out there actually knows how to design a game.
The characters are compelling and believable, and above all, sympathetic and complex. There's no painstaking "trying way too hard" gimmick you get from indie developers or big-name companies to appeal to post-pubescent children. The stylistic choices extend into the very heart of the gameplay's core concept, sending a clear divide between you and them, with no unbelievable 1vs1000 do-everything stubble-chinned antihero.
The sound's upbeat, bouncy, which on the surface doesn't reflect what you'd expect given the game's overall themes. That's because you rarely get a perspective of hope from this storyline which has undergone all too many tried-and-tired bad ending gamuts in previous media. The song may come off as repetitive, but it's inspiring and defining.
If there're any flaws, it's that it looks to be too short, like
You might get a little overwhelmed by all the chaos roaming the street when the marshmallow hits the fan, but this isn't really so much a flaw as what you should expect from mass rioting.
The controls are wonky. Oh, not with controllers. They're a peach then. Keyboard and mouse are a no-go. Rotating and moving need to be simultaneous which gets awkward with pressing letters. Controllers are your best bet, but there's a hitch. You're stuck with the monopolistic Microsoft Xbox controller everybody seems to fap over despite getting the placement of BAXY backwards and basically feeling like a New Age retro hippie's meditative glassware collection--and almost as heavy, too. Ordinarily you'd rely on x360ce to circumvent this, but somehow things don't go as they do automatically for just about every other game I've ever tried outside of Kero Blaster thus far. You'll get controller input, but then things get strange, which I certainly can't explain. Can you? If so, you'd be doing the human race a favor by sharing with the class. Basically the controls are mismapped--left joystick won't move, right joystick has the axis wrong, and the face buttons do whatever. And if you leave x360ce in the folder, you may lose the function of your trigger buttons when you cave in and use the Xbox controller you picked up at Gamestop because you had company over that one time in a blue moon's tenth anniversary.
And you will cave in. This game is cheeky and precocious. This game is flavorful and artful. This game is a video game. I've played over two decades of video games, with days upon hours of NES, SNES, Playstation, DS and so forth games under my belt, from back when Final Fantasy was compelling to the golden age of Castlevania which ended with Order of Ecclesia, from Animal Crossing to Smash Bros. Whatcha got there, buddy, if Anarcute's in your library, is a genuine video game.
You've played angsty marines shooting each other in the head and your 2D fighters with ludicrous button combinations a septillion times before. You've played your tiresomely edgy fantasy RPGs with twelve different flavors of humans and an Argonian, and you've played these things to death.
You might not be able to handle Anarcute.

Probably one of the most fun I've had in this type of game. Anarcute is a cuddly little animal game where you go against the establishment and take back your cute world. It's basically a top down shooter/fighter kinda game but you control a whole horde of cute animals on their rampage across the world as they take down a load of cops and helicopters with a load of weird futuristic weapons. There is a very big variety of enemies I have to admit and that definitely keeps it fresh, ontop of that there's loads of different traps all over each level that you have to watch out for. Luckily to help with all that you can pick up a few different enemy weapons which make all the difference, as well as unlockable abilites which you can use as long as you have picked up enough animals in the level so the game really makes you try your best to keep everyone alive.
There are also a bunch of unique and cool bosses that all require different strategies in order to beat them, they are definitely a highlight of the game. The game is kinda short though, took me just over 7 hours to beat all the levels and unlock all the animals, would of probably taken 5 or 6 hours if I didn't bother with extra stuff but I thought why not. Best to get the game on sale if you really want it to be worth it, however if you're a person who likes 100%ing games you'll definitely get a few more hours out of it. There is a bit of trial and error in the game but once you've figured out how everything works its not too hard, some levels can be frustrating at times but never has the game caused me to ragequit and I think that's great, the difficulty of this game is perfect.
The graphics and overall look of the game is great and really fits with the world and the characters. It's quite cartoony and basic but not too basic, the game could have done with a few more super dark levels (there's only one or two that are almost completely dark aside from a few street lamps and neon signs) because they make the game look a bit more pretty to look at. The sounds are pretty good too, they never get old or annoying. The music is also quite good but I think there should be a few more songs in there, I mean it says there's 22 tracks in the soundtrack but unless all the songs are similar I swear I've heard a bunch of them quite a few times.
On the bad side however the keyboard and mouse controls aren't great, and sure in the game it does say its best played with a controller but I doubt it'd be much better, the main problem is the camera and controlling the animals overall, I've played top down shooters that do it better so I know whats right but it isn't too much of a problem I guess. Aside from that I can't think of any problems I have with it, I mean personally I think there should be more content but that's just me.
Overall I'd give this game a solid 8/10, if cute animals and beating up cops is what you're into then definitely try this one out.

The best part about this game is hacking and slashing through a bunch of storm troopers within an extended universe story that (for my knowledge) doesn't exist anymore. You'll enjoy the horrid animations of the early 2000s, janky controls which need to be formatted, and unbelievably annoying and unfair lightsaber battles with NPCs who taunt you like a kid on the playground.  There are some things to keep in mind though, especially if you are looking to play this game:
-	You automatically deflect blaster shots and even on a harder difficulty the enemies are generally coded by a six year old child and run into you instead of for cover
-	Most of your deaths will be caused either by the environment or snipers who are immune to saber deflection (you need to counter-snipe them)
-	Unless you’re using a mod for textures on the environments, you have an easier time navigating this game while drunk
-	Unless you edit it in settings you automatically switch to third person to use your lightsaber. I mean, I guess you can play like that if you enjoy being a baby doofus.
-	Some of the best dialogue in the game isn’t in the cut scenes but between storm troopers before they notice you’re coming up on them. Makes you feel bad that you need to kill them, especially since you can take more time getting to know different Stormtroopers on an emotional level than the girl you need to save because of some stupid tied in love story no one could honestly care about
-	You can’t pick your lightsaber color in the story mode. Like really? Really? The character customization was the best part of the first one, even if the story was just as stupid.
-	The weapons which are Star Wars staples that people recognize are the lightsabers, E-11, bow caster, and thermal detonator. The rest are made up to make the game feel more like doom. And 90% of the time you only use the lightsaber anyway so….
-	Oh yeah, the story is stupid. You go to like, 6 places really.
-	I think the story is a continuation of Jedi Academy?
-	I’m pretty sure that’s not Billy Dee Williams voicing Lando in this one. Sorry guys.
All in all, the game is worth a few bucks. If you’re smart you’ll convince your friends to buy it too so you can spend countless minutes hacking each other apart in a multiplayer server (if you set one up) before you all retire to play Gary’s Mod and look at memes. I give Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast a solid 2.5/5 stars, not because of how bad or good it is, but because it reminds me of that kid who was supposed to be in remedial math, but was placed in honors because his older brother was on the varsity soccer team and his mom was banging the principal. Even though it falls short, it still gains merit because it has the Star Wars badge slapped over it. If it was any other universe or franchise, I could easily produce more effort to give up living  via onset aneurism then play this game.
In conclusion, I recommend this game because it helps you waste time on this pathetic rock known as Earth while dragging you across the universe on a story that doesn't really matter. You kill guys who don't like you because you don't like them, and in the end, isn't that what life is all about?        (Final Rating=   **.5 / *****)

1v1 swordfighting game, explains itself.
There are things that you might not know even if you search for it, that being the experience playing this game and meeting the community. But first as for the game itself it's pretty good, most people trying alternatives to this game like For Honor or Absolver end up coming back saying they were worse. This game does have problems like I just hinted, which mostly comes down to people thinking that the main competitive strategie is boring. Now it's actually not any more boring than a lot of other fighti/swordfighting games, meaning you use a very small set of attacks that are the best and play a safe defense.
Some loadouts take this to an extreme like katana judgement, which pretty much only uses one attack sometimes for entire rounds and without ever adjusting what they're doing. But if you don't mind defense and just like fighting 1v1 in general this game still is good.
To get more specific about this game, what divides this from a lot of fighting/swordfighting games is that movement limitations are very absent, you move really quickly and freely and this puts range and timing more central to the game than options, making the game feel less technical at times. Other times it makes it can feel very limiting because no matter what you choose you end up getting whiff punished by the same attack all over again, but that's because attack choice doesn't matter as much as positioning meaning you should look towards changing how you move.
This game is very unforgiving in the start and you can expect to get rolled a lot first few hundred hours, so if you aren't very committed to learning or winning at games in general either stay away or go on ffa servers and chat. Some people play this game just for the chill aspect so that is an idea to try.
Some people are toxic, don't mind them and if you do mind them don't play online games at all. Either that or accept that they exist and that they are not going anywhere.
The game allows for different character and sword combos to work, with fewer ones being bad than good in my opinion.

A thing people always loved about those cranky old-school ROGUELIKES was the fact that the worlds they presented adhered to rules and could therefore "play on their own". A foe could find a flask of poison you dropped, try it and die. A monkey could steal a bomb from your backpack, run away and explode around the corner, taking an enemy with him. That kind of thing. The game that REALLY popularized this concept was SPELUNKY and, I'm sorry to say, it has also soured games for me since. Many games following SPELUNKY'S example misunderstood this concept and bludgeoned the player with sheer randomness: BROFORCE is the pinnacle of this sorry development. Not a fan.
Anyways, CATACOMB KIDS gets it right. It gets it 100% right. Here's what happened today. I found a flask and ran into three Grumbuls. Even one of these dudes is a challenge - they fight smartly and chug potions to boost their skills - but three were a death sentence. I panicked and threw the potion at them - and I was really lucky because it turned out to be a potion of flames. One of the Grumbuls went down, another jumped into a lake to douse the flames and was eaten by pirahnas. The third attacked and I threw a ball of slimy goo in his face. He couldn't see me, so I charged, tripped a trap and killed us both while screaming BANZAIII.
CATACOMB KIDS. Never change. So good.

To be honest, I find it difficult to deny this project (it's not a game in any modern-day sense of the word) a healthy recommendation. But after "playing" it for over an hour, I feel like I can't do otherwise. Actual Sunlight zooms in on the themes of depression, suicide and the feelings of loneliness and uselessness in a very, very direct way, hitting one straight in the face time after time after time. It does so alsmost exclusively by using text, text one has to scroll through by hitting enter again and again and again. There's not much more "gameplay" except for walking around your depressive character in a generic environment and talking to objects and people. This triggers ... more text ofcourse. Whole the time, one gets confronted with ideas and opinions about how bad/gross modern society is to its core.
Now I don't have a problem with text-based games as such - back in the 1980's several excellent games were text-based -, but the actual texts used here, and the way the different themes are handled, is really too grim and too "in-your-face" for me. Having experienced the loss of a loved one to suicide quite recently, I could hardly bear playing this. Themes like these presented in such a direct way as here, should imo be the subject of therapy-sessions in a well cared-for, safe environment. To punch this through one's throat as it's being done here, may help in making a point, but it's not healthy for the ones playing or rather reading it.... So be careful, I guess, and try this one at your own risk.

I don't write reviews very often- mostly because I'm not very good at it and I don't really consider my opinion to hold much weight in any sense; however, something else that doesn't happen very often came with this game: LISA made me feel something.
I like LISA, it's a good game. Don't get me wrong, it's a fantastic experience. The jokes are funny, the writing isn't autistic, and it's an interesting story. My problem comes with the fact that no part of the game holds under any criticism I have.
Brad is the main character, he's deeply flawed and that's what makes him interesting. His family upbringing was complicated with him being abused and the brother to a sexually abused suicide victim who is the game's namesake. This trauma has led him to becoming a drug abuser as he woes over being unable to save his sister. This drug of fascination- Joy- mutates its recipients into disgusting, homunculus-like creatures.
Brad himself is somewhat unlikeable. His personality is dry and bland, but it's clear that's what the creator was going for. My only criticism is that no matter how you play the game, Brad ends up the same way.
The game is set in a post apocalyptic wasteland. The White Flash has robbed people of their civility and the world of its women. Brad finds the only female baby child, she gets kidnapped. That is the beginning of the plot.
I don't really want to go into describing the plot, but it's interesting enough. You look for the girl because you're her paternal figure and are worried that she will be taken advantage of in this wasteland. But there's one glaring problem with the story as it goes on: none of your decisions matter. Not a single thing you do will change the outcome of the game. That's fine, don't get me wrong- but with an ending so bitter sweet and unavoidable as it is, it really just drains me from playing this game ever again.
Additionally, the combat is just atrocious. I accidentally started my first (and final) run on hard mode, and I decided to not take the drug joy at all. This is the hardest set of conditions possible unless you want to further handicap (in details I go into later). This game isn't hard. There are too many abusable follower sets. Birdie is the most overpowered piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥I've ever seen in any video game and he literally destroys the game by existing. Perry and Terry anally devastate any enemy that lay in their way. The only way to actually make the game difficult is to use ♥♥♥♥♥♥ followers, which is just a bad gameplay mechanic.
On my hard mode, joyless run I lost one forgettable character who I threw away during an optional boss fight. I recruited every single character possible- yes, even Buckets. I just save scummed that♥♥♥♥♥♥
Despite not taking joy through the entire game, the aftermath of the game is the same. None of your decisions matter at all. It makes the game feel more like a visual novel with occassional button taps then an actual video game.
Characters are also two-dimensional, even party members I couldn't give less of a♥♥♥♥♥♥about; excluding maybe Terry Hintz, who actually has a personality. The only personality that some characters have is maybe how you first get them, or if they have an addiction or not- which is never talked about except in Birdie's and Nickles's case.
I really like the game's enemy design, I especially like Wally. The joy mutants get boring and I understand the purpose is for them to be unnerving, but there's nothing surprising about them. Peter is the grossest looking (unless I'm forgetting one. The doctor was pretty weird too), and the jumpscare that Harry gave me was gross too. This isn't really a criticism, but the mutants just come off to me as uninspiring. I don't really feel anything when I see them unless they have a jumpscare attached to their entrance like Peter or Harry.
LISA is $10.00. It's not a bad purchase. It took me ~9 hours to complete, but I did all the optional♥♥♥♥♥♥ You could probably beat this game in about 5 hours easy. Even on pain mode, all you need is:
-Terry Hintz
-Odyl for early game
-Rage for early game
-Perry (get him at the cross roads)
-Birdie (get him in area 2 easy)
and you're set.
All and all, the game is pretty good. I don't reccommend it at $10.00 though. If it's on sale for ~$5.00, get it for the experience.
Also the game is set in Olathe. It looks just as bland and dry as after the nuclear holocaust as before it. I think that's at least cool though. I don't see any of my friends so I think that they died.

A group of autistic Sonic fans got together to make their own game heavily inspired by Sonic. They accidentally made a good game instead. Name a Sonic game that's better than this. You can't.
This game has great music and beautiful 2D graphics; not indie retro garbage, but quality sprite graphics on par with Sega Saturn games.  The gameplay takes the parts from Sonic that are actually good, and fleshes it out with additional platforming and combat mechanics.
If I have a minor complaint, I think the game is too zoomed-in, and would benefit from giving the player a wider view. The game would likely be better at double the resolution. The postage-stamp sized view is enough for doing the necessary platforming and combat, but it really makes exploration tedious, so I ended up just gunning straight for the goal on every stage. It's a shame, because the level design is quite intricate: the levels are very large and have many paths.
You should know that all of the characters in the game are furry, and all of the playable characters are female, if that sort of thing will sway your decision.
The story is not as embarrassingly bad as I thought it might be, but I'll recommend you just play Arcade mode and spare yourself. (The remainder of this review will be about the story, so bail now if you aren't interested.) The script has fairly lengthy cutscenes in between every stage, and yet, doesn't amount to much. I suppose you can't expect better from people who think Sonic the Hedgehog is good.
The game has one giant plot hole that is so large it detracts heavily from the entire story. The protagonist, Lilac, and deuteragonist, Carol, seem to be extremely strong, as they are able to hold their own against legions of enemies, including soldiers, monsters, and giant robots. And yet, they are young enough to refer to themselves as children, and don't appear to have any special powers, or notoriety. At least Sonic has super speed as an explanation; it's paper thin, but it's *there*. Freedom Planet has nothing. That's the sort of sloppy writing you'd expect from a work of fiction aimed at children, but the complexity of OTHER parts of the story indicate that it wanted to be taken much more seriously than that.
The game makes a big deal out of hyping up its main antagonist, Brevon, an interstellar tyrant with access to superior technology who has killed countless heroes on countless worlds, and asks the question of why Lilac believes she can win against him. This question is not answered at any point, and yet Lilac prevails anyway. It seems like one of the game's most important plot points, and yet it is completely dropped. Even the standard cliche about the power of believing in yourself would have worked better than the big fat nothing the game offers.
Not only does the game not explain why the heroes are so strong, it also fails to explain why they decided it was their responsibility to save the world. For all the damn talking that goes on, the game hardly explores the two main characters at all. Not only do they lack any special powers, they lack any personal connection to the game's events.
The question of why Lilac decided it was her responsibility to save the world is brought up just once, when it serves the needs of the plot by splitting her and Carol up. Carol asks reasonable questions, and the scene makes Lilac look naive more than anything else. It's the sort of blind optimism that, narratively, invites an embarassing defeat. Sure enough, it leads her into a trap, where she is captured and tortured. But Carol instantly changes her mind immediately after their argument, and rescues Lilac, who ultimately learns nothing from the experience, and never pays for it again.
If the story was more simplistic, or the protagonist was silent, it wouldn't occur to me to ask these questions. But with the script as long as it is, they are glaring omissions. Instead of fleshing out its main characters, the game builds a complicated plot that focuses on the relationships between three countries, all with similar-sounding Chinese names so you're sure to confuse them. (Shang Mu and Shang Tu? Are you KIDDING me?!)  Who's on what side changes between each stage and it's difficult to keep up with, or to justify putting in the effort to bother. The story is definitely overcomplicated for a simple platformer like this. The time you will spend watching the story is ultimately not rewarded; it does not enhance the experience over the base game. If you play Arcade Mode, you still SEE the cutscenes without dialog, Sonic 3 & Knuckles-style, allowing you to imagine a better story than the one the game actually has.

is a retro-style platformer, originally designed to be a Sonic the Hedgehog fan game, only to evolve into a love letter to retro platformers in its own right. I'm happy to say this game is not too busy wearing rose-tinted nostalgia glasses to provide an entertaining challenge and a sense of childlike wonder when you first play it. It isn't so busy kissing retro gamers' feet to provide a satisfying game in its own right.
So what does
do right? I mentioned "childlike wonder," and the game certainly provides this in spades. Though dialogue between characters is immensely cheesy, it ironically manages to add to the game's appeal. The writing is not exactly sterling, and pretty much is exactly what I would expect from a game on Sega Genesis, which - given the aesthetic - is probably what GalaxyTrail was going for.
The gameplay is divided amongst three different characters, who each have a unique style of play. Lilac, the "spunky dragonoid," is a more offensive character who has the ability to basically spin dash in the air and ricochet off of walls, which is necessary in order to progress through levels. Similarly, Carol - the cat girl - has the ability to wall-jump, and has a motorcycle for a power-up that can drive up walls and ceilings, as well as use red platforms to jump between walls. The basset hound, Milla, is unlocked not even after progressing halfway through the game, which makes you wonder why the developer would even gate her off to begin with. Regardless, she has a much more unique style of play from the others. She can use ranged attacks, produce a shield to block attacks, and has the ability to fly for a short period of time, similar to Tails of Sonic fame. Each character has a health bar, but Milla has a decidedly smaller one, supposedly keeping with the theme that she isn't much of a fighter.
The inspirations from Sonic the Hedgehog are made abundantly clear in this game, and yet, the game has a far greater focus on platforming than speed, unlike many of the newer Sonic games. In fact, I would argue even unlike the original Sonic games. Speed almost takes a backseat: you aren't necessarily rewarded a ranking at the end of each level for how quickly you can complete a level. It's worth fighting enemies, as they tend to drop blue gems which you can collect to get extra lives (kind of like a retro platformer, huh?), but instead of 100, you must collect 150. Some enemies drop orbs which can be collected to unlock a bonus stage at the end of each level where you roll a die that you can hit repeatedly in order to reroll and hopefully get a different reward, whether it be a plethora of shields or 1-ups.
Speaking of shields, like the Sonic games, this game does have shield powerups, but they're rather unintuitive. There are several to choose from, and they all block you from taking damage, but what exactly the function of each one is is up to you to find out. A yellow, polygonal shield in the game lets you collect gems from a distance, a blue shield producing bubbles lets you breathe indefinitely underwater (an aside, this game has the most intuitive swimming controls I've seen in a platformer in some time), and a silver shield, fire shield, and pink sakura blossom shield that seem to make you invulnerable to certain attacks (the silver shield protects you from taking damage from spikes).
All of these mechanics come together to produce a retro platformer that is hard to forget, and that I find myself booting up repeatedly just to play through the same levels over and over again just to get better. It's a challenging platformer, the likes of which I simply don't see much of anymore - at least from the Mario and Sonic franchises. The absolutely stellar soundtrack composed by Woofle and the beautiful Genesis-era aesthetic are icing on the cake. Each level is nicely varied with its own, unique mechanics, and each boss provides an almost controller-biting challenge. One caveat, however, is that these bosses seem to have a slightly wonky difficulty curve, creating this curious scenario where a boss six levels into the game is somehow easier than one from two levels ago. I'm willing to chalk this up to subjectivity: whoever play-tested the game probably thought the bosses were the perfect difficulty curve, but I found ways to easily exploit some of them. Except the final boss, of course: he's impossible to fight if you don't practice.
At an MSRP of $15, I'm shocked at how few people own a copy of
. It's one of the best platformers of recent memory, up there with everyone's darling Shovel Knight. It's challenging, but not hardcore punishing in the way a game like Super Meat Boy might be. You'll have plenty of fun exploring the different levels, trying to best a boss without taking any damage, or even gathering all the collectible cards. (I guess it wouldn't be a platformer without collectibles...) Top it off with the most convincing retro stylization I've seen in a game attempting to appeal to retro sensibilities, and I find it impossible not to recommend.
This game was Kickstarted, but don't let that put you off of one of the best platformers of all time. If you're anything like me, you'll find yourself in absolute delight playing this game. The fact that it hasn't had anywhere near as much press as other fantastic indie games like Shovel Knight is almost criminal, to me. I can only hope my review will convince some people to pick it up and discover for themselves a love letter to Sonic fans that doesn't try desperately to clone the franchise it's inspired by. It's a better Sonic game than any of the recent Sonic games, and it's not even trying to be. I don't know if I could possibly praise this game enough.
Please, buy
. If you enjoy retro platformers, you will not regret this one.

You command a small space ship running away from the evil rebel fleet. Initially you try to survive through enough jumps to get back home to warn the empire, then you fight the rebel fleet itself. Rince'n'repeat.
What makes FTL click is the varied set of random encouters you come across every game. The encouters force you to adapt your plan depending on spoils of war you manage to grab on your way back home. Almost every game ends up being somehow different and you can further add variation by choosing a different ship altogether.
One game lasts maybe a bit more than an hour at maximum, which turns out to the be just right. Most games are enjoyable and satisfying without requiring you to commit to a daily grind or forcing you to sit down for hours to conclude a storyline that has run it's course already.
Gameplay wise FTL is slick. The UI works nicely, the hotkeys are well thought out and in general there's very little to complain. The visual style may look a bit dull at times, but it serves the actual gameplay with its clarity. The combat system may get slightly repetetive, but usually there's enough finesse and smaller variations that keep stuff fresh enough. Even at it's most repetetive, the short game span makes sure you still experience progress towards more interesting bits of the game. Once you start to feel comfortable with the base game, unlockables and achievements offer you more reasons to stray off from your routine solutions.
Overall, a highly enjoyable game that can be easily enjoyed even in smaller portions.

Well I thought I'd review this game after 150 hours. I want to write this review as I have noticed the recent reviews have been 'mixed'.  COH2 Is a very good RTS WWII game, in fact I would say that it is one of the strongest titles in the genre of late. Of course, there are fantastic WWII strategy games that have existed in the past, but this, in my opinion, sits at the top of the new releases. The reason for this is that it makes you feel like you are a WWII commander. Forming defensive lines, deciding when to push and when to retreat, taking risks and cutting supply lines and, most importantly, BIG GUNS. What makes this game is definetly the abundance of content in the modding hub. You can get increased population caps, free maps, skins, bulletins etc. I saw some reviews stating the AI isn't balanced as the hardest receive more resources making it impossible to get the upperhand. If i had only played this game for 20 hours I would be inclined to agree, however, this ridiculously hard AI setting is great for two very important reasons. 1) During the second world war there were so many instances where one side had more resources available but lost due to stupid tactics (this AI setting means you can try some of these and try out some creative solutions to very big problems like anti tank guns and anti-tank infantry) 2) It makes you a better competitive player to play harder AI - this game is all about speed, you must gather resources and positions quickly and produce an appropriate millitary early on! If you are considering buying this game I will tell you this, COH2 is unlike a lot of RTS games where the focus is more heavily placed on maintaining your supply lines and territory and building units rather than farming resources and building bases. It provides intense battles where you genuinely fear losing your men. Buy it if you like high energy RTS.
