This is a good game. If you like isometric RPGs, you'll love it. If you like story-heavy games, you'll love it. If you like cyberpunk stuff, you'll love it. I think we're very lucky that Harebrained Schemes was able to make Dragonfall and HK. They're both excellent and worth playing.
The obvious comparison for HK is with Dragonfall. The setting for both is somewhat exotic compared to the usual Shadowrun setting of Seattle. Both have similar setups. You lead a group of Shadowrunners on missions to pay the bills while a more personal, but more complicated mission slowly opens up to you. You have a hub zone with NPCs you can interact with and help/exploit. The combat is largely the same. If you liked Dragonfall, you'll like HK.
I do have some nitpicks, though. The NPC dialogue in the hub zone can get a little wordy. I'm no stranger to reading text in an RPG, but honestly after the third time having to run around the hub zone reading about everybody's multiparagraph problems, I started to lose interest and just skim. The decking sections where you're in the Matrix weren't implemented that well. It's a live-action stealth section where your movement isn't precise enough and the camera system limits your visibility in frustrating ways. I also found that the game tended to lag in the Matrix and in the hub zone and that the game takes a long time to save. I don't recall if this was also an issue in Dragonfall.
Overall, I had an excellent time with this and I highly recommend this game.

Shadowrun: Hong Kong, the third standalone title in Harebrained Schemes critically acclaimed Shadowrun series, is a turn-based strategy cyberpunk R.P.G. developed by Harebrained Schemes and published by Harebrained Holdings. Raymond Black is the man who took you and your foster brother Duncan Wu in as children and saved you both from living a harsh orphans life on the mean streets of Seattles crime ridden Barrens district. He raised, mentored and made the two of you into the men that you are today...you literally owe him your lives. Years later after receiving a highly cryptic message from Raymond, he desperately asks you to come to Hong Kong to meet with him. After immediately dropping everything and rushing to China, you find that Raymond mysteriously never shows up for the meeting and even worse you, your brother Duncan and some Shadowrunners are ambushed by the H.K.P.F.(Hong Kong Police Force). A vicious firefight ensues and you barely manage to escape with your lives quickly fleeing into the sewers with the help of the surviving Shadowrunners. Now branded as dangerous criminals on every newscast in the city and hunted by the full force of the entire H.K.P.F., you must find Raymond, attempt to clear your names and determine exactly what sinister event is happening in China. Prepare yourself to experience the most impressive Shadowrun title yet. Welcome to Hong Kong.
As always the feather in this franchises cap is the superb strategic turn-based combat and Shadowrun: Hong Kong continues to deliver, in my opinion, the best in the genre with this title. The combat is just as refined as ever with a slick, easy to use interface and very challenging A.I. that will flank, maneuver and attack appropriately as they engage your crew. The gameplay has also been tweaked with a completely rebuilt inventory U.I. and skill point distribution system that is much more polished than prior incarnations. One thing that I longed for in the previous titles was the ability to select who on your team would receive any items that you happen to pick up during a mission and this feature has thankfully been added to the latest game. There is also a newly added feature that gives you the option to sneak up and ambush unwitting opponents as soon as they come into your field of view. This is extremely helpful in that it gives you the opportunity to get your squad into strategic place and behind cover before the true battle initiates AND you can score some attacks before the enemy even has a chance to react which is a very welcome gameplay addition. No matter your playstyle be it Street Samurai, Decker, Shaman, Rigger or an amalgalm of the choices there is always a huge array of weaponry, armor, tech and spells, over 200, at your disposal as well as an abundance of new items that have been added to the list. Of particular note is the all new Cyberware skill tree and the Cyberware weapons that can be installed in your character's arms. From razor sharp blades, a whip to various other really cool armaments these new weapons are a blast to play with. As fantastic as the combat is though, the story has also been given the professional treatment. I won't discuss anything for fear of spoiling it but the narrative is extremely well written and truly compelling in it's execution. It's thought provoking and a tad terrifying at the same time while also steeped in Eastern mysticism. This title does a stupendous job of immersing you within the atmosphere of Asian culture, Shadowrun lore, corporate greed and urban strife with many of the "runs" that you go on being some of the most well thought out and unique missions of the entire Shadowrun franchise to date just super fun all around so my hats off to the developers for their hard work. The excellent non-linear gameplay also continues with this title as there are always different paths to accomplish the missions that you choose to accept with some methods bearing more rewards and consequences than others. To summarize, Shadowrun: Hong Kong's top notch gameplay, intense turn-based combat and thrilling narrative will keep you entertained for many hours as you enjoy this exceptional R.P.G. title.
Visually, this title excels in the isometric genre just as all the Shadowrun games do and really showcases the wonderful evolution of the franchise over the many years. Hong Kong is truly brought to life in game with an array of beautiful colors, gorgeous eastern architecture, very active N.P.C.'s and bright neon lighting that is just a pleasure to behold. Not to mention the fantastic atmosphere created with the truly excellent weather effects as the rain from an approaching typhoon plummets down on you while traversing through the streets of this eastern megapolis. As with every Shadowrun title one of my favorite things about their isometric gameplay is the amount of set pieces to look at in the environments and this game builds upon what the previous titles did and easily adds alot more new items to really flesh out the varied places that you visit both indoor and out. From the many buildings, equipment, vehicles, furniture, cables, etc. right down to the piles of trash everything is just so detailed, diverse and nicely placed. Over the course of the game you will visit a cornucopia of highly varied, interesting and beautiful locations from dilapidated shantytowns, bustling suburbs and massive cargo ships to high tech corporate highrises and beyond. Fans of this franchise are quite familiar with jacking into the matrix so you will be happy to know that the matrix visuals and aurals have been completely redone for this title and they look and sound absolutely fantastic. As far as the soundtrack goes, Jon Everist has done it yet again with a phenomenal musical score that is expertly suited to the game with a number of techno and orchestral tracks with an added asian flair that blends in quite wonderfully with the narrative. Yet another impressive feature is the gorgeous portrait art used during in-game dialogue between your character, your teammates and the various N.P.C.'s in the story. Shadowrun: Hong Kong isn't voiced but the exceptional art alone can convey so many thoughts to you the reader on the personality of the N.P.C. before you even read one word of their dialogue. Also of note, the aural quality of this title is top-notch as well with crisp high fidelity sound effects that easily immerse you within the dramatic storyline and engaging dynamic combat. For example if you happen to find yourself in a mahjong parlour, in the background you can hear mahjong tiles being played, patrons talking and laughing amongst themselves, drinks being poured and the aformentioned weather effects of the rain outside as it gently taps on the ceiling of the building. The game does an absolutely impressive job of making you feel as though you're actually where you appear to be both visually and sound-wise. In short, Shadowrun: Hong Kong's graphical and aural presentation is of the upmost quality and compliments quite nicely the superb narrative as well as the exceptional combat of this award winning game.
From the time that you first set foot in China, this title takes you on an unforgettable adventure through the beautifully realized futuristic streets of 2056 Hong Kong as you work the shadows, have intriguing conversations with friend as well as foe and engage in some of the best strategic turn-based battles in this genre. Option-wise there is a new editor for creating more user generated content for the Steam Workshop as well as Jon Everist's phenomenal soundtrack and there are a number of Steam Achievements to be hunted down but sadly no Steam Trading Cards to collect this time around. In conclusion, if you are a fan of cyberpunk, turn-based strategy or just great roleplaying games in general then your  library would be remiss without this superb pinnacle title as Shadowrun: Hong Kong is HIGHLY RECOMMENDED to any and all true R.P.G. gamers!

I bought this hoping it was a mature look into depression and how people deal with it. And it could have been that. Instead, this software -- I cannot call it a game as you are not allowed to make any decisions whatsoever -- is a short story about a depressed 30-something on his last steps to the end.
You never learn really how he is trying to deal with his depression or if he even tries to. The interactions you have with other characters are limited to short texts where you cannot choose your answers, and get bombarded by the wall of text instead.
I strongly advise against purchasing this. The story is an absolute downer and there is no gameplay other than pressing the button to get to the next scene.

Actual Sunlight is an exceedingly well-written and dangerous game. It's about an hour long and features almost no actual mechanics or choice--as the creator says, its intent is more to paint a portrait of an individual than serve as a traditional game. In that it succeeds.
You are--or, at least, you're watching--Evan Winter, a late twenty-something corporate deadender whose inexorable spiral into depression and suicide is the focus of the game. Evan's bleak, aphoristic thoughts on the world are sprinkled throughout in memos, monologues, imagined talk show appearance transcripts and conversations with his co-workers. They're a joy to read for anyone who likes dark and clever writing.
For five bucks, I'm glad I picked this up. It's a very short and human game, and I feel like I know the creator intimately after having gone through it. It's the sort of title that, if a) we were better at describing it all and b) we could convince ourselves to finish anything we start, could come from any member of our strangely disconnected generation who wanted to share their soul.
That said: If you're nearing thirty years old, have any doubts about where your life's headed or any sort of history with depression or suicide, I would avoid it. For those types, letting yourself surrender to this game's narrative is like going to be like playing with fire, or coming home to a familiar drug.

You are Evan Winter. A middle aged overweight failed writer. You live in apartment alone. You jack off every night. You hate your job, your co-workers don't really understand you and everyday you think about throwing yourself off of your apartment complex roof just to end it all.
This game goes through Evan Winters life and how monotonous and repetative it is. He wants to change to be a better person but it is already too late. He lies to his family saying everything is okay. His only escape is drinking.
Every day tasks are made into a complex puzzle and everything is questioned.
Slowly you see Evan getting more and more depressed to the point where he is borderline insane.
Evan Winter is an in-game representation of the developer as this is very similar to what he went through. The game breaks the fourth wall as the developer speaks to you directly and tells you not to ♥♥♥♥ up like he did.

It makes you think and contemplate your life and think where will I be in x amount of years.
The game is very short and only goes through about 3 days of Evans life.
Interact with EVERYTHING, seriously each object brings up new text or an event. Some of them are very clever.
This game will suprise you and shock you and has a sad ending.
I give this game a solid 9/10.

Super Time Force Ultra is a  side-scrolling action/shooter game by Capybara (Critter Crunch/Sword & Sorcery).
You start each level with a 60 seconds counter. You need to finish it before the counter hits 0. The levels are based on various points in history like the middle ages, dynosaurs and also the future.
You can go back in time to do things differently (you must do it each time you get killed) about 30 times each level.
The fun part is that you can actually "save" YOURSELF from dying if you kill the enemy before he kills YOU FROM THE PAST (woah). You need to make several time travels per level to finish it in time.
Each time that you make a time travel you can pick another character, there is a great variety of them (Aimy McKillin is my favorite, the sniper one). Plus, there is a well known character from a famous valve title in this game that needs to be unlocked ^~^
The game has no local co-op or online mode, which it's not a letdown in my pov, cause the game's concept doesn't fit well in a co-op mode. It would be really chaotic to make it, since both players would need to work together and make every time travel to be useful and to not mess up with the other's player timeline.
STFU (yeah) it's a excellent game with a creative proposal, well crafted retro graphics, funny history and addictive gameplay. I recommend it to anyone looking for a great 2D platformer experience.

Super Time Force Ultra is a fantastically fun game to play. I burned through the missions all night on a worknight, it was just that fun. The mechanics are inventive, the pixel-art platform-environments are beautifully created and challenging, the art style is perfectly suited to the tone of the game and the controls have a precision that would be the envy of many other larger titles in the action-platformer genre. The centrepiece of the game is a unique and brilliant mechanic that allows you to rewind and insert additional characters into your game, slowly turning what would be an overwhelmingly difficult platform landscape to your advantage using each character's unique skills in a complementary fashion to solve the challenges within a certain time-limit. Totalbiscuit put it best when he described it as Braid meets Contra.
Very little bad can be said about this game. Other reviewers have duly chastised STF for its dizzyingly stupid dialogue (and deservedly so - the game tries way too hard to be wacky and referential and what passes for humour is reminiscent of the sort of chat site lolz you might have enjoyed when you were nine), but ultimately the game is still a delight to play because of its focus on the gameplay and mechanics.
I thoroughly recommend Super Time Force Ultra.

Date: 2/28/16
Review Number: 30
Game:Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast
From (Creator Publisher): Raven Software/Lucasarts
Played On: Steambox w/Controller
Steam Price as of Review: $9.99
Total Time played: 60 minutes
Review:
Little bit of disclosure here, the actual game the wheel of morality picked was Dark Forces 2, Jedi Knight, but after spending fifteen minutes getting it to load properly only to find that the game would consistently crash on me on either of my machines, I gave it up as a bad job and moved to the sequel.  and honestly, what a sequel it is, or at least what a sequel I remember it to be, though the actual playtime I had reminded me of exactly how slow the game was to ramp up.  Now, I will say without a doubt that as far as first person shooters go, the Jedi Knight series was, and in a way still is, my favorite FPS series (though that title has been somewhat superseded by the bioshock series in recent years), and for many legitimate reasons outside the whole Star Wars fanboy thing.   The storylines are in depth and give you a characterization that is lost in so many of the other FPS genre, the character models were ahead of their time (that time being very long ago of course, so that doesn't hold quite as much water now) and the game did what I believe was the first well done implementation of third person perspective with a melee weapon that I had seen.  Not to mention all the nice force powers you would get as the game progressed into its later stages.  Though in a way, the end of that statement is one of the game’s flaws; because it's far more story oriented than other FPS games, the actual story itself can lend to slower gameplay, which in the FPS world is something that seems out of place now, even Bioshock was fairly quick to ramp up the special abilities and Plasmids, whereas in the 60 minute playtime I got with this game I wasn't even close to getting my lightsaber.
All that being said of course, this is no reason to dislike the game, it has just become one of those games that you want to take more time with, as opposed to the quick and dirty games that I've been reviewing lately.  This is a good thing, really, but it just means that I can’t really review this one as thoroughly as I can many other games.  But still, on the potential that one hour of playtime has on it's own, this game can certainly stand a cut above most of the other FPS games of it's time, and is a definite buy from me.
Game’s Fate: Uninstalled, but not for the merits of the game itself, just more that I know that Jedi Academy is better, so Ill wait for that to keep
Buy/No Buy: If you haven’t played it, you definitely should.  Even if Kyle is no longer canon, It's still a interesting story, and worth the playtime.  Buy

Runner 2 is the sequel to the award winning retro-themed runner game. Like the original, Runner 2 absolutely oozes charm and spirit with an undeniable aesthetic appeal that is equal parts game, visual and musical experience.
Like the original, this is a runner game where your character automatically runs forwards and you must dodge obstacles throughout each level and collect pickups. Pickups within each level interact and blend with each level's soundtrack to create a downright delightful, uplifting and enchanting audio experience while you play.
Runner 2 features a cast of colorful characters with a backstory and tons of extra unlockables including new characters, costumes, branching paths within game levels, alternate level paths via the game map and hidden levels based on the original game.
If you're a completionist there are also challenging achievements that present a decent amount of replayability as well. Runner 2 will test your reaction speed and memory. Initially some levels may seem frustrating but you'll get through them with a little perseverance and probably find yourself wanting to play "just one more" level.

PROS
+ Vast, beautiful areas to explore and traverse
+ Frequent checkpoints help mitigate frustration of frequent deaths
+ Interesting story and gameworld kept me playing
+ Lots of hidden areas and items to find
CONS
- Vast areas often lead to disorientation and confusion
- Some jumps are extremely frustrating
- Voice acting is average
- Achievements are difficult and are for hard-core fans only
- By the end I just wanted to get it over with to see what happens

I can't recommend this game. Mostly because the only thing it has going for it is the story which is... well.. poorly written. (look for a tl;dr at the bottom)
The game tries to make you care about your "best friend" Joe Barbaro. Unfortunuatly I came to actually hate him. Mostly because of the driving mechanic. I did not enjoy driving the cars, and unfortunuatly that's what you'll be doing most of the time. And why? Well, for one: You're the player, the protagonist, so you need something to do. For the other: It's because of the ***** idiot Joe. He gets himself into trouble quite a bit, which means you need to come by and pick him up. He makes decisions that I would never have made, and I wish I could actually make him pay for all the trouble he got me and the family into.
Besides my forced love for Joe (while I actually want to blow his brains out), you don't feel like you're part of the Mafia. Yes, you're doing Mafia stuff, although that's mostly about killing people. You're not actually going to stores asking for protection money and other kinds of making money, no you only get to shoot people.
Besides the, in my opinion, "lack of content" on that part, money is actually worthless.  You're part of the Family because you can make a quick buck,  however you can barely put that money to good use. There's no way you can buy cars, the only thing you'll be spending your money on is perhaps a repair on a car*, although you can always just steal another one (and faster one), or when buying new clothes because the cops are after you. So, why am I in the Family again if I can't enjoy that quick buck?
*Mostly you'll not even need to repair that car, not only because, as I said, you can just steal a new one and a faster one, but also because you'll be driving cars mostly of other people you're driving with. The question then is: Joe, why am I driving YOUR ***** car?
** SPOILER WARNING ** (If you're not going to buy the game, you can savely read on)
Joe gets himself in trouble, a lot. In the midnight you'll get a call from a bartender that he's drunk and swinging a gun around. To be honest, at first I found the driving mechanic actually forcing me to hate Joe, because of his troubles, I have to drive again. On arrival you convince Joe to come with you, however the stupid **** had to shoot the bartender, of course. Now I also need to drop Joe off AND make a detour to depose myself of the body. It's driving that was in no way neccessary, other than to explain a bit of the mechanics of car crushing (where you can make some money with). But please note: You don't need the money.
Later on, after the "final boss fight", you're going to celebrate that business got take care off, and you and Joe are put into seperate cars, of course, Joe's car takes a different route, because "Joe wasn't part of the deal". Unfortunately, you actaully (as the character) feel remorse for the fact that he has to go. But as the player, I was relieved, actually happy. He finally got what he deserved.
** END OF SPOILER **
tl;dr
- The story wants you to care for Joe, but you'll most likely end up hating him.
- Lack of content, you'll only get to shoot people, and drive them around.
- The driving mechanic is horrible, I really hated the driving in this game. (Especially because of the traffic AI)*
- There is no purpose for making money, you don't even need to buy guns, and why should you upgrade your car? You always get to drive someone else's.
- Overall poorly written story.
* When your light is green and you drive to cross the roads, the other side will drive as well, however, they may sometimes turn LEFT, which means they'll drive straigt into you. You're lucky if there are no cops around, because they will fine you otherwise for a "hit and run". Which makes no sense at all: after all he drove into me.

Note: I just completed this game as Carol who plays differently from Lilac.
Damn this is a good game. By selecting hard mode it was very challenging. There was a great blend of platforming and speed running. The production values were simply the best I've played for this genre. The voice acting and music were solid. The level design and enemies made it feel I was adventuring in a world instead of platforming in carefully constructed for gameplay stages. I've heard great things about Donkey Kong Tropical Freeze's environments but I doubt it has a story and impressionable characters like Freedom Planet does. Also each character had a wacky power set that just gave me interesting ways of abusing the game which can be a large part of the fun for some people.
I'm looking forward to a sequel and I hope they refine certain aspects that need more tuning. The story would've been fast and simple if the dialogue would keep scrolling without needing to press a button. Next time there needs to be an option for auto completion because it was tedious clicking a button to move onto the next line.
The boss battles were a treat but I found the 1 boss in the middle to be completely ineffectual midway through the game and the last 2 boss fights became impossible until I dialed down the difficulty setting from hard to easy. The biggest problem with these boss fights is that as Carol I felt my options to react to Brevon was extremely limited. I've seen videos were Lilac clearly jumps higher and dashes further than Carol. It's little differences like these that most likely made Brevon much harder to hit and avoid being hit. Carol doesn't need to play like Lilac but her ability to double dash mid air should have more directional options instead of being restricted to dashing the opposite direction. Then there is the animation delay between a bunch of her different moves could use tuning as well so pressing buttons on reaction against an enemy with random patterns is feasible.
I hope in the future the devs avoid disabling options. It doesn't make much sense to disable looking into the next screen on certain areas of the vertical levels. Having this type of look ahead tool should consistently work throughout the game.
Lastly just give a script a few more passes before committing to them. Milla's relationship with the main characters wasn't strongly established for someone we are supposed to feel a strong connection to. If Torque had gone through the same things she did it would've been more emotionally effective.
All in all I'm glad I purchased this. I was getting this out of nostalgia purposes but the way everything was put together reminded me in general how much a fun a finely tuned game can be.

This is a weird game. It's a 2D action rogue-light in the style of Binding of Isaac, only it's a sidescroller and feels more depressing than darkly comedic. You are best off going in as blind, so I'm going to go into as little detail as possible regarding the actual gameplay.
This game makes an extremely poor first impression. It leaves players to discover most of its core mechanics on their own, many of which are highly counter intuitive and left deliberately vague. For example, the options menu consists entirely of pictographs. It may take you a few moments to figure out how to simply quit the game without resorting to Alt+F4, assuming you do not delete your save data first.
You will be greatly confused throughout your first few hours with this game due to all the deliberate obfuscation. Many situations will initially seem unreasonably difficult, grindy or outright broken, but after deciphering the games mechanics you will realise that the game is much more forgiving than it may initially seem. Despite having some mechanics also found in idle games, it's not an idle game, nor one that wastes your time. However, it does not hold your hand, as you will need to rely on patience and careful observation to progress at a reasonable pace.
If you do become completely stuck, the major game mechanics are described in steam guides, but I recommend you avoid reading them for as long as your patience lasts. Like a good riddle, much of the fun is in the process of solving it.
I initially found myself taking each level slowly, inching along each level in an effort to avoid damage, but once I knew more of how the games works, I found myself running and gunning quickly through the stages in a way that puts the trailer to shame. The more I play the game, the more I enjoy it. If you have the patience to read through this wall of text, you might enjoy it as well.

This game is frakking great. I love the art (pixel art) and the writing is really goofy. If "blackbelt fightjitsu" makes you chuckle then you will enjoy every single thing Dr. Repeatski says. Gameplay-wise get ready for a bit of a mind-job you're first mission. You control an ever-expanding roster of heroes with the power to rewind time, drop in a different (or not!) teammate and try again *alongside your past teammate*. Special powers are granted if you can actually save a teammate that died previously. This lets you create all kinds of cool combinations and gang up on tougher enemies.

This game is both very fun and very funny.  The gameplay centers around the ability to rewind time, and although that is reminiscent of Braid in some ways, is also unique in the way you interact and team up with your former selves, each of which can be one of a number of different characters with different skills.  That makes it more than just a "try again" mechanism and instead it becomes one of the fundemental tools you need to use to complete the missions.

In just a few words, this game is amazing and worth a buy!
Why?
Well, first of all it is the first "Unleashed Sonic" game for the PC and that alone made me buy this game.
Oh and do you remember the Classic Sonic? The one from the Mega Drive/ Genesis games? Yeah, he's here too!
This game is basically a "Time Travel" type of game, because the modern and the classic Sonic meet and go through some old Stages (from previous Sonic Games) and each Sonic has it own style of gameplay!
Classic Sonic plays like the old Sonic games, and that's awesome because there were a LOT of people complaining because the new Sonic games did not look like the originals.
Modern Sonic plays like Sonic in "Sonic Unleashed" and "Sonic Colors", and I think that I don't need to say anything more.
Technically, this game is amazing, it runs at Full 60 Fps, so it's smooth as butter, and that's always nice... right? Yeah, it is!
Graphically, this game is gorgeus, Sonic Team did an amazing job turning 2D Classic Stages into fully 3D Stages with jaw dropping environments!
And I must not forget the Soundtrack, OH GOD! THE SOUNDTRACK! Once again they did an amazing job recreating songs from past games for this game! I can listen to the Classic City Escape song all day long!
Now for the bad part. For me the game was too easy and I could beat it in less of a day, but there's an HUGE dificulty spike (at least for me) between Rooftop Run and Planet Wisp. Planet Wisp was a pain in the butt for me (both Classic and Modern)!
There's also a ... bug? Yeah, let's call it bug. There's also a bug in the Ranking mode, that I experienced both on console and in my computer. Whenever you play a stage, the game will not save your time in the leaderboards. Although this is not a HUGE thing for me, it's something that I think they should fix.
But Overall, I think this game is worth a buy, even if you have the console version of this game!
Even though I have the Ps3 version, I bought the Pc version, because it plays at Full 60Fps, it's compatible with many resolutions and we must not forget the giant and great Modding Comunity for this game (and specially the Unleashed Project, that allows you to play all of Sonic's Unleashed Day Stages in Sonic Generations).
Final Veridict:
Buy it now! (Or the Sonic Hits Collection, because it's really worth the money)

After some flops in the Sonic franchise (Sonic '06, Secret Rings, etc.), this game gets the series back on it's feet, and then it does a backflip and wins the World Cup. In other words, it's really great.
Story: Sonic from the past and present, along with their friends, get sucked into a limbo of sorts. After playing through a few areas, the two meet up. Then they decide they need to help save his friends and return the locations back to the real world- erm, the games real world, the sonic world, Mobius. It's a really good plot. it engrosses the player, it does take a bit to start up however. It's still, nontheless, a great storyline. [Score: 8.5/10]
Presentation: The graphics for this game are amazing. I originally bought it for the PS3, then recently bought it on Steam as part of a Collection of Sonic games. The PC graphics are undoubtedly better, although you can't hate the PS3's graphics on this game either. The game looks great. [Score 10/10]
Gameplay: There are 2 Styles of gameplay, Classic Sonic, and Modern Sonic. Classic Sonic goes back to the roots of the series. Sidescrolling bliss. Modern Sonic goes with the style of playthrough from daytime Unleashed and all of Colors (save for the double jump). Not too much to say about it. Tight controls, high-speed gameplay, it's all really great. [Score 10/10]
Level Design: This game was released for Sonic's 20th Anniversary. This is probably why it remixes old stages from other games. The only new stage is the final boss. However, this isn't a bad thing, far from it! This is one of the many reasons this game was so successful. There are 5 stage types, Regular Stage Act 1, Regular Stage Act 2, Mini-Bosses, Bosses, and the final boss. The Regular Stages are for Classic, and Modern, respectively. The Minibosses are unlocked halfway through 3 of the 4 areas of the main hub. They are just reimaginings of older versions of bosses from older games. We have Metal Sonic from Sonic CD, Shadow from Sonic Adventure 2, and Silver from Sonic '06 (but acctually playable). The Boss fights, with the exception of the last one, are throwbacks to other final (or close to final) bosses from other games. These include: Death Egg Robot from Sonic 2, Perfect Chaos from Sonic Adventure, and Egg Dragoon from Sonic Unleashed. Each fight is really solid. The Final boss is Time Eater, in which Modern and Classic sonic both go super and you take them out in a way similar to The True Final Boss in Sonic 3 & Knuckles' The Doomsday Zone. My only real gripe is that Time Eater is a little bit unforgiving, it took me a few tries to beat it. That or I just suck. [Score 9.5/10]
Music: Along with the stages, the music is remixed from their respected stages (again, with the exception of the final boss), they are all really good. Some of my favorites include Death Egg Robot, Chemical Plant Zone Act 1, Metal Sonic, and my personal favorite, Time Eater. [Score 10/10 (although I wish it could be higher)]
Total Score: 48/50

This is old-school through and through. In both good and bad.
So what's good about it? It does not hold your hand. It does not restrict your actions or freedom. No QTEs of any description. It is bloody hard at places. I cosider myself a very experienced FPS player, and I've beaten this game earlier several times. But jumping into it on third(out of four) difficulty setting resulted in a pretty challenging playthrough, especially before protagonist's rejedification, when you have to rely on conventional weapons.
Fighting other jedi is just fantastic, and is still an eye candy after all these years. You can hack them with your lightsaber, use force powers, push them off the ledges, and even cheese them with conventional weapons sometimes, which is not an easy feat to accomplish. Even regular stormtroopers strafe and move around, making them very difficult to hit early on, until you get the hang of it.
But all this comes at a price too. Level design is just not very good at times from gameplay perspective. There is quite a bit of platforming, which is exactly as not fun as it sounds. Some environmental puzzles are just too obscure - even having beaten this game earlier I still had to use a walkthrough multiple times. Perhaps I was more patient back in the day... Sometimes you have to do things which are jsut counterintuitive. At one point player has to use force to move a crate to reveal the grate You can use force push and force pull on objects, but this particular crate had to be exactly pulled precisely from the left, it refused to move in any other direction and it made no sense.
Also, there is a special place in hell for aimbot rodians with disruptor rifles.
Still, this is an enjoyable game to play and replay, but if you are new to hardcore old-scool shooters - tread lightly.
P.S. The multiplayer is still alive! I've immediately found several populated servers with <50 ping at 2 A.M.

As of this review, the game is currently in Early Access for about $16, so its price and content may not be representative of its final product.
So continuing on to the actual part of the review, This Pixel-art Rogue-like game is amazing. I don't even know where to begin, so I guess I'll start off with the background. I originally torrented an earlier version of this game. Yes, I'm a terrible person, but keep in mind how hard it can be to judge a game from a trailer and some gameplay footage. (Hint: It's bloody difficult.) I did end up purchasing the game though, because I think that the content that they placed for early access was spot-on.
What piqued my curiosity from this game is the depth of this game. There's just so many interactions in this game that you simply would not expect a Triple A developing team would do. While I am comparing apples to oranges here, let's say you're in an Open-world RPG and you kill a goblin. Would you have been able to eat the goblin down to the bone? Would you have been able to eat the bones of the goblin and possibly choke on some while losing health? Simply put, you can in Catacomb Kids. For anyone playing, if you kill the purple slime and throw the ball toward the kombold, then it blinds the enemy allowing you to kill it or let it fall into the traps.
If you are able to, you can bottle a ball of slime and cook it in an open camp fire and drink the slime. Luckily for me, it was sweet. After going through some floors, you can meet a merchant, which sells a number of different equipment. Of course, on the off-chance that you don't have any money from killing the goblins, you can try and kill the merchant him/herself to acquire some loot. It's just these little things, like throwing a goblin into a lake of piranhas to get across without being gnawed to death, that is really fun.
Each time I enter a new floor,♥♥♥♥♥♥goes down. Quite literally; there are traps being activated with spikes from a pressure plate, flammable gases dispersed to blow up, mushrooms that extrude nauseous gases, and potions that can either freeze, zap, or burn you to death. Simply put, each floor is pretty unforgiving in its current state of the game, and on the off chance you step on a trap and it teleports you to the bottom of the stage, you better hope that you don't get stepped on like a goomba. Personal experience from that.
Gameplay aside, Controls in the game are top-notch, but a bit atypical from what I expected. If you have some experience using a Super Nintendo Emulator like snes9x, then you will get into this game a little bit smoother than others. I wish that the interaction between the ladder and wooden platform would be a little bit smoother, but that's something to wait for later I suppose.
As for graphics, the game seems to be currently set to a 4:3 aspect ratio resolution, but won't be a huge deal as most of the area will be covered in the shadows. There's no options for AA whatsoever or quality settings, but let me be honest here. You won't need to worry about having 800x600 screen to play this.
My main gripe at the moment is probably the music. It's not bad in that it doesn't fit, nor is it just poorly composed. I just wish I had an option to turn it off, even moreso it would be nice if the music would be muted when I'm on a different program. Other than that, it's quite soothing.
**
Overall, a lot of people have been saying to wait until the final product comes out. I don't disagree with this statement. I'd hate to be hyped up for a game only to be disappointed and regret investing my money into this team, but this game deserves my money. While I have not been able to get to the end of the game, the content they currently have out right now feels like enough content to be a full-fledged game. Just not for the same price value.
If anything though, I wish that there would be some more random interactions between heading to the next floor. So far, I've been able to see two different merchants, a kombold encampment, and a narrow dungeon. There would be times between each floor where I get a wad of cash, not knowing when or where I'll spend it. Perhaps a clergyman can heal players, a wizard that can imbue weapons, or a tailor can disguise you as a kombold. They're probably coming in the updates, but here's to hoping that this game will be worth the investment!

Catacomb Kids is a real-time roguelike platformer that draws more than a few cues from Spelunky, but approaches the genre in a manner all its own, resulting in a game that mashes roleplaying elements with platforming and inevitable death with a suprising degree of depth and tact.
Fromt the start, Catacomb Kids serves up a generous helping of character diversity, with two (and eventually six) different classes to choose from in the beginning, and an infinite pool of randomly-rolled characters with entirely different starting stats and equipment within each class, not to mention a randomly-generated appearance and name, just to reinforce how different each of your runs will be. Even in the game's current incarnation, the Bully and Poet classes offer an entirely different gameplay experience from the start, and even then, a vividly different experience depending on whether your chosen victi-er, "hero" is, say a clumsy, hammer-wielding powerhouse, a sneaky spear specialist, or a notorously messy eater who apparently realy likes daggers.
It only gets deeper from there, as progressing through each dungeon will yield such familiar roguelike experiences like identifying randomized potions, looting and eating fallen foes (for health and stat bonuses- there is no "hunger" stat), and learning your choice of spells from whichever magical tomes happen to be lying about. There is no "experience," either, at least in the traditonal sense, and level-ups are gained through locating a special orb that appears once per floor, meaning exploration takes the place of grinding, and combat is largely optional if you can navigate around it (unless you're interested in pilfering your fallen foes' gear and potions). Mind you, certain kids may possess a stat that enables them to gain experience in the use of specific weapons, but this is a circumstancial occurrence.
Each gained level nets you a point in a stat of your choice, followed by a character perk in that stat's as-of-yet invisible tree of skills, confering special abilities like charging your attacks, aiming your throws, and trampling your foes as you sprint through them, so by and large each of your runs will yield a very different character indeed.
It's almost sad, then, that for all this depth, each individual run is painfully short- and I use the term "painfully" on purpose. Like Spelunky, Catacomb Kids' levels have a single-minded interest in making your hapless dungeonman perish in whatever brutal way it can, sparing no expense in its "hidden deathtraps" budget, as well as pitting you against some fairly ruthless foes. Even mundane accidents like bringing electric-enchanted gear into the water, knocking over a torch and lighting the room ablaze, and choking on a bone while dining on your last meal will bring you down swiftly and mercilessly.
This is at once Catacomb Kids' primary appeal and its weakness- with no time limit for traversing each floor, players are free to take full advantage of the game's depth in fine-tuning their character's stats, equipment and spells to take their best shot at each obstacle as it arises, but ultimately, all that work can be undone in an instant, and more often than not, it will, over and over again, with individual runs rarely lasting more than a scant few minutes until players have built up some considerable skills (at which point, runs will -occasionally- last more than a scant few minutes).
For those who prefer a quick and visceral experience that doesn't feel like they're losing too much progress with each death, Catacomb Kids is an outstanding coffee-break game, and for those who want to feel like death is lurking around every corner and every moment of continued existence is a victory in itself, Catacomb Kids is a blissful challenge. However, for those who'd prefer to sit for an hour or two delving as deep into the dungeon as they can, Catacomb Kids' death-after-death-after-death gameplay grows stale rather quickly in its current two-class, one-environment state.
Still, to say this game has potential is an understatement- with an original and genuinely fun character progression system that's simple to comprehend and deep enough to play with at length, combat mechanics that are at once bluntly simple to learn yet intricately challenging to master, and a decidedly different character emerging with every run, Catacomb Kids has the makings of everything we love about Spelunky, The Binding of Isaac, FTL, and other genre-defining romps through random peril into the loving arms of near-certain demise.
If you've got a short attention span and a death wish, this game's definitely worth a play, and likely only getting better from here.

Anarcute is an action game where you’re super cute animals rioting against the evil capitalist. You want to take down the man who has suppressed these cute little animals. The evil must be stopped and we must riot with these adorable animals all the while listening to cute tunes!
As the name suggest the game features highly cute animals with a very cute art-style. The game looks very nice, not the best graphics in the world but it’s not meant to have those realistic sort of graphics anyways. The game looks like it’s made by Nintendo as it features those Nintendo Wii/Gamecube type art-style. The game ran over 100 FPS for me the almost all the time I played. I noticed some dips in FPS, though very rarely. The graphics menu has some customizations like resolution, SSAO, vsync, shadows quality, etc.
Just like the art-style the music is so cheery that It made my day just listening to the tune. Super cute and awesome music. I can listen to those tracks all day long. The audio effects and music have separate adjustable levels.
You’re a bunch of cute animal rioters. You start off with a short group of 1-4 animals and throughout the map other rioters are sleeping (I think symbolism?). You just walk next to them and they’ll join your party. Some rioters are trapped in cages and you must break these to have these rioters join you. If you get 10 or more rioters, you get the stomp ability which you can use to push some barriers. These can also be used to knockback enemies. Your animals can attack enemies, throw objects at them, even throw cars at them. Rioters can also knock down buildings once the number of rioters reaches high. You have a level bar indicating how many rioters you have and at certain points on that bar new powers get unlocked. The bigger the rioter crowd, the more powerful you’ll be. You can kill enemies by clicking on them or by throwing cars and other things at them. Stomping also does damage and knocks them back.
You start off in Tokyo and there’s a bunch of levels in it. Then there are 3 other cities like Paris, Miami etc. where you go to cause riots. Naturally, as you progress the missions get harder and harder. Missions include stuff like capture the flags throughout the map or take down certain brainwashing building (reference to media buildings I think), take down statues and structures etc. There are lasers, mines, snipers and many other traps. You must avoid these or you’ll start losing rioters. Once all rioters are dead, it’s game over.
You get coins when you complete levels and you can use these to get upgrades from the dispenser machine. Upgrades include stuff like walking faster, ability to double dash without having a cool down in between etc. You also unlock new animals when you free rioters from cages.
Each countries’ end stage features a boss battle where you have to beat it. These bosses have patterns and you must try to find their weakness and kill them. Once you beat the boss the evil capitalist dictator moves to the next country and that country gets unlocked to play in. All the countries have their own respective theme.

I hope this is doing well, it deserves to. It puts my mind in a weird place. Somewhere between quirky Japanese titles like Katamari Damacy, and extremely well-polished shareware games of the '90s. I absolutely adore it. The controls are honed to perfection (especially the auto-aim mode, which I wish was the default for keyboard & mouse), the gameplay is genuinely fun and unencumbered, and it's just all very silly.
It's also very typically French, which is beautiful. It has that... air about it. It's like how Britain is obsessed with monolithic super-governments, nanny states that think for you and control people. That's come up in so many of our shows and games, from Blake's 7 to the upcoming We Happy Few.
Anarcute is like that but more relevant to French culture and the concept of Anarchism and the revolution. So there's definitely something intelligent there behind all the colourful characters and the friendly, cartoony visuals.
I don't know. It's hard to explain. It feels fun to play. Not fun in a 'mobile game' sense (I'm not a fan of mobile game design), but fun in a sense that video games were in the '90s and early '00s. It's like a love-letter to that era but with more modern considerations regarding the gameplay. Only slightly more modern, though, really. The UI is really bright and vibrant, and getting an S rank on everything is actually really difficult!
But there's something more modern about it that really makes it sit well in ways that sometimes playing games from the '90s doesn't always. It's a perfect fusion. And it's something that I really wish I'd see pop up more often. If Ori & the Blind Forest is a pure Castlevania but modernised to just the right amount. This is that for Pikmin or Katamari Damacy.
It's brilliant!

Anarcute is an action game developed by a group of five French students; Anarteam, and published by Plug in Digital, releasing on PC and Xbox One in July 2016.
I was absolutely in love with this title right from launching it. The gameplay is simple yet has a keen eye for depth and just the right amount of difficulty. The aim is to roam around the world you are in, freeing captured companions who will join you in the game’s main aim, to cause anarchy and riots. It took me a while to get the pun in the title, but its Anarchy, and cute combined, because have you seen these animals?! Cute as a button!!  Back to the gameplay; the rioters which join your party will raise your threat level, allowing you to use your special abilities. The more rioters you have in your party the more threatening your group is. I particularly like the ability to knock down buildings to save potentially captured companions which are precariously stuck on the side of it! The missions that you carry out take place in various different countries around the world, but the idea is still the same regardless.  The combat is simple; you just hover your mouse around the general area of an enemy and your rioters will wreck them (or not?) depending on how much you outnumber them.
Whilst Anarcute may not look the most graphically impressive style game, but it just screams character. It looks just like a game from Nintendo and I love it! The cute animal companions you find scattered around the world are so cute. All of the character models are nicely designed as well as some nice smooth animations across the board. The soundtrack is completely on point as well, with some top of the range sound effects too.
The difficulty does increase as you would expect as you progress further into the game; but you can negate a little bit of this buy purchasing upgrades for your squad of rioters which will assist you such as being able to run on infinite amount of ammo and projectiles bouncing between enemies more often. Some levels will also require retrying multiple times in order to find the best route throughout it without losing half your squad to silly mistakes.
The game won’t take a huge amount of time to complete, there are 4 or 5 countries to fight in, and each country has about 10 levels in each, and these levels will have different objectives which can range from capturing flags, or playing a mission completely solo and having to avoid enemies line of sights. This game however screams for a co-op/multiplayer mode, it would just add a whole new level of content and replayability, hopefully the developers will find time to add it in a future patch.
I was a little disappointed to find that even though the game suggests at the start, that you use a controller, but I couldn’t get mine to work, this was with two separate xbox controllers, whilst the game is playable with mouse and keyboard, I can’t help but wonder how much easier the experience would have been if I got to use the prefered controller option.
Overall Anarcute is a hugely fun game to play, it was more fun than what I expected and I was expecting a lot just from the screenshots and info which was available. The cute character models and soundtrack are awesome, and fit perfectly well into the game’s addictive gameplay.

Anarcute is one of those games you can sit back and relax with, as you cause destruction of your own cities and overthrow the brainwash police. With a nice soundtrack and some great initial gameplay, you'll run around causing havoc with a goofy smile on your face. But then the game gets into a groove that turns into its main problem overall. When the game does change the pace, it does it rather well, with stealth sections or bomb escorts that force you to play a little differently. But it doesn't do it often enough, as you are forced in yet in what seems yet another level that you feel like you've played before. And while it can punish you for being reckless, the game's difficulty is really where the game doesn't deliver for veterans of the action strategy genre. For those looking for their first experience in the genre or looking for a game for kids, Anarcute does a great job as an introductory game in the genre. It just doesn't have the mechanics to keep you interested if you've played games like it in the past, and the KISS principle only goes so far. For me, it's a target sale title, as it has a relaxing feel to it. Well, as relaxing as anarchy can be.

Mega Man X plus GunStar Heroes plus Super Mario Bros. 2 plus Sparkster, multiplied by Sonic the Hedgehog, divided by the 16 and 32-bit eras of gaming=Freedom Planet. At first glance, this game appears to be nothing more than a Sonic clone. But if the aforementioned equation means anything to you, you can already tell that's not the case. While the game shares the same momentum-based physics, high speed action, and anthropomorphic of the classic Sonic games, the game distinguishes itself with its amalgam of varying playstyles between characters and its character driven story. The game features cutscenes that give the whole game a Saturday morning cartoon vibe, and each boss encounter feels more meaningful than just an indicator that the level is over. It's not RPG-quality storytelling, but it's lightyears beyond anything the Sonic series has seen in a while. I suppose I can just end this by saying that it's Sonic, but better in almost every way. The mechanics of Super Time Force Ultra are a lot of fun. A sidescrolling shooter, you can reverse time to 'double up' (and more) on yourself to help kill enemies and beat the level within the time limit. If you die, rewind and try to save yourself from dying by killing the thing that killed you before it has the chance!
The levels are varied in terms of art, each world has a level that mixes up the objectives and style, and each boss is really fun and zany. There's a lot of unlockable characters, each has their own style and abilities, giving you an ever-increasing pallette of tools to deal with the challenges you face.
The game isn't incredibly hard, but it is really fun, and the challenge level felt just about right for me. For the ultra-hardcore player, a hardcore mode unlocks on completion, that locks out a character completely if they die, unless you can travel back in time and prevent their death. Sounds like a lot of fun, but I'm certain it will make the game REALLY hard, so if you're after a challenge, there it is!
I enjoyed the game's art style, which reminded me of Bravest Warriors / Adventure Time, and the humour is really good. There are a few overlong cutscenes (namely at the start and the end of the game), but they're so well written and amusing you don't really mind.
There's a lot of unlockables and collectables too, so there's a significant amount to do after completing the game's stages. There's a lot to do and a lot of excuses to spend time with the game after completing it.
This is a great game. I hope Capy makes some sequels.

If you want to ice-skate around pitch black hallways looking for that obscure barrel or button that blends in perfectly with the scenery while enemies peck away at your health with hit-scan weapons and grenades, this is perfect for you.
I honestly can't see the fun in this, usually games play off their strengths and you can overlook the weaknesses, but in this game it plays completely off its weaknesses. You spend the first few hours walking around hallways looking for buttons that blend in with the scenery perfectly, by the time you learn what the button generally looks like they change it, you don't get the lightsaber in these few hours, you just spray wildly at things right infront of you. There's a decent Doom-like progression of weapons which leads you to believe you'll be using them a lot, you won't. I used the pistol and bowcaster once, the E-11 and sniper are the only blaster-type weapons I needed.
Once you get the lightsaber, you will be pumped, you will want to hack/slash and duel, you will want to master it. Too bad, from this moment on you're against bombers who drop a grenade on death and snipers whose shots can't be deflected by the lightsaber, so you'll be sticking with blasters yet again, but atleast you own the lightsaber now. You will also be doing a lot of jumping puzzles, this is absolute hell because your character is on rollerskates and when you land you slide a bit thus falling off platforms is an easy thing to do. Yet there are a number of jumping puzzles in this game, as I said, they're playing off the weaknesses.
The level design is even worse, I ended up watching a walkthrough where the guy doing the walkthrough had to stop to look up a walkthrough. I managed to get up to the waste disposal part before getting too frustrated, I had to blow up a random barrel that could only be shot via a grate and it made me realise I didn't have the patience. there are a lot of trip mines in random places for no other reason than to kill you for not noticing. My first 5 minutes of this game was walking into a store room to instantly blow up, it forces you to save every 5 minutes (each save seems to go to a new file, so have fun with that).
The game supports 2k resolution, yet not 1080p, it hates multiple monitors and I can't change the brightness to actually see what I'm doing. I installed this on my SSD yet it takes 10 seconds to load a save which gets frustrating when you're constantly loading a save before a stupid jump or an encounter with an oddly placed bomber and if you alt-tab it will constantly put itself infront of everything else making the essential task of looking at a walkthrough that much harder.
I can't say the same for the other games I bought in the bundle, but I'd give this one a miss, I've read that there's a forced stealth segment coming up so my hopes of it getting better were severely misguided.

There is a moment in Jedi Outcast where all of a sudden everything seems to fall into place. Level design, story pacing, game mechanics, sound, difficulty, scale. It's almost an audible click. Or maybe that familiar hum of a lightsaber being switched on.
Whilst the earlier levels are fun in the way that you're blasting Storm Troopers and working out puzzles, they're also a little clunky. Blasters are, paradigmatically, clumsy and random, and this is no lie in this game. You'll often find your shots missing through no fault of your own, leading to awkwardly long (and extremely hard if you're playing on Knight/ Master difficulty!) fire fights that aren't at all satisfying.
But wait it out. Whilst the game survives the first few missions on it's merits, it explodes into excellence once Kyle Katarn rejuvenates his force abilites and retrieves his saber. Suddenly an entirely new set of dimensions are opened up: huge vertical jumps, manipulation of the environment from afar, the slowing of time and the ability to knock your enemies about are not only responsive mechanics, they're incredibly fun to use.
All of that pales in a comparison against the lightsaber battles though. In all honesty it is hard to recall a more enjoyable, tense and dramatic experience than entering a duel with a Reborn. One wrong move and your dead or so badly wounded that the rest of the fight is going to see your opposition on the offensive. To become adept, you have to be agile and tactful at times and understand when to use brute force at others. You'll never forget the time you take on two saber wielding assailants. That's a feeling borne of a great game.
It's the closest thing to a proper progression system that I've ever played, with Kyle regaining his powers as the narrative progresses. Your ascent from novice to warrior-god allows you to feel powerful, but also like you deserve to be there. Like you yourself have mastered the force and lightsaber combat. As a huge Star Wars fan, to me, that sensation is deeply moving.
So yes, I recommend this game. It's one the best games I've ever played, mainly because I can't think of anything (apart from it's sequel Jedi Academy- also excellent) that comes close to it's blending of character and story progression. If you're a Star Wars fan, you owe it to yourself to play through this. If you just want something to become obsessed with and master over time, then you're in for a treat to.
May the force be with you.

I recieved this game in the humble bundle monthly bundle. I do like the style, and the gameplay, or at least what I can figure out, is fun. Unfortunately this game is more frustration than fun. I can't compare it to much, but I can at least put in my two cents, for what that's worth.
So, the game is lovely, and the basic controls are fun. Unfortunately the inital teaching of those controls is a bit poor. Enough that I was confused until a few minutes in, when I suddenly had an "OH, That's how that works!" moment. The problem is, this wasn't a good thing. My immediate after thought wasn't "I learned a new trick." but instead "Why didn't they just SAY that."
And that gets to the core of the problems. Words, or lack thereof. I understand mystery, wanting a game to tell a story that unfolds as you learn, or even wanting to make something artsy. But the lack of instruction, and the lack of explanation is what truly stunts this game in my eyes. Simple explanations would make this game far more enjoyable. I wouldn't stumble around wondering what to do. I wouldn't be confused about how things work as much. It's fine to teach me new skills, or leave extra unique powers free for discovery. But leaving the player with only vague understanding is no fun.
I admittedly have not played much of this game, and I hope to come back to it, but I think it says a lot that the game couldn't keep me wanting to play, but instead pushed me away with its obtuse and unpleasant habit of leaving the player confused.
In any case, I can't say I recommend the game. It's difficult in the wrong way. But I can't say I hate it either. I just...don't like it as much as I want to.

Let me start by saying this game is GOOD, but not great. Yes, I realize it's in alpha. That's probably why - it has some rough edges it needs polishing. The devs also realize that by making it early access they are making it available for review. This game does a lot of things really well, and a few things poorly, mostly in design choices of game rules. Let's start with the general discription:
If you liked Spelunky, and like traditional roguelikes, you'll love this game, even for how frustratingly hard it is. I could almost describe Spelunky as easier than Catacomb Kids (CK). CK takes traditional fantasy elements and a fun yet dark aesthetic and imerses you in a really compelling world where gear, character stats and unidentified potions control the way you play the game. At it's current price, it's a great value. I've already dumped hours into this game.
PROS:
-Tight, mostly responsive controls make this game a joy to play on a gamepad.
-Fantastic sound and good music.
-Megapixel GFX do not seem trite, and are rather well done for a aesthetic that's easy to love.
-Combat is varied, strategy is deep, builds are different enough to make it interesting.
-Monsters have fairly solid AI and will force different approaches to each one.
-Unique character generation means you can continually roll bunches of 6 Kids with different gear and builds until you pick your favorite or try something new.
-The environment plays a lot into your strategy. Why take on a Grumbel face to face, when you can throw a rock and knock over the torch right next to him?
CONS:
-Completely useless characters are rolled fairly often. No one is ever going to play a Kid with 2 HP.
-Humanoid monsters are faster, tougher, more accurate and better at climbing than you are. It's almost like fighting the Spelunky shopkeeper five times on every floor.
-Once in a while you'll find yourself in places in the dungeon you can't get out of. Probably just an alpha issue.
-As far as I can tell, there's only one tileset.
That being said, it's a good game and will probably keep getting better with each update.

"This game is not a game: It's a portrait."
We could talk about graphics, sure.  It's RPG Maker VX Ace with custom artwork.  We could talk about length.  It clocks in about 20-30 minutes depending on your reading speed.  Gameplay?  Think Gone Home, or Dear Esther.  It's much more about art than it is about needing to fit in the mold of the medium it occurs in.
I think the big thing about this game, though, is message.  It's not a cautionary tale, it's not trying to save its protagonist or give you the opportunity to try and save him, you're not trying to see how many imaginary points you can earn in keeping the unfortunate and unavoidable end from occuring.  This is his life, and this is how it is; a picture of a sad, lonely, fat 30ish year old locked in a downward spiral.  Say what you will about the rest of the presentation, but the writing is great (fortunate because you'll be doing a lot of reading).  Fascinating character study and relatively unique, both in what it tries to do and especially what it is about.
One additional detail: sometimes games like this are accused of being so un-game-like that they should have just been in another medium, a graphic novel or a film or something, maybe. I think the nature of it being a game, and more importantly a game that offers you false, meaningless choices, is important to the portrayal that Actual Sunlight is trying to achieve. Simply watching it or reading it wouldn't give you the connection to just how meaningless and routine Evan Winter feels that his choices are.

Actual Sunlight studies three chapters of Evan’s life, each seeing him slip further and further into a downward spiral entirely of his own making. It’s easy to dismiss him as a hopeless loser and leave it at that, but the wit and insight he offers into his situation through his writings turn him into an introspective critic of his own self destruction.
Full review //

This isn’t your typical game and deals with mature themes that some might find difficult. The story is about a man named Evan who is facing middle age and not having achieved what he wanted out of life. On a very serious note if you are suffering with depression you should think twice about playing this game. As you are pulled more into the story and start to relate it can become difficult to separate your feelings from that of Evan’s.
The majority of the game is done through text with some interactive elements in the environment but the main pull is the story.

If Shovel Knight is an ode to the NES/SNES, then this is an ode to the Genesis. It takes level design similar to Sonic and speed focus like Sonic, but if you were to try to just compare it to Sonic the Hedgehog 1-3, you would find yourself finding little the two have in common. The gameplay is fast-pased and fun, leaving little to be desired. It takes the normal gameplay stuff that was common from that era and re-imagining it. The game has fun combat, allowing all characers to attack each with a special ability and special movement. Although I have not played through all of the stories of the game, I don't feel I need to. The bosses are fun and unique, each having awesome designs I instantly fell in love with. The music is fantastic, now where can I buy it?! The game looks fantastic with vibrant colors and extremely various areas that are really awesome to look at. And most of all, the one thing that this brings to the table that I was not expecting, was the voice acting. With the exception of a fairly "meh" performance of someone in the intro, all of the voiceactors are FANTASTIC with all of them being just a bunch of people from the internet. What I loved the most about them was that the writing for them, and the actors themselves, make the characters come to life in your mind. Each has a personality that is portraid by the voiceacting that surprised me! I honestly had some very emotional moments where I nearly cried purly on the fact that the voiceactors made the characters pain, arguments, and fears real. They were not just sprites on a screen, but real people.
I cannot say this enough, BUY IT if you like platformers like this. You might not, and that is fine, but I still highly reccomend this game. This truly is the 16-bit Shovel Knight focused on the 90s, and it is fun!

TL;DR

Freedom Planet is a good indie title that calls out to the import Sega Saturn era-type games of old. Lush sprite art, and boss designs gives the game that "Treasure" feel to it: as the platforming and boss battle aspects to it pertains to Dynamite Headdy, and Gunstar Heroes, respectively. However, in some levels of the game the level designs could use a bit more work, as sometimes too much is going on in the background; causing you to wonder where to go, and what to do. Moreover, they tried to incorporate the fast paced level design of Sonic the Hedgehog into the level design, which falls flat in my opinion, as the levels don't offer a constant flow for the characters to move at a very fast pace for an appropriate period of time. Loop de loops and slopes have that "Sonic 4 Sticky Shoes" feel, instead of the natural physics of momentum that Sonic had, thus making speed feel cheap and unrewarding. Not to say Freedom Planet is a bad game, it has a certain charm and challenge that outweighs the bad aspects of it, just if there is a sequel to it, they'll expand it to make it more like a Treasure game rather than a Sonic Team one.

Super Time Force Ultra is a very mediocre game saved by its one very elegantly executed mechanic, but that mechanic is not worth much more than five dollars. Ten if you're a perfectionist. It's cool and fun, but I wouldn't recommend it unless it's on sale. I guess I'll give it a thumbs up, but only because I bought it for five dollars, and I believe that is the fitting price
When I say the game is mediocre, I mean it. The level design is incredibly simple, derivative, trite, and forgettable. Some of the bosses are kind of neat, but that's the extent of it. They have a bunch of similar versions of two or three puzzles, all of which are either solved by having two heros shooting on opposite sides or having Shieldly block something. Every and all parts of the main campaign can be completed by shear brute force, and there's no reward for being clever besides a sticker and the sake of being clever. If that's enough for you, then the game's design is sufficient. If that's not, then you'll get bored real fast, as did I.
Unlocks suffer from a similar issue. You either unlock a character by collecting a certain percentage of collectibles (yes, really), or going down somewhere in the level. Literally every character hidden in a level is just in an obvious basement somewhere, or hidden in plain view with a panning camera. Some of the characters are somewhat unique, but they still manage to become incredibly redundent. I promise you that you only need half the cast to get everything done flawlessly, and I quickly min-maxed almost all my play-time into three or four characters who excelled at certain situations. Minor, less essencial characters just feel like reskins and button remaps. It's like adding a dozen slightly worse but slightly different sniper rifles in Counter Strike. Neat the first use, but then entirely useless.
The puzzle portion of the game helps demonstrate the clever mechanic of the game, but the puzzles are, just like most of the game, is very derivative. If you like puzzle platformers, you've seen all the levels before. It's boring.
Apparently this game is funny? Could've fooled me.
The one saving grace is the main mechanic, the time travelling. It's fantasically executed. It has a brief learning curve, but after a bit you'll start to think along with the game. During the end-of-mission replay, you get to truly see how clever and unique the game is. To experience this little original addition to puzzle-platformer game mechanics is a joy within itself. However, even this one great aspect of the game sells itself too short
I usually hate it when people say a game is too short. I think it's ridiculous and misguided to expect a game, or any experience, to be worth a certain price per hour or minute. Way too often do games over stay their welcome and drag out what could have otherwise been a satisfying and complete experience in order to make themselves seem larger than they are. However, Super Time Force Ultra is that rare scenario when a game is honestly too short. It introduces itself, it builds up new characters that all add new dynamics, then it suddenly ends. The game shows you its cool little idea that it worked really hard on, does a little song and dance with it, but leaves just when you were beginning to get into it leaving a trail of half-baked puzzle levels in its wake.
At the asking price, I would not recommend this game. It can be beatten in under five hours, yet somehow still feels repetitive and overly familar a halfway in. For five, perhaps ten dollars, it's worth that short fun adventure of getting the hang of the game's one interesting and polished mechanic. Wait for a sale if you're really interested in puzzle platformers or shoot 'em ups, pass if you're not.

After playing Undertale by Toby Fox a friend told me about Lisa. He said "You like Undertale, don't you? I recently played Lisa, which is similar to it. Give it a try, you won't regret" so I thought about this and I decided to do it.
The game appeared to be a little bit different. I mean, the transition from the calming view of the Ruins, Snowdin, Waterfall and so on, to a post-apocalyptic world is a little bit tough.
I got over that easily and I started playing. I thought "Lisa" will be a little bit awful because of the dark humor, just like another one i played in the past, but even so, it touched me in a way I wasn't expecting.
I began to live through Brad's emotions and feelings. I made myself new friends, I made mistakes that cost me a lot. I even got to the point where I killed people who were close to me just to try to reassemble my "family" as it's called at a certain point in the game. I didn't want to do all of the killing blows to them. I hardly tried not to be so damn genocide, but at that point, I knew I couldn't change my fate. I became a killing machine just to retry to live my miserable life again through someone else. I understand this somehow: as a parent you just want to make your children avoid bad things which happened to you and also want them to achieve goals you couldn't reach. I know that your child must be your first priority in your life, but this doesn't mean you have to kill everyone just for the sake of your "ideas".
About the "technical" characteristics of the game, well, the combat interface brings up a new way to fight, letting you to perform several attacks in one go (it's like battling in Civilization V xD). Also the overall platformer and the walking simulator style give the game a touch of originality.
To sum up, I'll say that Lisa it's a game with a heartbreaking story, but also with a challenging and unique combat. It's a game that reflects perfectly one man's psychological illness in the reach of something he will never be able to have again, in the circumstances given: a new life.
